AGENCY Parties to the Contract of Agency 

´N A DISPUTE BETWEEN P and A, all defenses relating to legal capacity are available, e.g., infancy, insanity. If the suit is based upon an agency formed by contract, defenses in contract, e. g., fraud, duress, may also be asserted. Where, however, P is sought to be held by T because of the acts of his agent, the personal disabilities of the latter will not relieve him. Thus an authorized contract made by an infant agent cannot be avoided because of the agent's infancy. 

However, the incapacity of P would be a defense. 

Casey v. Kastel, 237 N. Y. 305.

An insane person may appoint an agent but such agent's acts may be voided by the insane principal. Where the parties can be restored to status quo, knowledge of the insanity by T is immaterial. If there can be no such restoration the insane principal is bound if T did not have reasonable ground to believe that P was insane. Where, however, the agent is appointed after P has been judicially declared incompetent, the appointment is void and A's acts do not bind P. 

McCarthy v. Bowling 182 A.D. 18, 169 N.Y.S. 463 ·

Though a spouse is not the agent of the other merely because of the marital relationship, where a contract for an improvement on realty is made with a husband or wife and that realty belongs to the other or both, the husband or wife contracting is presumed to be the agent of the other, unless the latter having knowledge of the improvement shall within ten days after learning of the contract give the contractor written notice of his or her refusal to consent to the improvement. This presumed authority only authorizes T to file a mechanic's lien against the improved property. It does not permit the entry of a personal judgment unless the agency is proved as a fact.

Stanley Patch etc. Co. v. Barry 148 Misc. 376; Lien Law § 3 

Creation of an Agency

An agency can be created orally; in writing, with and without a seal; by implication; by estoppel; by necessity. 

An agent can always be appointed orally unless the statute requires the appointment to be in writing. Even in the latter instance as between the principal and the agent, there is an agency though the liability of the principal to T may not be legally estab- *In this discussion "A" refers to agent or servant; "P" to principal or master; "T" to the third party dealing with A or P. 21

lished. The statute requires that an agent appointed to contract for the conveyance of or to actually convey any interest in realty or to contract for or make a lease for a period over a year, must have his authority in writing. But even in these cases where P orally asks A to sign for him in his presence, P is bound despite the fact that A acted under oral appointment. 

Real Property Law §§ 242, 259 

Other contracts to be executed by an agent, which are required by the Statute of Frauds to be in writing, may properly be made by the agent though his appointment was orally created. 

One partner may orally delegate authority to the other to act on behalf of the partnership in any situation, regardless of any of the above rules.

If there is a representation by P by word or act that A is his agent and T acts on this misrepresentation, P is estopped from denying the agency unless the third party knows or is put on notice that in fact the agent is acting without actual authority. 

Thus where a mortgagor pays the interest to a lawyer who closed the deal for mortgagee and who properly retains and exhibits the bond and mortgage, it would be a good payment as against the mortgagee, since leaving the bond and mortgage in the lawyer's possession gave the apparent authority to collect. 

Crane v. Gruenewald 120 N. Y. 274.

It should be noted, however, that the mere giving of possession of an article to another without anything more does not create such apparent authority as to permit the passing of a valid title. 

Smith v. Clews 105 N.Y. 283

Delegation of Authority by the Agent to Another 

An agent may appoint another to assist him if he was so authorized, but if no express authorization was given he may do so and the sub-agent's act will bind P, if (1) The act is purely ministerial or mechanical and not personal in its nature; or (2) If the nature of the work is such as to require help. Where 

A is employed to buy land he may engage an attorney to close the title. If A is to manage a large business he may employ help. When a depositor deposits a check with his bank, drawn on a foreign bank, it is known that the first bank will require the service of a foreign bank to complete the transaction. The correspondent bank is acting for the depositor rather than for the first bank. 

Negotiable Instruments Law § 350d 

Commercial Bank v. Norton 1 Hill. 501 (3) Where circumstances arise requiring aid to execute the agency. Where a chauffeur delivering furniture for P could not find the street of destination, he had implied authority to invite plaintiff on the truck to point out the way. 

Gross v. Mertz 216 A. D. 726, 214 N. Y. S. 198.

AGENCY 

23 If a servant, without authority, express or implied, engages another to do his work, the master is not liable for damage caused by the person so engaged if the latter was competent. If, however, the servant engages one who is not competent, or if the servant directly supervises or controls the acts of the person he engages, the employer is liable for any damage caused T by this subservant. 

The basis of the master's lability is the negligence of the servant in the execution of his selection, and this negligence is fused with his agency and is attributed to the master. Thus, if P engages Al to drive a team of horses, and Al without authority, permits A2, who is totally incompetent and inexperienced, to drive the team, the master is liable to T for damage caused by the negligence of A2 to T. 

Grant v. Knepper 245 N. Y. 158.

In cases where A may properly appoint subagents, A is not responsible for their acts unless he was guilty of fraud or gross negligence in choosing them.

The Relationship Between Principal and Agent 

Even in situations where the relationship between principal and agent is based on contract, the rules of agency favor a qualification of the doctrine of consideration to the extent that when a promisee relies upon a gratuitous promise of another who begins to act for the promisee, he may recover from the promisor for failing to act properly. 

Siegel v. Spear 234 N. Y. 479.

An agent is under an obligation to aid his employer in the work for which he is engaged. He must do nothing to make profit for himself at the expense of his principal, without the full knowledge and consent of the principal. Thus where P's salesman secretly procures a lease of P's premises to take effect upon the termination of P's lease, the salesman can be forced in equity to assign his new lease to P. It was his duty to aid his employer in his endeavor to continue to carry on his business On the same principle an agent may not embark on a venture on his own account in a business which is similar to that for which he has been engaged to act as agent and make a profit for himself, which profit might reasonably have been made by his employer had A not so acted. 

He is a trustee for P of any profits thus made. An agent who violates his trust forfeits his right to compensation for work rendered by him. 

Kinney v. Glenny 231 A.D. 311, affd. 257 N.Y. 560

Lawdin v. Bway Surface Adv. Co. 272 N.Y. 133 

Beatty v. Guggenheim Exploration Co., 265 N. Y. 380.

An employee who breaches his contract is not entitled to receive money not yet due him even though earned at the time he abandoned his employment.

Sundland v. Korfund Co., Inc., 260 A. D. 80.

If an agent is hired to buy stock for his principal, he cannot secretly sell to the latter his own stock, even though the sale may be a bargain for the principal. An agent cannot buy from himself. 

The principal can have the transaction set aside. 

Taussig v. Hart 58 N. Y. 425.

The penal law forbids a purchasing agent to get any commission from one who sells to P, or the seller to give the purchasing agent any commission for purchasing from him on behalf of P. 

Penal Law § 439. 

When an agent is authorized to sell an article for a specified sum and he sells such article for a larger amount, the larger amount belongs to the principal. 

Greenslete v. Ferguson, 191 A. D. 745, 182 N. Y. S. 198.

Under proper circumstances an agent may represent both parties to any transaction, e. g., both parties agree that A is to be their agent in the transaction. Of course, if his own interest is opposed to that of his principal, he cannot serve as agent. 

Jarvis v. Schaefer 105 N. Y. 289.

A servant who commits a tort is liable to the master should the third party recover from the master because of the tort. Although the master and servant are not joint tort-feasors in such cases, a release to one discharges the other. Where the master notifies the servant of the action against him, the latter is bound by the result of the suit against the master. The master may bring in the servant as a party defendant. 

Kinsey v. Wm. Spencer 165 Misc. 143, affd. 281 N. Y. 601

These are the implied obligations resting upon a master. Actions against him lie in tort for negligence and not on the promise. (1) That he shall provide suitable appliances and a reasonably safe place to work as the hazards incident to employment will permit. (2) That he shall provide other servants when required, sufficient in number and skill so that the servant may not be exposed to unnecessary risk. 

Dittiger v. Isal Realty Co. 290 N.Y. 492 

Adlam v. Kowalinka 291 N. Y. 40 

Daurizio v. Merchants' D. T. Co., 152 Misc. 716, 274 N. Y. S. 174

Where two or more are appointed agents, they must act jointly unless the appointment otherwise provides. 

In re Julliard's Will 171 Misc. 661, affd 259 A. D. 828.

Termination of Agency 

An agency with two exceptions may be terminated at the will of P or A despite the existence of a contract. Of course the party who breaches the contract may be made to respond in damages. 

The two exceptions are: (1) An agency coupled with an interest in the subject matter of the agency. If a power is given as security for a debt and the property which is the subject-matter of the power is delivered with the

AGENCY 

25 power to the creditor as part of the transaction, this power is coupled with an interest and is irrevocable. 

Terwilliger v. Ontario R. R. Co. 149 N. Y. 86.

In this connection it should be noted that if P owes A $500 and says to A, "Sell my race-horse and take your debt out of the sale," this authority is revocable, even if P had said that it was to be irrevocable. The mere fact that he was to take his debt out of it does not make it an agency coupled with an interest. The “interest did not grow out of that agency" as it did in the first case. 

Haiss v. Becker 198 A. D. 23, 189 N. Y. S. 791. (2) An agency coupled with an obligation.-A spends some of his own money while acting for P, it being understood that A is to recoup his expenditures out of the returns from the agency. After 

A has spent the money, the agency becomes irrevocable. A can go through with the deal so as to protect his expenditures and P cannot revoke the agency.* 

In re Driscoll 131 Misc. 613, 228 N. Y. S. 335.

If P has revoked the agency, which was not an agency for one particular act, but rather a continuing agency, and T, who had dealt with A continued to do so without knowledge of the revocation, P would be bound. P is required to give actual notice of the revocation to those who had dealt with A previously. As to others who had merely heard of the agency, but had not dealt with A, no notice is necessary. 

McNeilly v. Continental Life Ins. Co. 66 N. Y. 23.

Death of P revokes every agency (except one coupled with an interest or an obligation), and even though neither A nor T knew of his death. This rule applies regardless of the hardship on T. 

Glennan v. Rochester Trust Co. 209 N. Y. 12.

Insanity of P terminates the agency if T knew of the insanity or there was a formal adjudication of insanity even without T's knowing it. The insanity of A likewise terminates the agency. But if T cannot in these instances be put in status quo and was ignorant of the insanity (there being no adjudication), P is bound. 

The adjudication of bankruptcy of A or P terminates the agency over matters affected by the bankruptcy. If A becomes a bankrupt and his authority extends to merely formal acts not involving financial liability, the authority is not terminated. *This rule does not apply in the case of attorney and client, An attorney engaged for a special cause may be discharged by his client at any time, with or without cause. All that need be paid is the reasonable value of the services rendered up to the discharge if the discharge was without cause. The contract figure is not the maximum that may be allowed. It is a partial guide for ascertaining quantum meruit. If the termination of the contract is a result of death. or disability of the attorney, recovery is limited to the contract price. In re 

Montgomery's Estate, 272 N. Y. 323.

Where a trial of the cause of action has been had and an adverse judgment rendered, there is no obligation upon a party to further carry on the litigation simply because his counsel desires to do so. And this is so though the counsel be engaged on a contingent fee. Crowley v. Wolf 281 N. Y. 59.

Knowledge of Agent as Knowledge of Principal 

As a general rule the principal is bound by notice to or knowledge of his agent in all matters within the scope of the agency, obtained during the agency or then present in the mind of the agent. But this rule does not apply where information is given to the agent by T under circumstances as to warrant the inference that the agent will conceal his information from P. Likewise when the agent is engaged in a scheme to defraud his principal, his knowledge of certain facts is not notice to the principal so as to bind the principal with that knowledge. In one case T applied to P for a loan. P sent A to appraise T's equity in realty which was to be the security for the loan. A learned of an unrecorded lien but in collusion with T, he kept the knowledge from P. The loan was made and when P tried to foreclose, the owner of the prior lien defended claiming that although his lien was unrecorded it was known to P because A, his agent, knew of it. This was held to be no defense. 

When an agent attempts to defraud his own principal, his knowledge is not that of the principal. 

Henry v. Allen 151 N. Y. 1 

Constant v. University of Rochester 111 N. Y. 604 

Hurley v. John Hancock L. Ins. Co. 247 A. D. 547, 288 N. Y. S. 199.

The Relationship Between Agent and Third Party 

Where an agency and the identity of P are disclosed in the contract and the contract is within the authority conferred, the agent is not personally bound unless there be clear evidence of an intention to substitute or superadd the liability of the agent to that of his principal. If the agent acted without or beyond his authority, he is liable for breach of an implied warranty of authority. No action will lie for such breach until the original contract is broken by the principal. 

Moore v. Maddock 251 N. Y. 420 

Voss v. Lowry 225 A.D. 507, affd. 252 N. Y. 587 

Lewitus v. Brown 228 A. D. 146, 239 N. Y. S. 261.

An agent committing an act involving an individual tort such as, assault, trespass, fraud or conversion is personally liable for the tort whether or not the agency is disclosed. But if the plaintiff first brings action against the master for the servant's negligent act and fails to prove negligence on the part of the servant, he may not bring action against the servant. An agent may not be held liable for inducing in the course of his employment, the breach of a contract by his principal.

Greyhound Co. v. Commercial Casualty Co. 259 A. D. 317 

Wolf v. Kenyon 242 A. D. 116, 273 N. Y. S. 170.

If the third party has advanced money to the supposedly authorized agent to be given to the principal, the injured party in an action for moneys had and received cannot recover from the agent moneys paid to the agent and later delivered to the principal, for the agent has never received such moneys. They would be recov-

Harris v. Tams 258 N. Y. 229 

Mack v. Latta 178 N. Y. 525.

An agent does not impliedly warrant the legal capacity of the principal.* 

Hall v. Lauderdale 46 N. Y. 70, 75.

Scope of Authorities in Various Agencies 

The burden is on the person dealing with the agent to show that the agent has the real or apparent authority, which he assumes to exercise. 

In re Welton's Estate 143 Misc. 830, 257 N. Y. S. 590.

No obligation can be imposed upon the principal by an unratified act of an agent outside of his real, implied or apparent authority; but a ratified contract made by the agent on behalf of the principal may be rescinded by the third party if tainted by fraud in its inception, though the principal was himself innocent of any fraud. 

That is because a principal who asserts the validity of a contract made by the agent holds the contract subject to any invalidity or taint in its inception. 

Harriss v. Tams 258 N. Y. 229

In one case a landowner had signed a deed which was blank as to the name of the grantee. He temporarily entrusted it to a friend that he might exhibit it to a third person, a prospective buyer. The friend filled in his own name as grantee, and mortgaged the land to a bank which loaned him money. It was held that the owner was not estopped by his carelessness from asserting the invalidity of the instrument. Consciousness of peril to strangers, in the careless execution of instruments of the negotiable type, would induce the reasonably prudent man to exercise attentive care that the peril might be avoided. In the case of instruments of the non-negotiable type, the risk involved is less easily perceived; correspondingly the duty of care less frequently arises. 

Hulbert v. Walker 258 N. Y. 8, 19. (1) Warranties.-If the business in which A is engaged for P is one in which it is customary to give a warranty, it is implied that a warranty may be given by A. This is so, even if P expressly orders 

A not to warrant, provided this order is unknown to T. Ín what business a warranty usually is given is a question of fact. If A sells by sample it is implied that he can warrant goods to be like the sample, and where P furnishes A with a circular to be shown to *But see Goldfinger v. Doherty, 153 Misc. 826 affd. 244 A. prospective buyers as a means of inducing sales, A would have implied authority to warrant the goods to conform with statements of fact in the circulars which if made by P would be warranties.

Sharlette v. Lake Placid Company 194 A. D. 844, 185 N. Y. S. 543 · (2) Credit. A selling agent has no power to sell on credit unless it is the known usage of the trade to do so; nor pledge; nor receive payment, unless in possession of the goods to be delivered, in which case power to receive payment is implied. 

Iroquois Mfg. Co. v. Davis 122 Misc. 273, 203 N. Y. S. 607. 

An agent authorized to sell for a specific price on credit, who, takes cash and absconds, binds P to the sale. Private instructions are not limitations on T, if T does not know of them. 

A has no implied power to buy on credit unless credit is indispensable to carry out his duties; nor may he execute negotiable paper in payment for the goods. 

The agent must buy in the manner authorized. If authorized to buy commodities for cash he cannot buy them for part cash and part as exchange for other goods. Should the principal fail to ratify this latter transaction, the agent cannot recover for any money advanced by him, as he is deemed to have bought for himself. (3) Contracts.-Where A has been engaged to carry out the provisions of a contract, he has not implied authority to waive any of the contract provisions. 

Dudley v. Perkins 235 N. Y. 448. (4) Real Estate Agents.-A real estate broker is a mere negotiator. Having brought the parties to agree on terms, his task is completed. If such broker in his zeal to carry out his own purposes makes false representations as to the condition of the property, the principal is not bound, His fee is earned when the contract of sale is signed unless the contract of employment provides that the sale must be consummated and the title pass. Even in such cases the fee is earned though title does not pass if the reason is the act of the seller which renders performance of the contract of sale impossible. 

This is because of the rule that one may not take advantage of a condition precedent, the performance of which he himself has rendered impossible. 

Friedman v. N. Y. Telephone Co. 256 N. Y. 392 

Stern v. Gepo Realty Company 289 N. Y. 274.

A general power given to an agent to manage property does not by itself include authority to bind the principal to negotiate commercial paper. (5) One holding an unindorsed commercial paper has no implied authority to collect on it. There is a presumption that brokers in possession of negotiable instruments such as bonds, have authority to sell. 

Kittredge v. Grannis 236 N. Y. 375 

Gussenhoven v. Turner 260 N. Y. S. 514.

Factor's Act 

An agent entrusted with the possession of a bill of lading, customhouse permit or warehouseman's receipt for the delivery of merchandise or an agent without the document but in proper possession of the goods for the purpose of sale or pledge, has authority as a matter of law to sell or dispose of the merchandise (including a chose in action created by the sale) for money advanced or a written obligation given upon the faith thereof. A pledge by such an agent for an antecedent debt is not protected. Nor is a pledge protected if the agent was entrusted with possession for the purpose of sale as a result of common law larceny on the part of the agent, e.g., he falsely told the owner that he had a customer, but really intended to pledge it for his own benefit. 

I. W. Sweet v. Provident Society 254 A.D. 242, affd. 279 N. Y. 540

Personal Property Law § 43 

In the case of a proper pledge, the true owner may get back the goods upon prepayment of the money advanced. The contract between the third person and the agent is valid even against the true owner if he fails to make prepayment within a reasonable time after knowledge of the contract. 

Mann v. Simpson 286 N. Y. 450.

Liability of a Master for the Torts of His Servant A master is responsible for the torts of the servant within the general scope of his employment, while engaged in his master's business, and done with a view to the furtherance of that business. 

Thus in an action for false imprisonment, where it appeared that the plaintiff was arrested by servants of a department maintained by the defendant company for the purpose of investigating criminal complaints, adjusting differences and doing such acts as might lead to the recovery of articles stolen from customers, it was held •Attorneys have charging liens and retaining liens. The latter depend upon possession. Where the retention of papers may embarrass a client, the attorney may be required to surrender them upon receiving proper security for his compensation. Leviten v. Sandbank 291 N. Y. 352.

that whether the servants were acting within the scope of their authority was a question for the jury. 

Mott v. Consumers' Ice Company 73 N. Y. 543 

McLoughlin v. N. Y. Edison Company 252 N. Y. 202.

A principal is not liable for a loss caused to another by reason of the latter's reliance upon a deceitful representation of an agent, unless the representation was actually or apparently authorized. 

Notice of a limitation of an agent's authority to make a certain representation prevents recovery against the principal. 

Ernst Iron Works v. Duralith Corvoration 270 N. Y. 165. 

The liability of the principal for the acts of his agent or servant has been carried over to situations where A does damage because of an incidental negligent act done while in the very act of carrying out the business of the agency. In one case, A was employed at P's garage to sell gasoline. While the gasoline was flowing from the pump to a customer's car, A flipped a cigarette over the car. Sparks ignited the flowing gasoline and the explosion which followed injured the plaintiff. P was held liable, as it was A's negligent act while in the very act of doing his proper work. 

Wood v. Saunders 228 A. D. 69, 238 N. Y. S. 571.

Where the act is unlawful, such act wilfully done by the agent will not be considered impliedly within the scope of an agency. 

The master will not be held liable unless he actually authorized or ratified the act. Therefore, if A, while collecting rents for P, or while running the elevator for P's apartment house, assaulted a tenant, for the latter's refusal to pay the rent, or for uttering a criticism, P cannot be held liable for the assault. This case is to be distinguished from the cases where an employee has legal authority to exercise reasonable force to perform his duties, such as a railroad conductor in removing a disorderly person from his train. 

Zucker v. Lannin 217 A. D. 487, 217 N.Y.S. 65 

Trebitsch v. Goelet 252 N. Y. 554.

There are some exceptions to this rule, e. g., common carriers, inn-keepers. Here the duty of the master toward T is contractual in its nature and recovery may be had in tort as well as in contract. 

The right of action has been extended to bath house proprietors and by a recent lower court decision to restaurants, saloons and barrooms. Thus a plaintiff in a barroom who was assaulted by an employee to whom a complaint about a drink was made, was allowed to recover against the proprietor. 

Schell v. Vergo 166 Misc. 839, 4 N. Y. S. (2d) 644.

Where there is notice to the principal that an employee is in the habit of acting in a manner dangerous to others, there is a duty to exercise skill and care commensurate to the damage which may reasonably be anticipated. And where an employee without authority on an isolated occasion invited a stranger on the premises without the master's knowledge, the latter was not responsible for the negligence of the stranger invited by the employee. 

DeRyso v. N. Y. Central R. Co. 275 N. Y. 85.

31 The fact that A, in the exercise of his duties, did not use the best or shortest method in the execution of his duty is immaterial. If a driver, A, sent to a station in the southern part of the town drives the wagon south, but takes the longest route through the park, so as to see his friend on the way, his master as well as he, A, would be liable to T if T were hurt by A's negligent driving on the way. But the distinction between a "roundabout" way and a "different" way should be noticed. It is generally for the jury to determine the period when A was outside the scope of his employment.

The doctrine of respondeat superior does not apply to a public official and his subordinates.

Effect of Statute Governing Operation of Motor Vehicles 

By statute many of the common-law principles of the law of agency have been changed in cases involving motor cars. If an owner of a motor vehicle expressly or impliedly permits X to use his automobile, the owner is liable for any damage caused by the negligent operation of the automobile while X is using the automobile, upon a public highway in New York, even though the use be only in the business of X. The burden of proving the permission to use the motor vehicle is upon the plaintiff. The injured party may be an invitee in the car with the approval of the owner. The liability of the operator and owner is joint and several.* 

Vehicle and Traffic Law §59; Cherwein v. Geiter 272 N. Y. 165 

Cohen v. Neustadter 247 N. Y. 207.

When a trailer is joined with an auto truck or tractor, they are considered one motor vehicle. Accordingly, if an owner of a trailer engaged an independent contractor to attach the latter's motor tractor and thus transport the former's freight over a highway, the owner of the trailer and tractor are jointly liable for the negligence of the operator of the combined vehicle. 

Vehicle and Traffic Law §59a. 

What is "use with permission of the owner" under the statute has been the subject of many decisions. If the owner specifically prohibits the use of the car by the borrower in a certain territory, a collision in the proscribed territory would not subject the owner to *If a joint owner is a passenger in a car being driven by the other joint owner, the negligence of the driver is not imputable to the passenger if the latter sues a third person who caused injuries. Jenka v. Veeder Contracting Co. 290 N.Y. 810

any liability as the borrower then would be using the car without permission. On the other hand, if the limiting instructions relate to the manner of operation, e. g., speed to be applied, though the instructions be disobeyed, nevertheless the use is with "permission" of the owner. It thus follows that if the owner permits the borrower to have a guest in the car and the borrower permits the guest to drive the car with him in it, the owner would be subject to liability for damage caused by the guest's negligence. This would be true even if the owner had clearly instructed the borrower that only he was to drive. The thing forbidden related to the operation of the car, not to the use which might be made of it. If the borrower permits the guest to use and entirely control the automobile borrowed without the presence of the owner, the owner would not be liable for any damage caused by such guest. "Use" also includes control while the car is being repaired on the road. 

Owen v. Gruntz 216 A.D. 19, 214 N.Y.S. 543 

Eckert v. Farrington Co. 262 N. Y. 9 

Arcara v. Moresse 258 N. Y 211; Chaika v. Vandenberg 252 N. Y. 101.

An owner who leaves an automobile with an independent contractor to be repaired is liable for the independent contractor's negligence while giving the automobile the customary and necessary road test. 

Zuckerman v. Parton 260 N. Y. 446.

The statute does not change the common law rule respecting the owner's rights to recover from third persons when his car is damaged while being operated by another not in the owners' business but with his permission and in his absence. In such cases the negligence of the driver is not imputed to the owner. It is imputed only in actions brought by third persons against the owner or if the owner sues and he was in the car at the time of the accident so that he had the legal right to control its operation. 

Mills v. Gabriel 259 A.D. 60, affd. 284 N.Y. 755 

Gochee v. Wagner 257 N. Y. 344.

Where a servant is given the use of a motor vehicle to be used in connection with his work, the statute does not apply. Should the vehicle be used outside the scope of the agency, the owner is not liable.

Psota v. Long Island Rail Road Co. 246 N. Y. 388. 

If the motor vehicle was sold to A under a contract of conditional sale, so that title was in the vendor, A is the sole "owner" for the purpose of this rule, despite the terms of the contract between the parties under the conditional sale, declaring title to be in vendor. 

A chattle mortgagee of a motor vehicle, out of possession, is not the "owner" for the purpose of this rule. 

Vehicle and Traffic Law § 59. 

Liability of an Independent Contractor 

The general rule is that the owner of property is not liable for the negligent act of an independent contractor with whom he has

AGENCY 

33 an agreement for the performance of work. But a question frequently arises whether A is an agent or an independent contractor, so as to determine P's liability in case someone is injured by A or his help during the work. This is really best determined by the circumstances. What the parties call themselves is not binding on a third party. A is an independent contractor if he (1) used his own tools, (2) directed the work, (3) paid the help, (4) had the sole right to hire and discharge the help, (5) contracted with P for a lump sum or its equivalent, so that A was put in a position of profiting or losing. If some of these situations exist and some do not, it would seem that it is then a question of weight. 

Beach v. Velzy 238 N. Y. 100

Robins Dry Dock v. Navigazione etc. S. A. 261 N. Y. 455 

Dutcher v. Victoria Paper Mills 219 A. D. 544, 220 N. Y. S. 625

The same difficulty arises where A takes orders from several on one job. The rule has been expressed in this way: He is deemed to be the master who has the supreme choice, control or direction of the servant, and whose will the servant represents, not merely in the ultimate result of his work but in all its details. 

Ramsey v. Bennet Contr. Co. 245 N. Y. 66 

Bartolomeo v. Bennet Contr. Co. 245 N. Y. 66.

There is no duty arising upon an owner or a general contractor to inspect the machinery and tools used by a subcontractor, which that contractor exclusively possesses and controls; nor of any duty after an inspection disclosing defects, to maker repair of a defective appliance. lacano v. Frank & Frank 259 N. Y. 377.

There are some exceptions to the main rule. The principal remains liable for the acts of the contractor as if the latter were an agent. (1) If the work which the contractor is hired to do constitutes a public nuisance. (2) If the owner interferes with the work of the independent contractor and as a result the plaintiff is injured. (3) If the independent contractor is hired to do unlawful work. (4) If the employer is bound to repair by contract or statute, his obligation cannot be avoided by engaging others to do the work. 

Thus a lessor who was under obligation to keep the roof of the leased premises in good repair was held liable for damages to a lessee's goods by rain coming through the roof poorly repaired by an independent contractor whom the lessor had hired. 

Komar v. Wynn 125 Misc. 176, 210 N. Y. S. 422. (5) If the work to be done is inherently dangerous. An owner cannot absolve himself of liability by hiring a contractor to demolish a building. Where work is to be done on a public highway, which unless carefully done will create conditions dangerous to the public, duty to use care cannot be delegated. Thus, if a contractor leaves an insecure pile of iron rails in a street under construction by him, the principal is liable to a child who is hurt by its fall while

playing near the iron. Disagreement has arisen in the attempted application of the doctrine because of varying views as to what is inherently dangerous.* 

Boylhart v. DiMarco 270 N. Y. 217 

Berg v. Parsons 156 N. Y. 109 

Hanley v. Central Bank 255 A. D. 542, affd. 280 N. Y. 734 

Kowalsky v. Conseco Co. 264 N. Y. 125 

Paltrey v. Eagen 200 N. Y. 83; Wright v. Tudor City 276 N. Y. 303

No responsibility rests upon an owner to a contractor or the latter's servants because of a dangerous condition which he has undertaken to repair. The assumption of such work includes an assumption of the risk. Ratification

The rule of ratification applies if (1) A names his principal and (2) acts without or in excess of his authority. It is sufficient if P is so described as to be capable of later identification. A could under this, insure a house for "the benefit of those concerned" and anyone concerned could ratify. Once P ratifies, he is bound. After the ratification and notice to T, T cannot withdraw even with A's consent, for it now has become P's contract. The agent is then no longer responsible to the other contracting party. It becomes a case of an agent having contracted for a disclosed principal. 

Though ratification must be by a positive act, there can be ratification by silence in cases where A exceeded his authority. In such case P is bound to disavow A's act within a reasonable time after the knowledge of the facts comes to him. Where A had no authority at all to begin with, it depends on the particular circumstances of the case whether mere silence will operate as presumptive proof of ratification. If the circumstances are such that the silence of P would induce T to rely upon an agency and to act upon such reliance to his detriment, then such silence or inaction may be considered as a ratification. 

Ketcham v. Morsland 18 Misc. 450, 42 N. Y. S. 7.

A ratification must be of the entire act and not of a part and must be made in the same manner that the authority of agency would have had to be given originally. If the authority should have been in writing, the ratification must be in writing. 

Hyatt v. Clark 118 N. Y. 653.

To constitute a valid ratification, P must know all the facts of importance when he ratifies. A deliberate ratification without investigation, is a valid ratification. Yet when A was originally authorized to do a certain act, and he goes beyond his instructions, there is at once a presumption that P has ratified, which presumption can be overcome by evidence to the contrary. 

Merritt v. Bissell 136 N. Y. 521. *For a valuable list of cases on this subject see Kuhn v. J. P. Carlin Construction Co., 154 Misc. 892, 278 N. Y. S. 635.

AGENCY 

35 Ratification dates back to, the creation of the contract between the unauthorized agent and the third party. Where, however, the subject-matter of the contract is destroyed before the ratification, the ratification is invalid. In a leading case, A, an insurance broker, placed insurance with T Insurance Company for P, without authority. The insured building burned and then P ratified A's act. It was held that the ratification was invalid.

An executor's power relates back to the decedent's death. He may ratify an act done between the time of the decedent's death and the time of his appointment.

Ratification can be applied to cases where A committed a tort, in which case a sharing of the fruits of the tort would be considered ratification. In such an instance both A and P would become liable. 

But note that a forged instrument can be ratified. The crime of forgery, however, is not excused thereby. By the ratification the sig nature becomes valid only for purposes of suit in civil cases. 

Though an insane person can ratify, he cannot do so while he is non compos mentis. 

Undisclosed Principal

Where A deals in his own name, and later T learns that A was really P's agent, T can elect to sue A or P. Any set-off that T might have against A may be asserted against P, when T learns of his identity. 

Foreign Trade Banking Corp. v. Gersetta Corp. 237 N. Y. 265

A satisfaction of a judgment against A or P bars any suit against the other. But if T proceeds against or obtains judgment against A although aware of P's identity, it is not an election. He may continue to pursue his rights against both until paid. 

Civil Practice Act § 112b. 

Where A signs a written contract in his own name merely, which contract does not upon its face show that he was acting as the agent of another, he will be personally bound thereby even if he had orally disclosed the name of his principal. Even if A had signed, “A, president of Z Corporation," A would be liable, as the signature would be A's, with the rest of it only descriptive of A. If, however, the contract on its face indicates even to a slight degree that A, though he signed the contract in his own name, was acting for a disclosed third person, the question of whether the contract was executed by him as agent or principal is one of fact for the jury to determine. This, of course, permits parol evidence to discharge the agent. 

Meyer v. Redmond 205 N. Y. 478.

The undisclosed principal could be held liable unless the document was a negotiable instrument. A person unnamed on a negotiable instrument cannot be sued upon that instrument. 

Casco National Bank v. Clark 139 N. Y. 307.

If the agents signs a contract with T, as agent of P, he cannot sue

T in his own name when nothing on the face of the agreement shows that he is a party to, or a beneficiary of, the contract. 

If A contracts as agent for P, without the authority of P, A cannot be held as a principal and thus held to the contract. A may only be held liable on his breach of warranty of authority. Therefore if 

A contracts as agent for the P corporation, to purchase realty from T, the fact being that the P corporation is not yet organized but is going to be, specific performance cannot be compelled against A should this P corporation not be in existence when the day for the passing of the title arrives. A's liability rests only on the warranty of authority. 

Weiss v. Baum 218 A. D. 83, 217 N. Y. Ş. 820. *The common law effect of a sealed instrument no longer exists. The presence of a seal does not prevent a suit against one not named in the instrument. The presence of a corporate seal purported to be executed by corporate authority, constitutes a rebuttable presumption that the instrument was so executed. 

Civil Practice Act, § 342; General Corporation Law § 14.

Bailment and Sale

IN 

BAILLMENTS 

´N ORDER that a bailment exist, there must be (1) an actual or constructive delivery by the bailor, (2) of personalty, (3) which is accepted by the bailee, actually or constructively. An owner, by the mere delivery of the chattels to another even though the latter be a dealer in similar merchandise is not estopped from asserting his title thereto against any one else. 

Deferred Payment Plan, Inc. v. Bennett 263 A. D. 694 

Webster v. Lane 125 Misc. 868. 212 N. Y. S. 298.

Where a patient leaves his overcoat in the reception room of a dentist, there being no closet in which to deposit wraps, the dentist is the bailee of this overcoat. 

Where A delivers goods to B, who is to remodel, reshape or do other work upon these goods and return them in altered form to A, we have a bailment. The fact that it will be necessary for B to add some of his own material to A's goods does not alter the situation. 

The title to the material used by the bailee and added to the article worked on, passes to the bailor by accession. If B is to return other goods in exchange, it is a sale. 

Title to the goods which are the subject of a bailment remains in the bailor; in a sale, title is in the vendee, regardless of possession. 

Should a sheriff levy on bailed goods in the bailee's possession under an execution issued by a judgment creditor of the bailee, the sheriff is liable because title was in the bailor. When bailed goods are destroyed through no one's fault, the bailor stands the loss. 

Where the goods are delivered to A for safekeeping, A being given an option to buy, it is a bailment until A actually buys. 

Bailment for Sole Benefit of Bailor

In such bailment the bailee is liable only for gross negligence by which is meant an intentional failure to perform a manifest duty in reckless disregard of the consequences. A gratuitous bailee in the absence of statutory authority, may not sell the bailor's goods without permission. If he desires to terminate the bailment he must request the bailor to remove them to storage and notify the bailor. 

But he may not sell them. A warehouseman may sell for storage charges after notice. 

Crosby v. 20 Fifth Avenue Hotel 173 Misc 595, affd. at p. 604.

A gratuitous agreement to undertake a trust in the future is not obligatory. But if the trust is entered upon, the gratuitous bailee is responsible on his undertaking. 

Siegel v. Spear & Co. 234 N. Y. 479. 27

The negligence of a bailor contributing to the loss will exonerate the bailee from liability 

Osborn v. Cline 263 N. Y. 434.

Bailment for Sole Benefit or Profit of Bailee 

In a bailment of this kind, the bailee is liable for even slight negligence on his own part. If, however, the property is stolen, damaged or destroyed through an independent agency, the bailee is not liable if he has exercised ordinary care in respect to the property entrusted to him for safekeeping. 

Hobbie v. Ryan 130 Misc 221, 223 N. Y. S. 654.

The fact that it was agreed that the bailee was not to be liable in case of theft does not mean that he is not liable if he is negligent. 

To be relieved of liability in this case it is necessary to stipulate that he is not to be liable even if negligent. 

Balice v. Erie R. R. Co. 208 A. D. 427, 203 N.Y.S. 636 

Bailments for Mutual Benefit of Bailor and Bailee (1) Pledges.-There must be actual or constructive delivery of the property to constitute a pledge. If the pledgee parts with possession, his lien is destroyed. If, however, possession is restored to the pledgor for some special purpose and then to be returned, the lien remains a lien against all except bona fide possessors. 

Matter of Bickford 265 A. D. 266.

Title remains in the pledgor. The pledgee obtains only possession with a right to sell the property at a public sale in case of the pledgor's default and after demand. Notice of sale must be mailed to the pledgor at least ten days prior to the date of the sale. A sale by the pledgee before the pledgor's default is absolutely ineffective as against the pledgor. If the pledge consists of stock, it is the pledgee's duty to collect dividends and apply them to the reduction of the indebtedness. The parties may enter into a contract expressly removing these restrictions and giving the pledgee the power to sell at a public or private sale without notice and to become the purchaser. In a private sale the pledgee must adopt all reasonable modes of procedure so as to obtain the best price. 

Cole v. Manufacturers Trust Co. 299 N.Y.S. 418 

Brown v. Provident Loan Society 282 N.Y. 453 

McCoy v. American Express Co. 253 N. Y. 477.

Though the relationship between pledgor and pledgee is that of debtor and creditor when collateral is sold after default and a surplus is at hand after the sale, the claim for such surplus may be maintained in an equity action for an accounting. 

South Shore Thrift Co. v. National Bank 276 N. Y. 465.

A wrongful use of the pledged property by the pledgee does not terminate the pledge. The pledgee remains liable for any resulting damage. If he is unable to restore the pledged article upon the payment of the debt, he is liable in conversion for the actual loss suffered.

BAILMENTS 

39 The pledgee owes a direct duty to the pledgor to be reasonably careful in his custody of the pledge so that no harm should come to it through his act.

Little v. Acceptance Corp. 215 A. D. 427, 213 N. Y. S. 606. 

A pawnbroker has no recourse against a pawner, but can look for reimbursement only to the pawn as the sole security upon which the loan was made.

In re Adam's Estate 159 Misc. 827, 288 N. Y. S. 924. (2) Hire of Chattels.—The care to be used by the bailee in this bailment is the same as that of a pledgee. He impliedly warrants the article to be fit for the purpose for which it was hired. One who installs a loaned tank for gasoline storage impliedly warrants that it is reasonably fit and suitable for such purpose. A dealer who supplies sacks for bagging peas, in order that they may be unloaded from a ship, is liable for damages if the sacks, while being hoisted, break because of their insufficiency. 

In re People 250 N. Y. 410 

Standard Oil v. Boyle 231 A. D. 101, 246 N. Y. S. 142.

The continuing in possession of personalty after the expiration of a lease thereof does not act as a renewal of the lease. 

Hood Farm v. Roberts 254 A. D. 383, 5 N. Y. S. (2d) 513. 

Particular Bailments (a) Storekeepers.-A store proprietor is a custodian for profit of such articles which are necessarily laid aside by a customer in participating in acts essential to carry on the business at hand. There is an invitation by implication extended by the defendant to lay aside a coat worn by a customer, while trying a new one. If a plaintiff, in order to try on a new hat in defendant's store, laid the hat she was wearing, on the counter with her purse underneath the hat, the defendant would not be liable for the purse if stolen, as that article was not involved in the transaction. And a proprietor was not held liable for money stolen from trousers left in a booth while the proprietor took measurements for new trousers. 

Powers v. O'Neill 89 Hun. 129; Bunnel v. Stern 122 N. Y. 539.

Even the liability as to articles necessarily laid aside exists only for the time necessary for the completion of the business at hand. 

McAllister v. Simon 27 Misc. 214, 57 N. Y. S. 733. (b) Restaurateurs.—A restaurant owner is not liable for the loss of a guest's overcoat when the coat is hung on a hook in close proximity to the guest's seat and which the guest can take with him at any time. The fact that the waiter helps him remove the coat or hangs it up for him does not alter the situation. 

Wieler v. Silver Standard Ins. 263 A. D. 521. 

(c) Check rooms.-As to property deposited by a guest or patron in the check room of a hotel or restaurant, the proprietor is not liable beyond $75, for property there deposited for which no fee is charged, unless the excess value of the article is stated in the re-

ceipt. If the value is so stated the proprietor is not liable beyond $100, unless the property was lost through the negligence of the restaurateur or stolen by him.

Honig v. Riley 244 N. Y. 105; General Business Law. § 201. 

To take advantage of the statutory limitation, there must be evidence that there was a posting of the statute as specified in Section 

206 of the General Business Law. 

Gardner v. Hotel Roosevelt Inc. 263 A. D. 268. 

(d) Theatre Owners.-The occupants of a box in a theatre cannot recover for loss of apparel hung upon hooks attached to the wall of the box. The hooks are for the convenience of the occupants.

Burden of Proof of Bailee's Liability 

A plaintiff bailor may make a prima facie case of conversion or negligence against the bailee by showing a delivery to the bailee and a failure to redeliver upon due demand. The burden of going forward then shifts to the bailee. The bailee may make out a prima facie defense by showing that the loss occurred through no fault of his own. It then becomes the plaintiff's duty to again go forward and show that the loss was caused by the defendant's negligence or affirmative act. The concession on the part of the bailor that the article was stolen from the defendant bailee does not destroy the prima facie case nor relieve the bailee from the necessity of showing that the theft was not through the fault of the bailee. The ultimate burden of proof is upon the plaintiff bailor.* 

Castorine v. Rosen 290 N. Y. 445.

If the bailee was to use the bailed article in a certain manner or for a certain purpose, he is liable in conversion for any slight departure. Thus if A hires a car to go to Plattsburg and goes instead to Rouse's Point past Plattsburg and the car is damaged, A is liable to his bailor though the damage occurred without the fault of A. Innkeepers

The innkeeper's liability at common law did not originally extend to cover property not within the walls of the inn or the buildings used in connection therewith. Whether that is the law in New 

York today is an open question, though the Court of Appeals has hinted that this common law rule is to be preferred. Where an innkeeper maintains a system for the transportation of baggage of guests from the station to the hotel, the limit of liability for loss is $250, unless at the time of delivery a written receipt stating a higher value is given. In that event the limit of the innkeeper's liability is $500 unless the loss occurred through his fault or negligence. 

Davidson v. Madison Corp. 257 N. Y. 120. *A bailee may show that the bailed article was stolen from him through no fault of his own, under a plea of general denial.

BAILMENTS 

41 An innkeeper is an insurer of the safety of property of his guest, brought infra hospitium. He is liable for its loss, whether by burglary, theft or negligence, unless it arises from the neglect or misconduct of the guest, an act of God, or of public enemies or by fire not caused by the negligence of the innkeeper. 

Under the statute, if (1) the proprietor of a hotel provides a safe in the hotel for the safekeeping of the jewels, ornaments, money or bonds and notes of guests and (2) notifies the guest of this by a notice containing a copy of the statute,* posted in a conspicuous manner in the office and public rooms of the hotel, and (3) the guest neglects to deliver such valuables for deposit to the person in charge of the office, the proprietor is not liable for loss of such valuables, unless the loss is due to the fault of the innkeeper personally. If the guest offers to deliver such valuables to the person in charge, the innkeeper may refuse to accept and be liable for over $500. If the innkeeper does accept more than $500, the liability of the innkeeper in the event of loss, not due to his negligence, would not exceed $500 unless there were a special agreement in writing to the contrary. A watch while ornamented with diamonds, is not a jewel within the meaning of the section if the watch is in daily use. 

If an employee removed objects from the safe, the statutory limit ations of liability would still apply. 

General Business Law, §§ 200, 201 Kennedy v. Bowman Biltmore Hotel, 157 Misc. 416 

Millheiser v. Beau-Site Co. 251 N. Y. 290 

Glinsky v. Dunham, 230 A. D. 470, 245 N. Y. S. 359 

Epp v. Boroman, 171 Misc. 338, 12 N. Y. S. (2d) 384.

If property other than jewels, ornaments, money or securities is stolen from a room, the limit of the innkeeper's liability is $500. 

The duties of an innkeeper are non-delegable. If in this performance he selects third parties, the latter are not deemed independent contractors, but are agents of the innkeeper. 

Davidson v. Madison Corp., 257 N. Y. 120.

An innkeeper is not, and was not under the common law, an insurer of the safety of the person of the guest. He must exercise only reasonable care for his safety and comfort. There exists an implied warranty that the premises are, for the purpose of personal use by the guest, as safe as reasonable care and skill on the part of anyone can make them. 

Friedman v. Shindler, 224 A. D. 232, affd. 250 N. Y. 574

To be able to hold the innkeeper to his liability as such, one must come to the inn as a guest, and be ready to pay for the accommodations. One attending a function at a hotel or one who merely leaves his baggage at the hotel and does not stay there is not a guest. 

If however, a person intending to be a guest sends his baggage ahead and later becomes a guest, the responsibility relates back to the time of the delivery of the baggage. The fact that one registers

Liens 

Rapee v. Beacon Hotel Co., 293 N. Y. 196

One who alters or repairs, or enhances the value of, or shapes personalty at the owner's request, has an artisan's lien while the goods are in his possession. Title does not rest with the artisan. The lien is limited to the article upon which work was done. If A delivers a suit to be repaired and lends the tailor his scissors for the work, the tailor has no lien on the scissors for the price, as he did not alter, repair or enhance their value. Moreover, the lien is a specific lien, i.e. the lien is good only as to that article. If he returns the suit to A and 

A does not pay, the lien is lost. If A brings another suit the next day, this second suit cannot be held until the price of the first is paid.

Lien Law §180. 

In one case the defendant wrapped newspapers for the plaintiff, a publisher and addressed them and mailed them to the plaintiff's customers. It was held that the defendant did not have a lien upon the newspapers, as no artisan's lien was shown. 

N. Y. Dem. Pub. Corp. v. Lang 132 Misc. 57, 229 N. Y. S. 45.

A lienor who stores, maintains, keeps or repairs a motor vehicle or while in the possession supplies fuel thereto at the request of the legal possessor, obtains a lien superior to the rights of a chattel mortgagee, despite the fact that title may be in the mortgagee. 

Lien Law & 184 

Courtlandt v. Yellow Cab Co. 217 A. D. 4, 215 N. Y. S. 789

The right to retain the property under the lien is exercisable only as to that possessed. The possession may be actual or constructive. 

The owner of the article who obtains possession from the lienor by force, fraud or trick does not thereby destroy the lien. But if the owner obtains lawful possession and during such lawful possession sells the article to a bona fide purchaser, the lien is destroyed. Thus, if the bona fide purchaser should take the article, e.g., an automobile to the lienor for repairs, the lienor cannot retain the car because of a lien he may have had for labor when the car was owned by the seller. If the artisan has made any contract inconsistent with the lien, the lien is waived. Thus, if the property was to be delivered before payment was to be made, the bailee has no lien. 'Kamaran v. Sidney Garage 137 Misc. 744, 244 N. Y. S. 337.

An innkeeper's lien is given by statute to a keeper of a hotel, apartment hotel where food is also served if required, inn, boarding or rooming house. It extends to any personalty the guest brings in, even though it does not belong to the guest. It might even have been stolen-provided the innkeeper does not know that the goods when brought in are not those of the guest. 

Lien Law § 181.

43 A lienor may pledge the article upon which the lien exists, but the owner can get back the article by payment or tender of the amount due from him, despite the pledge.

A bank has no lien upon the account of a depositor who may be indebted to the bank. Thus, if a surety for the depositor paid the latter's debt to the 'bank after default, the surety would not be subrogated to the deposit. The bank could continue to pay the depositor out of his account with it.
