Gifts Inter Vivos 

There are three requisites of a valid gift of personalty: (1) An intent to make an immediate gift; (2) An unconditional and complete delivery either actual or constructive, to the donee, or to one in his behalf, operating to divest the donor of possession and dominion over the thing given. A mere promise to give an article of personaltv, is insufficient to constitute a legal gift inter vivos. A gift inter vivos cannot be made to take effect in possession in futuro for this amounts only to a promise to make a gift. (3) An acceptance by the donee.* 

Gannon v. McGuire 160 N. Y. 476 

In re Peno's Estate 128 Misc 718, 221 N. Y. S. 205, 218

There is no presumption in favor of a gift or of delivery. The possessor must prove delivery. It may be shown by the former owner's admission that the property belongs to another. To prove intent, evidence of prior declarations of the donor, showing intent to give, is admissible as corroborative evidence of a gift. Subsequent declarations tending to show a gift are admissible as they really are declarations against interest. 

In re Brown's Ex'r 130 Misc. 865, affd. 252 N. Y. 366 

Van Cleef v. Maxfield 196 A. D. 734, 188 N. Y. S. 322.

In one case a testator placed certain bonds in an envelope across the face of which he wrote, "property of Miss Lizzie Beck." The envelope was placed in his safe-deposit box to which he alone had access. It was held that this fact did not prove a gift to Miss Beck. 

The element of delivery was missing. 

Beck v. Staudt 133 N.Y.S. 529, affd. 208 N.Y. 566 

Cf. Mutual Life Ins. Co. v. Holley 280 N. Y. 330.

If the donor gives the donee the key of a vault or the combination of a safe or the key of a trunk, with words of gift of the contents, we have a good gift, since the article is incapable of manual delivery.

It is not less a gift because it is accompanied by a condition that *Joint control negatives any idea of a gift. Matter of Bashford, 178 Misc. 648.

it is subject to defeasance by the death of the donee before the death of the donor. 

People's Trust Co. v. Dickson 126 Misc. 580 affd. 220 A. D. 742.

Money or jewelry though not intended as outright gifts but which are given as a token of the engagement to marry, cannot be recovered back if the engagement' was breached, since it is a recovery sought for breach of contract to marry and such action is barred by statute. Where the contract is not breached, but is, by mutual consent rescinded or abrogated, recovery for such items may be maintained. 

Andrie v. Kaplan 288 N. Y. 685; Unger v. Hirsch 180 Misc. 381.

Delivery and the intent to make a gift need not occur simultaneously. Where a bailee has possession, a declaration by the owner that the bailee may consider the article given as a gift, transfers title. 

Bank Accounts as Subjects of Gifts 

It follows from what has heretofore been said, that if A transfers his savings-bank book to B, signifying his intention to present his account there to B, a valid gift inter vivos is established. 

In re Keating's Estate 214 A. D. 802, 210 N.Y.S. 588

The delivery of the bank book of a check account does not create a gift of the amount in the account. The distinction is this: A savings-bank book is evidence of debt and the bank is not obliged to pay the depositor except upon the production of the bank book, but in the case of a commercial account, it is not necessary to present the bank book in order to withdraw money. In the latter case the depositor controls the fund though the book may have been given away. The book is not evidence of a debt but only a memorandum. 

Brophy v. Haeberle 220 A.D. 511, 221 N.Y.S. 698

Since a check is merely an order on a bank to pay money and is not a transfer or delivery of that fund, such check is not a gift. 

In re Gibbons' Estate 234 A D. 153.

Let us consider some variations of this situation. A deposits his own money in a bank, in X's name, without any qualification. Title does not pass to X. A trust in favor of X is not implied from these facts. Nor is there a gift, because there was no delivery of the thing given or a symbol which would represent possession. 

Beaver v. Beaver 117 N. Y. 421. 

Totten Trusts

Where A deposits his own money in his own name as trustee for X, it is a tentative trust revocable at will. Should A predecease X without revocation, a presumption arises that an absolute trust is created as to the balance on hand at A's death. The tentative rights of the beneficiary may be ended by the depositor by a decisive act of disaffirmance. The rights may become vested by making a completed gift. 

Matter of Totten 179 N. Y. 112.

BAILMENTS 

45 The revocation of the right of the beneficiary may be accomplished by closing or changing the form of the account; by the prior death of the beneficiary; by a disaffirmance in a written instrument. 

Joint Bank Accounts

If a husband and wife each contribute to a joint investment or to the purchase of a security, and the title is taken in their joint names to be held by them, no presumption arises that either intended to make a gift of his or her share to the survivor. They hold as tenants in common. But where a husband buys personalty with his own funds, and takes title in the joint name of himself and his wife, there is a presumption, in the absence of other evidence, of an intent to confer upon his wife the right of survivorship and to leave him with complete control and right of disposition. 

In re Blumenthal's Estate 236 N. Y. 448, 452.

A bank account in the name of husband and wife, in the absence of evidence to the contrary, creates a right of survivorship whether or not there has been a delivery of the bank book. 

Brumer v. Brumer 223 A. D. 186, 228 N. Y. S. 63.

If a bank account is opened in the name of "A or B, payable to either or survivor," a presumption at once arises that the interest of the depositors is that of joint tenants.* This presumption is not conclusive and may be overcome by proof that the depositor when making the deposit had no intention to create a joint tenancy. For the bank which has paid, the form of the account is an absolute protection, unless notice has been given not to pay. 

Upon the death of one of the depositors in the absence of fraud or undue influence at the opening of the account to be pleaded and proven, this presumption becomes conclusive in favor of the survivor as to any moneys then left in the account. It continues to be a mere presumption as to any moneys previously withdrawn. The withdrawal did not destroy the joint tenancy or the title of the survivor, if a joint tenancy had been created. It did, however, open the door to competent evidence, if any was available, that the tenancy created at the opening of the account was in truth something different from the tenancy defined by the presumption. 

In re Juedel's Estate 280 N. Y. 37 

In re Porianda's Estate 256 N. Y. 423 

Marrow v. Moskowitz 255 N. Y. 219

Nothing prevents one joint owner from destroying the joint ownership in the entire deposit to the extent of his withdrawals of no more than his equal share for his own use, although, if the entire account were withdrawn, the result might be otherwise. The disposition by the joint tenant of his undivided interest may take any form, e.g., sale, assignment, gift, mortgage, pledge. 

In re Suter's Estate 258 N.Y. 104; Matter of Ĥoffman 175 Misc. 607

This presumption is not applicable to deposits in national banks. As to such deposits, intention is the test of the nature of the deposit. In re Hickmott's 

Estate, 166 Misc. 536, affd. 256 A. D. 1047.

Gifts Causa Mortis 

The following elements are all essential in order to constitute an effective gift causa mortis (1) The gift must be of personalty. It cannot include future earnings. (2) There must be such a delivery and acceptance as vests in the donee control and domination over the property. Delivery to a third person to hold and then upon the death of the donee to deliver to a named donee is insufficient, for there has been delivery only to the donor's agent and not to the donee. Upon the death of the donor the agency terminated. (3) An intention that it take effect on death; and (4) An existing peril and an apprehension of death. (5) The donor must die of the ailment from which he suffers at the time he delivers the article. But note that if the donor thinks he is suffering from one disease but is actually suffering fron another, and he dies of the latter, the gift would be good, for he did die of the disease from which he was suffering. A voyage in dangerous waters is not the kind of peril which forms the basis for a gift causa mortis. 

In re Duffy 127 A.D. 74, 111 N.Y.S. 77 

Beaver v. Beaver, 117 N. Y. 421, 428; Matter of Reardon 175 Misc. 1002

The gift becomes void by recovery from the ailment and it is revocable by the donor. It also becomes void by the death of the donee in the lifetime of the donor. The burden is on the donee to establish, by a fair preponderance of credible testimony, that a gift was intended. 

Ridden v. Thrall 125 N. Y. 572, 579. Finders

Though generally a bailment depends upon a contractual relation, there are situations where the element of lawful possession, however created, plus the duty to account for an article as the property of another, creates a bailment. For that reason, finders are bailees. 

Armstrong v. Sisti 242 N. Y. 440.

When one abandons an article which is found by another, the finder obtains title and the former owner cannot reclaim it. If an owner loses an article, the finder's rights are good against everyone but the owner. As against him, the finder is bailee. 

If a person forgets a package on a street car or train, the company obtains custody and possession. It is the duty of a passenger who picks it up to turn it over to the company. 

Foulke v. N. Y. Cons. R. R. Co., 228 Ñ. Y. 269.

What Is a Negotiable Instrument?

HE MOST frequent forms of negotiable instruments come as (1) promissory notes, and (2) bills of exchange (drafts).

A promissory note is an unconditional promise to pay a definite sum of money at a definite time, to the order of some person or to bearer. A bill of exchange is a direction by one person to another person to pay to the order of a third person a definite sum of money at a definite time. $600.00

Example of A Promissory Note 

New York, N. Y., July 25, 1945 

Ninety days after date I promise to pay to John Smith the sum of Six Hundred and 00/100 with interest at 6% per annum at Corn Exchange Bank of New York 

Value received. or order .......Dollars

Example of A Bill of Exchange RICHARD ROE 

$600.00 

At twenty days sight pay to John Smith or order the sum of Six Hundred and 00/100 

New York, N. Y., July 25, 1945

Dollars and charge my account. 

To John Doe, 9 Rockefeller Plaza, N. Y. C. 

RICHARD ROE

To be negotiable the instrument must contain each of the following six characteristics. (1) The promise to pay or the order to pay must be unconditional. If the instrument calls for payment to be made out of a particular fund, or out of "my profits on the building job" or if a cer- *A trade acceptance is a draft or bill of exchange drawn by the seller on the purchaser of goods sold and accepted by such purchaser. Dubler v. Toscana, 142 

Misc. 369, 254 N. Y. S. 464. 47

tain ship arrive, or provided the maker is able to pay, or when A shall marry, it is not negotiable and the later happening of the event does not make it negotiable. So far as determinable on the date of execution the condition might never occur. But if an order was to pay "out of account No. 1 first," it is not conditional but an order to pay and to charge the general account of the drawer if the sum stated is more than the designated fund consists of, and the instrument would be negotiable. 

Negotiable Instruments Law §22 

Fulton v. Varney 117 A. D. 572, 102 N. Y. S. 608. (2) What is to be paid must be United States money or foreign coin. A promise in an instrument to pay "with a good wagon worth $500," or in bonds, renders the instrument non-negotiable. (3) The money to be paid must be a definite sum. The fact that interest or attorney's fees are to be added to a principal sum does not make the payable sum indefinite.* (4) The money must be payable either on demand (this is called a "sight instrument") ** or at a fixed or definite time, or after a certain occurrence. A promise to pay "ninety days after my reaching the age of 21," makes the instrument non-negotiable, for the time is neither fixed nor definite, nor certain. But an instrument "payable 20 days after my death" is negotiable, for death is certain to Occur. (5) The instrument must be payable to the payee's order or to bearer. (6) When the instrument is addressed to a drawee, he must be named or otherwise indicated with reasonably certainty. 

Negotiable Instruments Law §§ 20; 23 

Hegeman v. Moon 131 N. Y. 462.

The negotiability of an instrument is not affected if (1) It fails to have a date, seal or to mention consideration or place where drawn or where payable; or if or (2) It authorizes the sale of any collateral; or if (3) It authorizes a confession of judgment if not paid on time; (4) If payment may be accelerated by the happening of some event, e.g., non-payment of an installment or the filing of a lien; or (5) If the holder is given the right of choosing between having something done instead of getting his money. If it only contains a promise to do something other than pay money, or to do something and pay money, it is not negotiable. 

Negotiable Instruments Law §§ 24, 25 

Glide v. Sheridan 173 Misc. 542, 18 N. Y. S. (2nd) 339. *Where the sum payable is expressed in words and also in figures and there is a discrepancy between the two, the sum denoted by the words is the sum payable. Negotiable Instruments Law § 36. 

**A demand or sight instrument is payable at once when issued and the Statute of Limitations begins to run at once. Parol evidence is inadmissible to show that a date was set for payment.

Acceptance of Bills of Exchange 

Since a bill of exchange is merely an order on the drawee, and not an assignment, the drawee is not liable until he accepts, i.e., writes "Accepted" or a similar word, and date and signature, across the bill. When the drawee does accept he becomes primarily liable. 

The acceptance may be written on a separate paper, but in such a case the acceptor is bound only to those bona fide holders who acted on the faith of the acceptance. The acceptance can be executed before or after the bill is signed or completed, or even after the bill of exchange is due.

Negotiable Instruments Law §§ 222, 226. 

Acceptances are either general or qualified. The general acceptance assents without any qualification to the order of the drawer, but a qualified acceptance varies the effect of the bill as drawn. 

The qualifications may be (1) As to the amount, i.e., a partial acceptance, as when the drawee accepts as to $50, whereas the draft was for $100. (2) As to time, e.g., the draft is payable in ten days and it is accepted as payable in twenty days. (3) As to place. It should be noted that if the acceptor indicates a place of payment, as "payable at the Corn Exchange," it is not a qualified acceptance. But if it is restricted to that place only, as "payable only at the Corn Exchange," it is qualified. (4) If not all the drawees accept but only some of them. 

If the acceptor imposes a new condition, as "payable when drawer sends me more money.”

Negotiable Instruments Law §§ 227, 228, 229. 

The effect of a qualified acceptance is to bind the acceptor only according to the tenor of his acceptance. The holder need not receive the qualified acceptance. If he does, he is bound by it; but all prior parties, including the drawer, who do not agree, are discharged from further liability. They are deemed to have assented, unless they signify dissent within a reasonable time after notice of the qualified acceptance.

Negotiable Instruments Law § 230. 

No acceptance is valid or complete until notification or delivery of the acceptance. But the drawee has 24 hours in which to accept or refuse. If he finally does accept, the acceptance dates as of the presentation for acceptance. Should the drawee refuse to return the bill after 24 hours, and the holder demand it, it is deemed accepted as of the time of presentation..

Negotiable Instruments Law §§ 224, 225. 

The holder may wait until maturity and then present his bill to the drawee for payment, without bothering to have it accepted. But it may be presented for acceptance at any time, and if acceptance is refused, the bill is considered dishonored at once, even though it may have a year to run. There need be no further presentation for payment.

However, there are three cases where the holder must present the bill for acceptance within a reasonable time or else negotiate it to someone else within a reasonable time, who in turn must so present it for acceptance or negotiate it. These cases are: (1) If the bill orders payment within a definite number of days after sight, e.g., "Please pay 30 days after sight." In such a case the time of asking for the acceptance fixes "the sight" and that fixes the date of maturity. The holder must in such a case present for acceptance, otherwise there will not be a date of maturity. (2) Where the bill says that it must be presented for acceptance. (3) Where the bill is payable at a place other than the drawee's home or place of business.

If there are joint drawees (there cannot be two or more in the alternative), presentment must be made to all, unless one has authority to accept for the others. If a drawee is dead, presentment should be made to his personal representative. If bankrupt, presentment for acceptance can be made to the bankrupt or to his trustee. 

Negotiable Instruments Law § 242. 

Bearer Paper 

An instrument is payable to bearer- (1) When it is expressed to be “payable to bearer." (2) "Payable to payee or bearer." But not if it said "to the order of the bearer, Ralph Jones," for then the word “bearer” is merely descriptive of a definite person. (3) Payable to a person known by the one primarily liable to be dead or non-existing or fictitious. (4) When the last indorsement is in blank. (5) When it is payable not to a specific person, as "to the estate of John Smith."

Negotiable Instruments Law § 28 

Shipman v. Bank of New York 126 N. Y. 318, 330.

The Holder in Due Course 

A holder in due course is one who (1) in good faith, (2) pays value for an instrument, (3) without knowledge of any defenses which there may exist in favor of those apparently liable upon the instrument, (4) before maturity. Value may even be an antecedent debt. 

Frank v. Von Bayer 236 N. Y. 473.

Every holder is deemed prima facie a holder in due course; but when it is shown that the title of any person who has negotiated the instrument was defective, the burden is on the holder to prove that he or some person under whom he claims acquired the title as a holder in due course.

Negotiable Instruments Law, §§ 98, 91. 

Where there is fraud, the presumption is that he who is guilty will part with the note for the purpose of enabling some third party to recover upon it, and such presumption operates against the

holder and it devolves upon him to show that he is a holder in due course. Even proof of value will not avail unless coupled with proof that the value was given without notice of the fraud. 

Negotiable Instruments Law § 98 

New York Bankers v. Duncan 257 N. Y. 160

If a person takes the note or check of a corporation in payment of a personal obligation of its officer, he is not a holder in due course, for this fact is sufficient to put him on inquiry. Where, however, a reasonable inquiry on the part of the taker of the note even if made, would have resulted only in dispelling the idea of fraud on the part of the officer, the taker is a holder in due course. 

Reif v. Equitable Life Assn. 268 N. Y. 269.

A bank is liable for the amount of checks of a corporation, indorsed by the president thereof and deposited in such bank for his personal use unless such act is authorized or the corporation is negligent or has otherwise deprived itself of its right to recover against the bank. The bank is not liable to the corporation for misappropriation of that fund by the officer if it has on file a proper resolution of the corporation, authorizing that officer to endorse checks for the corporation. 

Weissman v. Banque de Bruxelles 254 N. Y. 488.

Negotiabe Instruments Law § 95. 

The purchase of an instrument a short time before its maturity at a large discount requires the submission of the question of good faith to the jury. A 10% discount on paper payable in two months was not enough to constitute bad faith. 

Coopersmith v. Maunz 237 A.D. 795, 263 N.Y.S. 33 

Becker v. Hart 135 A. D. 785, 120 N.Y.S. 270

Where the transferee receives notice of any infirmity in the instrument or defect in the title of the person negotiating the same before he has paid the full amount agreed to be paid therefor, he will be deemed a holder in due course only to the extent of the amount theretofore paid by him. 

Negotiable Instruments Law § 93 

Freeport Bank v. Viemeister 227 A. D. 457, 238 N. Y. S. 169. 

Note this case: A holder in due course passes the instrument to

X, who knows that the note had been procured by fraud. Yet X, if he has not himself been a party to the fraud, can recover against the maker. He got title from a holder in due course, and he therefore succeeds to the rights of the holder in due course. If X was a party to the fraud at the time of the transfer, he cannot recover as his previous knowledge of defects in title is revived. 

Gruntal v. Natl. Surety 254 N. Y. 468.

Under the same reasoning, a payee of a note unenforceable because of lack of consideration does not acquire the rights of a holder in due course by a repurchase of the note from a holder in due course before maturity.

Crawford v. Debevoise 136 Misc. 838, 241 N.Y.S. 65 

Suppose the holder, Smith, transfers an order note to Robert

Jones without an endorsement. Jones thus gets the note subject to all the equities. Then Jones learns that Smith had obtained the note by fraud. This is a defense as between the immediate parties, but not against a holder in due course. So Jones demands Smith's indorsement. Smith indorses. Jones does not become a holder in due course, because the indorsement takes effect as of the date it was actually made, and when the indorsement was made Jones knew of the fraud and so was not a taker in good faith. 

Negotiable Instrument Law § 79. 

When a note is marked, "This note is secured by a chattel mortgage," such verbiage is sufficient to put a holder on notice of a defense of payment. Where a note contains the verbiage, "This note is subject to the terms of a conditional sales agreement executed by the maker on this date," the promise of payment is not absolute, the note is not negotiable and the holder is put on notice.* 

Old Colony Trust Co. v. Stumpel 247 N.Y.S. 538

Securities Investment v. Maxwell 131 Misc. 160 affd. 224 A. D. 872. 

Real Defenses Against a Holder in Due Course 

There are these defenses, called real defenses, which the maker, acceptor or drawer can use to defeat a recovery upon the instrument, even by a holder in due course: (1) Where he (the maker, acceptor or drawer) had no contractual capacity, as where he was an infant or adjudged lunatic at the time he bound himself under the instrument.

Negotiable Instruments Law § 41. 

(2) Where he did not consent, as for example where the defendant's signature was forged and the instrument was passed on to an innocent holder for value. The latter cannot then recover from the one whose signature was forged. But note that fraud in the inducement would not be a case of lack of consent. 

Negotiable Instruments Law § 42 

(3) When the instrument is void by statute. So negotiable instruments given for gambling debts, or delivered under a usurious rate of interest, are not good in the hands of a holder in due course. 

Suppose M makes a note to P's order for $1,000, for P's accommodation, and P takes it to B and obtains $700 for it. B cannot recover from M, even though he thought it was not an accommodation. It was a usurious negotiation. Where the note is not usurious in its inception, but later becomes so, usury is no defense. The legal inception makes impossible the existence of usury. 

Hinman v. Brundage 13 N. Y. S. (2nd) 363. 

*But cf. Petroleum Acc. Corp. v. Queens Avenue Laundry 265 A.D. 692 

where the indorsee was held to be a holder in due course even though, at the same time, he became the assignee of a contract which required the assignee for a stated period to keep lighting equipment in repair. It was for this service that the note was given. The decision pointed out that the breach of contract occurred after the negotiation and that the assignment of the contract put no burden upon the assignee.

In one case M gave P a check in payment for goods. P, losing at a card game, indorsed that check to X, the winner. X collected as that check had a valid inception. 

Bernstein v. Fuerth 132 Misc. 343, 229 N. Y. S. 791

Where P loaned money to D and received notes bearing 6% interest therefor, and in addition an undertaking that D was to repay the sum advanced, plus the interest, in any event, plus an additional sum if D made a certain profit in the venture in which he was to use the money, the transaction and the notes were usurious. 

It does not matter that the additional rights are contingent. It is a right, and this right plus the legal rate of interest constitute a usurious interest. 

Webster v. Roe 212 A. D. 756 affd. 241 N. Y. 570.

If the consideration alone is merely illegal (as payment by note for helping in a crime or illegal transaction), the note in the hands of a holder in due course is good. 

Howard Mfg. Co. v. Cohen. 207 A. D. 588, 202 N. Y. S. 449.

A bank which discounts notes for full value and without notice of any usury may recover upon such notes, although usurious in their inception.

Reel v. Porcella 263 A.D. 621 

If the holder obtained the instrument through the indorsement of a foreign corporation, which could not collect on the instrument because of a failure to file a certificate of doing business with the Secretary of State, he cannot be defeated by such defense if he would otherwise be holder in due course. 

Allison Hill Trust Company v. Sarandrea 134 Misc. 566 affd. 236 A. D. 189.

Defenses Available Only Against Those Not Holders in Due Course 

Such defenses are called personal defenses and are not available against holders in due course. (1) Fraud in the inducement. Where the defendant was induced to sign a note for the price of worthless stock, fraudently represented by the payee to be valuable, and the payee sold to a holder in due course, the defendant is liable to the holder in due course but not to the payee.

Negotiable Insrtuments Law § 94. 

(2) Failure to deliver a complete instrument. If a complete negotiable instrument is stolen and passed or negotiated without any forged indorsement to a holder in due course, the latter gets a good title. Even if the holder in due course negotiated the instrument to one who knew of the theft, the recipient would have good title, for he was not an immediate party and took the rights of the holder in due course.

But if an incomplete instrument is obtained otherwise than by delivery, e.g., by theft, and filled in without authority, there exists a defense even against a holder in due course.

Negotiable Instruments Law § 34.

The rule illustrated in the "theft" case applies if the maker gives the payee a note complete on its face to hold for a while and to return it later. This is not delivery. Should the payee pass it on to a holder in due course, the latter can collect, because failure to deliver a complete instrument is no defense against a holder in due course. It is that only between the immediate parties. (3) Want or failure of consideration. Every negotiable instrument is deemed prima facie to have been issued for valuable consideration. Lack of it must be proved by the defendant. Credit given on an antecedent debt is sufficient consideration. 

Merchants Bank v. Home Deposit Co. 128 Misc. 446 affd. 221 A. D. 828. 

Placing the proceeds of a discounted note to the credit of an indorser at a bank is not such payment therefor as to render the bank a holder in due course. It is only when the indorser has drawn against the credit that the bank becomes such holder. 

Citizens State Bank v. Cowles 180 N. Y. 346.

Partial failure of consideration is a defense pro tanto. But where the contract is entire and it is impossible to determine the price of each article, partial failure of consideration is no defense pro tanto. 

Negotiable Instruments Law § 54; Kelso v. Ellis 224 N. Y. 528. (4) Payment is no defense against the holder in due course, but is as between the immediate parties. If the holder is paid, he cannot collect again. But if when paid he is not required by the maker to give up the note and passes it on to a holder in due course, the latter can collect. We are not considering the maker's right against the person who fraudulently passed the note. (5) When the negotiable instrument is delivered to the payee with the understanding that it is not to be used unless a certain thing is first done by the payee, and that thing is not done, the payee's title is defective. If the instrument is transferred in violation of the agreement, the burden is upon the holder to show that he acquired title as a holder in due course. 

Silverman v. Loan Assn 125 Misc. 843, 211 N.Y.S. 491

To constitute notice of an infirmity in the instrument, or a defect in the title of the person negotiating, the person to whom the instrument is negotiated must have actual knowledge of the infirmity or defect or such knowledge that his taking the instrument amounts to bad faith. Mere negligence or mere evidence creating suspicion is not enough.

Negotiable Instruments Law § 85 

Blanks 

Dutch v. McMahon 210 A. D. 203, 219 N. Y. S. 321.

Whoever signs and puts in circulation a blank negotiable instrument impliedly confers authority upon a subsequent holder to fill in the blanks at will within a reasonable time. Of course it may not be urged against innocent third persons, that the words thereafter inserted were contrary to the authorization actually given or were inserted after such reasonable time. 

Hulbert v. Walker 258 N. Y. 8

If X had seen the instrument before it was complete, and then saw P fill in the blank, X would not be a holder in due course. 

Although a holder of an incomplete instrument has prima facie authority to fill in blank spaces, it does not aid X, who saw the blanks. He takes the note subject to all the equities. If, however, X had then passed the complete instrument to Y for value, Y would be a holder in due course, if acting in good faith. 

Negotiable Instruments Law § 33 

Greenblatt v. Miller 5 N. Y. S. (2nd) 388.

Note that there was delivery of an incomplete instrument. But if there had been no delivery of an incomplete instrument, but X had obtained the signed unfilled instrument by stealing it, it could not have been valid in anyone's hands.

If a check, complete on its face but exhibiting blank spaces wherein additional figures or names may readily be inserted, is signed in that condition by a drawer, and the instrument is altered by the introduction of other figures or words, the drawer may not recover the amount taken from his account from an innocent drawee who has paid the check, because his negligence had facilitated the forgery. 

Hulbert v. Walker 258 N. Y. 8 

Natl. Exchange Bank v. Lester 194 N. Y. 461. 

Negotiation and Indorsement 1 An instrument payable to bearer may be negotiated by delivery. 

If it is payable to order, it may be negotiated by the indorsement of the holder plus delivery.

The indorsement must be written on the instrument or on a paper attached to it, and must order the payment of the whole sum to the transferee. A purported indorsement to two or more, severally, is not a negotiation. It is, however, treated as an assignment and gives legal title to the indorsees of their separate shares. 

They may all sue together, or any one or more sue, provided all the indorsees are brought in as parties. But "to pay X and Y jointly" is not a partial indorsement and there can be valid negotiation or delivery.

Negotiable Instruments Law §§ 60, 61, 62 

Blake v. Weiden 291 N. Y. 134.

By signing a non-negotiable document on the back, the signer does not become an indorser, but he becomes liable as a maker or guarantor. 

Scott v. Palmer 286 N. Y. S. 453 affd. 273 N. Y. 471.

There are five kinds of indorsements: 

(1) Blank The payee indorses in blank by merely writing his name, usually on the back of the order paper. The order instrument is now bearer paper, and the indorsee or holder can negotiate by mere delivery. An instrument is considered payable to bearer if the last indorsement is one in blank.

Jones." This keeps it order paper. There cannot even be a further transfer of the instrument without the indorsement of Robert Jones, much less negotiation.

If an instrument on its face is payable to bearer, and is then indorsed specially, it remains a bearer instrument. But the liability of the special indorser exists only in favor of such later holders as are the indorsees of the one to whom he indorsed specially. 

Negotiable Instruments Law § 70 

(3) Qualified. Where the holder writes on the back, "Pay to 

Robert Jones or order without recourse," and signs his name, the paper remains negotiable, but the holder who indorses incurs no liability for the non-payment. 

A writing on the back of a promissory note which read "I hereby assign all my right and interest in this note to Richard Fay in full" was held an unqualified indorsement. To render an indorsement qualified, the words "without recourse" or words of similar import must be used. If the same writing had been put on a separate paper not attached to the note it would have been a mere assignment. The statute does not permit the interpretation that the word "assign" on the back of the instrument meant a transfer "without recourse." 

Negotiable Instruments Law § 68; Fay v. Witte 262 N. Y. 215.

Obviously either a blank or special indorsement may be made qualified. (4) Conditional. Such an indorsement transfers title to the indorsee subject to the fulfillment of a stated condition. The paper remains negotiable. If the contingency does not occur, the indorsee is entitled to no money. Conditional Indorsement

If the condition had been on the face of the instrument it would have made it non-negotiable. 

The maker may disregard the condition and pay to the indorsee or his transferee, whether the condition has been fulfilled or not. 

But if the indorsee or transferee is paid, he holds the proceeds subject to the rights of the conditional indorser. "5 (5) Restrictive.-"Pay to Robert Jones only," "Pay to Robert 

Jones for my use," "Pay to Robert Jones for Arthur Rose's use,' "Pay to Robert Jones for collection," "John Smith (holder), for deposit." This kind of indorsement renders the paper non-negotiable. The form of such indorsement gives notice of the non-negotiable character of the instrument to all parties into whose hands. it might come.

Negotiable Instruments Law § 66 

Mizell v. Hicks 8 N. Y. S. (2nd) 158.

The indorsee of an instrument for collection may sue the maker thereon in his own name, and this even though the indorsement is restrictive. 

Carson v. Federal Reserve 254 N.Y. 218, 237

Negotiable Instruments Law § 67 

Marine Trust Co. v. Lauria 213 A. D. 64 affd. 244 N. Y. 577

Restrictive Indorsement 

Pay to Robert Jones for Arthur Rose's use 

John Smith

An indorsement by the holder "for deposit" or "pay any bank or banker," or equivalent, is a restrictive indorsement and indicates that the indorsee bank is only an agent for collection. The indorser, however, does guarantee to subsequent holders the genuineness of prior indorsements and authority of prior indorsers to indorse. 

Very often holders indorse instruments in blank when depositing them for collection. The bank may change the indorsement to a restrictive indorsement by writing over the signature of the indorser such words as "for deposit" or "for collection," to negative the presumption that the bank of deposit is the owner. 

Negotiable Instruments Law § 350c. 

Suppose a holder, H, strikes out the indorsement of an indorser. 

The one whose name is stricken out and all those who indorsed after that name up to H are released.

Negotiable Instruments Law § 78. 

Negotiation is deemed prima facie to have been effected before maturity and at the place where the instrument is dated. 

Negotiable Instruments Law §§ 75, 76. 

Liability of Maker and Acceptor 

The maker and acceptor are both primarily liable. At maturity the holder need not make any formal demand. The maker or acceptor must be ready to pay at the place of payment. If payment is not made at maturity, suit may be started at once. 

A failure to present the note does not bar the holder's right to recover against the maker, though the note be past due. If the maker was able and willing to pay at the place of payment at maturity, and had the funds there available for that purpose, there has been tender though no payment which stops interest running. 

Shapiro v. Weber 220 A. D. 667, 222 N.Y.S. 471

Negotiable Instruments Law § 130 

The holder of a note though holding collateral to secure the note, may sue the maker on default without first tendering the collateral. 

The maker is entitled to the collateral upon payment of the amount due. The proper procedure for the maker is, when sued, to set up a counterclaim, and in it demand the return of the collateral upon payment of the amount due. 

Natl. Bank of Rochester v. Erion-Haines R. Co. 213 A. D. 54

The acceptor warrants the genuineness of the drawer's signature and his authority to draw, the payee's capacity to indorse, and that the drawer has sufficient funds with him. He also engages that he will pay according to the original tenor of the instrument. Accordingly, he cannot assert the forgery of the drawer's signature as a defense. But he cannot be held liable for a raised amount since he does not warrant the genuineness of the amount. Nor does he warrant the genuineness of subsequent indorsements. 

Negotiable Instruments Law §§ 110, 112 

Though the indorser is an infant, he can pass good title and one who holds through an infant may recover from the maker though the infant may use infancy as a defense.

A corporate maker cannot set up a defense of usury. If an individual is a co-maker with a corporation, the individual may set up a defense of usury. If, however, the individual co-maker was an accommodation party and not a victim of the usury, he cannot set up the defense of usury.

Astra Pictures Inc. v. Schapiro 182 Misc. 19 

Rockmore v. Epstein 127 Misc. 526, 217 N. Y. S. 76 

A note which reads: "We promise to pay, etc.," is presumed to be a joint obligation only. This presumption is rebuttable. On the death of one of two joint makers, the survivor remains liable in law. Equity might permit recourse to be had against the estate of the deceased maker, if the survivor were insolvent. 

First Natl. Bank v. Knickerbocker 126 Misc. 467, 214 N.Y.S. 465

An agent who signs a note as an agent of a disclosed principal is liable on the note itself, if he had no authority to so sign as agent. 

New Georgia Bank v. Lippman 249 N. Y. 307.

The drawer and indorsers are secondarily liable. Indorsers are liable prima facie in the order in which they indorsed, but evidence is admissible to show that among themselves they agreed otherwise. 

Negotiable Instruments Law § 118 

Faigelman's Estate, in re 142 Misc. 167, 254 N. Y. S. 161.

One who negotiates by delivery or by a qualified indorsement warrants the genuineness of the instrument, his title thereto, capacity of prior parties to contract and that he has no knowledge of any facts which would impair the validity of the instrument. Where the negotiation is by delivery only, the warranty extends in favor of no holder other than the immediate transferee. It thus follows that if A negotiates a usurious instrument to B by delivery or by qualified indorsement, he would not be liable if he did not know of the defect. His warranty extended only to his knowledge. 

One who indorses generally warrants the genuineness of the instrument, his title, capacity of prior parties to contract, that the instrument is valid at the time of his indorsement and that on due presentment it shall be paid or accepted as the case may be, and if dishonored and the the necessary proceedings on dishonor duly taken, that he will pay.

Negotiable Instruments Law §§ 115, 116.

Presentment 

There must be presentment by the holder or his agent in order to charge those secondarily liable, even though the indorsement be made after maturity. If the note is a demand note, it must be presented within a reasonable time. Whether or not there was a reasonable presentment of the demand note depends upon particular facts. 

In some cases a few months may not be a reasonable time-in other cases five years may be a reasonable time,e.g., the holder delayed presenting the note in accordance with the request of all the parties liable thereon. 

Klemann v. Collins 223 A.D. 161, 227 N.Y.S. 589

To constitute due presentment to the maker or acceptor so as to hold the indorsers, the instrument must be ready to be delivered. 

A demand over the telephone is not a sufficient presentment. 

Gilpin v. Savage, 201 Ñ. Y. 167.

If no place of payment is specified in the instrument, the presentment must be made at the maker's residence or place of business. If payment is to be made at a bank, presentment must be made during the banking hours. The maker has till closing time to pay before there can be dishonor. If payment is to be at a business place, then presentment must be made during business hours. 

Negotiable Instruments Law §§ 132, 133, 135 Notice of Dishonor 

After the instrument is dishonored, notice must be given to those secondarily liable, personally or by mail. If it is a foreign bill of exchange (a bill which is either drawn or payable in another state) it must be protested formally. The protest is the making of a public record, usually by a notary, of the facts showing that the instrument has been dishonored. Notes never need a formal protest. An oral notice of dishonor is sufficient if it sufficiently describes the instrument and states that it has been dishonored. 

Negotiable Instruments Law, §§ 160, 167, 189. 

Suppose X is the holder; A, B, C and D are indorsers. Upon dishonor X gives notice of it only to D, the last indorser. This makes 

D responsible. If D wants to protect himself, he should notify the prior indorsers. If he serves notice only on two, B and C, they are each responsible to those indorsers that came after them. But they can get nothing from A, as he was not notified. The notice to A may be given by anyone in the name of the one entitled to give a notice. 

Negotiable Instruments Law §§ 161, 162. 

The notice of dishonor, if the parties live in the same city, must be given before the close of business on the day following dishonor, or if it is given at a residence, before the usual hours of rest, the next day following the dishonor. If sent by mail, it must be deposited so as to arrive during these hours the next day. But should the instrument be in the hands of the holder's agent, the holder is given an additional day in which to give notice of dishonor. 

Negotiable Instruments Law §§ 174, 165.

Where a note was dishonored Friday, May 27 and the notice sent at 10 A. M. on the next day was received on Tuesday because Saturday was half-holiday and Monday a legal holiday, the notice was held timely, since if the following day were not Saturday the notice would have been received that day. The holder was not required to know the practice of the postoffice department in curtailing Saturday deliveries. 

Weil v. Aronsohn 147 Misc. 605, 264 N.Y.S. 292

If the parties live in different places, then it must be deposited in the post office in time to go by mail the following day, or if there be none, the next mail after that. The sender is not responsible for miscarriage in the mails. If an address has been added to the sig nature, the notice of dishonor is to be sent to that address. If not, then it is to be sent to the post office nearest his place of residence. 

The notice in the latter case may be sent to his place of business. 

Negotiable Instruments Law §§ 175, 176, 179. 

The testimony of an indorser that he did not receive the notice does not, standing alone, raise any question of fact as to whether the statute has been complied with, once the notary's certificate showing the dishonor and the mailing of the notice of protest has been put in evidence. To create a question of fact, evidence must be given to the effect that the certificate is false in its statement that a notice was mailed.* 

Trusts and Guarantee Co. v. Barnhardt 270 N. Y. 350

Asbury Park v. Simensky 160 Misc. 921, 290 N. Y. S. 992. 

Where a party receives notice of dishonor he has the same time for giving notice to prior parties, after he gets his notice, as the holder had after dishonor.

Negotiable Instruments Law § 178. 

If those primarily liable were partners when they accepted or made the note and no place of payment was specified, presentment may be made to any one of them, even though they are no longer partners. The same is true of notice to partners who are indorsers. 

If they are joint debtors and not partners, then presentment must be made to all. The same applies to a notice of dishonor. 

Negotiable Instruments Law §§ 137, 138, 170, 171. 

If the drawers or indorsers know that there will not be any acceptance or payment, presentment need not be made to charge them. This would occur when (1) the drawee is a fictitious person or (2) when presentment was waived by the indorser. But if the maker is insolvent, it is not an excuse for failing to present the instrument.

Negotiable Instruments Law §§ 129, 142. 

*It would seem, however, that where a defendant indorser serves upon the adverse party within 10 days after joinder of issue, an original affidavit to the effect that he has not received notice of non-acceptance or non-payment, he has thus put the plaintiff to his common law proof and the person who claims to have sent the notice must so testify and be subject to cross-examination. Civil 

Practice Act, § 368.

or Notice of dishonor to the drawer may be dispensed with when (1) the drawer and drawee are the same person; (2) the drawer had no contractual capacity; or (3) the drawer has no right to expect payment or acceptance, as when the drawer knows that he has no money with the drawee, unless the circumstances are such as to lead one to reasonably expect that there will be funds to meet the bill of exchange when it is presented. 

Mazukiewicz v. Hanover Nat'l Bank 240 N. Y. 317

Negotiable Instruments Law § 185 

Notice of dishonor to the indorsers may be dispensed with when (1) the indorser was an accommodated party; or (2) the indorser was the one to whom the instrument was to be presented for payment; or (3) the drawee was a fictitious person; or (4) the drawee had no contractual capacity, and this was known to the indorser when he indorsed; or (5) such notice cannot be given after the exercise of reasonable diligence. 

Negotiable Instruments Law § 140, 183, 186.

Notice of dishonor may be waived, either before or after dishonor, by making payment or by promising to pay, despite a failure to receive due notice. Consideration is not needed to support the waiver. 

Kraut v. Nordlinger 215 N¸Y.S. 496, affd. 243 N.Y. 649

Negotiable Instrument Law § 180 Commonwealth Fuel Co. v. Powpit Co. 212 A. D. 553 

Successive accommodation indorsers are not co-sureties so as to be entitled to contribution among themselves, unless they agree to be bound jointly and not severally. 

A clear, unequivocal promise to pay waives the indorser's right to refuse to pay because of failure to receive notice. A request by the indorser that the holder extend time of payment is a waiver. 

Even though the indorsers may be able to successfully resist any action on the note because of failure to give him notice, or because the action is barred by the Statute of Limitations, property pledged by the indorser to insure payment is not released. 

Reynolds v. Doyle 125 Misc. 778, 211 N.Y.S. 509 

Discharge of a Negotiable Instrument 

There are three ways of discharging a negotiable instrument: (1) A negotiable instrument is discharged if it is paid off to the real holder by one primarily liable, or cancelled by the holder, or if the principal debtor becomes its owner at or after maturity. If the principal debtor pays for and receives it before maturity and resells it to a holder in due course, the latter can recover against the maker, *Under the Negotiable Instrument Law § 214, when drawer and drawee are the same person, the holder may treat the instrument either as a bill of exchange or a promissory note.

acceptor, drawer and indorsers. Until the date of maturity the bill is alive.

Negotiable Instruments Law § 200. 

A payment to the holder of a promissory note by an indorser, not as agent for the maker, but simply in discharge of his own obligation as an indorser, where the note was executed by the maker for value does not inure to the benefit of the latter. In an action upon the note, the maker is liable for the whole amount. To the extent of the money paid, the indorser becomes equitably entitled to be substituted to the rights and remedies of the holder, and becomes, pro tanto, the beneficial owner of the debt; so that the maker's obligation to pay the note in full, at first due to the holder solely in his own right, becomes after the first payment by the indorser still wholly due to the holders, but partly in his own right and partly as trustee for the indorser. 

Seventh Nat'l Bank v. Cromwell 131 Misc. 276, 226 N. Y. 721. (2) Alterations.—When there is an alteration the instrument and all the parties to it at the time of the alteration are discharged. It differs in nature from a cancellation only in that a cancellation must have been effected intentionally by the holder. To get the effect of an alteration so as to discharge the instrument, the alteration may have been made even by a stranger, and that even against the holder's will. But should the instrument be sold to a holder in due course, who knows nothing of the alteration, he is protected only as to the terms of the instrument before the alteration. 

The alteration, to be effective, must be a material one. This includes a change in the date; sum payable, either principal or interest; time of payment; place of payment; number or relation of parties; or the currency in which the instrument is payable. 

Negotiable Instruments Law §§ 204, 205, 206. 

At common law a material alteration of a negotiable instrument voided the instrument even in the hands of a holder in due course. (3) A holder may at any time renounce his rights against any party to the instrument. The renunciation must be in writing when no consideration passes for such renunciation or where the instrument is not delivered up to the person primarily liable thereon. An absolute renunciation by the holder of his rights against the principal debtor at or after maturity, discharges the instrument and all the parties thereto. The holder in due course is not affected. 

Negotiable Instruments Law § 203 

Bank of U. S. v. Manheim 264 N. Y. 45.

When the instrument is discharged all parties, primary and secondary, are no longer liable. But it is possible that those secondarily liable may be discharged, even though the instrument itself may not be. This we have already seen in the case where the holder scratched out the signature of an indorser. This discharged the one whose name was scratched out and those who indorsed after that one. In fact, a discharge of a prior party, in any manner,

or a tender by him discharges the subsequent indorsers. Thus a release by the maker of the holder and the first indorser releases the second indorser, under the Negotiable Instruments law. Yet under 

Debtor and Creditor Law § 234, a later statute, co-obligor A is not released if the obligee in writing as part of the same transaction, expressly reserves his rights against A when releasing co-obligor B. 

Therefore it has been held that if the first indorser and maker are released and then a written reservation executed holding the second indorser, the latter remains obligated. Should he pay the holder he can recover from the maker and first indorser despite the release.

Negotiable Instruments Law § 201 

Brill v. Brandt 176 Misc 580 affd. 289 N. Y. 581.

If B, C, D and E are indorsers and E has indorsed it back to B, all those who are indorsers subsequent to B are not liable to him. Having been a prior indorser, he is liable to them. To allow him to sue on his later indorsement would only create a circuity of actions. 

Where the holder releases the principal debtor, or the holder obligates himself by a binding contract to extend the time of payment, all those secondarily liable are released unless the holder has expressly reserved his rights against them. 

Assume there are five indorsers, A, B, C, D and E. The first, A, is liable to the other four. The second only to the last three, and so on down the line. Since payment by an indorser does not discharge the instrument, but only allows him to get reimbursement, a payment by an indorser does not relieve prior indorsers. If D paid, A, B and Cremain liable. And if the holder sues B, B must pay the holder, even though the holder has been paid by D. The holder must, however, hold the proceeds he receives from B in trust for D. 

B, of course, can collect from A, and so on up the line. Checks

A check is in reality only a negotiable bill of exchange which is drawn on a bank and payable on demand. It is not a transfer or delivery of that fund until presented at the bank and paid, because until payment the fund still remains subject to the control and order of the drawer.

Negotiable Instruments Law § 321 

In re Gibbons' Estate 234 A. D. 153.

A drawer of a check is different from a drawer of a bill of exchange. The former is regarded as the principal debtor. 

A drawer undertakes that there shall be paid by the drawee, to the holder of the check, the sum of money mentioned, at the place named, when the check is presented. Ordinarily where a check is delivered at the same place where the bank is located, it must, in the absence of special circumstances, be presented during the business hours of the next regular business day after it is received. If the holder fails to present it within that time, the loss resulting from neglect to so present the check falls upon the holder. Thus if while

holder holds the check the drawee becomes insolvent, or the money deposited with the drawee to meet the check depreciates, the drawer is discharged. Where the item is received by mail by a solvent drawee or payor bank, it is deemed paid when the amount is finally charged to the account of the maker or drawer. One who becomes a holder of a check, which has been negotiated for an unreasonable length of time after its issue, is not deemed to be a holder in due course.

Negotiable Instruments Law §§ 322, 350f 

Weinberg v. Goldstein 226 A. D. 479, 235 N. Y. S. 529.

What is a reasonable time depends upon usage. The next day is usually the customary time for presentation. It is worthy of note that, in cases of bills, further negotiation extends the time of presentment. But such is not the rule in the case of checks.. 

In the absence of some agreement between the drawee and the payee, by which the payee may be induced to delay presentation, an interval of nine months is an unreasonable delay as a matter of law. 

Ferrari v. First Nat'l Bank 246 N.Y. 382

It has been held that a deposit by the payee in his own bank for collection on the day following receipt of the instrument and presentation by the collecting bank on the day thereafter, is a sufficiently prompt demand. 

Jaysee Holding v. Block 138 Misc. 294, 245 N. Y. S. 351.

If a depositor dies and the bank does not know of the death, the bank is not liable if it pays the amount of the check. But if it knew of the death, it is liable if the obligation represented by the check was not owing. 

The drawee bank unless subject to special engagement, is bound to honor the depositor's signature, and it may do so without liability even where the signature is not written exactly as the specimen signature in the bank's possession, if the bank has not been put on notice that the check is of questionable validity. A notice to à drawee bank by one claiming to be an assignee of the depositor, does not justify a bank in refusing to honor the depositor's order on his check. The assignee in order to protect himself should file the assignment itself, bearing the signature of the depositor, with the bank. 

Gibraltar R. Co v. Mt. Vernon Trust Co. 276 N. Y. 353.

A wrongful dishonor of a depositor's check by his bank makes the bank liable for the damages to the credit of the depositor. The payee of the check, however, cannot maintain an action against the bank even though the maker has on deposit sufficient funds to pay the check, for the reason that the payee is merely a stranger to the bank. 

Katz v. Pacific Bank, 212 A. D. 601, 209 N. Y. S. 497.

If a payee violates an agreement not to present a check for payment until a certain date, the maker may rescind the transaction and stop payment. 

Stadtmauer v. Lukin 126 Misc. 318, 213 N.Y.S. 33

Collection of Checks 

A bank with whom a check is deposited for collection is the agent of the depositor. Until payment by the drawee title remains in the depositor and the latter can by notice to the drawee revoke the authority of the collecting bank to collect.* 

Wolf v. T. G. & T. Co. 251 A. D. 354 affd 277 N. Y. 626.

Forgery of Payee's Name 

Where the endorsement of a payee is forged and the drawee bank pays out of the drawer's account, the bank must make good to the depositor for it has not paid on the drawer's genuine order. The liability is dependent upon the depositor's giving notice of the forgery within two years after the return of the voucher. The maker's rights are not affected by a certification of the check. Where a person has been induced by fraud to draw a check to the order of an' existing person whose name and identity have been fraudently assumed by an imposter and to deliver the check to the imposter, an endorsement by the imposter is not a forgery and the drawee bank may pay upon such endorsement. The bank has carried out the maker's intent to pay to the person with whom dealings were had by the drawer even though that person was designated by a name he did not bear. Such intent is deemed to exist when by prior dealings the imposter has caused the belief that he is the intended payee. 

Consequently if X is the owner of a lot being purchased by B and a check is drawn to the order of X in payment, should the imposter walk in at the closing claiming to be X, receive the check and endorse X's name and receive payment from the drawee, the latter would be liable for here we have a forgery. If, however, this imposter had on a former occasion convinced B that he was X the owner and had thereafter received the check, there would be no forgery so as to throw liability upon the drawee. The impostor in the latter instance was the intended recipient of the check. 

Negotiable Instruments Law § 43 

Cohen v. Lincoln Savings Bank 275 N.Y. 399.

When an instrument is payable to the order of a fictitious person and the maker is induced to believe that he is describing an existing person, no other person can acquire any right or title to the instrument.

Certification of Checks 

Though checks cannot be accepted, something similar is effected by certification. By a certification the drawee bank represents that the signature of the drawer is genuine; that it has funds of the drawer in its possession sufficient to meet the check, and it engages not to permit a withdrawal from the funds to the prejudice of any bona fide holder of the check. If it does not certify, it is in no way *See infra, the subject of "Trusts" on the question whether moneys collected constitute a trust fund.

responsible to the holder for such refusal. By certification the bank does not guarantee the body of the check. The certification must be in writing and signed by the drawee. On certification procured by the holder, the drawer and those indorsers prior to the certification are discharged. But note that if the drawer himself had his bank certify the check, he remains liable as well as the bank. 

Negotiable Instruments Law § 324. 

A banker or trust company which has certified a check, note or other instrument for the payment of money at the request of the drawer, payee or holder cannot, however, be required to refuse payment at the request of any party thereto. 

Negotiable Instruments Law § 325 

The refusal on the part of the drawee bank to certify the check at the request of the holder is not tantamount to a dishonor, which would render presentment for payment unnecessary. The bank owes no duty to certify any checks; and it is no part of the contract between the maker of the check and the payee. A bank is obligated to honor and pay checks when properly presented if the drawer has sufficient funds in the bank's possession. When a holder of a check requests certification instead of payment, he enters into a new contract with the bank, and one which was not within the contemplation of the drawer upon such certification. 

Wachtel v. Rosen 249 N. Y. 386.

If a check was in fact certified by mistake and if plaintiff's position was not in fact changed on the faith of the certification, the bank has an equitable defense. 

Metropolitan Life Insurance Co. v. Bank of U. S. 259 N. Y. 365. 

Nor does the negligence of the bank, in certifying a check at a time when the depositor did not have on deposit a sufficient sum of money for payment, prevent the bank from recovering from the maker an overdraft, for as between the bank and depositor an overdraft is a loan for which the depositor is liable to the bank. 

T. G. & T. Co. v. Emandee 136 Misc. 328, 240 N. Y. S. 36.

Where a holder in due course presents a certified check to the bank on which the depositor's signature has been forged, and the bank pays, the bank cannot get back its money from the holder in due course, and it must make good to the depositor. This protection is not extended to a holder whose competent agent dishonestly procured an acceptance while suspecting the forgery. 

Banca Commerciale Italiana v. Clarkson 274 N. Y. 69.

Duty of Depositor After Forgery 

Suppose a check is raised, or the maker's signature forged, and the bank, not noticing it, pays out the amount according to the tenor of the check. The depositor does not notice the fact that too much of his money has been paid out, until more than one year has passed, and then tells the bank. The bank is not liable; its liability lasted to the end of the year after the return of the vouchers, and

when a year went by and the depositor failed to inform the bank, its liability ceased. This one-year rule applies only to cases where the maker's signature has been forged or where the check has been raised. It does not apply to a case where an indorser's signature has been forged. In the latter case the period of limitations is two years after the return to the depositor of the vouchers of payment. 

Negotiable Instruments Law § 326 

Kleinman v. Chase Nat'l Bank 124 Misc. 173, 207 N. Y. S. 191

But it should be noted that, even if a year had not gone by, and the same kind of forgery had been successful several times, and nothing was said because the depositor had been negligent in not learning of the forgery, the depositor could get back from the bank only the loss caused by the first forgery.

A depositor upon the return of his vouchers from the bank, must in order not to be considered negligent (1) compare the returned vouchers (2) the balance in the bank's statement, with his own record or check stubs. 

Stumpp v. Bank of New York 212 A.D. 608, 209 N.Y. 396

Screenland Magazine v. Nat'l. City Bank, 181 Misc. 454 

This duty calls for no more than the exercise of ordinary care. 

The depositor may intrust the examination of the account and vouchers to a competent employee and thus discharge his duty to the bank. 

Takenaka v. Bankers' Trust Co. 132 Misc. 322 affd. 225 A. D. 860.

The depositor is under no duty to ascertain whether the indorsements are genuine or forgeries. 

Fitzgibbons Boiler Co. v. Nat'l City Bank 287 N. Y. 326.

If the negligence of the depositor enables one to easily alter the check and so causes the bank to pay on a forged order, the depositor is estopped from disputing the bank's authority to pay. If the bank and the depositor were both negligent, the bank must make good to the depositor any payment on the forged order. 

Gutfreund v. East River Nat'l Bank 251 N. Y. 58.

When Negotiable Documents Are Considered Payment 

If a debtor gives his creditor a check, the debt is not extinguished until the drawee pays, unless there is a special agreement or circumstance which implies that the giving of the check was complete payment. Even though the creditor give a paid receipt for the debt when he receives the check, this in itself does not evidence an intent on the part of the creditor to take the check in absolute payment. And this is true even though the check is certified by the drawee at the debtor's request. Should the drawee bank refuse to pay, the creditor may elect to bring an action on the check or on the original debt. Where the check is transferred or indorsed over to a third party, there is an election by the creditor to release the debtor on the original debt, and the debtor's liability exists only upon the check. 

Bernstein v. Fuerth 132 Misc, 343, 229 N. Y. S. 791.

Where the debtor gives the creditor an uncertified check, and he has funds in the bank at the time the check is given, if the creditor is guilty of laches in the presentation of the check, and in the meantime the drawee bank becomes insolvent, the debt is discharged to the extent of the loss. 

Williams v. Brown 53 A. D. 486, 65 N. Y. S. 1049.

Similar rules apply to notes. Unless a note is paid at maturity there is no payment of the debt represented by the note, in the absence of a special agreement to the contrary. Where, however, the note of a third party is given by a debtor to the creditor, the presumption is that it was taken in absolute payment of the debt, provided the debt was contracted contemporaneously with the giving of the note. If the note of a third party is given for a precedent debt, there is no such presumption, and the note must be paid before the debt is cancelled. 

Bank of Taiwan v. Schild 236 A.D. 128, 258 N.Y.S. 331 

Dibble v Richardson 171 N. Y. 131

CARRIERS What Is a Common Carrier? 

COMMON CARRIER is one who indicates to the public that he will for a specified compensation, transport property from one place to another, for all persons that may see fit to employ him, up to the capacity of his facilities. Some examples of common carriers are: express companies, omnibuses, hackmen, railroad companies, ferries, porters, truckmen, wagoners, cartmen and parties who undertake to carry goods for hire as a common employment. 

Re Motor Haulage Co. v. Maltbie 293 N. Y. 355

Common carriers never hold themselves out as such for other common carriers. They may not unreasonably discriminate between its shippers. 

Root v. L. I. R. R. Co. 114 N. Y. 300.

Railroad carriers are under a duty to furnish cars promptly on demand, to transport goods when this can be done with reasonable diligence and without unfair discrimination. 

Walrath v. Amer. Ry. Exp. Co. 217 A.D. 83, 216 N.Y.S. 545

Common carriers may refuse to carry goods if they are not of the kind carried by this carrier; or they are not tendered at the proper time and place as fixed by the carrier; or they are not safely packed; or the facilities are insufficient because of some unusual circumstance which exhausts the carrier's facilities. 

Liability of a Carrier in the Transportation of Goods 

Common carriers are insurers of goods upon their receipt for immediate transportation, so that if there is an accidental loss the carrier is liable. This rule does not apply where live animals and birds are shipped. The common carrier is not liable for injuries caused to such, arising from their nature and propensities, and which could not be prevented by foresight and care. 

Clay v. N.Y.C.R. Co. 224 A. D. 508, 231 N.Y. S. 424.

It is the obligation of the carrier to use reasonable effort and due diligence to carry and deliver the goods within a reasonable time from the date of receipt, and it is liable for failure to do so, except for certain specified causes. The breach occurs upon the expiration of a reasonable time from the delivery to the carrier. 

Geismer v. L. S. & H. R. Co. 102 N.Y. 563 

Aristo Hosiery Co. v. Atlantic Coast Line Co. 129 Misc. 305.

The liability of the carrier for not delivering within a reasonable time is limited to such damage as may reasonably be presumed to have entered into the contemplation of the parties, or which has resulted from the delay after the carrier was informed of a special 70

CARRIERS 

71 circumstance, e.g., the merchandise was to be used for the presentation of a particular theatrical performance on a stated day. 

Chapman v. Fargo 223 N. Y. 32, 36 

Rives v. Amer. Ry. Exp. 227 A. D. 375, 237 N. Y. S. 429.

The publication of a timetable imposes upon the carrier the obligation to exercise reasonable care and diligence to make the movements of trains correspond thereto, but the obligation is not absolute. If obstructions, e.g., snow, are to be removed, all available means for removal should be used.* 

Cormack v. N. Y. N. H. & H. R. R. 196 N. Y. 442.

The certain specified causes which will exempt a carrier from liability for delay or for any damage to the goods are these: (1) An Act of God.-The damage in such a case must have been caused without the intervention of any human agency. If a district is overswept by a flood and the goods deteriorate because the carrier fails to keep them ventilated during the period of delay, the loss falls on the carrier. The flood is an act of God but the negligence during the delay contributed to the damage. Note that if because of a snowstorm lights are not lit by the city employees, and because of this there is an accident, it would not be an act of God. 

There was human intervention even though not the fault of the carrier's agents; and even though an act of God caused human intervention, the carrier is liable. If there is a special contract to deliver at a certain time, inevitable accident or an act of God is not a defense. (2) Acts of a nation (or its subjects) at war with this country. (3) Inherent nature of the goods. (4) Public authority, e.g., the goods are removed by valid legal process, and the bill of lading surrendered or impounded by the court.

General Cigar Co. v. Reading Co. 205 A. D. 322. 

When a common carrier furnishes a bill of lading, this bill is a receipt, and prima facie is a contract to carry safely and deliver. 

Will v. Canadian Nat'l. Ry. Co., 216 A. D. 239, 214 Ñ. Y. S. 513

The carrier may by inserting in the bill of lading the words: "shipper's weight, load and count," or other words of like purport, indicate that the goods were loaded by the shipper and the description of them made by him; and if such statement be true and the shipment is in carload lots, the carrier is not liable for damages caused by improper loading or misdescription. 

Personal Property Law § 209 

Robinson v. N. Y. Central R. 245 A. D. 378 affd. 270 N. Y. 659. 

Erroneous Delivery by Carrier

The general rule is clear that any delivery of property by common carrier thereof to a person other than the one designated by the owner of the property to be the recipient of the property, con- This rule applies to the transportation of goods and passengers.

stitutes a conversion, irrespective of the question of negligence or the exercise of due care. 

M. &T. Trust Co. v. Export Corp. 143 Misc. 1 affd. 262 N. Y. 92.

A shipment of goods sent C.O.D. contemplates that the carrier will act as bailee and as agent to collect the amount specified, in cash. A carrier accepts a check at its peril. Should the check be dishonored, the carrier must pay the loss caused the shipper. 

Mogul v. Lavine 247 N. Y. 20

If a shipper orders the carrier not to deliver to the consignee, and gives the carrier ample notice, the carrier is negligent in delivering the goods to the consignee, and the shipper can recover. 

Bond v. American Ry. Exp. Co. 124 Misc. 619, 208 N. Y. S. 643.

If a railroad is forced to deliver up a shipper'; goods to a sheriff, it must notify the owner at once if it desires to be held free from liability.

Where a freight agent who issued bills of lading against goods given to the railroad conspires with his dishonest friend to get up a bill and drafts falsely, showing that merchandise has been delivered to the railroad company, and these drafts are attached and delivered to a bona fide purchaser for value without notice, the railroad company is liable to the bona fide purchaser. This is the New 

York rule and the Federal rule. 

Josephy v. Panhandle & S. F. Ry. 235 N. Y. 306.

Connecting Carriers 

A common carrier receiving goods for shipment inter-state is liable for loss caused by it or any connecting carrier. The initial carrier cannot exempt itself from liability. 

U. S. Code, Title 49 § 20 sub. 11. 

If a connecting carrier refuses to take the goods, the first carrier becomes a bailee from the time of the tender. If there is no tender, the first carrier remains liable as a carrier. 

Contracts Exempting Carriers from Liability for Goods 

Contracts which purport to totally exempt carriers from liability for negligence are void as against public policy. A carrier may limit its liability for damages caused even by its own negligence, if a lower rate of transportation upon an agreed valuation is afforded the shipper upon condition that recovery is to be limited to such valuation, or where the limitation is the consideration for other benefits to the shipper. 

F. A. Strauss v. Canadian Pac. Ry. 254 N. Y. 407 

Kilthau v. International M. Marine Co. 245 N. Y. 361.

In order that the company should be limited in its liability, the instrument on which its liability is mentioned must be of such a nature as to represent a contract. So an oral agreement, which is contradicted by a bill of lading given later by the company without the shipper's assent, would be binding despite the bill of lading. 

But an express receipt, or a bill of lading given without any previ-

CARRIERS 

73 ous agreement, is binding.* When a person signs a statement for a carrier declaring the value of the goods shipped on his ticket, and which valuation determines the rate, the shipper is bound by the terms of the statement, even though he never read the statement when he signed it. 

Bostwick v. B. & O. Ry, Co. 45 N Y. 712 

Minturn v N. Y. Cent. R. R. Co. 220 A. D. 222, 220 N. Y. S. 789.

When a shipper nonfraudently misstates the contents of a package which he ships by freight, and because of his misstatement a lower rate is charged, it does not excuse the carrier for loss of the goods in transit.

The Carrier as Bailee of Goods. 

After notification to the consignee of the arrival of the goods and the passing of a reasonable time (a question of fact), the carrier becomes a bailee and is subject to the rules of bailment. The time of notification counts from the time of mailing the notice to the consignee. If the consignee is not notified because his whereabouts are unknown, the company after such reasonable time is a bailee. 

Rotundo v. Erie R. R. Co. 198 N. Y. 688 

Porter v. Penn. R. R. Co. 217 A. D. 49, 215 N. Y. S. 727.

If the consignee is known to the carrier, and the carrier sells the goods without notifying the consignee of their arrival, it is a con version.

If a transportation company has unclaimed freight or baggage (not live stock or perishable goods) in its possession for 60 days, it may, at its own option, deliver the same to any person engaged in the warehouse business in the State of New York. Upon taking the receipt the carrier is discharged from its liability. 

If the carrier holds the goods for a year, it may sell the goods at public auction after four weeks from the first publication of the notice of sale.

Railroad Law § 68 

Erie R. R. Co. v. Kieser 216 A. D. 500, 215 N. Y. S. 576.

If the transportation was free, the carrier is not an insurer during transportation, but a bailee. 

As to articles carried by a passenger in the same car with him, the carrier is only a bailee. 

Posner v. N. Y. Central 154 Misc. 591, 277 N.Y.S. 671.

A Carrier's Liability to Passengers 

A carrier must take reasonable care that a passenger shall have safe passage to the train, protecting him from any unnecessary danger or from a danger of which the railroad company is or ought to be aware. This includes protection against threatening danger from fellow passengers. If the common carrier actually takes a passenger aboard, it is obligated to use care, fully commensurate with As to whether "checks" for parcels or parking include contract terms, see infra, pp. 113, 114.

1 the situation and all the circumstances presented, in order to protect the passenger. If the passenger is a small hild, that must be taken into consideration, and more care should be taken in watching him than in the case of an adult.

Kearns v. B. & Q. T. Co. 254 A.D. 779 

White v. N. Y. Cent. R. Co. 228 A.D. 50, 239 N.Y.S. 90 

Longacre v. Yonkers R. Co. 236 N.Y. 119

Crawford v. M.M.T. Co. 254 A.D. 582 

Sannucci v. N. Y. Cent. R. Co. 223 A. D. 517, 228 N. Y. S. 505.

If a carrier is negligent and a passenger is therefore hurt, the carrier is, of course, liable. But if a passenger when alighting, slipped on something placed on a step by a person for whom the carrier was in no way responsible, the latter is not negligent, unless it had actual or constructive knowledge of the presence of the foreign substance and an opportunity to remove it. Where a passenger on a subway train was pushed in or out of the train by a passenger behind her when the doors were opened at a station and her foot sank in a space between the car and the platform so that the passengers in the rear stepped over her because there was no guard on the car or platform to regulate the crowd, it was held that this was negligence on the part of the carrier and the plaintiff recovered. 

Nelson v. Murray 255 A. D. 884, 7 N.Y.S. (2nd) 969 

Fidelman v. N. Y. Rapid Transit Corp. 246 N.Y. 564 

Moll v. Niagara Gorge R. Co. 238 A. D. 528, 264 N. Y. S. 761

Negligence may also consist of a failure to use the best appliances.
