But if the carrier in selecting its appliances had done everything reasonable to get the best, and they turned out to be bad, the carrier is not liable for injury because of the defect. It is the absolute duty of a railroad to furnish safe locomotive boilers. The exercise of ordinary care in providing a boiler is not sufficient. 

Luce v. N. Y. C. etc. Co. 213 A. D. 374 affd. 242 N. Y. 519.

If an employee injures a passenger even maliciously, the carrier is liable.* This rule differs from the ordinary rule of master and servant, for the company has the affirmative duty of carrying passengers safely, and it is responsible for the way the employees execute that duty. Only if the passenger threatened the servant with acts of personal violence would the carrier not be liable. Thus where a conductor negligently assisted a passenger in alighting, the company was held liable, though it was no part of the conductor's duty to help people off. 

Gillespie v. Brooklyn Heights R. R. Co. 178 N. Y. 347 *Where an employee of a carrier assaults a passenger, the action may be maintained in contract as one for breach of contract of carriage or in tort. For the purpose of the Statute of Limitations it does not matter whether the form of the action is ex contractu or ex delicto. The liability is referable to the question of the carrier's negligence and the three year Statute applies. Barad v. N. Y. Rapid 

Tr. Co., 162 Misc. 458, 295 N.Y.S. 901; Loehr v. East Side Omnibus Co. 259 

A. D. 200; affd. 287 N. Y. 670.

As a general rule there can be no recovery for mental suffering resulting from a breach of contract. An insulted or publicly ejected passenger or hotel guest may however, recover, Jacobs v. Harmeling 180 Misc. 1070.

CARRIERS 

75 If the plaintiff was not a passenger at the time of the injury, there can be no recovery unless the employee rausing the injury was acting within the scope of his employment. Thus, where a ticketseller sells tickets to X, and later has X arrested for passing counterfeit money of which X is innocent, the company is not liable, for the ticketseller was not dealing within his scope with a passenger, but rather as a private citizen. If he had held X just before selling him a ticket, or immediately on selling the ticket and as part of the same act, the company would have been liable, as the agent would have then been acting within the scope of his employment. 

An invitee of a conductor permitted to ride without the carrier's authority, cannot recover for injuries received through the carrier's negligence, since he was not a passenger.

Liability of Carriers to Free Passengers 

A carrier can contract to exempt itself from liability to passengers in return for a lower rate, provided the passenger had the option to pay full rate without giving any exemption. Where one is carried gratuitously, the stipulation contained in the pass, exempting the carrier from liability in case of injury through negligence, has been held valid. The degree of negligence is then immaterial. 

Montalbano v. N.Y.C.R.R.Co. 267 A.D. 617 Conklin v. Canadian-Colonial Airways 266 N. Y. 244 

If a person traveling on a free pass exempts the carrier from liability for negligence, this does not exempt a joint tort-feasor. The release is interpreted as speaking of the future, as regards the carrier alone. This agreement, however, accrues to the benefit of all other companies recognizing the pass and whose facilities the plaintiff uses during the trip gratuitously, as part of the benefits of the free pass. 

Wilder v Penn. R. R. 245 N. Y. 36.

Liability for Freight Charges 

The consignor is ordinarily liable for freight charges. The fact that the bill of lading stipulates that the consignee is to pay, imposes no obligation on the carrier to insist on payment before delivery to the consignee. The carrier may neglect to collect from the consignee, and collect from the consignor. But the consignee may become liable for such charges by his own act. He becomes liable because of presumptive ownership, acceptance of the goods and the services rendered and the benefits conferred by the carrier for freight charges.

The consignee is not liable for transportation charges, under the Interstate Commerce Act, if the consignee is an agent only and has no beneficial title in the property, and he notifies the carrier of this in writing prior to the delivery of the property. 

Erie R.R.Co. v. Rosenstein 249 N. Y. 241 

N. Y. C. R. R. Co. v. Warren 234 N. Y. 261.

Under the terms of the Sales Act, it is presumed that title to the

goods is in the consignee. Therefore, unless this presumption is overcome, the right to sue the carrier for any breach of contract of carriage is in the consignee. It has been held, however, that where the contract between the consignor and consignce fails to comply with the Statute of Frauds, the consignor may sue for breach of contract of carriage, since no actual transfer has taken place. The same is true if by mutual rescission, title has been revested in the seller. 

Fein v. Weir 129 A. D. 299, affd. 199 N. Y. 540 

Krulder v. Ellison 47 N. Y. 36; Rosenberg v. Buffum 234 N. Y. 338 

Telegraph Companies

Ordinarily individuals and corporations engaged in quasi-public business cannot contract to absolve themselves from liability for their own wilful misconduct or gross negligence. If a telegraph company because of gross negligence fails to transmit an unrepeated message and the plaintiff sender is damaged thereby, he may recover the full amount of the damage. If the action is not based upon gross negligence and the message is not repeated, the damages are limited to the amount received by the telegraph company for sending the same, provided the contract so stipulates. An inadvertent or mistaken act of incorrectly transmitting the message, or a delay due to atmospheric or other conditions to which telegraphic messages are subject, is not a case of gross negligence.. But an absolute failure to deliver a message, unexplained by the defendant, is prima facie gross negligence as a matter of law. 

Krivitsky v. Western Union 129 Misc. 431, 221 N. Y. S. 525.

There seems to be a limitation upon the above rule Where the terms of the telegram disclose the general nature of the transaction which is the subject of the message, the company is answerable for the natural consequences of its neglect in the matter. Where the message gives no hint of the nature of the transaction, liability is for nominal charges, or for the tolls if they have been prepaid. 

Kerr S. S. Co. v Radio Corp. of America 245 N. Y. 284.

A telephone corporation is required to provide instrumentalities and facilities as shall be adequate and in all respects just and reasonable. It is liable for damages caused by the negligence in the performance of its duties. But a claim that the defendant corporation failed to furnish adequate telephone service as a result of which the services of a physician could not be secured until too late to save the life of the plaintiff's intestate, states no cause of action. 

The company assumed no such indefinite risk on failure of service. 

Emery v. Rochester Telephone Co. 271 N. Y. 306.

The sendee of a telegram also has a cause of action against the telegraph company should it fail to deliver the message. Whether the theory is that of third party beneficiary or in "ort is not clear, but it has been decided that the terms of the contract between sender and company bind the sendee, except where because of the

CARRIERS 

77 nature of the transaction the sendee should not be bound. Thus though the sender would be bound by a contract provision giving him 60 days within which to file a claim if there is non-delivery, the sendee would not be bound by such provision. He would have a reasonable time not exceeding 60 days, after he should have discovered the failure to send.

MacDonald v. Western Union Tel. Co. 176 Misc. 427.

Presumption that New York Law Applies

IN THE absence of proof of what the law of a foreign jurisdiction is, it is presumed that the common law of New York applies, provided that that foreign jurisdiction has adopted the common law from England. Where the law of a foreign jurisdiction is not proven, and the law of that jurisdiction is not derived from the English common law, the law of New York, both common and statutory, applies. 

Gregg v. Gregg 133 Misc. 109, 231 N.Y.S. 221 

Gavin v. Matherbe 146 Misc. 51, affd. 264 N.Y. 403

Brassell v. John Hancock Mut. Life Ins. Co. 134 Misc. 274 

Smith v. Compania Litagrafica 127 Misc. 508 affd. 220 A. D. 782

When the Law of the Forum Applies When litigants air their dispute in a New York court, the laws of procedure of the New York court will be followed, for all remedial matters are decided according to the laws of the forum. What the actual rights of the parties are is goverened by the law of the state or country where the rights arose. What is a matter of procedure and what of substance is determined by the lex fori. 

Murray v. N. Y. O. & W. R. Co. 242 A. D. 374, 275 N. Y. S. 10.

Rules of evidence, burden or proof, Statute of Limitations, service of process, are all remedial points, and the law on these points is that of the state where the trial takes place. It is, of course, competent for parties to a contract to establish a shorter or different limitation to the right of action thereunder than that given by statute. The intent to do so must clearly appear from the contract itself.* 

Reilly v. Steinhart 217 N. Y. 549 

Franklin Sugar Refining Co. v. Lipowicz 247 N. Y. 465 

Russel v. Societe Anonyme des Etab. Aeroxon 268 N. Y. 173.

Domicile and Residence 

Frequently the domicile of a party is very important in order to determine the forum whose laws are to govern. A man has but one domicile, though he can have more than one residence. Residence means bodily presence as an inhabitant in a particular locality, but domicile requires bodily presence with intent to make it a fixed and permanent home. A person continues a "resident" of a state where he is domiciled even though temporarily absent from the state. 

Rawstorne v. Maguire 265 N. Y. 204. *Whether the Statute of Frauds involves the remedial side of a litigation or the substantive rights of the parties is a question not entirely settled in this state. 78

The essential requirements for a change of domicile are abandonment in fact of the former domicile and residence in a new locality with intent to remain there and make a new and sole domicile there. An existing domicile continues until a new one is acquired and the burden of proof rests upon the party who alleges a change. Thus where a person domiciled in Ireland left that country with intent to remain permanently in New York and died en route it was held that the domicile in Ireland continued since there had been no change. Even the bringing of the body to New York did not effect the change. 

In re Armstrong 167 Misc. 592, 4 N.Y.S. (2nd) 413 

In re Newcomb's Estate 192 N. Y. 238, 250.

A woman upon marriage takes the domicile of her husband by operation of law. If he changes his domicile, the wife's domicile follows his. Her physical presence would not be required to effect the change. If a wife is living apart from her husband without good cause his domicile is her domicile.* Where a husband refuses to take his wife with him or abandons her or casts her off or attempts to change the domicile in a way as would be utterly unreasonable because of the peril to her health, the matrimonial domicile remains where last established and he does not establish a new one by moving away. 

In re Daggett's Will 255 N. Y. 243

Matter of Wandmayer 178 Misc. 464 

Heller v. Heller 172 Misc. 875 affd. 285 N. Y. 582

The domicile of origin of a child born in wedlock is that of the father and when the father changes his domicile, it changes that of the infant. The domicile of a child born after the father's death is that of the mother. When a minor child becomes emancipated, he may establish his own domicile.

Cohen v. Delaware L. & W. R. Co. 150 Misc. 450. 269 N. Y. S. 667. 

Validity of Foreign Divorces 

If a divorce decree has been granted in one state where there has been a proper domicile of the plaintiff and there have been met the proper procedural requirements of due process, that judgment must be given full faith and credit in every other state. Due process exists where the summons is published and the defendant notified by mail or served personally in another state. Lack of appearance by the defendant does not affect the rule. Nor does it concern the state, that the plaintiff has abandoned the defendant in another jurisdiction. If neither party is a domiciliary of the state when the complaint is filed, the appearance by the defendant does not suffice to confer jurisdiction of the subject matter upon the court. 

Williams v. North Carolina, 63 Supreme Court Reporter 207 

Matter of Lindgreen 293 N. Y. 18 *It would seem that this statement may not be accurate in the instance where a wife leaves her husband to permanently reside in another jurisdiction and there commences an action for divorce. Apparently she may maintain the action as a domiciliary. See next caption.

Want of jurisdiction over the person or subject matter is open to inquiry notwithstanding the recital of jurisdictional facts in the decree of the sister state, according to our Court of Appeals, but the Supreme Court of the United States expressly left open the question as to the power of a state to question the finding of a sister state granting the decree, that there was a bona fide domicile established there. Furthermore, it gave no minimum standards of domicile in the divorce state sufficient to warrant the application of the full faith and credit clause. 

Matter of Holmes 29 N. Y. 261

Although the husband fails to appear in his wife's action for divorce in another state, his subsequent filing of a petition for a modification of the decree creates a binding adjudication upon him regardless of the question of the validity of that foreign divorce decree. It would follow that a later charge of adultery by him against his wife because of her subsequent marriage would be unfounded. 

Vernon v. Vernon 289 N. Y. 503; Matter of Bingham 265 A. D. 463.

Where the defendant in the divorce action remarries despite the fact that the foreign divorce is invalid, he accepts the benefits of the decree and he is then estopped from asserting its invalidity in order to assert rights incident to the continued existence of the original marital status e. g. election against the will of the plaintiff who had obtained the original decree. 

Matter of Bingham 265 A. D. 463; Carbulon v. Carbulon 293 N. Y. 375.

Where a wife left her husband in New York and obtained a divorce in Massachusetts without proper service it was held that despite the invalidity of the divorce she was barred from claiming as his widow upon his death. When a wife divorced by her husband in another State by proceedings which were invalid because no jurisdiction had been obtained of her, sued her husband in New York for separation, he was permitted to institute a counterclaim for divorce on the groud of her adultery. He was not estopped from going behind his own decree because in this case the Court was being asked to pronounce judgment directly upon the marital status, a relationship to which the State was a party, and the result he was seeking in the second action was no different from what the foreign decree had declared. It is only when personal advantage is being sought that one is estopped from disregarding a decree which he himself has obtained.* But where a husband is sued by his second wife for a separation he may defend on the ground that the divorce obtained by his first wife against him is invalid and that his marriage to the plaintiff is also invalid. 

Krause v. Krause 283 N. Y. 355; Cross v. Cross 177 Misc. 347 

Querze v. Querze 290 N. Y. 13; Stevens v. Stevens 273 N. Y. 157

Estoppel against a husband in favor of a second "wife" suing for separation, will not be invoked to bar him from asserting that a di *For a detailed discussion of the question of foreign divorces see Standish v. 

Standish 179 Misc. 564.

vorce obtained by him was invalid, where his second "wife" urged getting the invalid decree and was aware of all the circumstances. 

Amerling v. Amerling 180 Misc. 701.

If the plaintiff had gone to another State to commence a divorce proceeding on the grounds not recognized in New York and the defendent appeared in the action, New York will recognize the foreign decree because of the full faith and credit clause of the United States Constitution. But a divorce obtained in Mexico by a New 

York resident when neither party had at any time ever resided there was held invalid although the defendant appeared in the action. If a foreign court divorce is recognized, it is a matter of comity. 

Glaser v. Glaser 276 N. Y. 296; May v. May 251 A. D. 63.

Crimes A criminal prosecution must be brought in the county where the crime is committed. New York will not enforce the criminal laws of any other state, though it may hold the one charged with the crime for extradition. The accused will be surrendered only where he was actually present in the demanding state at the time the act complained of was committed. Constructive presence is not enough. 

People v. McLaughlin 247 N. Y. 238

Only the Federal government may surrender a fugitive who has fled from a foreign country to one of the states. Such act is a part of the "foreign relations" controlled by the Federal government. 

A state court has no jurisdiction over crimes committed exclusively against the United States, nor will it assume jurisdiction of questions which have been adjudicated in the Federal courts. 

Madole v. Gavin 222 A. D. 698, 225 N. Y. S. 407. 

A crime is committed where the last essential act is done. If S in 

State I sends his agent to New York to commit a crime, though the crime is begun in State 1, it is completed in New York, and S can be prosecuted in New York. It should be noted that in the case of homicide, the crime is committed where the fatal injury was inflicted, even though the death took place in another state. 

New York will not enforce the tax, revenue or penal laws of any other state. Suppose a railroad company was, according to the laws of Statel 1, to pay $10,000 if by its negligence it caused a death. If this railroad was sued for the $10,000 in New York, under the statute of State 1, there would be no recovery, for New York would not enforce another state's penal laws. 

In re Martin's 136 Misc. 51, affd. 229 A. D. 714 

Beadall v. Moore 199 A.D. 531, 191 N.Y.S. 826

The fact that alimony and counsel fees are demanded in an action in which merely the marital status is otherwise involved does not mean that a personal advantage is sought. Alimony is not a "private" claim arising from the marriage. That right comes from the statute. Querze v. Querze, 290 N. Y. 13.

There is a disagreement in the cases about estoppel against the husband sued by the second "wife," when he seeks to put in issue the validity of their marriage because of a questionable divorce obtained by her from her former husband, with his knowledge and assistance. See Heusner v. Heusner 181 Misc. 

1015 and Rosenberg v. Perles 182 Misc. 727.

Torts When one commits a tort against another's person, the latter gets a right to compensation, and each state, because of comity, will aid the injured to enforce his right. But no state will enforce such a right acquired under the laws of another state if to do so would violate its own public policy. 

Loucks v. Standard Oil Co. 224 N. Y. 99.

In personal injury actions, the lex loci (law of the jurisdiction where the injuries were inflicted) governs the rights of litigants, while the lex fori (law of the place where the trial takes place) controls matters relating to procedure. Where a gratuitous guest sues here for injuries received in an accident in Massachusetts, he must bear the burden of proving his own freedom from contributory negligence despite the fact that in Massachusetts the burden would be on the defendant to prove it. The rule governing proof of freedom from contributory negligence is a matter of procedure. 

This situation is not to be confused with one in which a foreign statute gives a cause of action to a plaintiff even though his negligence has contributed to the accident but in a lesser degree than that of the defendant. The rules of the foreign jurisdiction (where the accident occurred) govern the substantive rights of the parties since the cause of action exists only because of the laws of that jurisdiction. But the lex fori still controls on the question of procedure. 

Fitzpatrick v. Inter. Railway Co. 252 N. Y. 127 

Wright v. Palmison 237 A. D. 22, 260 N. Y. S. 812.

The court in its discretion may decline to exercise jurisdiction in an action between non-residents, including foreign corporations though doing business here, where the action is brought to recover for personal injuries caused by an act of negligence committed outside the State. The usual justification for the refusal to exercise its jurisdiction is that there is not any relation between the tort and the business being done in this State. 

Waisikoski v. Philadelphia & Reading R. R. 228 N. Y. 481. 

It seems that the New York courts will exercise jurisdiction in an action between non-residents where the negligent act took place in the state. 

Hunter v. Hosmer 142 Misc. 382, 254 N. Y. S. 635.

If the act that caused injury to a person is not a tort in the state where the act is done, the injured cannot bring action in New York, where the same act, if done in New York, would have been a tort and given rise to a cause of action. The converse is also true. 

So, if the injury in State 1 gave rise to a good cause of action in State 1, and the action is actually brought in State 2, the plaintiff as to remedy is governed by the law of the state where he brings the action, though as to the substantive part of the case he is governed by the laws of the place where the tort was committed. 

Mastruzzi v. Aloi 269 N. Y. 637.

Who obtains the right to sue for wrongful death is a matter of

substantive law. If a tort resulting in death is committed in a jurisdiction where the right to sue lies with the consort, ascendant and descendant of the deceased, an action brought in New York by the plaintiff, as administrator will not lie here. And if a wife brings suit against her husband based on a tort which arose in a state giving her no such cause of action, New York will dismiss the complaint. 

Coster v. Coster 289 N. Y. 438 

Sapone v. N. Y. C. & H. R. R. Co. 130 Misc. 755, 225 N. Y. S. 211.

Where a statute in another state limits amount that can be recovered for the death in a negligence case and X is killed there, the New York court would recognize the limitation were the suit brought here. Since the amount is mentioned in the statute, it is part of the substantive law on the point and not a part of the remedy. 

Loucks v. Standard Oil Co. 224 N. Y. 99.

Suppose the New Jersey law says that if an employer pays a sum to an injured employee under the Workmen's Compensation Act for an injury sustained in the course of his employment, the employer can get back any sum up to the amount paid, should the employee recover in another action for the same injury. The employer pays $1,000 in New Jersey. Later the employee recovers $800 in a 

New York court. The employer can get from the employee the $800 in a New York court, because the right is a New Jersey right, and New York courts of equity will prevent the double recovery and enforce the substantive rights under rules of another state. 

Hartford Acc. & Ind. Co. v. Chartrand 239 N. Y. 36.

Contracts 

All matters bearing on (1) validity, (2) interpretation, (3) execution of a contract, including (4) the capacity of a party to act are controlled by the law of the place where the contract is made, unless a contrary intention plainly appears. 

Vanderhost v. Kittredge 229 A. D. 126, 241 N.Y.S. 302 

Union National Bank v. Chapman 169 N. Y. 538, 543

A contract is made where the acceptance occurs. If an offer is mailed from State 1 to the offeree in New York, and the acceptance is mailed from New York, the contract is made in New York. 

Suppose a valid contract is made in New York between H and Mrs. K., a married woman. The action is brought in State 2, where a contract with a married woman is invalid. State 2 would allow recovery, for the question involves rights and not remedies. Since it is a question of validity, the law of the place where the contract was made governs unless a contrary intent is shown. 

Franklin Sugar Refining Co. v. Lipowicz 247 N. Y. 465.

All matters connected with the performance of a contract are regulated by the law of the place where the contract, by its terms, is to be performed. In one case A gave B a check for a gambling debt in Florida drawn on a New York bank and payable in New

York. B sued upon the check, and it was held, that although it was to be presumed that the Florida law was the same as the common law, which held a gambling contract valid, yet the plaintiff could not recover, as the check was an executory contract, by its terms to be performed in New York, and the New York law holding a gambling contract illegal would be followed. If the plaintiff had sued on the contract made in Florida rather than on the check, it might have been presumed that the gambling debt was valid in Florida, and it could then be enforced in New York. 

Beadall v. Moore 199 A. D. 531

Holzer v. Deutscher Gesellschaft 277 N. Y. 474 

Thuma v. Wolf 132 Misc. 56, 228 N. Y. S. 658

If no place of performance is mentioned in the contract, a presumption arises that the parties intend that it should be performed where it was made. 

Vanderhorst v. Kittredge 229 A. D. 126, 241 N. Y. S. 302. 

Where a contract is made in another state, to be performed in New York, the parties are presumed to know the law of New York State, even though they may be citizens of a foreign jurisdiction. 

De Witt v. Brisbane 16 N. Y. 509, 514.

Where the place of performance is in different states or countries, the lex loci contractus (the law of the place where the contract is made) controls.

Smith v. Companio Litagrafica 127 Misc. 508 affd. 220 A. D. 782. 

The validity of an assignment is determined by the law of the place where it is mailed to the assignee. 

Jackson v. Talmadge 216 A. D. 100 affd. 246 N. Y. 133.

Despite the above rules, a provision of law in a jurisdiction whose laws ordinarily control, will not be applied in New York against New York citizens if the application of such provision would furnish no defense to the New York citizen as against the fraud or breach of the other party. A short statute of limitations may accomplish such result. Under our law a purchaser is given a reasonable time within which to make a complaint of breach of warranty before he may be held to have waived the breach. Where the application of the foreign statute would deprive a New York citizen from having such reasonable time, the New York rule will be applied. 

Gutkind v. George Lueders & Co. 267 N. Y. 320.

Marriage Contracts 

The validity of a marriage depends on the laws of the jurisdiction where the marriage took place, except where the marriage is incestuous or polygamous or otherwise contrary to our public policy. If a citizen of a foreign country, in which polygamy is legal would bring his half dozen wives to New York, the marriage of the six spouses to the one spouse would not be considered legal or valid by us. There is no comity where public policy is involved. 

Incuria v. Incuria 155 Misc. 755. 280 N. Y. S. 716.

Bills and Notes 

A note is regarded as made where it is delivered, and if it is mailed, it is considered made where it is mailed. Ordinarily, the law of the place where the instrument is made governs. Thus, where a note is made outside New York, bearing a rate of interest lawful in that state but unlawful in New York, the New York courts would hold the instrument valid. 

Hennenlotter v. De Orvananos, 114 Misc. 333, 186 N. Y. S. 488 

Hibernia Nat'l. Bank v. Lacombe, 84 N. Y. 367.

The nature of the instrument e.g., whether it is or is not a bearer instrument will be determined by the laws of the state where the instrument had its inception. 

Swift v. Bankers Trust Co. 280 N. Y. 135.

The obligations of the drawer are (a) that the instrument will be accepted and paid on due presentment and (b) if dishonored and the necessary proceedings taken, he will pay. Matters connected with presentment, acceptance and payment are regulated by the laws of that place. The engagement to pay upon dishonor contemplates performance at his place. Secondly as to days of grace, manner of making protest, and person to whom protest is to be made, the law of the drawee's place controls. The necessity of making a demand and protest are incidents of the drawer's original contract and are governed by the law of the place where the bill is drawn. 

Amsinck v. Rogers 189 N. Y. 252.

The indorsement of a negotiable instrument is an independent contract and is governed by the law of the place where it is created. 

Thus a forged instrument and delivery in a foreign country would give good title to an endorsee if its law so provided. 

Heidelberg v. Heidelberg 171 A. D. 106, 155 N.Y.S. 933 

Real Property

The law governing personal property is that of the state of domicile of the owner and not where the property is located. As to realty the law of the place where the land is situated governs. Thus a wife's right to dower must be determined by the laws of the state where the realty is situated. 

Lowe v. Plainfield Trust Co. 216 A. D. 72, 215 N. Y. S. 50.

It also follows that a judgment of a foreign court will not avail, of its own force, to transfer title to land in this state, despite the fact that a conveyance can be executed by an agent of the court in fulfillment of its mandate. Where, however, the owner himself executes a conveyance of land in this state, title passes even though the owner act under compulsion directed by the foreign court. 

If the conveyance in the foreign jurisdiction was compelled by the court in an insolvency proceeding dealing with the insolvency of the conveyor, the title of the conveyee would be subordinate to the rights of local creditors with executions or attachments against the goods of the creditor. 

Deschenes v. Tallman 248 N. Y. 33.

Wills and Decedents' Estates 

The rules of construction, a power created by will to appoint chattels or other movables, the validity of the question of revocation of a will are determined by the laws of the testator's domicile at the time the will was executed if personalty is involved. As regards realty, the laws of the place where the land is situated govern. 

In re Dialogue's Will 87 N.Y.S. 237 

In re McCready 236 A. D. 390, affd. 263 N. Y. 602 

City Bank Farmer's Trust Co. v. Meyer 263 A. D. 671.

The validity and effect of a testamentary disposition of personal property are governed by the law of the domicile of the decedent at the time of his death unless such law contravenes some rule of public policy. 

In re Gifford's Estate 279 N. Y. 470.

A will executed outside of New York State will be probated here, provided it is in writing, subscribed by the testator, and meets the requirements of the place where it was executed or of the testator's domicile or of this state.

Decedent Estate Law §§ 22a, 23. 

Transfer of Personalty

The essential validity of a conveyance of a chattel is determined by the law of the state where the chattel is situated at the time of the conveyance. This applies to negotiable instruments and also to other intangible personal property when no one can get the benefit of ownership except through and by means of the paper which evidences such intangible property, e.g., shares of corporate stock. 

These have a situs apart from the domicile of the owners. 

The title of a foreign assignee or receiver is upheld upon the principle of comity. If the title is by virtue of a voluntary transfer, it is sustained against everybody. But if it depends on a foreign statute or judgment it is sustained against all except domestic creditors. 

Hastings v. Byelesby 286 N. Y. 468. Trusts

When we consider trusts of personalty we must differentiate between testamentary trusts and trusts inter vivos. The rule is that the essential validity of a testamentary trust of personalty must be determined by the law of the decedent's domicile. Where a nonresident establishes a trust inter vivos situated within this state, no invariable rule can be formulated. The intent controls. Thus where the situs of the trust and the domicile of the trustees are in New York, and the intent of the settlor is that the laws of his own domicile shall not control, the New York law will control regardless of the place of execution of the trust instrument. If a trust instrument valid in New Jersey but invalid in New York is drawn by a New Jersey resident in New York, and the res is located, the trustee domiciled, and the trust administered in New York, the New Jersey law would nevertheless apply if the intent of the settlor was that in all

matters affecting the trust, the law of his domicile should govern. 

Shannon v. Irving Trust Co. 275 N. Y. 95

Hutchinson v. Ross 262 N. Y. 381; Personal Property Law § 12a. 

Powers

The general rule is that an estate created by the execution of a power takes effect in the same manner as if it had been created by the deed or instrument which originally created the power. It has been held to follow from this that the law applicable to the deed should be the law applicable to the construction of the instrument which exercises the power, unless there is a contrary intent expressed in the deed. 

Chase Bank v. Central Hanover Bank 265 A. D. 434.

Conferring Jurisdiction by Stipulation 

The parties may stipulate that the laws of state X are to govern in the transactions, no matter where the case is tried if the stipulation is made in good faith, if it bears on some element in the transaction, so that there is reason for that state being selected, and if the party who would ordinarily have the right to sue in New York is not being deprived of important rights under the arrangements. But if a state's laws are selected merely because they are most liberal or most stringent, and for that reason alone, the arrangement will not be recognized. 

Sliosberg v. N. Y. Life Ins. So., 217 A. D. 685, 217 N. Y. S. 226

An agreement by which a New York resident as a party to a contract undertakes to confer exclusive jurisdiction on a foreign tribunal over controversies, is void as against public policy. This refers only to the jurisdiction of the court over the subject-matter. 

Sudbury v. Ambi Verwaltung, 213 A. D. 98, 210 N. Y. S. 154. 

Foreign Judgments

A judgment of another state is conclusive as far as to preclude a retrial of the merits in New York except 

1. Where the judgment is tainted with fraud; or 

2. Where the foreign court had no jurisdiction of the person of the defendant or of the subject matter of the action. 

Oberlander v. Oberlander 179 Misc. 459. 

Thus a contention that a judgment of another state is erroneous as a matter of law will not be maintained. The question should be disposed of in the state where the judgment was obtained.* 

Franklin v. Lee 233 A. D. 592, affă. 259 N. Y. 532 

Cowans v. Ticonderoga Pulp Co. 219 A. D. 120 affd. 246 N. Y. 603.

The foreign judgment may be attacked collaterally for want of jurisdiction, or for fraud perpetrated upon the court or upon a third party. The fraud in such case is made up of the same con- *The law seems not to be definite on the question whether the fact that there is a lack of reciprocity between New York and the particular foreign jurisdiction involved, is material as regards the conclusiveness of the judgment.

stituents as is fraud in any other case. The defense of lack of jurisdiction must be raised by the answer. 

Hall v. Hall 139 A. D. 120, 123 N.Y.S. 1056 

Humnicki v. Pitkowa 154 Misc. 407, 277 N. Y. S. 417.

There are two classes of exceptions to the general rule of invalidity of foreign judgments where no personal service had beeneffected in the foreign jurisdiction: (a) where the foreign law of process is held to be binding upon a defendant, by reason of his citizenship or residence in the foreign state and in recognition of the allegiance which he owes in consequence to such state, (b) where the defendant is a corporation doing business in a foreign state, whose laws provide a method of service upon foreign corporations, and condition the right to do business within the state upon subjection to such laws. 

Rhodesian Gen. Fin. Ltd. v. Mac Quisten 170 Misc. 996. 

Foreign Confiscatory Decrees

The decree of a foreign government by which private property is confiscated so as to affect a contract not made nor to be performed there, or which may affect property in New York, is given no recognition here because such decree is contrary to our public policy. 

It does not matter that such government is recognized by the United States. Thus corporations destroyed by the decree of an unrecognized government and functioning elsewhere have been regarded as living outside of government territory. But an unrecognized government in control of its own territory is a de facto government and its acts affecting property within its own borders are sovereign acts. Thus where the unrecognized government confiscated oil in its own territory owned by its own nationals and then sold such oil to the defendant, an American, the defendant is not liable in conversion. The act was in the territory of the unrecognized government. 

M. Salimoff v. Standard Oil Co., 262 N. Y. 220.

When the unrecognized government is recognized, the effect is to validate all acts of that government from the commencement of its existence. But even under such rule, the decree of the foreign government may not prejudice the claims of our nationals to property within our jurisdiction. 

U. S. v. President and Directors of Manhattan Co., 276 N. Y. 396.

Suits Against Foreign Governments 

A foreign sovereign may not be sued here not because of comity, but because there has been no submission to our jurisdiction. That there has been no recognition of a foreign de facto government does not change the rule. Nor does the fact that we are at war with the foreign sovereign power affect the immunity. And if the defendant is an instrumentality of the foreign sovereign, as distinguished from an autonomous, corporate body, a suit is not maintainable. 

Telkes v. Hungarian Natl. Museum 265 A. D. 192

CONSTITUTIONAL LAW Eminent Domain THE 

THE POWER of eminent domain is the right of the state as a sovereign power, to take private property for public use upon making just compensation. This right may be delegated by the Legislature to a corporation or individual to whom has been delegated some public duty or function by some act of the Legislature, which act must state the specific purpose for which the delegation is made. 

If it is delegated to a municipality, the specific purpose need not be stated. 

People v. Pendergast 220 A. D. 351, affd. 248 N. Y. 215.

The necessity or expediency of taking private property for public use is a legislative question, and the courts cannot interfere in its determination. Whether the use for which the property is proposed to be taken is a public one is a judicial question for the court to decide and as to this the determination of the Legislative may be reviewed. 

In re Cosgrave 238 N. Y. 84 

Little v. Ford 223 A. D. 559, affd. 249 N. Y. 495.

Private property can never be taken by the state for any private use. Hence a railroad could not have property condemned so that it might erect a storage house for customers on it for that would be a private use. 

Matter of City of New York, Saratoga Avenue 226 N.Y. 128

Where property has previously been devoted to public use by a corporation having the power of eminent domain, it cannot be taken by another corporation to which has been delegated the power of condemnation, unless the authority so to do has expressly or by necessary implication been conferred by the Legislature, and this rule applies to municipalities as well as to public service corporations. But this rule has no application where the taking is by the sovereign. The right to retake is inhérent in its sovereignty. 

In re Highway 234 A.D. 129, affd. 259 N. Y. 530 

In re Cruger Avenue 238 N. Y. 84; Board v. Ponda 249 N. Y. 445

There is no constitutional provision for compensation when public property is taken for a public use. Accordingly the legislature may authorize the appropriation of municipal property devoted to a public use e.g., streets, for a different public use without the allowance of compensation. 

People ex rel. Palmer v. Travis 223 N. Y. 150, 167.

The Compensation 

The sum to be paid as compensation is fixed by the state, or by a jury, through majority decision, or by the Supreme Court, either 89

with or without a jury, or by three Commissioners appointed by the Court.

The amount to be given is the fair market value of the property for all available uses and purposes taken in terms of cash as of the date of taking plus consequent damage to the remainder caused by the loss of a useful part. When there is no market value as of a date, evidence may be introduced of the fair market value of the property, if in substantially the same condition, at the nearest earlier date when there was a fair market.

Re Board of Water Supply 277 N. Y. 452 

The fact that the property has not been used to best advantage does not mitigate against any of the owner's rights to have the value assessed so that he may get the highest compensation, but he may not swell the damages beyond the fair market value by any consideration of probability that some time in the future the property may be used for some purpose to which it is adapted, unless it appears that the market value of the property is enhanced by the chance of probability. On the other hand, benefits which the owner may derive from the public use for which the property is to be taken, are not to be considered in the appraisal of direct damages, though they may be considered in fixing consequential damages. 

City of N. Y. (Exterior St.) 285 N. Y. 455.

Where part of a parcel is taken, compensation is based upon the difference between the fair market value of the entire property and that of the remainder including compensation for damages resulting to the part not taken, not only by reason of the taking but also by reason of the use to which property taken is put. Benefits resulting by the use of the part taken to the part not taken, may be offset only against consequential damages. 

In re Whitlock Avenue 278 N. Y. 276 

City of New York (Norwood) 266 A. D. 677.

If a grantee, holding under words of "limitation" and using the land as it was to be used under his grant, lost the land through its being condemned, the grantee gets the full award, and the grantor's heirs get nothing. The heirs have a mere posibility of reversion. 

In re Water Front on East River 213 A.D. 187, 210 N¸Y.S. 387

Art I, § 7 Constitution of New York 

N. Y. Central Ry. Co. v. Maloney 234 N. Y. 208

Where any realty under lease or other contract is taken by condemnation, all the covenants, contracts and engagements between landlord and tenant or any other contracting parties, respecting the same, or any part thereof, upon the vesting of the title in the city, cease and are absolutely discharged. 

In re Allen St. & 1st Avenue 256 N. Y. 236.

A tenant is entitled to compensation for his fixtures or structures annexed to realty in such a manner that injury to them or to the realty would result if removal took place, whenever the city in taking the realty destroys the leasehold interest of the tenant. This compensation is required even where there is a clause in the lease

CONSTITUTIONAL 

91 

LAW 

stating that the tenant is to receive nothing for his leasehold interest in the event of a condemnation of the premises, and that he may remove his annexations at the end of the lease. 

In re Whitlock Avenue 278 N.Y. 276 

In re Allen St. & 1st Avenue 256 N. Y. 236 sup- The award of the commissioners must be based on, and have port in the record and on whatever knowledge they may have acquired in viewing the premises. What the commissioners learn outside of the record is not to be taken into consideration in determining the award. 

In re Chittenango-Cazenovia 130 Misc. 516, 223 N.Y.S. 833 

Board of Supervisors v. Beardslee 140 Misc. 894, 252 N. Y. S. 10.

Although the courts will not interfere with an honest compensation award, the Legislature may provide for a review by some one of the tribunals which might have been selected to award. 

In re School Site 222 A.D. 554, affð. 250 N. Y. 588

Police Power and Due Process Clause 

The State and Federal Constitutions both say that no person (and this includes corporations and municipalities) shall be deprived of life, liberty, or property without due process of law. The guarantee of due process demands only that the law shall not be unreasonably arbitrary or capricious and that the means selected shall have a real and substantial relation to the object sought to be maintained. Decisions of the Supreme Court of the United States are binding upon the State courts in defining the scope of the due process clause in the Federal Constitution. Technically, the New 

York courts have power to reject decisions in defining the same clause in the State Constitution, but they do not do it. 

Noyes v. Erie etc. Co-op Corp. 281 N. Y. 187

Art I, § 6 Constitution of New York United States Constitution 14th Amendment 

Central Savings Bank v. City of New York 280 N. Y. 9

The rights under the due process clause are not entirely superior to the public interest. The State may establish regulations reasonably necessary for the general welfare, the protection, general prosperity and safety of the health and morals of the people, even though the rights of private property be thereby curtailed or the freedom of contract abridged. This is the state's "police power.' 

Any law adopted by the Legislature must be reasonably calculated to effect such ends in order to be considered under the heading of police power.

People v. La Fetra 230 N. Y. 429 

People v. Teuscher 129 Misc. 94, affd. 248 N. Y. 454

Under police power rights the state can reasonably regulate child and woman's labor conditions; employment agencies; junk dealers; auctioneers; moving pictures; material from which houses must be built, so that a law prohibiting frame houses in certain districts is constitutional; size of homes; location and regulation of

slaughter houses; use and preservation of wild forest land; zoning regulations; the sale of soft drinks; acts permitted on Sundays. 

People v. American Wool Stock Co. 286 N. Y. 77 People v. Board of Appeals 234 N. Y. 484 

Wulfsohn v. Burden 241 N. Y. 288; Cronin v. People 82 N. Y. 318 

Assn. for Protection of Adirondacks v. McDonald 253 N. Y. 234

A tax levied on an individual with discrimination, making him pay almost all the money necessary to support the village would be void. But a tax levied as a special assessment because of a local improvement, by which the property of one or of a few alone benefited, could be made to be borne by these few. 

An ordinance prohibiting the operating of a particular business in one part of a town and allowing it in another is contra to the due process clause. It doesn't regulate the business all through the city, nor does it do so in other parts where the same neighborhood conditions exist. An ordinance prohibiting the construction of a gasoline tank within 1,000 feet of one specific dwelling house is unconstitutional. 

A zoning resolution which prohibited the use for business purposes of any structure, unless it had a frontage of at least 20 feet and à depth of at least 50 feet was held unconstitutional, because it was arbitrary and unreasonable and did not serve a purpose either useful or aesthetic, nor in any way promoted public health, morals, public safety or general prosperity. 

Oppenheimer v. Kraus 221 A.D. 773, affd. 246 N.Y. 559 

Allowing farmers to sell vinegar of a low standard, while others must conform to a higher standard, deprives those not farmers of means of competition with discrimination, and thus deprives them of property in an unfair manner. It is an unconstitutional law. 

Since a man has a duty to give evidence when called upon, he can be subpoenaed in New York to give evidence in a different state. 

This is not depriving him of liberty, for it is his duty. This applies only to criminal cases for in a civil case a deposition can be taken. 

A deposition cannot be taken in a criminal case, as every man must be confronted by his accusers. 

A right of review by appeal is not an essential element of due process of law. 

In re Foote 129 Misc. 2, 221 N. Y. S. 302.

Construction of Statutes 

The courts favor such construction of a statute as will render it constitutional wherever possible. The court assumes that the purpose of the legislature was legitimate. Whether the purpose was wise is not for the courts to consider. 

Schieffelin v. Goldsmith, 253 N. Y. 243.

The Court will act only if an actual case is before it requiring a decision concerning the constitutionality of a statute. 

One who challenges the constitutionality of a statute, must show that he will be affected unfavorably if the statute is upheld and he

CONSTITUTIONAL LAW 

93 must also show its unconstitutionality beyond a reasonable doubt. 

People v. Harnett 224 A. D. 127, affd. 249 N. Y. 606

People v. Teuscher 129 Misc. 94, affd. 248 N. Y. 454. 

Any state law or any act of any department of the state which is contrary to, or in conflict with a Federal law, is invalid. 

A statute may be constitutional as applied to one set of circumstances and unconstitutional when it is made to cover another situation. It may be valid when enacted and may become invalid by a change in the conditions to which it is applied. 

Realty Revenue Corp. v. Wilson 181 Misc. 802. 

The words of a treaty are to be taken liberally in the light of evident purposes. When two constructions are admissible, one restrictive of rights and the other liberal, the latter is preferred. 

Matter of Zatelewski 292 N. Y. 332 

Interstate Commerce

Though the Federal Government has absolute power over interstate commerce, a state has some control over any articles or any situations which play a part in interstate commerce. A state may make rules governing the inspection of goods entering the state to ascertain its kind, quality or weight; it may tax property in the state used in interstate commerce; it may tax motor bus owners engaged in interstate commerce at the rate of one cent per mile for each mile of highway in that state over which such vehicle traveled, although intrastate buses were taxed upon a different basis. The classification was held to be reasonable and not discriminatory. 

A state cannot interfere with the expression of Congress over an interstate matter even though the state ruling is made in the interests of public safety, and in the exercise of the police power of the state. In circumstances where compulsion upon a foreign corporation engaged in foreign or interstate commerce to submit to suit in the state court upon a transitory action arising in a different jurisdiction would result in an unreasonable burden upon interstate commerce, the foreign corporation is entitled to an order prohibiting the state court from attempting to exercise jurisdiction. In the adjudicated cases the foreign corporation has been a carrier. 

Banque de France v. Supreme Court 287 N. Y. 483 

Rueffer v. Dept. of Agriculture 279 N. Y. 16

People v. Public Service Comm. 226 A. D. 43, 234 N. Y. S. 342. 

A common carrier passing through a foreign state, en route between termini in the originating state, is engaged in interstate commerce, unless the route is unreasonable or a subterfuge for the purpose of taking advantage of federal statutes. 

Bus Corp. v. Davis 225 A. D. 182, 232 N. Y. S. 536.

Rights Upon Arrest: (a) Before the Magistrate 

The "information" is the allegation made to a magistrate that a person has been guilty of some designated crime. It is the basis upon which a magistrate is authorized to act in issuing a warrant. 

People v. Knapp 152 Misc. 368, 274 N. Y. S. 85.

A defendant is entitled to be taken before a magistrate and arraigned without unnecessary delay after his' arrest. The failure to do so may be considered by the jury as bearing upon the question of the treatment to which the prisoner was subjected during the interval between his arrest and arraignment. When a confession is obtained during this interval the length of time becomes important if coercion is claimed.

People v. Cohen 243 A. D. 245, 276 N. Y. S. 851. 

On coming before the magistrate, the defendant must be told what the charges against him are, that everything he will say may count against him and that he has an immediate right to counsel. 

He has the right to stand mute and no presumption can be created against him from his failure to take the stand. Should the defendant desire to make any statement, he makes it not under oath and he may be asked about any circumstances which may aid him. 

Code of Criminal Procedure §§ 188, 198 

People v. Russo 261 A. D. 176, 295 N. Y. S. 457.

The answer of the defendant to each question must be distinctly read to him as it is taken down. He may thereupon correct or add to his answers until it conforms to what he declares to be the truth. 

The fact that no minutes are taken down does not deprive the one convicted of the right to appeal. 

People v. Cittrola 213 A. D. 674, 210 N. Y. S. 21.

A committing magistrate is not required to exact the full measure of proof necessary to secure a conviction, but is obliged to hold the accused if there is proof that a crime has been committed and there is reasonable ground to believe that the accused is guilty of the crime. If the magistrate does not dismiss the defendant he may hold him for an information, or an indictment by the Grand Jury. 

People v. Munro 150 Misc. 41, 268 N. Y. S. 404.

The magistrate may exclude from the examination every person except the clerk of the magistrate, the complainant and his counsel, the district attorney, the attorney-general, the defendant and his counsel, and the officer having the defendant in his custody. 

Code of Criminal Procedure § 203. 

(b) Waiving Examination

In cases where the magistrate has not exclusive jurisdiction in the first instance, he is without power to take any proof or make any finding, if the defendant waives examination and elects to give bail, though the magistrate may examine witnesses conditionally and preserve their testimony. The accused has the right to have the testimony given against him heard by that tribunal which shall try him on the merits or by the grand jury. This election to waive examination before the magistrate is not an admission of guilt. 

Hodge v. Skinner 254 A¸D. 42, 4 N.Y.S. (2d) 406 

(c) The Indictment 

The first pleading on the part of the people is the indictment. Its purpose is to acquaint the defendant with the charge made. The

CONSTITUTIONAL LAW 

95 indictment must contain (1) the title of the action, specifying the name of the court to which the indictment is presented, and the names of the parties; and (2) a statement of the specific crime charged, to include the name of the crime if it have one, or if it be a misdemeanor having no general name (e.g., libel, assault,), a brief description of it.

Code of Criminal Procedure § 295 b and c. 

The Grand Jury which consists of from 16 to 23 persons, is the body authorized to find an indictment. The Grand Jury ought to find an indictment when all the evidence before them, taken together, is such as in their judgment would, if unexplained and uncontradicted, warrant a conviction by the trial jury. 

Code of Criminal Procedure § 258. 

Twelve must agree to the indictment, and if 12 do not, it means that the charge is dismissed so far as this grand jury is concerned. 

But since a hearing before a grand jury is not "being placed in jeopardy," the court may submit the facts to other grand juries as often as the court thinks necessary.

Code of Criminal Procedure §§ 224, 268, 269, 270. 

At common law a prosecuting attorney might resubmit a charge to a grand jury without obtaining an order of the court permitting such resubmission. Grave abuses arose out of such practice, and it was to correct such abuses that the statute was enacted requiring an order of the court before a charge could be resubmitted to another grand jury after it had been dismissed by one.

People v. Barr 259 N. Y. 104; Code of Criminal Procedure § 270. 

(d) The Trial 

The defendant is entitled to a speedy and public trial and to counsel. He may produce witnesses in his behalf and he must be confronted with the witnesses against him in court, except where the charge has been preliminarily examined before a magistrate and the testimony reduced to the form of a deposition. If the right of cross examination has been complied with, the testimony of a witness upon a former trial who is dead, insane or cannot with due diligence be found in the state, may be read and it does not matter how far the proceedings have progressed in the former trial nor how it had ended.

Code of Criminal Procedure § 8; People v. Hines 284 N. Y. 93, 115. 

The accused has a right to have compulsory process for obtaining witnesses. Where a court refuses to issue an order directing the sheriff to produce as a witness for the defendant a person then in jail under an indictment, it was held reversible error although the testimony already introduced was strong against the defendant and the witness could have properly refused to answer on constitutional grounds.

People v. Wells 272 N. Y. 215. 

Defendants who are jointly indicted may be tried separately or jointly in the discretion of the court. The discretion is to be exer-

4 cised as to insure justice and a fair trial. And the trial court need not discharge all the defendants being jointly tried because it becomes necessary to declare a mistrial as to one defendant. 

People ex rel Epstein v. Lawes 297 N. Y. 386 Code of Criminal Procedure § 391; People v. Snyder 246 N. Y. 291 

After the commencement of the trial, the people shall not be required to elect between the counts of any indictment, except that for good cause shown, and in the interest of justice, the court may in its discretion, require an election as to one or more counts. 

Code of Criminal Procedure § 279a. 

Bail

The State Constitution contains a prohibition against excessive bail, but it does not follow it has been held, that refusal to fix any bail violates the prohibition. By statute, admission to bail before conviction is a matter of right in misdemeanor cases only. It is discretionary in other cases. This discretionary power cannot be exercised arbitrarily. Since an order denying bail is not appealable, the way to test out the question of proper exercise of discretion is by habeas corpus. On the return of the writ, the Supreme Court has before it only the legality of the denial of the bail e.g., whether the denying court has abused its discretion by denying bail without good reason. But this does not give the court entertaining the writ the right to fix other bail, since this would be really an appellate act affecting an order not appealable.

People ex rel. Shapiro v. Keeper of City Prison 290 N. Y. 393. 

Constitutional Rights Which May or May Not Be Waived

Under the Fifth Amendment to the Federal Constitution and also under the New York State Constitution (Article I, § 6) no person can be held to answer for a felony unless on presentment or indictment of a Grand Jury. Under this section a New York statute was held unconstitutional which permitted a defendant to waive an indictment or presentment before being tried for a felony. 

People v. Christian, 249 N. Y. 314.

Constitutional safeguards which may or may not be waived can be divided into two classes: those which belong to the accused alone and which can be waived, and those which belong to the public as well and cannot be waived. The Legislature may make provision for waiver of a jury in criminal cases where the crime charged is not punishable by death; a person may waive his right to a jury trial in civil cases; his right not to testify against himself; his right to compensation for property taken for public use; his right not to be searched without a warrant; his right to counsel; his right to be confronted by his accusers or the People's witnesses;* his right to offer a plea in open court.

Art. I. § 2, Constitution of New York. 

*The rule of confrontation does not preclude the receipt in evidence of a record made by a public officer in the course of his official duties. People v. 

Nisonoff 267 A. D. 356.

CONSTITUTIONAL LAW 

97 One cannot waive the provisions in regard to freedom of religion; his right not to be twice put in jeopardy; his right to be tried by a court for a crime. 

People v. Sugarman 248 N. Y. 255.

In capital cases a defendant cannot waive his right to be present. 

A verdict rendered in his absence or after a trial from which he has been absent is defective and a conviction must be reversed. In cases of felonies not punishable by death a defendant may waive his right to be present at the trial or any part thereof or at the rendition of the verdict.

The presence of the judge is essential. Even temporary absence warrants reversal.

People v. La Barbera 274 N. Y. 339; People v. Parisi 276 N. Y. 97. 

Double Jeopardy

The Constitution prohibits any one being tried twice for the same offense and thus placed in "double jeopardy." This rule applies to all indictable offenses and misdemeanors. The test is not whether the defendant has been tried for the same act, but whether he has been put in jeopardy for the same offense and against the same sovereignty. Where an act is an offense against both the Federal and 

State laws, it is possible for the defendant to be found guilty in the state court and then tried in the Federal court. 

People v. Eklof 179 Misc. 536. 

The purpose of the rule is to prevent persecution and oppression; under the following circumstances therefore, there is no double jeopardy and a new trial may be had: the trial is terminated by a disagreement of the jury; mistrial because of an incident during a trial created by the defendant and prejudicial to the prosecution; discharge of jury pursuant to law, or by the consent of the accused, or through extreme or absolute necessity, e.g., illness or death; death or incapacity of the judge. He has been put in double jeopardy and cannot be prosecuted again on the same charge. In the absence of any of these, once the defendant has pleaded to a valid charge, a jury sworn and evidence given in court having jurisdiction, there is a jeopardy. 

People v. Cignarale 110 N. Y. 23

People ex rel Blue v. Kearney 181 Misc. 981, affd. 292 N. Y. 679 

People v. Collins 238 A. D. 592, 265 N. Y. S. 475. 

An indictment by a grand jury or an examination by a magistrate, or a trial which ends in a disagreement of the jury are not considered a trial so as to prevent a retrial. 

People v. Steurnthal 154 Misc. 130, 276 N. Y. S. 689.

A court having jurisdiction finished a two day trial on Sunday. 

Defendant was found guilty and sentenced on Sunday. He was released on a habeas corpus. When it was attempted to try him again his plea of former jeopardy was sustained.

People ex rel. Meyer v. Warden of Nassau County 269 N. Y. 426. 

In one case the court declared a mistrial and discharged the jury

after its retirement before a verdict, because it had received information of the defendant's prior conviction of a crime which had the effect of turning the charge of the crime for which the defendant was being tried, from a misdemeanor to a felony. It was held that the defendant was immune from further prosecution on the ground of former jeopardy.

People v. Thrum 143 Misc. 7, 256 N. Y. S. 586. 

A conviction under the wrong section of the Penal Law is not a jeopardy and if the conviction is reversed, the state may have the defendant indicted under the proper clause. 

People v. Smith 177 A. D. 152, affd. 221 N. Y. 590.

If a judge sets aside an acquittal, his decision must be reversed without any trial, for a trial would be double jeopardy. 

Where a single set of acts is done causing harm to several individuals, a criminal prosecution resulting in an acquittal based upon the acts which violated the rights of one of the individuals will serve as a bar to prosecutions based upon the same acts which violated the rights of other individuals. Where a defendant is charged with burning 35 houses by the single act of setting fire to one building, an acquittal upon an indictment charging arson as to one of the buildings would be a bar to an indictment for burning any of the others. 

People v. Barr 259 N. Y. 104; Woodford v. People 62 N. Y. 117.

A single act may be an offense against two statutes, but if each statute requires proof of an additional fact which the other does not, an acquittal or conviction under either statute does not exempt the defendant from prosecution and punishment under the other. 

This is illustrated in a case where a man is indicted and tried for burglary and then for larceny which took place in connection with the burglary. Burglary may be shown by proving the breaking into and entering a building with intent to commit a crime therein. No larceny need be proven. If the crime intended is larceny there need be proof of the intent alone. A conviction for burglary would not bar a trial for the larceny. In the latter case, there must be shown the additional fact of a taking or appropriation. 

People ex rel. Kwatkowski v. Trenkle 169 Misc. 687 Ex Post Facto Laws 

The Constitution of the United States forbids the passing of any ex post facto law either by the national government or by the states. 

An ex post facto law has been defined as a law: (1) that makes an act, done before the passing of the law and which was innocent when done, criminal, and punishes such act. (2) that aggravates the crime or makes it greater than it was when committed. (3) that changes the punishment and inflicts a greater punishment that was annexed to the crime when committed. A statute reducing punishment may apply to a crime before the enactment of such statute.

CONSTITUTIONAL LAW 

99 (4) that alters the legal rules of evidence and permits the reception of testimony less than or different from that required at the time of the commission of the offense in order to convict. 

People v. Hayes 140 N. Y. 484; Pincus v. Adams 274 N. Y. 447.

The ex post facto rule applies only to criminal cases, penal statutes and vested rights. Accordingly, rules of evidence may be changed making admissible in ordinary civil cases evidence which previously was inadmissible; a new law may prescribe additional qualifications for jurors; the Legislature may establish a statute of limitations where none existed before or make it shorter, provided a reasonable time is allowed for actions to be brought; it may extend the statute provided an offense barred at the time of the new enactment is not revived. 

Campbell v. Evening Post 245 N. Y. 320 

People v. Adams 74 N. Y. 447 

Dee v. State Tax Commission 257 A. D. 531, affd. 282 N. Y. 617. Self-Incrimination

A witness need not answer any question, or produce any real evidence if the answer or the real evidence will tend to make him liable to a punishment for any crime or to expose him to a penalty or loss of land. This rule applies also to questions put by a grand jury. If complete immunity is given by a statute to one who may testify, such person is then compelled to testify. However, the fact that testimony required to be given because of an immunity state statute, may be used against him in a prosecution under a Federal statute, does not invalidate the immunity statute. The immunity from prosecution like the privilege against testifying which it supplants, pertains only to prosecutions in the same jurisdiction. 

Feldman v. United States 64 Sup. Ct. Rep. 1082

Civil Practice Act § 355; Matter of Doyle 257 N. Y. 244. 

If a public officer, upon being called before a Grand Jury to testify concerning the conduct of his office, refuses to sign a waiver of immunity against subsequent criminal prosecution, or to answer relevant questions, he can be removed from office. 

New York State Constitution Article 1, § 6. 

If a person against whom a Grand Jury inquiry is directed, is compelled to testify before that body and indictment is found. against him it should be dismissed. Any conviction would have been invalid. 

People v. Gillette 126 A. D. 665, 111 N. Y. S. 133.

Where it is desired to identify a defendant he may be ordered to stand up; his wig may be removed to show that he is bald. Such acts are not evidence tending to incriminate him but serve merely as a closer inspection of the object before the court to wit: the witness. A murderer may be forcibly taken before his dying victim for identification; a thief may be forcibly examined and stolen property taken from his person and brought into court for his identification; he may be forcibly shaven; the shoes of an accused

may be taken from him and placed in foot marks leading to the house of a murder victim; one charged with operating a motor vehicle while intoxicated may be examined and the police physician may testify concerning the condition of the accused. 

Schmidt v. District Attorney 255 A.D. 353, 8 N.Y.S. (2nd) 787

People v. Strauss 174 Misc. 881. 

An attorney against whom disbarment charges have been brought is not privileged when the answer to a question would tend to make his disbarment certain. Disbarment is not punishment for a crime. 

In re Becker 229 A. D. 62, 241 N. Y. S. 369,384. 

Unlawful Search and Seizure

The Constitution provides that the right of the people to be secure in their persons, houses, papers and effects against unreasonable search and seizure shall not be violated. A warrant cannot be issued except upon probable cause supported by oath and describing the place to be searched and the things seized. 

Act I, Constitution of New York

Civil Rights Law Sec. 8 

There is a right to search and seize without a warrant, persons lawfully arrested and to find and seize things connected with the crime. But a seizure is unlawful when the purpose is merely to discover possible grounds as yet unknown, for arrest or accusation. 

There is therefore a right to resist a seizure if no arrest is contemplated and there is merely a suspicion of the commission of a crime. 

This is true though in fact a crime is being or has been committed. 

People v. Richter 291 N. Y. 161

Even though seizure of property has been unlawful, what has been seized is competent evidence against the defendant in the Courts of New York. The rule is the same whether the seized items are innocent articles or contraband. 

People v. Richter 291 N. Y. 161 Voters

To vote in New York, one must be a citizen of the United States for at least ninety days and a resident of New York for a year, of the county four months, and of the election district for thirty days before election.

Soldiers and sailors on active duty or those individuals who are away because of the necessities of their business, e.g., traveling salesmen, may vote despite these "resident" provisions. Nor does one gain or lose residence for voting purposes while working for the Government, or while confined to a poorhouse or asylum in an election district which is not the one in which the citizen votes. 

The bare intention of a student to change his residence to that of the institution is not sufficient to constitute the change for vot ing purposes unless circumstances independent of his presence at the school evince an actual intent to change the place of his home. 

Art II §§ 1, 19, 3 Constitution of New York 

Watermeyer v. Mitchell 275 N. Ý. 73.

CONSTITUTIONAL

LAW 

The right to vote is not a natural right of the citizen; it is a political privilege and emanates from the people of the state. 

O'Brien v. City of Saratoga Springs 121 Misc. 728, affd. 224 A. D. 124. The Legislature The Legislature of New York State is composed of a Senate and an Assembly. A majority constitutes a quorum in either House. 

An military officer is ineligible to membership in the Legislature. 

An officer of the Federal Reserve Corps is not a military officer. 

Any bill may originate in either house of the Legislature. In this respect it differs from the United States Congress, where revenue bills originate only in the House of Representatives. 

Before a bill can be passed in the Legislature, it must be on the legislator's desks for three days, unless it be a bill of extreme importance in which case the Governor may send a certificate of public necessity and dispense with the three day requirement. 

Art III §§ 2, 10, 13, 15 Constitution of New York 

A bill to become a law must receive a majority vote of each branch of the Legislature, with a quorum present, unless the bill is a tax measure or an appropriation, in which latter cases the quorum consists of three-fifths of the members elected to each House, and not a majority as in other cases. Should the bill pass in both 

Houses, it goes to the Governor for his approval or veto. If he retains the bill for over ten days, Sundays excepted, the bill becomes law unless the Legislature has adjourned within these ten days. In case of such adjournment, the bill cannot become law unless the Governor actually signs the bill within thirty days after the adjournment.

Art. III § 25; Art. IV § 9 Constitution of New York. 

If the Legislature wants to grant public (state) money or transfer property for local or private purposes, the assent of two-thirds of the members elected to each house is necessary. So an appropriation for improving the navigation of the Boquet River from its mouth to the Falls is for a local purpose, as it promotes the interest of the people of the Falls and does not serve a general public service. So also is a bill to vest the state land inside a city, in the city, local. Two-thirds assent would be needed to pass such a bill. 

Art. III § 20 Constitution of New York. 

'Franchises to run a street railway, for example, are granted by the Legislature, or by the city so empowered by the Legislature, for the absolute control and ownership of the streets is in the state. The city is in the position of a trustee of the streets. 

People v. Kerr 27 N. Y. 188.

The Legislature cannot confer jurisdiction on the Court of Claims over a claim, if the claim would have been barred because of the Statute of Limitations had the claim been against a private individual instead of against the state.

No private or local bill shall embrace more than one subject, and this subject must be expressed in the title. So, a title reading “An

Act to Incorporate the Economic Power Co." is an insufficient title to include provisions allowing the corporation to use highways. 

A Legislature has no power to extend the limits of a municipality by adding territory to it, because the Legislature cannot pass any private or local bill (1) incorporating villages. In addition the 

Legislature cannot pass a private or local bill (2) Changing the names of individuals. (3) Laying out, working on or discontinuing highways, or draining swamps. (4) Locating or changing the county seat. (5) Changing the place of voting. (6) Changing the fee of officers who do not receive fixed salaries. 

Providing for a change of venue in civil or criminal cases. It does not apply to condemnation proceedings. (8) Providing for election of local supervisors. (9) Selecting grand or petit jurors. (10) Granting to a private corporation or individual any exclusive privilege or franchise or any exemption from taxation. (11) Regulating the rate of interest on money.

A law relating to a matter of state concern and applicable to all municipalities or localities in a class based upon population or nearness to large populations may be a general law though one locality fits that description. Of course the law must have a reasonable relation to the limited number who fit the description. Thus a condition due to difference in population may be the subject of legislation which covers only cities of over 1,000,000,000, although the law could relate only to New York City. 

Stapleton v. Pinckey 293 N. Y. 330

Art. III 18 Constitution of New York. 

No law shall authorize the construction or operation of a street railroad without the consent of the owners of one-half in value of the property bordering on the part of the highway through which the railroad is to go. The consent, once given, is irrevocable. In addition to these consents, the local authorities controlling the highway must consent. If the owners will not consent, the Appellate 

Division of the Supreme Court may, on application, appoint three commissioners, who, after hearings, may determine for the owners. 

The court's confirmation of the report is necessary. 

The Executive 

The executive power is vested in a Governor and Lieutenant- Governor, elected for four years, who must be thirty years of age and New York residents for at least five years preceding election. 

Art. IV § 1 Constitution of New York. 

The Governor is the commander-in-chief of the militia, which consists of all able-bodied male ciitizens between eighteen and fortyfive. The militia officers are appointed by the Governor and their terms expire with that of the Governor. 

Art. XI § 4 Constitution of New York.

The Governor has the power to call either House for a special session. He can pardon all crimes except treason and the results of impeachment proceedings. In the case of treason, the Governor can suspend execution of the sentence until the Legislature meets and acts on it. 

The Governor can commute a sentence for a crime, with any restriction. The commutation can provide that if the prisoner is later convicted of another felony he is to serve out the term for which he was conditionally pardoned. The reprieve or commutations of sentences may be revoked at any time prior to the actual discharge of the prisoner. The Governor may, therefore, revoke the commutation, even after it has been delivered to the warden of the prison, provided the prisoner had not yet been discharged.*
