In case an appropriation bill has one or more items which are objectionable, the Governor can veto the objectionable items without affecting the rest of the bill.

Art. IV § 9 Constitution of New York. 

The Lieutenant-Governor is president of the Senate and can vote only in the event of a tie. He becomes Governor on the death or disability of the Governor and acts as Governor during the Governor's absence from the state.

Art. IV § 6 Constitution of New York. 

The State Judiciary 

The courts of New York State have no jurisdiction of crimes against the United States, unless the act constituting such crime is also a crime against the State of New York, in which case the state court would enforce only the state laws. 

People v. Conti 127 Misc. 244, 216 N. Y. S. 442. 

The Supreme Court is the court of general law and equity jurisdiction. There are four judicial departments, and in each department an Appellate Division. The Appellate Division justices are 

Supreme Court justices appointed to the Appellate Division by the Governor for five years, or to the end of their term as Supreme Court justices if it is less than five years away. In case of need, additional justices may be appointed temporarily by the Governor. 

The term of the Supreme Court justice is fourteen years. If a vacancy occurs, a member is voted for at the next election, which must be at least three months away, for a full fourteen-year term.

Until January 1 next after election, the Governor appoints a judge An executive pardon does not wipe out guilt even if the pardon recites that it is given because the executive believed the convicted person to have been innocent. with the advice and consent of the Senate, if then in session. If it is not in session he can appoint without it. (The same applies to vacancies in the Court of Appeals.)

Art. IV § 4 Constitution of New York. 

No person can hold office of judge or justice of a court longer than the last day of December next after he shall be 70 years of age.

This rule does not apply to the municipal courts. 

In re Moore 125 Misc. 607, affd. 215 A. D. 655. 

Judgments and orders rendered by a judge past the age of 70 are valid and cannot be attacked by private persons. The authority of the judge is open to attack only by the state. 

Sylvia Lake Co. v. Northern Ore Có 242 N. Y. 144.

The Court of Appeals is the highest court in the state. It has seven judges elected for fourteen years. Five make a quorum and four are necessary to a decision. The Governor may appoint temporary judges if needed.

Art. VI § 7 Constitution of New York. 

Judges of the Supreme Court and Court of Appeals may be removed from office only by two-thirds vote of both houses of the Legislature. Other judges, except justices of the peace, magistrates and justices of the municipal court of the City of New York, may be removed by-two thirds vote of the Senate alone upon the Governor's recommendation.

Art VI § 11 Constitution of New York Compensation of Public Officials 

A person accepting a public office, with a fixed salary, cannot legally claim additional compensation for the discharge of these duties, even though the salary may be very inadequate remuneration. Nor does it alter the case that by subsequent statutes or ordinances his duties within the scope of the charter, powers pertaining to the office are increased and not his salary. Whenever he considers the compensation inadequate, he is at liberty to resign. 

Salaries and terms of officials provided for in the State Constitution cannot be changed by the Legislature to be effective before the end of the term of the official whose salary or term is affected. 

This applies to the Governor, Lieutenant-Governor, Attorney General, and Comptroller.

Art. V § 1 Constitution of New York. 

The same restrictions concerning salaries apply to judges of courts created by the Constitution. These courts are Supreme Court, including the Appellate Division, Court of Appeals, County Court, Surrogates' Court, Court of General Sessions, City Court of the City of New York. Since the Municipal Court of the City of New 

York is not a court created by the Constitution, the Legislature can do with it as it pleases and may at any time reduce the compensation of its justices. 

Haggerty v. City of New York 267 N. Y. 252.

IM Any amendment may be proposed in either House. It must be passed not only by a majority in each House, but by two successive Legislatures. It is then submitted to the voters. If a majority are in favor, it is then a part of the constitution. 

In 1916 and at least every twenty years thereafter, and whenever the Legislature may at other times direct, the electorate decides whether there is to be a constitutional convention. The work of such a convention is submitted to the voters. If accepted, the constitution proposed by them becomes law. 

Art. XIV Constitution of New York. 

A treaty, if in force, is the supreme law of the land, and supersedes all local laws inconsistent with its terms. 

Techt v. Hughes 229 N. Y. at p. 240. Assessments

An action in equity to vacate an assessment and restrain its collection cannot be maintained merely because the assessment is for any reason invalid or illegal. Nor can an action at law be maintained to recover back money paid upon an illegal assessment, not void upon its face, so long as the assessment remains unvacated and unreversed. The action of the assessors is regarded as judical and the assessment in the nature of a judgment. The action may, however, be maintained to vacate an assessment as a cloud upon title, when it is invalid, but does not appear so on its face. 

Lewis v. City of Lockport 276 N. Y. 336.

Property owners may not be assessed for paving more than the original cost of the paving. 

Segfried Construction Co. v. New York 126 Misc. 689, 214 N. Y. S. 385. 

Suits Against the State

As the State of New York is a sovereign power it cannot be sued without its consent. It may withdraw that consent pending suit, in the absence of statute. Neither the doctrine of estoppel nor that of laches can be made to apply against the state. The state is not governed by the Statute of Limitations. Its property cannot be acquired by adverse possession.

In re Certain Lands in City of New York 127 Misc. 710. 

By statute, the state will not contest the right to the possession or title of real property where there has been adverse possession for forty years.

Civil Practice Act. § 31. 

Where there is a moral obligation on the part of the state to reimburse one who has suffered loss, an enabling act permitting the Court of Claims to pass upon such claims is constitutional. 

Cuvillier v. State 250 N. Y. 258

One state may maintain an action against another state and the state may maintain an action against an individual. 

An individual cannot, without the consent of the state, interpose a counterclaim against the state in an action brought by the state.

Full Faith and Credit* 

A judgment of a sister state may be assailed for want of jurisdiction over the person or the subject matter. As to defenses which might have been asserted at the time the action was brought, the judgment is conclusive.

Oral evidence of a defendant is competent to controvert jurisdiction of the person. It is not, however, competent to challenge the correctness, authenticity or conclusiveness of the judgment because of a mistake of law. 

Phillips v. Griffen 236 A. D. 209, 259 N. Y. S. 105.

The judgment of a court of competent jurisdiction of a territory of the United States is entitled to the same full faith and credit as the judgment of another state. 

Butler v. Butler 179 Misc. 651. *See Ante p. 79 for a discussion of the validity of foreign divorce judgments under the full faith and credit clause.

OUTLINE OF THE CONSTITUTION OF THE UNITED STATES 

THE PURPOSES of the Constitution as stated in its preamble are (1) to form a more perfect union, (2) establish justice, (3) insure domestic tranquility, (4) provide for the common defense, (5) the general welfare, and (6) to secure the blessings of liberty to ourselves and our posterity. 

The original constitution is divided into seven articles. Article 

I declares the legislative power to be lodged in Congress, which consists of (a) a Senate, and (b) a House of Representatives. 

A member of the House must be at least 25 years old, 7 years a citizen, while a senator must be at least 30 and a citizen for 9 years. 

Each must be a resident of the state from which he is elected and each is elected by popular vote. The House is composed of members chosen every second year. The number from each state is based upon the population of the state. 

The senate is composed of two members from each state, elected for six years by popular vote. One-third are elected every second year. Each branch elects its own officers but the presiding officer of the Senate is the Vice-President, who has no vote except to decide a tie.

The Senate alone may try federal officials who are impeached. 

When the President is tried the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court presides. A two-thirds vote of the Senators present is required for conviction, which conviction effects a permanent removal from office, and the offender may be further prosecuted. 

Each branch of Congress decides the qualifications of its own members; punishes its own members for disorderly behavior. A majority of the members is necessary for the transaction of business, except adjournment, or compelling the presence of an absentee. 

Each branch must remain in session while the other branch is in session, except that an adjournment of three days or less is permitted. 

Congress must meet at least once a year, in January.

Members of Congress are exempt from arrest while attending their session, or in going to and returning therefrom. This exemption does not exist in cases of treason, felony or breach of the peace. 

Members may not be arrested or questioned in any other place for any speech or debate made in either House. No member may accept any federal office created during his term, or the salary of which was increased during his term; and no person holding any government office may at the same time become a member of either House. 107

All bills for raising revenue must originate in the House, though the Senate may propose such bills. 

Before a bill becomes a law it must be approved by both Houses and by the President, unless when the President disapproves of any measure, it is passed over his veto by a two-thirds majority in each House. If a law approved by both branches is sent to the President, and the President does nothing within ten days, Sundays excepted, the law becomes effective as if the President had approved. 

Congress has the following powers besides those mentioned: (1) provide for the raising of money by taxation and duties, which provisions must be uniform throughout the country; (2) borrow money on credit; (3) regulate interstate and foreign commerce; (4) establish uniform rules on naturalization; (5) enact bankruptcy laws; (6) coin and issue money and punish for the counterfeiting thereof; (7) fix standards of weights and measures; (8) establish post offices and postal rates; (9) enact copyright and patent laws; (10) establish Federal courts inferior to the United States Supreme Court; (11) punish for crimes committed on the sea, and acts which are in violation of international law; (12) declare war, raise and support armies, though such appropriations of money shall be for no longer than a term of two years; (13) maintain a navy; (14) make treaties; (15) govern the district which is the seat of the government, now Washington, D. C.; (16) make all laws necessary and proper for carrying into effect the foregoing powers. 

Congress is not permitted the following: (1) to suspend the writ of habeas corpus, except in the case of rebellion or invasion when the public safety is threatened; (2) take away the property of a person condemned to death (bill of attainder); (3) pass a criminal law to govern any facts committed prior to the enactment of the law (ex post facto laws); (4) tax any article exported; (5) give any preference to any port of any state over that of another, or to compel vessels doing an interstate business to pay duty; (6) grant any title of nobility (an office-holder may not accept any present, office, or title from any foreign land or its head without the consent of Congress).

The states are prohibited from (1) making any treaty; (2) granting any letters of marque and reprisal; (3) coining money or issuing paper money on its credit; (4) providing for anything but gold and silver coin as legal tender; (5) passing any bill of attainder, ex post facto law or any law impairing the obligation of contracts; (6) granting any titles of nobility.

Each state is prohibited, unless permitted by Congress, from (1) laying any duty on imports or exports except what may be absolutely necessary for executing its inspection laws, and such collections shall be for the use of the United States Government, and under congressional control; (2) taxing tonnage of vessels; (3) keeping armies or warships during peace times; (4) making treaties with a state or foreign power, or engaging in war unless actually invaded, or in such imminent danger as will not permit delay.

OUTLINE OF CONSTITUTION OF THE UNITED STATES 

109 Article II deals with executive power vested in the President. He holds office for four years. The method of electing the President, and the Vice-President, is as follows: Each state elects electors, equal to its number of senators and representatives in Congress. These electors may not hold any office under the government. They vote for two persons, one as President, and the other as Vice-President. 

The person having the highest vote for the presidency becomes the President, provided he has a majority of the whole number of electors appointed. If he fails to have a majority, the House of Representatives being represented by at least two-thirds of the States, selects the President from the three names having the highest number of votes, this selection being by a majority vote; the representatives of each state vote as a unit, and each unit is one vote. If the 

House fails to choose the President, the Vice-President acts as President.

The Vice-President is also chosen by the electors, and the person chosen must have a majority vote. If he fails to obtain a majority of the number of electors, the Senate by majority vote selects the Vice- President from the two having the highest vote. At the time of the voting, two-thirds of the senators must be present. 

The time for choosing and the voting dates are chosen by Congress.

The President and the Vice-President must be born in the United States and have been a resident of the country for 14 years, and be 35 years old.

The Vice-President becomes President if the President is removed from office, dies, resigns or is unable to perform his duties. The salary cannot be changed during the term. 

The President is the Commander-in-Chief of the Army and Navy; he may pardon or grant reprieves for offenses against the United 

States, except in cases of impeachment.

With the advice and consent of the Senate, he may make treaties. 

The necessary assent required is two-thirds of the Senators. With the approval of the Senate, he may nominate and appoint ambassadors, judges of the Supreme Court, cabinet members. 

The Constitution requires the President, from time to time, to give Congress information concerning the condition of the government; to recommend legislation; to call special sessions when necessary; to receive foreign representatives; to fix time for adjournment of Congress if the House disagrees; to execute the laws. The 

President and Vice-President, as well as other civil officers of our government may be removed upon impeachment, after conviction of treason or bribery, or other high crime or misdemeanor.

Article III deals with the judicial power which is lodged in the Supreme Court and the lower courts established by Congress. The judges thereof hold office for life during good behavior, and their compensation cannot be diminished while in office. 

The judicial power extends to law and equity cases which pertain to the Federal Constitution, the laws of the United States and its

treaties, or which affect ambassadors or other public ministers, or which deal with controversies arising on the opean seas in which the government is a party, or in controversies involving two states, or one state and the citizens of another state, or between citizens of different states, as well as cases between foreign states and its subjects.

The Constitution requires a trial of all crimes excepting impeachment to be by jury, and to be held in the state where the crime was committed. Where a crime was not committed within any state, the trial is to take place as Congress by law directs. 

Treason is defined as the levying of war against this country, adhering to its enemies, giving them aid and comfort. Before a person can be convicted of such crime, the testimony of at least two witnesses, or the confesion in open court by the accused, is necessary. 

Article IV enumerates some of the rights of the states and the citizens thereof. Each state is directed to give full faith and credit to the laws, records and judicial proceedings of every other state. The citizens of each state are to have all the privileges and rights of the citizens of the other states. Provision is also made for extradition of persons charged with treason, felony or other crimes from one state to another. Each state is guaranteed a republican form of government and protection against invasion or domestic insurrection. 

Article V provides for amendments to the Constitution, which may be made whenever two-thirds of both Houses propose the amendments, or in the alternative, when the legislature of twothirds of the various states, after a convention called for that purpose, approve of an amendment, provided the proposed amendment is ratified by three-fourth of the states or by conventions in three-fourth thereof.

No amendment can be made which deprives a state without its consent of equal representation in the Senate. 

Article VI declares the Constitution, the laws of the United States made in pursuance thereof, and all treaties, to be the supreme law of the land. It also requires that no religious test shall be required as a qualification to hold any federal office. 

The seventh division consists of the amendments made to the 

Constitution subsequent to its ratification.

The first ten amendments, adopted within two years after the original Constitution, make up the Bill of Rights. These amendments are: 

1. That Congress is to establish no religion or prohibit any individual from exercising his religious belief; or abridge the freedom of speech or press; or prevent the people from assembling peaceably or from petitioning the government for redress for any grievances. 

2. That the right of the people to keep and bear arms shall not be infringed. 

3. That soldiers are not to be quartered in any house without the consent of the owner in times of peace, and in times of war only in accordance with the law.

OUTLINE OF CONSTITUTION OF THE UNITED STATES III 

4. Unreasonable searches and seizures are prohibited, and provision made for warrants for search and seizure only upon sufficient evidence by sworn facts describing the place and things to be searched or taken. 

5. No civil person is to be held to answer for infamous crime unless upon a presentment or an indictment; no person is to be put in jeopardy for the same offense more than once; nor be compelled to testify against himself in a criminal proceeding; or to be deprived of life, liberty or property without due process of law; nor his property taken for public use without just compensation. This amendment applies only to the Federal Government. 

6. Speedy and public trials in criminal prosecution by an impartial jury are ordered, and the accused is to be confronted with the witnesses against him, and has the right to compel witnesses to come to court and to have the assistance of counsel. 

7. In lawsuits involving over $20, the right to a jury trial is preserved. 

8.Excessive bail or excessive fine or cruel and unusual punishment are prohibited. 

9. The rights given under the Constitution are not to limit other rights and privileges the people might have. 

10. The rights not expressly given to the Federal Government nor prohibited to the States are left to the States and the people. 

11. Abrogated the right of citizens to sue states in Federal Courts. 

12. This amendment changed the old method of electing the President and Vice-President to conform to the manner described above. 

13. Slavery was abolished within the United States. 

14. All persons born or naturalized in and subject to the jurisdiction of the United States are declared to be citizens of the United States and of the state of their residence; no state is permitted to deprive any person of his life, liberty or property without due process of law; each person within each state is entitled to the same protection of the law; representatives are to be apportioned according to the number of persons in each state, and provision is made for a proportional reduction from the representation of any state which deprives any person entitled to vote from voting. 

15. Gives the right to vote to all citizens regardless of race, color or previous condition of servitude. 

16. The tax on incomes is permitted. 

17. A change is made in election of Senators so as to provide for their election by popular vote. 

18. The manufacture, sale or transfer of intoxicating liquors within the country or the importation thereof is prohibited. This was repealed by the twenty-first amendment. 

19. The right to vote is extended to females. 

20. The so-called "Lame Duck" Congress was abolished. The term of Congress begins on the third day in January and the term of the President and Vice-President on the twentieth day of January. 

21. Repeal of eighteenth amendment.

CONTRACTS 

Unilateral and Bilateral Contracts Contracts are either unilateral or bilateral. If one party promises to do something in return for a specific act of the other party, we have the elements of a unilateral contract. No enforcible obligation is imposed upon the promisor until the specified act is performed. Where one party promises to do something in exchange for a promise, we have the elements of a bilateral contract. Promises must not be merely formal words, having no probable or potential value. 

Matter of Lord 175 Misc. 921, 923

Nassau Supply Co. v. Ice Service Co. 252 N. Y. 277 

It may be stated as the general rule that there are these elements necessary for the formation of a contract: (1) an offer; (2) an acceptance of that offer in its exact terms; and (3) there must be consideration. Each will be considered separately. 

The Offer 

Offers must be unqualified and definite. Often an invitation to negotiate is mistaken for an offer. "If you should be interested in my lot, would be glad to hear from you, size 20x100, price $1,000." was held to be an invitation to negotiate and not an offer to sell. 

Where a request is made of a merchant for prices, the sending of a catalog of prices is not an offer to sell but only an invitation to negotiate. An auctioneer solicits offers from the bidders. The acceptance takes place when the hammer is knocked down. 

Patrick v. Kleine 127 Misc. 88, 215 N.Y.S. 305 

Cerreta v. Costello 212 A. D. 687, 209 N. Y. S. 257

An offer to pay a "fair share of the profits;" "to convey 70 acres❞ not further described; to continue in the defendant's employ without stating the term, compensation or services to be rendered, would all be considered to be too indefinite to allow for an acceptance. Where a promisor retains an unlimited right to decide later the nature or extent of his performance, the promise is too indefinite for legal enforcement. 

Varney v. Ditmars 217 N. Y. 223 

Chiapparelli v. Baker 252 N. Y. 192

Although an agreement is uncertain and therefore invalid in the first instance because of the indefiniteness of the offer, it may be rendered valid by subsequent acts, facts or by agreement of the parties which clarify the uncertainties. So although an acceptance of a promise to pay "a sum of money" for services to be rendered would not create a valid contract, the giving of notes for a definite sum of money would remove the indefiniteness. An agreement "to 112

CONTRACTS 

113 make a fair and reasonable settlement for personal injuries sustained by the plaintiff" is not enforceable where the amount to be paid is not set forth; but a promise to pay expenses of the plaintiff's illness is a definite promise. Agreements to sell or buy what would be "needed" or to lend an amount "sufficient to carry on your business" have been held definite enough to be enforceable. 

Wood v. Aetna 224 A. D. 628, 232 N.Y.S. 53 

King v. Krischer 220 A. D. 584, 222 N.Y.S. 66 

Stern v. Premier Shirt Co. 260 N. Y. 201

Habgood v. Van Dyke 128 Misc. 884, affd. 220 A. D. 801 

A promise that was originally too indefinite may by performance become definite, and as the other party to the bargain must be regarded as continuously assenting to receive such performance in return for his own promise, a valid unilateral contract arises on receipt of such performance. A promise or offer to buy or sell all the cans needed in a canning factory; all the coal needed for a foundry; all the iron refined during a certain period, is definite as to quantity, since the quantity can be determined. 

Schlegel Mfg. Co. v. Cooper's Glue 231 N. Y. 459 

Grundt v. Shenk 222 A. D. 82, affd. 248 N. Y. 602.

If goods are obtained under an agreement for their hire or sale and no price is fixed, it is presumed that a reasonable price is intended. A "reasonable" price is a definite price for the purpose of a contract, as the jury can fix that definite price. 

The Acceptance 

An acceptance to be effective must be an acceptance of the offer in its exact terms. Where an offer is sent by a telegraph company and the latter delivers an inaccurate transmission, an acceptance of the erroneous figure makes no binding contract. The company is not the agent of the sender but an independent contractor. 

Amerop Travel Bur, v. Postal Tel. Co. 146 Misc. 591, 262 N.Y.S. 304

Spratt v. Paramount Pictures 178 Misc. 682. 

If the offer looks toward a bilateral contract, i.e., the offer requests a promise from the other side, the acceptance in such case must consist of a binding promise. Commencement of the work which was to be promised is in itself not sufficient; the promise was what was asked for and that is what must be given. Conversely, if the offer requests an act, i.e., unilateral contract, the promise to perform the act is not an acceptance of the offer; an act was asked for, and only that act in accordance with the offer can constitute an acceptance. 

White v. Corlies 46 N. Y. 467.

The offer must be brought home to the notice of the offeree. An offer to reward a person who finds and returns a lost article is accepted when the article is returned by the finder who did so knowing of the offer of reward. 

Reynolds v. Eagle Pencil Co. 285 N. Y. 448.

One who receives a ticket, on paying a consideration, for having his package taken care of for a time, or his car watched in an en-

closure during a ball game, is not bound by a statement on the back of the ticket that the watcher is not liable for damage to the baggage or car, unless the notice is brought to the attention of the owner, so as to be made part of the contract. 

In some cases, however, although the "offeree" does not note or read the undertaking, he is considered as having accepted it. These cases are such where by usage and custom or by the actions of the party, he is considered as having "accepted." Thus, a person who buys a steamship ticket with conditions of the company's liability for damage to a passenger's baggage stamped on it, is a passenger subject to these conditions, even though he never reads them. Every part of a steamship ticket is a part of the contract. The fact that the purchaser did not read the ticket is immaterial. Curiously enough this rule has not been applied to railroad tickets; only if the conditions printed on the ticket are brought home to the purchaser, or are known by him or are so printed as to be very conspicuous, is the purchaser held to be subject to the printed conditions. 

Rosenthal v. Compagnie Generale 170 Misc. 426, 12 N.Y.S. (2nd) 102 

Murray v. Cunard S. S. Co. 235 N. Y. 162 

Hutchins v. Penn R. R. 181 N. Y. 186.

Ordinarily, one who signs an instrument is conclusively bound thereby. If he could read the instrument, not to have read it was gross negligence. If he could not read it, not to procure it to be read was equally negligent. In either case the writing binds him. This rule does not apply if the signer is illiterate or blind, and the contents are misread or misrepresented to him by the other party or even a stranger, unless the signer is negligent. 

Pimpinello v. Swift Co. 253 N. Y. 159 

In re Smith's Estate 243 A. D. 348, 276 N. Y. S. 646.

Before an acceptance by a promisee is binding upon the offeror, the acceptance must be received by the offeror. But if the offer is made through the mails or sent by telegram, it is implied that there can be an acceptance in the same manner, and the moment the offeree puts his acceptance in the mail box, or sends a telegram of acceptance, the contract is complete. This mail box may be that of the Post Office, or it may be the private mail box of the offeror. But if A sends an offer by telegram and B accepts by mail, or vice versa, it seems that the acceptance must be received in order to complete the contract, for the same method was not used in accepting as was used in offering. 

White v. Corlies 46 N. Y. 467

Webster v. Casein Co. of America 206 N. Y. 506 

A condition that the proposed contract shall not be obligatory unless the acceptance is received in a specified time, governs even though the offer and acceptance were both sent by mail. 

Where the offeror requires an acceptance "by return mail," he does not necessarily mean the mail immediately following the receipt of the offer, if the offeree lives in a city where there are several mails every day.

CONTRACTS 

115 Even though both parties suppose that a binding contract exists between them, it is not conclusive, unless in fact such an agreement had actually been made. 

Machinery Utilities Co. v. Fry 224 A. D. 392, 231 N. Y. S. 148. 

Rejection of the Offer

A proposal on the part of the offeree to accept the offer with a stated slight change or an intended acceptance subject to some conditions is equivalent to a rejection of the offer. Upon such rejection the parties are in the same position as if an offer were never made. 

Glens v. Ryerson 195 A. D. 769, 162 N. Y. S. 427. 

Revocation of the Offer

An offer remains open for the time stated in the offer, or if no specified time is stated, for a period which is reasonable considering the subject-matter of the offer or the surrounding circumstances, or until the offer has been revoked by the offeror. Before the offer can be said to have been revoked by the offeror, the revocation must be received by the offeree. If a valid acceptance is mailed in acceptance of a mailed offer, the acceptance dates from the time it is mailed. 

A revocation dates from the time it is received. It thus follows that if the acceptance is mailed at 11 a.m. and received at 5 p.m., and the revocation mailed at 8 a. m. and recived at 3 p. m., a valid contract exists, since the mailing of the acceptance occurred before the receipt of the revocation. 

Stein-Gray Drug Co. v. Michelson 116 N. Y. S. 789.

Where the offer is made publicly through the newspapers, it may be revoked through the newspapers by giving the revocation similar publicity; and even though the one who reads the offer has not read the revocation, the offer no longer exists. 

Death or insanity of the offeror automatically revokes a revocable offer if either occurs before valid acceptance. 

Jones v. Union Central Ins. Co. 265 A. D. 388, affd. 290 N. Y. 883.

If an oral offer declares that it will remain open for a stated time, the offeror, if he has received no consideration for his promise to hold it open, may withdraw it before the stated time has elapsed and thus render any subsequent acceptance ineffectual because there is no longer an offer to be accepted. If the offer is accepted before its withdrawal or termination, it ripens into a contract. If such offer is in writing signed by the offeror or his agent* it is not revocable during that period because of the absence of consideration. If the written offer does not state a period of irrevocability, it is considered irrevocable for a reasonable time. 

Real Property Law § 279 (4); Personal Property Law § 33 (5). 

If the oral offer is one to enter into a unilateral contract, it can be withdrawn at any time before the act requested has been performed. The offer may be withdrawn even though the offeree has *If a realty interest is affected, the agent's authority must be in writing.

begun to perform or is seen approaching with the intention of proffering performance, subject, however, to the statement in the preceding paragraph.* 

Petterson v. Pattberg 248 N. Y. 86. Consideration

Consideration, the third element, is the doing or promising to do what one is not legally obligated to do, or the refraining from doing what one may legally do, for a promise or act which is the motive for the promise, the doing or refraining. The detriment to the promisee is not consideration merely because the promise induced the detriment. The promise and the consideration must purport to be the motive for each other. Thus, if A promises B a sum of money, and in reliance upon that promise B purchases a home intending to use that money to pay for it, B cannot enforce A's promise merely because he has suffered a detriment. The promise and the detriment were not the motive each for the other. Likewise, a voluntary_payment by P of D's debt to X, does not require a payment by D to P.

Olmstead v. Olmstead 138 Misc. 839, 247 N. Y. S. 350. 

These have been held sufficient consideration to permit the enforcement of a promise given in exchange: refraining from smoking for a period of years, at the request of another; a promise to advocate the cause of the promisee; a promise not to file a petition in bankruptcy against another; an agreement to withhold suit, though no set period is agreed upon. If no fixed time is set, the time must be reasonable. If the person who so agrees to withhold suit honestly and reasonably believed his claims to be at least doubtful, forbearance to sue is good consideration. A withdrawal by a girl's father of his objection to her marriage to a promisor is good consideration though the girl did not require her father's consent. A parent has a right to try to induce his child not to marry a specific person. 

Fredenburg v. Fredenburg 159 Misc. 525 

Hamer v. Sidway 124 N. Y. 538; Post v. Thomas 212 N. Y. 264 

Strong v. Sheffield 144 N. Y. 392; Miller v. Vanderlip 285 N. Y. 116, 125

If A plans to default in his contract with B, and C then promises A an additional sum if he does not break his contract, C's promise cannot be enforced. A has given up no legal rights and he cannot collect from C, for being already bound to carry out his contract with B, A, by promising not to default, has not given any consideration for the additional promise of C. 

Vanderbilt v. Schreyer 91 N. Y. 392.

The court in two sets of circumstances has held that A could collect from C, the second promisor. *By statute, a unilateral offer binds the offeror when the performance is tendered if the offer was in writing, for the purpose of satisfying all or part of a then existing obligation. See infra page 123.

117 (a) In one case the defendant owner of premises, contracted for the building of his house. The contractor sub-contracted the building of the foundation to the plaintiff. During the progress of the work the plaintiff told the defendant that he intended to abandon his contract as he felt the contractor was not financially responsible. 

The defendant thereupon promised to pay when he finished the work. On default of payment by the contractor, plaintiff sued the defendant and recovered. 

Manetti v. Doege 48 A. D. 567, 62 N. Y. S. 918. (b) In the second instance a marriage contract was involved. A was engaged to marry the daughter of C, and the latter promised A to pay him and the daughter an annuity after the marriage. The court held that in such cases the other party to A's contract (the daughter in this case) was linked with A, and C's promise to A was to be read as follows: "If you and my daughter will not rescind or modify your contract to marry, I will pay you an annuity of $10,- 

000." Undoubtedly, if C promises A and B jointly to give them $10,000 to induce both not to rescind or modify their contract, C's promise can be enforced, as a legal right has been given up by them. 

De Cicco v. Schweizer 221 N. Y. 431 

Past Consideration

Past Consideration is not sufficient to render an oral promise enforceable. If A paints B's house without having been requested to do so, a later oral promise by B to pay is unenforceable, since the consideration for B's promise was past. The promise was not the motive for the detriment. If, however, a promise is in writing and signed by the promisor or his agent*, and the consideration is expressed in writing, the promise is enforceable despite the above rule, if the consideration is proved to have been given. 

Real Property Law §§ 279 (2); Personal Property Law § 33 (3) 

There are additional instances where past consideration would be a valid consideration. In all these instances the background is moral consideration, i.e., it seems just that a claim should be satisfied. But the elements of a good contract must have existed though some defense created by law bars recovery on the contract. The additional promise for past consideration removes the bar which existed prior to the additional promise. These instances are: (1) The Statute of Limitations has already run to completion. 

A promise or acknowledgment then made can be enforced if made in writing; or, in case of a debt, if part payment of principal or interest is made. The promise, acknowledgment or payment starts the statute running again.

Civil Practice Act § 59. 

To make payments effective against a party to save a claim from the statute of limitations they must have been made by him or for him by his authorized agent and must be made with intent to make *If a realty interest is affected, the agent's authority must be in writing.

future payments. Payment by a trustee in a bankruptcy or by an assignee pursuant to a general assignment is not a voluntary payment by the debtor and does not revive the statute. Nor does the application of receipts of the sale of collateral by the creditor constitute such part payment sufficient to toll the statute, even though the original loan instrument authorized the creditor to sell. 

B'klyn. Saving Bank v. Wechsler 259 N. Y. 9 

American Woolen Co. v. Samuelson 226 N. Y. 61 

United Trust Co. v. Burgess 175 Misc. 511. (2) A debt discharged in bankruptcy is revived and becomes actionable only by virtue of an unequivocal statement in writing in which the debtor expresses his assumption of an obligation to pay the debt. Partial payment by itself is not sufficient to waive the bar. 

The promise must be clear, unequivocal and express, and may be made after the petition is filed. A written statement "If I can get going again the bankruptcy will mean nothing-every dollar I owe will be paid" was held not to amount to a new promise. 

Linzer v. Weitzen 292 N. Y. 306 

Meyer v. Price 250 N. Y. 370

Stern v. Starr 282 N.Y.S. 516; Personal Property Law § 31. 

The action in either of the above two instances may be maintained upon the new promise or upon the original cause of action. 

Dusenbury v. Hoyt 53 N. Y. 521. (3) A promise by an adult to perform a contract made during his infancy is enforceable and infancy cannot be set up as a defense. (4) An endorser discharged because he received no due notice of dishonor waives the discharge by a clear promise to pay. The promise need not be in writing. 

Ross v. Hurd 71 N. Y. 14. (5) Where a contract is unenforceable because it is oral and therefore within the Statute of Frauds. it is enforceable when it is later put into writing.

Illegal Consideration 

Where there is a single consideration for one or more promises and any part of that consideration is illegal or against public policy, the promises cannot be enforced. If there are several such considerations the promises are also unenforceable. Where there are several considerations and several promises and each consideration can be correspondingly apportioned to each promise, recovery may be had upon the promises which are supported by the legal considerations. 

Remington v. I. B. Machine Co. 167 Misc. 108, 3 N. Y. S. (2nd) 515.

A promise in consideration of illicit cohabitation or of the suppression of evidence or the commencement of any action in divorce though the parties are living apart, is void. An agreement to waive the Statute of Limitations at the inception of liability contravenes public policy and is unenforcible. 

Fidelity & Deposit Co. v. Palmer 252 A. D. 55, 297 N.Y.S. 646 Pine v. Okoniewski 256 A. D. 519, 11 N.Y.S. (2nd) 13 

Angresani v. Tozzi 245 N. Y. 558; Gould v. Gould 261 A. D. 733

CONTRACTS 

119 It is not contrary to public policy for a person having a proper interest in another to restrict marriage along certain lines, as infancy and relationship. In fact, all reasonable restraints designed to prevent hasty or imprudent marriages are permissible. But agreements creating general restrictions on first marriages are void. 

Re Estate of William Burnside 176 Misc. 562.

Subscription to Charities — Promissory Estoppel 

A mere naked promise to contribute a sum to a named charitable institution would seem to lack the element of consideration. Certainly the request that other subscribers make contributions in reliance on the promisor's contribution even if stated as a consideration in the subscription agreement, is not consideration to support the promise. The courts, however, have leaned toward enforcement of these promises. The subscription agreement is treated like an offer to make a unilateral contract which when acted upon by incurring liability, becomes a binding obligation. An invitation to carry on the charitable work need not be expressed in the subscription agreement- it may be implied. Where the request that the promisee go on with his work cannot be implied, the court will invoke the theory of promissory estoppel, provided the charitable institution has in some way relied on the promise to pay. 

I & I Holding Co. v. Gainsburg 276 N. Y. 427

Where A promises a sum of money and requests that the fund bear his name or the name of some person, and the donee accepts a part of the gift or acts in conformity with the request, there is a direct detriment to the promisee, declared by the court to be the motive for the promise, and an enforceable contract exists without resort to the doctrine of promissory estoppel. 

Keuka College v. Ray 167 N. Y. 96 

Allegheny College v. Bank 246 N. Y. 369 

Mutuality Rule

When parties effect negotiations looking toward the creation of a bilateral contract, there must be mutuality of obligation to effect a binding contract. A promise by one party to perform cannot be enforced by the other party if the latter is left free to perform or not. 

If A writes B, "As long as your purchases amount to not less than $10,000, I will give you exclusive agency in New York," B cannot enforce A's promise for the exclusive agency if A desires to terminate it, as there is nothing in the agreement compelling B to purchase anything. There was no mutuality of obligation. 

Smith v. Diem 223 A. D. 572, affd. 249 N. Y. 590.

Where the plaintiff, a jobber, entered into an agreement with the defendant by which the latter agreed to furnish plaintiff's requirements for resale during one year at a fixed price and there was no promise by the plaintiff to take any definite quantity, the court held the promise unenforceable for lack of mutuality. 

Schlegel Mfg. Co. v. Cooper's Glue 231 N. Y. 459.

A promise made to purchase all the items of a specific nature needed by the promisor in exchange for consideration would ordinarily be binding. But if the promisor at the time of the promise was not engaged in a business needing such items and had no present or future outlook for such need, a promise to buy means nothing under such circumstances. 

Ehrenworth v. Stuhmer 229 N. Y. 210

Nassau Supply Co. v. Ice Service Co. 252 N. Y. 277. 

A contract wherein a corporation agrees to buy back its stock from one who purchases or owns it is unenforceable because a corporation is permitted under the statute to buy its stock out of a surplus only. There is the possibility that the corporation will pay out its surplus as dividends, an act lying entirely within its own power, and thus is making a promise to do what it can by itself make legally impossible of performance. 

Topken, Loring & Co. v. Schwartz 249 N. Y. 206.

In this connection it has been held that if the contract to purchase was only part of an otherwise valid contract, e.g., a contract of employment, there would be mutuality. The contract then would be good unless it could be shown as a defense that the stock would have to be bought out of capital, there being no surplus. 

Richards v. Wiener 207 N. Ỹ. 59. 

Contracts of Employment 

A hiring is at will unless a definite period of service is specified. 

The master may discharge, and the servant leave, at any time. A hiring at so much per day, week or month or year, is an indefinite hiring, and no presumption arises that it was even for a day, but only at the rate fixed for whatever time the party may serve. If the servant seeks to make the hiring one of a definite term, the burden is upon him to establish it by proof. 

Watson v. Gugino 204 N. Y. 535.

In an action to recover a salary for the remainder of a term of em ployment after the plaintiff's discharge, the jury must pass upon (a) whether the plaintiff made diligent efforts to secure other employment of a similar character, and (b) if he secured other employment, what the compensation was, and (c) whether the compensation was as much as he could have earned in good faith during the unexpired part of the contract. 

Schwed v. Kennedy 220 A. D. 189, 221 N.Y.S. 179

The Statute of Frauds - Contract for Services 

A contract which by its terms is not to be performed within one year from the making thereof or the performance of which is not to be completed before the end of the lifetime of a person, not necessarily one of the contracting parties, must be evidenced by a note or memorandum in writing, subscribed by the party to be charged or his lawful agent, otherwise it is voidable as a contract. The day in which the contract is made is not counted as part of the year.

CONTRACTS 

121 The year begins on the day following the making of the contract though it be a Sunday. Thus an oral contract made on February 15 to end next February 15, is outside the statute. 

Bayreuther v. Reinisch 264 A. D. 138, affd. 290 N. Y. 553

Goon v. Fu Manchu Restaurant 253 A. D. 531, 2 N. Y. S. (2nd) 879. 

Nothing short of full performance by both parties will take the contract outside of the operation of the Statute of Frauds. Where there has been part performance there can be recovery only in quantum meruit. 

Tyler v. Windels 180 A. D. 698, affd. 227 N. Y. 589.

Where payments are made upon such contract and the defendant is in default, the money paid may be recovered back in an action for money had and received. In this respect it differs from a contract for the sale of merchandise of $50 or more. There part delivery dispenses with the need of a written memorandum and the contract becomes enforceable. 

Personal Property Law § 31 

Sophie v. Ford 230 A. D. 568, 245 N.Y.S. 470 

Kremer v. Kremer 243 A. D. 66, 276 N.Y.S. 212

Power v. Matthews-Kadetsky Co. 242 A.D. 1, 273 N.Y.S. 44 

David Taylor Co. v. Fansteel Products 234 A. D. 548, affd. 261 N. Y. 514.

The courts have shown a marked tendency to consider a situation to be outside the statute wherever possible. So, an oral contract to build a house within fifteen months; to account to the plaintiff for all proceeds from the sale of realty, provided the defendant should not be required to pay any sum due before a year from date; to pay upon the determination of a suit; on the marriage of a third person; upon the restoration of health, were all held to be outside the statute as the contingency might occur within the year. 

Sherrill v. Bull 129 Misc. 623, affd. 222 A. D. 792 

Gallagher v. Finch 211 A. D. 635, 207 N. Y. S. 403.

An oral contract to make a written contract is unenforceable where such an oral contract embodying the same terms as the intended written contract would itself be unenforceable because of the Statute of Frauds. 

Deutsch v. Textile 212 A. D. 681, 209 N. Y. S. 388.

If we have an express contract of employment for a year, and the employer permits the employee to continue working after the beginning of the ensuing year, it is not clear whether the law implies, as a proper inference of fact, that the employment is to continue for for another year*. If during the first year of employment the parties discuss their relationship for the coming year and new terms are orally agreed upon to begin at the termination of the year's employment, this contract is within the Statute of Frauds, as the oral contract could not by its terms be terminated within a year from the making thereof. 

Lonsdale v. Migel 222 A. D. 197, 225 N. Y. S. 593. *See Foster v. White 3 N.Y.S. (2nd) at page 459.

Every agreement made in consideration of marriage must be in writing.* 

The memorandum, to satisfy the Statute of Frauds must contain all the material terms of the agreement fixed by the parties. An incomplete writing may not be supplemented by testimony of oral promises omitted from the writing. But a complete agreement is not necessarily void though the writings sets forth only the promises upon which there has been discussion and agreement. The relationship between the parties and the circumstances may be such that the terms not written down and not discussed may have been taken for granted by both. Then the agreed terms written into the memorandum together with those assumed, become the enforceable contract. 

Stulsaft v. Mercer Tube Co. 288 N. Y. 255.

Agreement to Settle- Accord and Satisfaction 

If A is indebted to B in a fixed sum which is undisputed, an oral promise by B to accept a lesser sum in full settlement is not binding on B if there was no consideration for his promise to take less, for when A promised to give less he did not promise to do any thing he was not already bound to do. But a writing executed after 

April 13, 1936, releasing all or part of the claim or lien is enforceable though without consideration. 66 

Jaffray v. Davis 124 N. Y. 164.

When the amount involved is unliquidated, a lesser sum paid may settle the claim. Thus if a creditor after an honest dispute retains for an unreasonable length of time or deposits a check marked full settlement," or so retains or deposits a check not so marked when the buyer says it is to be in full settlement of a disputed claim without any objection, it is a full accord and satisfaction. If the check was marked "in full settlement," the fact that the seller endorsed it "Received this check on account" does not change the situation; it is a full accord and satisfaction, and therefore binding. 

Byrne v. Padden 248 N. Y. 243, 249; Schnell v. Perlman 238 N. Y. 362 

Schuttinger v. Woodruff 259 N. Y. 212.

Where A acting as P's agent for the sale of merchandise collects a sum of money, deducts 10% therefrom as his commission and returns the balance by check in full settlement, the acceptance of this check does not bar recovery by P of the sum deducted on the ground that there was nothing due to A, for there was no dispute at the time the check was sent; what was sent was due to P in any event 

Hudson v. Yonkers Fruit 258 N. Y. 168. *Before the statute abolished actions for breach of promise to marry, mutual promises to marry did not have to be in writing. **Besides, the law will not suffer an agent to withhold moneys collected for a principal's account by the pressure of a threat that no part of the moneys will be remitted to the owner without the approval of deductions beneficial to the agent. Such conduct is a flagrant abuse of the opportunities and powers of a fiduciary position.

123 Suppose J owes K $1,000. They agree that J is to give $800 and his horse as full payment. K tries to sell the horse but can obtain no more than $100 for it. He then sues for the other $100. He cannot recover. Any consideration (the horse in this case) except "money for less money" is good and valid in law. 

If a bilateral contract is made for the performance and acceptance at a future time of a stipulated performance in satisfaction of all or part of a present claim, contract, lease or mortgage, it is enforceable if in writing signed by the party to be charged. If this agreement is not performed by one party according to its terms, the other party may assert his right under the original claim or under the subsequent agreement at his option. 

If a written offer signed by the offeror or his agent is made to accept a designated act in discharge of a present claim, contract, lease or mortgage, the tender of such performance by the offeree before revocation of the offer, makes the offer binding upon the offeror, though he refuses to accept the performance.* 

Personal Property Law §§ 33a, 33b; Real Property Law §§ 280, 281. 

Novation

To constitute a novation there must be an extinguishment of the original obligation and an executed mutual agreement among the parties to both the old and the new obligation whereby a new party is substituted for the old. The theory is that the new debtor contracts with the old debtor that he will pay the debt, and the new debtor also so contracts with the creditor. There is therefore a complete novation where P accepts the promissory notes of S for his (P's) entire claim against D, all three parties consenting. 

Henderson v. Sheppard 231 A. D 610, 248 N. Y. S. 89.

A creditor when advised, after he has entered into a contract with two or more, that one of them has retired from the contract and the others have assumed the debt, may (1) insist upon the continued liability of the retiring debtor, or (2) by continuing so to deal with the new debtors as to evidence his intention, he may enter into a new contract to accept them as solely liable. If he does the latter, he cannot hold the retiring party on the original contract. The assent of the creditor to the substitution must be established but the consent to enter into the new contract may be implied by conduct. 

Thus where the creditor of a partnership after dissolution thereof, knowing that one or several of the partners have agreed with the others to assume and pay the debts of the firm, takes the negotiable notes of those who should pay, in payment of the debts of the firm, he thereby cancels the claim against the firm and discharges the other partners. 

Schloss Bros. v. Bennett 260 N. Y. 243. *If a realty interest is affected, the agent's authority must be in writing.

Modification of Written Agreement 

An executory agreement cannot change, modify or discharge a written instrument which states that it cannot be changed orally, unless the executory agreement is in writing and signed by the party against whom the change, modification or discharge is sought or by his agent.*

Personal Property Law § 33c; Real Property Law § 282. 

Contracts of Infants 

The contracts of a person under 21 years of age, are valid but are voidable at the will of the infant. The fact that an infant has intentionally and fraudulently misstated his age and thus induced X to contract with him, does not estop him from setting up his infancy as a defense, for the courts will not permit an adult to enforce a contract by converting a cause of action in contract into one in tort. 

International Text Book Co. v. Connelly 206 N. Y. 188.

The disaffirmance must take place either before his attaining majority or within the period of the Statute of Limitations if the contract is executory or if the contract is executed, within a reasonable time after attaining his majority. 

Levenberg v. Ludington 152, Misc. 735, 274 N. Y. S. 193.

The cases are confusing as to the obligation of the infant to return the benefits received until disaffirmance. The present trend seems to be that the infant, in a contract involving personalty, may recover the consideration with which he parted, if he makes a demand before bringing the action and tenders back before suit whatever he has received which is still in his possession or control or if out of his hands, the reasonable value therefor. Thus where an infant buys an article for cash and then desires to avoid the contract and get back his money, he must return what he has and account for the deterioration in value. If he has deposited stock with a broker on a margin account and the stock was properly sold and a balance left with the broker, the infant disaffirming after the sale can recover only the amount remaining, since the sale when made was valid. A 15-year old infant was not permitted to recover the fare he paid for airplane transportation used. Recent cases have gone even further and have held the infant liable for what has been received by him. Thus where an infant used premises under a lease and was dispossessed for non-payment of rent, he was held liable for the reasonable value of use and occupation. An automobile repairer was held entitled to hold an automobile under his lien against an infant who would not pay for work he ordered.** 

Joseph v. Schatzkin 259 N. Y. 241; Pieri v. Nebbia 178 Misc. 388 

Sternlieb v. Normandie Natl. Sec. Co. 263 N. Y. 245

Vihnes v. T. & W. Air Inc. 173 Misc. 631 

Casey v. Kastel 237 N. Y. 305; Rice v. Butler 160 N. Y. 578 *If a realty interest is affected, the agent's authority must be in writing. **It is difficult to approve the rulings of the lower court decisions requiring an infant to pay for what he has received before he can be allowed to disaffirm when he is sued and is not seeking affirmative relief.

CONTRACTS 

125 If realty had been sold by the infant, and the purchase money had been squandered, the infant can avoid the contract and obtain his realty, provided he avoids the contract within the statutory period of limitations (10 years,) which commences to run on his attaining twenty-one. Mere delay in avoiding the sale is no ratification until the statutory period has passed. 

O'Donahue v. Smith 130 A. D. 214, 114 N. Y. S. 536.

An infant can affirm his contract for the sale of realty after majority. His affirmance must consist of an actual act of confirmation with the intention to affirm. Mere passive acquiescence, even for a length of time but short of the period of limitations, is not sufficient. Where, however, an infant who had purchsaed realty continued in possession, control, occupancy and management for a year after majority, the court held it to be an affirmance of the purchase. 

Whitman v, Home Guardian Co. 135 Misc. 598, 238 N. Y. S. 301.

Payments on account made shortly after attaining majority are not in and of themselves ratification as a matter of law. Ratification is a matter of intention and the payments are merely evidence. 

Hook v. Harmon N. R. Estate Co. 250 A. D. 689, 295 N. Y. S. 249.

An infant is liable for necessaries contracted for by him during his infancy. What constitutes "necessaries" depends upon the station in life of the infant. Usually they include food, lodging, medical attendance, and common education. The infant is liable in quasi-contract and so only for the reasonable value of the necessaries, if the plaintiff can show that the parent or guardian has not the means to pay or will not discharge his duty in furnishing the necessaries or that the infant is emancipated. 

Stetson v. Russell 130 Misc. 713, 225 N. Y. S. 139.

The defense of infancy is sufficiently set up when the defendant alleges that he was an infant and that the articles contracted for were not necessaries at the time of the contract. 

Morgan v. Smith 130 Misc. 412, 224 N. Y. S. 400 

Wilkinson v. Fleishman 238 A D. 858, 263 N.Y.S. 18

Regardless of the above rules, a contract made after April 13, 1941 may not be disaffirmed by an infant above 18 years of age on the ground of infancy, where the contract was made (a) in connection with a business in which the infant was engaged and (b) was reasonable and provident when made. The burden of establishing the elements (a) and (b) is upon the one seeking to enforce the contract.

Debtor & Creditor Law § 260. 

Contracts of Insane 

Contracts of one adjudged insane are absolutely void. Contracts of a person of unsound mind not yet judicially declared incompetent are voidable at his election upon recovering his reason or at the election of his committee or representatives or heirs. What the insane person received he must return. 

McCarthy v. Bowling 182 A. D. 18, 169 N. Y. S. 463.

Mistake

This section and the two following relate to the formation and not to the interpretation of a contract. 

Where parties deal face to face and the seller intends to transfer title to a person of good financial standing, a transfer of title to the person in front of him who falsely represents himself to be some other person, is a voidable transfer. The purchaser can pass good title by selling to a bona fide purchaser for value. 

If Jones, claiming to be Y, had personally obtained the goods, not upon credit, but by giving a forged check naming Y the maker, as the consideration, Jones would have been guilty of larceny. Jones would have obtained no title at all, and he could therefore pass no title even to a bona fide purchaser for value without notice. 

Amola v. Bernstein 214 A. D. 469, 212 N. Y. S. 518.

If a vendor and vendee negotiate by letter, and the vendee, who is A, signs as B, there is no contract and no transfer of title, even though the goods are shipped. Nor would there be a contract if A had come in person and falsely said he was B's agent. In these cases, the person with whom the vendor thought he was dealing was not actually before him. A sale by A to a bona fide purchaser would pass no title. 

Phelps v. McQuade 220 N. Y. 232 

Brotchener v. Üllman 141 Misc. 102, 252 N. Y. S. 244.

When the subject-matter is non-existent, unknown to both parties, there is no contract. So if T and S buy and sell a ship, which unknown to both had sunk the day before, no rights are conferred on either party. 

Duncan v. N. Y. M. Ins. Co. 138 N. Y. 88.

When there is a mutual mistake of identity, or quantity, or price, there is no contract. So if T and S buy and sell cotton from a ship called the "Peerless" and there are two such ships, and T means one, and S means the other, there is no contract. 

Misrepresentation and Fraud* "Misrepresentation" as used here refers to a quality and incident which do not involve the substance of the agreement. It is a false statement made by one who does not know of the falsity, but believes what he says to be true. If the representation is a component part of the contract, and is the essence of the agreement, it is a condition which justifies a rescission. But if the representation, though a component part of the agreement, is not of the essence, it is a warranty, and so justifies an action for damages and not rescission. 

Fraud to be actionable must be (1) Material to the inducement that brought about the contract; (2) About a fact and not an opinion; *For the remedies available to a party claiming to have been defrauded, see heading "Rescission of Contracts" in the subject "Equity," infra p. 220.

CONTRACTS 

127 (3) With knowledge of the falsity of the fact, or in reckless disregard of its truth; (4) The statement must have been made with the intention that it be acted upon; and (5) It must have been acted upon so that damage resulted. 

Owens v. Waterhouse 225 A. D. 582, 233 N. Y. S. 535.

If X, while insolvent, obtains goods from P on credit, the fact that X omitted to mention his insolvency to P will not be sufficient to avoid the sale. If, however, there is an intent never to pay at the time the goods are purchased, title does not pass to the purchaser. 

Hotchkin v. Third Natl. Bank 127 N. Y. 329.

Duress 

"Duress" is a threat of violence by one contracting party against, or imprisonment of, the person contracting or his near relative. It renders the contract voidable at the insistance of the victim of the duress. A threat to take legal proceedings does not constitute duress. 

O. P. R. R. Co. v. Forrest 128 N.Y. 83 

Crossways Apts. v. Amante 213. A. D. 43, 210 N.Y.S. 346 

Jaeger v. Canter 13 N. Y. S. (2nd) 414

Contracts for the Benefit of a Third Party 

The tendency has been to allow P as beneficiary of a contract between A and B to recover although P has furnished no consideration for the promisor's promise. At the present time the law on the point can be summarized by saying that the beneficiary P can sue on a contract made for his benefit if one of these conditions exists: (1) If there was a pecuniary legal obligation running from the promisee to the beneficiary at the time the promise was made by the the defendant for the benefit of the beneficiary. The fact that A, the promisee, owed an obligation to P, the beneficiary, links P up with A and makes P a privy to the consideration, given by A to B. 

Lawrence v. Fox 20 N. Y. 268.

Suppose a broker employed by a lessee to find someone to take over the balance of the lease, succeeds in getting such person. The lessee is unable to get the landlord's necessary consent to the arrangement and the deal falls through. Several months thereafter the landlord deals directly with the proposed tenant and arranges to give the latter a new lease and promises this new tenant to pay the broker his commission which he would have earned if the tenant had given his consent originally. The broker can not recover from the landlord because at the time of the promise there was no debt owing to the broker by the promisee. 

Freed v. Tishman 119 Misc. 721, 197 N. Y. S. 259.

By statutory enactment the grantee of realty is liable for all or a part of the mortgage debt evidenced by a bond and mortgage executed together, then a lien on the conveyed premises, if the grantee assumes payment of such debt in whole or in part, provided the grantee shall simultaneously with the conveyance to him of such realty, or upon an extension agreement or modification of the mort-

gage indebtedness, execute and acknowledge before an officer authorized to take acknowledgements of deeds, a written statement that he assumes the debt, giving the specific amount assumed. The grantee's signature and acknowledgment in a deed containing the assumption would also be sufficient.

Civil Practice Act § 10336. 

(2) If the beneficiary P, at the time the promise sued upon is made to the promisee, stands in such esteem and affection in the eyes of a party to the contract as a child or parent would stand. The actual relationship between them would permit the conclusion that a moral obligation to benefit the beneficiary should exist. A beloved niece, a wife, and an illegitimate child were permitted to recover as beneficiaries. 

Seaver v. Ransom 224 N. Y. 233; Todd v. Weber 95 N. Y. 181 

Buchanan v. Tilden 158 N. Y. 109. (3) If the contract is a "public contract," as where a municipality seeks to protect its residents by contracts for their benefit. Two tests are applied by which the right to maintain the action is determined: (a) whether or not the contract by its terms shows that it was intended for the benefit of the plaintiff; (b) whether or not there was some obligation or duty owing from the city to the third party.

Where a water company contracted with the city to furnish water to the residents at a certain rate, a resident was permitted to enjoin the collection of an increased rate. Likewise a resident near a canal was allowed to collect in contract from a contractor who damaged his house while blasting, because of a clause in the contract between the contractor and the city which stated that any damage to “structures along the canal" shall be remedied by the contractor. But in another case a taxpayer whose property was destroyed by fire was held not entitled to recover against a Water Company for a negligent breach of contract with the City to furnish water for fire hydrants for a rental paid by the city. For the inhabitant to be considered a beneficiary under a contract between the city and another, the benefit must be primary and immediate and show the assumption of a duty to make reparation directly to the individual member of the public. If a promisor undertakes to supply fuel for heating a public building, he is not liable for breach of contract to a visitor who finds the building without fuel and contracts a cold. The service was toward the city as an entity, and not toward individual customers.'

Lewis v. Dunbar 178 Misc. 980 

Pond v. New Rochelle Water Co. 183 N.Y. 330 

Moch v. Rensselaer Water Co. 247 N. Y. 160 (4) If the promise runs directly to P, at the request of a party to the contract, although P does not furnish the consideration. *For a good summary of public contract cases see Creedon v. Automatic Voting 

Machine Co., 243 A.D. 339, affd. 268 N. Y. 583.

129 (5) If the promisor acted so as to later cause a person to suffer a legal detriment while relying on the promise, the promisor will be estopped to assert the defense of "no consideration." 

McClaire v. Mass. Bonding Co. 266 N. Y. 371.

By their mutual agreement, the promisor and promisee may revoke the beneficiary's right before the latter ratifies it.* 

Kessler v. Haile 127 Misc. 413, 217 N. Y. S. 182 

Morales v. Joanon 146 Misc. 515, 262 N. Y. S. 468.

If A had an assignable contract with B, he can assign it to P and P can sue B in his own name, regardless of the above rules. Note that it is an assignment to which the reference is made and not a contract made by two for the benefit of a third person. Assignments

An assignment may be made either for value, as a gift, or for the purpose of enabling the assignee to sue though he be obligated to account to the assignor. In the absence of an agreement to the contrary, all rights to a sum of money arising after a breach of contract are assignable. An option is also assignable.** If the assignment is in writing signed by the assignor or his agent*** absence of consideration is no defense. 

Gellens v. 11 W. 42nd St. Co. 259 A. D. 435 

Farone v. Hall 128 Misc. 794, 220 N.Y.S. 1

Real Property Law § 279 (3); Personal Property Law § 33 (4). 

A bilateral contract for personal services cannot be assigned by either party as such a contract involves a personal relationship, and since performance cannot be delegated, the contract cannot be assigned. Thus, in one case it was held that an employce, who worked for X under a contract not to enter into similar services for another within a specified territory for eighteen months after leaving X's employ, could not be enjoined from so working for another by Y, who had purchased X's business, and this despite the fact that the employee worked for Y subsequent to the sale. The services were not personal in nature. 

Ave. Z Laundry v. Yarmush 129 Misc. 427, 221 N. Y. S. 506.

The following are not assignable-all claims to recover damages for personal injuries, such as libel, slander, malicious prosecution, assault and battery, false imprisonment, and other actions for personal injuries. A cause of action for injuries affecting estates, rather than persons, like conversion or deceit, is assignable. 

A "public officer" may not assign in advance his salary or other pay to be earned and to become due; the reason for this rule being *But cf. dictum in McCarthy v. Pieret, 281 N. Y. at page 410 where the court said that contracts for third party beneficiaries are executed contracts where the promisee is unable to revoke the arrangement or control the promisor in the fulfillment of the promise. **A corporation or an individual in the collection business is prohibited from accepting an assignment of a claim for the purpose of suit. that such an assignment tends to prevent the office holder from having the interest in his work he otherwise would have, to the public detriment. 

Diehl v. Sheehan 251 N. Y. S. 254, affd. 258 N. Y. 624.

An assignment of something which has no present, actual, or even potential existence when the assignment is made, does not operate to transfer the legal title to that thing when it does come into existence. Such an instrument, if made in good faith for a valuable consideration and not void as against public policy, operates as an executory contract to transfer such after-acquired property and creates an equitable lien thereon between assignor and assignee. But the legal title remains in the assignor, and at law that title is not transferred until either the equitable lien is enforced by judicial decree or some new act intervenes by which the assignor puts the assignee in possession thereof. An heir or expectant legatee or devise may assign his expectant or contingent interest, and the assignment will be enforced in equity, if made in good faith, for an adequate consideration and without fraud. 

In re Heye's Estate 149 Misc. 890, affd. 241 A. D. 907 

Nugent v. Smith 202 A. D. 739, affd. 234 N. Y. 611 

In re Merrihew's Estate 171 Misc. 541.

The parties to a contract may agree that rights thereunder are not assignable. It is one thing to agree that a chose in action shall not be assignable. It is another thing if the owner of the chose in action merely covenants with the obligor that he will not assign. In the latter case the assignment if made is good. The only consequence would be that the assignor would be liable for breach of his agreement not to assign.

Sacks v. Neptune Meter Co. 238 A. D. 82. 263 N. Y. S. 462. 

The assignee in every case takes subject to all the equities up to the time the debtor is notified or learns of the assignment. Whether or not the debtor assents to the assignment is immaterial. Therefore a bona fide purchaser for value does not acquire good title to a chose in action which he has bought from one who procured it by assignment from the owner by duress. 

Barry v. Equitable life Assur. Soc. 59 N. Y. 587.

The vendee is not liable to his assignee for the amount of the consideration for the assignment where the contract failed because the vendor was unable to perform. The assignee bought what his assignor had. But an assignor of a chose in action impliedly warrants that the claim is genuine and enforceable to the amount specified in the assignment.

Sabael v. Harrison 221 A. D. 879 22 N.Y.S. 633 County Securities v. Warwick 176 Misc. 272 

It is not necessary for the assignee to notify the debotor, in order to protect the assignment. Should the assignor assign the same credit to a second assignee, the latter would obtain nothing, because the assignor no longer had anything to assign. If, after the first assignment, the assignor or the second assignee received payment from the

131 debtor, the recipient would be liable to the first assignee. The monies collected would be held in trust for the first assignee and the latter would be entitled to an accounting in equity. Who did or did not give the debtor notice, is legally immaterial. 

The debtor, if he paid the second assignee in reliance upon notice from the assignor and without knowledge of the first assignment, would be discharged.
