Transfer of choses of action are within the Statute of Frauds exactly in the same manner and under the same conditions as transfers of goods.

Contracts Implied in Law and Fact 

Implied contracts are of two classes. One class is evidenced by the acts of the parties. These are contracts resting upon an implied promise in fact. Thus, if A enters B's store and in B's view takes an article from the counter, then nods to B, receiving B's nod in return we have a contract implied in fact. The actions of A implied the offer to buy at the regular price, and the actions of B implied the acceptance. Moreover, these actions expressed the real intention of the parties.

The second class consists of contracts implied by law where none in fact exists, i.e., quasi or constructive contracts created by the law rather than by the intentions of the parties. Such contracts rest upon the equitable principle that a person may not enrich himself unjustly at the expense of another. In reality no contract exists there is only a law-created obligation. If one man has obtained money by imposition, extortion, trespass or conversion, such money may be recovered back, for the law implies a promise from the wrong-doer to restore it to his rightful owner, although it is obvious that this is the very opposite of his intention. 

Miller v. Schloss 218 N. Y. 400.

A carrier can demand payment for freight charges from the consignee who accepts the goods despite the fact that the consignor is ordinarily liable for it. When the consignee accepts the freight in capacity of an owner, the law implies a promise on its part to pay. 

N. Y. C. R. R. Co. v. Warren 234 N. Y. 261.

Implied Conditions 

In every contract there is an implied undertaking on the part of each party that he will not intentionally do anything to prevent the other party from carrying out the agreement on his part. Thus, if the contract calls for A to do some work with implements furnished by B, the other contracting party, there is an implied condition that the implements furnished by B are suitable for the purpose, and if they are not, B cannot recover for breach of contract. 

In re People 250 N. Y. 410.

When a person by express language engages absolutely to do an act not impossible or unlawful, an unavoidable unforeseen accident will not excuse non-performance. The party should have protected

himself by appropriate excusatory stipulations in the contract. But there are cases where the law inserts conditions of its own accord. 

The doctrine of implied conditions is asserted to overcome the hardships of the strict enforcement of the letter of contract law in certain cases and do justice. Where a situation arises which clearly was not to affect the contract and for which the parties naturally enough failed to provide, or contemplate, the law will think for them along equitable lines and will imply such conditions as would have been in the minds of all the parties, had they thought of them. Thus where the defendant agreed to run cars every half hour over land it sold to plaintiff, for a certain period, or in case of breach, to refund the purchase money, the court held that failure to adhere to the schedule during a snowstorm was not a breach sufficient to permit the plaintiff to demand his money. The court implied the condition that the defendant would be relieved from the consequences of a slight breach of non-performance under the above rule. 

Maidment v. Krause 225 A. D. 492; Stewart v. Stone 127 N. Y. 500 

Buffalo & Land Co. v. Bellevue Land Co. 165 N. Y. 247.

When performance depends on the continued existence of a given person or thing and such continued existence was assumed as the basis of the agreement, death or destruction puts an end to the obligation for the contract is subject to an implied condition that the person or thing shall exist when the time of performance arrives. In every contract of personal service there is an implied condition that insanity, sickness or death shall be an excuse for nonperformance. This rule, however, does not apply where the condition to be performed consists of the payment of money. Where a policy of life insurance contained a clause forfeiting it in case of non-payment of premium when it became due, it was held that the insanity of the insured did not effect a waiver of the forfeiture clause. 

Wheeler v. Connecticut Mutual Life 82 N. Y. 543 

Buscini v. Paterno Const. Co. 253 N. Y. 256.

Where repairs are to be made on the buildings of another, there is an implied condition on both sides that the buildings on which the repairs are to be made shall continue in existence. The destruction of them without the fault of either party will excuse complete performance. The repairer recovers the contract price for the finished work and in quantum meruit for those party finished. If equipment had been installed the plaintiff may recover for such equipment and for the equipment delivered on the premises but not yet installed, but recovery was not allowed for the equipment prepared and not delivered on the premises. 

Gabler v. Evans 129 Misc. 911, 223 N.Y.S. 408 

Whelan v. Ansonia Clock Co. 97 N. Y. 293.

If B engages to do an act lawful at the time, but which is un- *It seems that where an employee's service under a term contract is interrupted by illness, the employer is obligated to pay wages until such time as he is justified in treating the contract of employment breached and he elects to terminate it. See Clark v. Irondequit Coal Co., 257 A. D. 63.

CONTRACTS 

133 lawful on the date of performance, B need not perform. There is an implied condition that an unlawful act will not be required. 

Boer v. Garcia 240 N. Y. 9

Vanetta Velvet Co. v. Kakunaka 256 A. D. 341, 10 N. Y. S. (2nd) 270... 

A defense is insufficient which attempts to explain away a failure to manufacture and deliver goods on the ground that the merchandise mentioned in the complaint if manufactured by the defendant, would have infringed patents of other parties. The defendant, having undertaken to manufacture and deliver the product was impliedly required to obtain a license from the patentee. Nor are scarcity of labor, of material, strikes, increased taxation excuses. 

Planetlite Co. v. Gleason 234 A. D. 304, 255 N.Y.S. 109 

Freund v. Zephyr Laundry 180 Misc. 249, affd. 266 A. D. 734. 

Conditions Precedent and Subsequent

Contracting parties may properly stipulate that the contract is not to have effect until the happening of a certain event or performance of an act or that the contract is to be considered terminated upon the happening of an event; or they may agree on certain conclusions to follow on any conditions existing. Thus, a clause can provide that the contractor shall be given an extension of his time for building the house if there is a strike among his workmen. 

This would mean that if the men went on strike (even if the contractor himself caused the strike) the contractor would be given more time.

If the parties have signed a full and complete contract, the fact that it provided that a more formal paper should be executed the following day does not make it less binding and effective. 

Hohauser v. Berwin 125 Misc. 834, 211 N. Y. S. 580.

Before a plaintiff can recover, he must allege and prove that he has duly performed or tendered performance of his part of the contract except as may have been prevented or waived or non-performance has been excused in some other way. If a condition precedent has not been performed because of the defendant's fault, the latter cannot take advantage of the failure. 

Aimes v. Wesnofske 255 N. Y. 156 

Rosenthal v. Natl. Folding Box 226 N. Y. 313, 322.

Failure to perfectly perform a contract to erect or improve a structure will not deprive the plaintiff of his right to recover for substantial performance where the work not done or defectively done, is not of great importance and the omission has not been deliberate. The plaintiff must show the defect to be unsubstantial and unintentional. An amount may be deducted from the contract price sufficient to make good any shortcoming. 

Blanchard v. Saratoga Springs 241 A. D. 193, 271 N. Y. S. 573.

It is the general rule that in contracts of purchase and sale, the conditions with respect to payment and conveyance are concurrent. 

But where part of the price is to be paid prior to conveyance, the covenants are not concurrent, but independent. If payment is to be

made upon a certain day and the consideration for the money is to be performed at a later date, the performance of the consideration is not a condition precedent to the right to recover the money payment. Where, however, the person entitled to payment in advance of the performance of the consideration neglects, upon the default of the payor, to sue for such payment until after the time set for performance of the consideration, the obligations which at first were independent become dependent and concurrent. It would in the latter case be a defense to the action for the money that the plaintiff has not performed his part. 

Loliver v. Palladino 226 A. D. 391, 235 N¸Y.S. 243 

Kennelly v. Shapiro 222 A. D. 488, affd. 250 N. Y. 523.

Very frequently building contracts contain a clause that no payment is to be made to the contractor unless a certain named architect or engineer gives his certificate of approval. Despite this condition precedent before becoming entitled to payment, recovery can be had where the certificate has been wrongfully or unreasonably refused. 

Nolan v. Whitney 88 N. Y. 648.

If, however, a contract for the sale of goods is involved and the contract provides that the approval of a certain named expert, not the buyer's agent, must be obtained before the buyer need accept the goods, an unreasonable refusal by this expert to give his approval is sufficient excuse for non-acceptance by the buyer. Only collusion or dishonest control of this party by the buyer can permit the seller to recover for this non-acceptance. 

Van Iderstine v. Barnet 242 N. Y. 425.

Where one is employed under a contract requiring him to do work which must meet with the satisfaction of his employer and he is discharged before the termination of the contract, a defense that he failed to satisfy would fail if the employer was unreasonable or arbitrary in his dissatisfaction. But if the contract was one involving fancy, taste and judgment, the unreasonableness of the employer plays no part. The only question is whether the dissatisfaction was feigned or genuine. The burden of coming forward with evidence to show that the discharge was because of his dissatisfaction, is on the employer, but the burden of the whole case must be sustained by the plaintiff employee who must show that the dissatisfaction was not genuine. 

Applegate v. McFadden 214 A. D. 221, 212 N.Y.S. 67 

Zitkin v. Max Heit Dress Co. 151 Misc. 241, 271 N. Y. S. 275

If A is bound by a contract with B for a definite period of time, and C deliberately and unjustly induces A to breach the contract, C is liable to B for damage. The rule is different where there is no employment for a definite time, or definite purpose, so that either party may leave the employ of the other at will, under the terms of the contract. 

Campbell v. Gates 236 N. Y. 457 

Vail-Ballou v. Casey 125 Misc. 689, 212 N. Y. S. 113.

CONTRACTS 

135 Waivers

A waiver is the voluntary abandonment or relinquishment by a party of some right or advantage. It is applied by the courts in order to defeat forfeitures. For that reason no consideration for the waiver is required, nor any prejudice or injury to the other party. 

Fisher v. U. S. Casualty 138 Misc. 307, 245 N. Y. S. 406. 

Where a party is entitled to receive payments at a specified date under a contract, the right to enforce a penalty for failure to pay may be considered waived and the plaintiff would be estopped, when the parties have established a usage to pay only after a written reminder or within a grace period or after the due date. Of course the effect of the usage may be terminated by giving notice that in the future strict compliance will be required, or the contract itself may provide that a specific indulgence must not be considered a waiver of the rights under the contract.

Montant v. Moore 135 A. D. 334; Moore v. Mootchnick 232 A. D. 705 Traynor v. John Hancock Ins. Co. 273 N. Y. 230. 

Anticipatory Breach

Renunciation of a continuous executory contract by one party before the day of performance gives no right to the other party to sue for damages before the time for the defendant's performance has arrived. There are two exceptions in which suit can be started at once: (1) in cases of personal service contracts and (2) contracts for the manufacture or sale of goods. 

Indian River Islands v. Mfrs. Trust Co. 253 A. D. 549. 

Contracts in Restraint of Trade 

Suppose D owns a dairy store and sells it to E. E, desiring to protect himself, has a stipulation put in the contract of sale that D is not to engage in the dairy business anywhere within five blocks of the store. This contract, even though it is unlimited in time and is in restraint of trade, would be an enforceable contract, because the protection that E gets is a fair protection for his particular contract, and does not interfere with the interests of the public. 

Lappono v. Marmone 204 A. D. 496, 198 N. Y. S. 433.

For similar reasons a provision in a contract restraining employment will not be enforced if it is more extensive as to time and space than will afford a reasonable protection to the employer's business. If the covenant unreasonably restricts the employee's right to pursue his trade, it is void. A clause restricting an inventor from entering the employ of a rival company for a year following the termination of his employment is a valid provision. A contract, however, by an ordinary workman not to enter other like employment for eight years after leaving his employer, when there is no element of secret or valuable information which he could impart, would be a contract in restraint in trade, unreasonable in its scope, and void. 

Clark v. Stenacker 236 N. Y. 312; Interstate Tea Co. v. Alt 271 N. Y. 76.

Price-Fixing Contracts 

A contract relating to the sale or resale of a commodity which bears a trade mark or trade name and which is competitive, may provide that the buyers will not resell the commodity except at the prices stipulated by the seller. It may also include a provision that any dealer to whom the commodity may be resold shall agree that he will not in turn resell except at the stipulated price. 

This restriction does not prevent the purchaser of a commodity from removing the brand, thus separating physical property which he owns from the good will which does not belong to him. When the brand is removed and the good will not utilized to aid the sale, there can be a sale at any price. Nor does the restriction prevent the sale at a lower price if the owner is closing out his stock for the purpose of discontinuing the sale of such commodity or sale of damaged goods.

General Business Law § 369a 

Guerlain v. Wooworth Co. 170 Misc. 150, 9 N. Y. S. (2nd) 886.

Illegal and Enforceable Agreements* 

Illegal contracts are generally unenforceable. Where a contract which violates a statutory provision is merely malum prohibitum and there is no statutory provision depriving a party of a right to sue and public safety is not involved, this rule will not necessarily be followed if the denial of relief would be wholly out of proportion to the requirements of public policy or would inflict undue punishment. So although it is a misdemeanor to sell securities to the public without first filing a notice with the Department of State, the plaintiff cannot rescind his subscription to the defendant's stock because of the failure to file the notice. The required statement had no relation to the transaction and the statute did not say that the sale was invalid. No recovery was allowed for liquor delivered without a license. Liquor traffic affected public health and welfare; likewise gambling, wagering and usurious contracts, a completed act of brokerage by an unlicensed real estate broker, work by an unlicensed plumber, detective agency, lawyer, physician, dentist, cannot be recognized. The licenses are not required for revenue purposes, but for public protection. 

Carmine v. Murphy 285 N. Y. 413 

Shorten v. Milbank 170 Misc. 905, affd. 256 A. D. 1069 

J. E. Rosasco Creameries v. Cohen 276 N. Y. 274

Though it is a misdemeanor for a person to enter a hospital and obtain a release for personal injuries within 15 days after the injuries were sustained, the release so obtained is not ipso facto void. 

Thorne v. Columbia Cab Co. 167 Misc. 72, 3 N. Y. S. (2nd) 537**. 

Where there is an agreement to pay more interest than 6% per *Illegality of a contract which is contrary to public policy, need not be pleaded affirmatively. When such illegality is apparent, the Court of its own motion will deny relief. Attridge v. Pembroke, 235 A.D. 101. **Reversed on other grounds, 168 Misc. 255.

General Business Law §§ 374, 379 

A contract between A and B cannot be enforced when its performance would require A to defraud X or to betray the confidence of X, or which would require A to destroy the effect of another contract between X and others, which contract A was under legal duty to protect. In a recent case (A), a newspaper man contracted with a news agency (B) to send radio messages while a passenger on the Graf Zeppelin (X) in reply to messages sent to him by his friends. The news agency made arrangements to collect the messages for publication as news of the flight. Newspaper man (A) at the time he engaged passage on the Graf Zeppelin (X) agreed that he would give no interviews and send no reports of the flight while en route and for eight days after the completion of the flight. The owners of the Graf Zeppelin (X) had contracted the exclusive news rights of the flight to a third party (Y). Newspaper man (A) apparently had full knowledge of the contract for exclusive news rights. When the newspaper man sought to collect under his contract with the agency, relief was denied. The court held that the contract was born in tort. 

Reiner v. North American Newspaper Alliance 259 N. Y. 250.

A seller cannot recover the price of goods sold where he has paid a commission to the purchaser's agent. Nor can the purchaser's agent recover a promised commission. This was the common law and is now part of the statutory law. 

Penal Law § 439 

Sirkin v. 14th Street Store 124 A. D. 384, 108 N. Y. S. 830.

Money advanced under an executed illegal contract cannot be recovered back where both parties were in pari delicto. Where the parties are not equally in guilt, or when it benefits the public interest to give relief to the more innocent of the two contracting parties, the contract will be set aside and the injured party will be restored to status quo as far as possible. In one case money paid to a marriage broker was recovered, even though marriage broker contracts are against public policy. The purpose was to discourage the business of marriage brokers. Similarly a casual bettor who has lost money to a bookmaker on a horse race may recover back such money. 

The statute permits recovery of money thus lost and paid. The bookmaker cannot recover back or offset money he has lost. In the *The Penal Law (Secs. 991-994) provides that a winner of a wager cannot recover from a welching loser and that the loser may recover any payment made.

A maker of a note who gave his note to a bank, knowing that it was to be treated as an asset of the bank solely for the purpose of deceiving the government's bank examiners and other depositors as to the solvency of the bank, was held estopped from pleading "no consideration," when sued by the bank upon the note. 

Bay Parkway Natl. Bank v. Shalom 270 N. Y. 172.

PRIVATE CORPORATIONS Forming the Corporation 

CORPORATION is formed by filing a certificate of incorporation with the Secretary of State in Albany, and paying the necessary fee and tax. This certificate contains (1) the name, (2) the purpose of the corporation, (3) the amount of stock, common (with par value and amount without par value) and preferred, including the dividends to be paid on the latter as well as preferences, privileges and voting powers of shares of different classes, (4) the ctly and county in which the principal office is to be, (5) the intended duration of the corporation, (6) the names and addresses of the directors (who must be at least three in number), the names and addresses of the subscribers to the certificate and the number of shares the latter take, (7) a statement that (a) the subscribers are of full age and at least two-thirds are United States citizens; (b) at least one is a New York resident, and (c) at least one director is both a United States citizen and a New York resident and (8) that the Secretary of State is designated as the agent of the corporation upon whom process in any action or proceeding may be served. The certificate must also contain the address to which the Secretary of State shall mail a copy of process served upon him. 

Stock Corporation Law § 5. 

The certificate is signed and acknowledged by each incorporator. 

A corporation other than a railroad corporation, which shall not do corporate business within two years from the date of its incorporation, may be dissolved in an action by the attorney general. 

General Corporation Law § 36. 

If the Secretary of State refuses to file a tendered certificate on the ground of alleged non-compliance with the statute, the validity of his objections may be determined in a court proceeding to compel the filing.

The certificate of stock issued by the corporation must have (1) the signature of the president or vice-president, (2) that of the secretary or treasurer or their assistants, and (3) the corporate seal. 

Stock Corporation Law § 65. 

The certificate as a legal concept is but evidence of title to the property right which its owner has in the corporate stock. Nevertheless, it is considered property for all practical purposes. A conversion of a certificate of stock is a conversion of the stock itself. 

Pierpont v. Hoyt 260 N. Y. 26.

The Corporate Entity 

The corporation is an entity separate and apart from its stockholders. The owner of even all the capital stock of a corporation 139

does not thereby become the legal owner of its property, but title to the latter is vested in the corporate entity. 

Brock v. Poor 216 N. Y. 387.

While a corporation will ordinarily be regarded as a legal entity, quite separate and apart from its stockholders, officers or directors, and from other corporations with which it is connected, the law will not permit this fiction to be carried to such an extent as to become a cloak for fraud or illegality. The courts will look beyond the fiction of corporate entity, where one is so organized, related to or controlled by the other as to be its mere instrumentality, or alter ego. 

While it is difficult to reconcile all the cases, the broad rule is that where one corporation acquires sufficient stock in another to control it, the corporate entity of the two organizations will be preserved where such acquisition is resorted to for the purpose of participating in the affairs of the owned corporation in the normal and usual manner. But where such stock ownership is acquired with the design of so dominating and regulating the subsidiary company that it becomes a mere dummy or department of the holding company, the court will not permit the owner to escape liability for the acts of its alter ego, and will deal with the real party in interest, as if the dummy did not exist. 

Pagel v. Harmon Paper Co. 236 A. D. 47, 258 N. Y. S. 168.

In one case the plaintiff sought to hold the defendant liable for personal injuries received through the negligence of a motorman who was operating a car on the tracks of the Forty-Second Street, Manhattan & Saint Nicholas Avenue Railway. Each company had the same executive officers, and practically the same board of directors. The Third Avenue Railway Company owned substantially all the stock and second mortgage bonds of the Forty-Second Street Railway Company, but only a part of its first mortgage bonds, and made large loans to it from time to time. All the cars which ran over the tracks of the two companies were marked the "Third Avenue System." Cars were purchased by the Third Avenue Railway Company and leased to its various subsidiaries. But the wages of the motormen and conductors operating on the tracks of the Forty- Second Street Railway Company were paid by that corporation, as well as many other expenses for maintenance and repair. The corporate entity of the two corporations was recognized and upheld, and the plaintiff was denied a recovery against the dominant company. 

Berkley v. Third Avenue Railway 244 N. Y. 84.

If a corporation has been dissolved by proclamation of the Secretary of State for non-payment of franchise taxes and its directors do business in its name, they would be individually liable. 

Poritzky v. Wachtel 176 Misc. 633. 

Ultra Vires Contracts 

Any contract made which is not within the corporate purpose is considered ultra vires (beyond its powers). Whether the courts will

PRIVATE CORPORATIONS 

141 enforce an ultra vires contract depends upon how far the transaction has gone. If the contract has been executed and performed on both sides, the court will not interfere, but will leave the parties as it found them. If neither side has performed, so that the contract is entirely executory, the court will not aid either party in the enforcement of the contract. But if the corporation alone has performed, the court will give the corporation relief, for whatever harm can be done has already been done. If the other party alone has performed, the corporation cannot be held unless it has received a practical benefit from the other party's performance. If both sides have partly performed, there can be a recovery on the basis of quantum meruit. 

Appleton v. Bank 190 N. Y. 417; Stock Corporation Law § 16 

Leinkauf v. Lombard 137 N. Y. 417 

Whitney v. Barlow 63 N. Y. 62; Jemison v. Bank 122 N. Y. 135

When, however, an ultra vires act affects only the interests of the stockholders, it may be sanctioned by the assent of the stockholders. 

Behrman v. Zeman 130 Misc. 846, 225 N. Y. S. 385.

Stockholders who consent to an ultra vires act cannot thereafter be heard to complain concerning the act of which they themselves approved. The consent may either be a positive act or neglect to act promptly to condemn the unauthorized act. 

Santos v. National Bank 130 Misc. 348, 223 N. Y. S. 817.

A corporation is not bound by agreements between promotors made before its formation, unless adopted after incorporation. 

Corporate Rights (1) Changing Bonds to Stock.-With the consent of two-thirds of the capital stock, the directors may allow bondholders to change their bonds into stock. If there is not enough stock to supply the demand, the capital stock may be increased to meet the demand. 1 

(2) Right to Change Its Name.-A corporation may change its name by filing a certificate giving the old name and the new one. 

The holders of all outstanding shares must sign and acknowledge their signatures on the certificate filed for that purpose with an affidavit of the secretary or assistant secretary authenticating their authority but the president or vice-president and secretary or assistant secretary may do so if they are so authorized by a majority of the votes of all outstanding shares at a meeting called for that purpose. 

General Corporation Law § 40. 

(3) Right of Merger.-Any stock corporation, authorized to do business in New York, that owns all the stock of another corporation authorized to engage in a similar business in this state, may merge with the latter corporation which becomes liable for the obligations of the merged corporation. The combined corporation may assume the name of either corporation.

Stock Corporation Law § 85. 

Even a guaranty agreement held by the merged corporation may

be asserted against the guarantor by the absorbing corporation subsequent to the merger. 

Bank of U. S. v. Glickman 241 A. D. 92, affd. 265 N. Y. 539. (4) Purchase of Stock.-A corporation may buy its own stock but only out of its surplus and not out of its capital stock.* 

Cross v. Begullin 226 A. D. 349, affd. 252 N. Y. 262.

A stock corporation may own, sell or pledge stocks, bonds or notes of any other corporation if the certificate of incorporation permits, or if the corporation whose stocks, bonds or notes are acquired is engaged in a similar business or is engaged in work necessary or useful to the business of the other corporation. 

Stock Corporation Law § 18. 

2 A stock corporation with the consent of the holders of record of two-thirds of the outstanding shares entitled to vote thereon, at a meeting properly called for that purpose, may sell its property, franchises, privileges and rights to any corporation, but its franchise can be sold only to a domestic corporation. 

While the sale of the assets of a corporation changes the character of the business of the vendor corporation, and establishes the right of a dissenting stockholder to have his stock appraised, it does not necessarily amount to an actual dissolution. 

In re Clark's Will 257 N. Y. 487; Stock Corporation Law § 20. 

Any stockholder not voting in favor of the proposed sale may at any time prior thereto, object and demand payment for his stock. 

If notice of the meeting was not mailed to him at least twenty days prior to the taking of the vote, the stockholder may object and demand payment within 20 days after the mailing. The objection and demand must be in writing and filed with the corporation. Thereupon within 60 days after such demand and upon 8 days' notice to the other, either the stockholder or the corporation may apply to special term of the supreme court in the judicial district in which the office of the corporation is located for the appointment of three appraisers. A majority of these appraisers may determine the value of the stock, subject to the court's approval. The value is fixed as of a time just prior to the taking of the action to which the objection is made. It should be noted that an objection without a demand on time is insufficient.

Stock Corporation Law § 21 

In re O'Brien 182 Misc. 577. (5) Right to Consolidate.-Two or more domestic corporations may consolidate. A certificate must be filed with the secretary of state giving facts about the new corporation, e.g., location, directors, terms of consolidation, etc. The certificate is signed in a fashion similar to that of the certificate of change of name.

Stock Corporation Law §§ 88, 89, 90. 

(6) Right to Mortgage Its Property.-Every stock corporation other than a moneyed corporation shall have the power to borrow money and contract debts when necessary for the transaction of its business, or for the exercise of its corporate rights, privileges or franchise, or for any other lawful purpose of its incorporation; and it may mortgage its property and franchises to secure the payment of such obligations, or of any debt contracted for such purposes. 

The consent to the execution of such mortgage, except a purchasemoney mortgage, by the holders of not less than two-thirds of the total number of shares outstanding entitled to vote thereon, given either in writing or by vote at a meeting of the stockholders called for that purpose, shall be required. Without such consent a corporate mortgage, is deemed invalid and ineffectual to create a lien on corporate property.

Maryland Cas. Co. v. Schaefer 141 Misc. 629, affd. 256 N. Y. 663. 

(7) Right to Issue Stock. A corporation may issue stock only for property or money or services actually received from someone, not necessarily the purchaser, for the use and lawful purposes of the corporation, to the extent of the full value of the stock issued. If less is received, creditors can hold the stockholders liable to the extent of the inadequacy of the consideration for which the stock was issued. But neither a promotor, nor anyone else, can get stock for services rendered before the corporation actually existed. The directors, if there is not any fraud, are the final judges of the value of the property or the services.

(8) Guaranty of Obligations.-A stock corporation may guarantee an obligation for the payment of money (a) when the guaranty is made in connection with and incidental to the exercise of corporate rights and purposes; (b) or with the negotiation by sale or otherwise of an obligation owned by it; (c) if the guaranty is that

of another corporation at least a majority shares of which is then owned, directly or iindirectly by the guarantor corporation and the guarantee is approved by a resolution of the latter's board of directors; (d) when the guaranty is approved by the holders of 2-3 of the outstanding shares entitled to vote thereon at a properly called meeting, or by the written consent without a meeting of all the outstanding shares entitled to vote thereon. 

Stock Corporation Law § 19. 

Liability of a Corporation for Crimes and Torts 

A corporation is liable on its contracts, for its torts, and for its crimes. În its crimes or torts it does not matter if the corporation was then engaged in ultra vires acts. Although an artificial body can hardly be said to have criminal intent, the courts have said that if the authorized officials commit a crime in the corporate name, the corporation is liable to a fine (you cannot imprison the corporation) or the charter may be taken away. The agents of the corporation who personally participate can be imprisoned. 

A director ignorant of a defect which caused the injury, may recover against his corporation in tort, though the other directors may be aware of the condition. Notice to them or their knowledge is not imputed to the plaintiff. 

Stearns v. Schenectady Day Nursery 288 N. Y. 574.

Stockholders' Rights 

Ownership of stock carries with it the enjoyment of any rights or privileges attached to the stock. The stockholder whom the corporation need recognize is not the indorsee of the stock or the actual holder. It is the holder of record as shown on the corporate books, unless the corporation has knowledge of the real owner. Nevertheless, as between the record holder and a purchaser from him, the seller becomes a trustee for the purchaser and must account for benefits received. 

Holbrook v. New Jersey Zinc Co. 57 N. Y. 616 

Broderick v. Aaron 264 N. Y. 368, 268 N. Y. 260. (1) Rights to Dividends.-A dividend belongs to the stockholder who owns the stock when it is declared and the relationship between that stockholder and the corporation, is that of creditor and debtor. 

Dividends of stock sold after dividends are declared but before they are payable, belong to the seller. Dividends declared before the death of the life tenant belong to his estate, although they are not payable until after that event. Even though the corporation declares that the dividends are to be paid at a later date without specifying a date on which the stockholders entitled to such dividends are to be determined, the dividends belong to the owner on the day of the declaration. But when directors provide that it shall be payable only to stockholders of record on a day certain, only stockholders at the time so fixed are entitled to the dividend. A corporation is pro-

The assertion that no pre-emptive right may vest in a stockholder in respect to unissued authorized stock has been disavowed as being too broad. Under this new rule if an amended certificate (a) alters or abolishes any preferential rights of any outstanding shares having preferences, affecting the holders of such shares adversely; or (b) creates, alters or abolishes any provision or right in respect of the redemption of any outstanding shares or of any sinking fund for the redemption or purchase of any such shares or of any sinking fund

If notice of the meeting was not mailed to the stockholders entitled to receive notice of the meeting at least 20 days prior to the taking of the vote, then the objection may be made within 20 days after the mailing. With the objection, there must be a demand for payment of the stock.

The objection and demand must be in writing and filed with the corporation. If the action is effected without a meeting, the time to file the objection and demand shall expire on the 20th day after the mailing to such stockholder of a notice stating the nature of the action and the date on which the amended certificate was filed. 

Liabilities of Stockholders 

When a person enters into a subscription agreement with a corporation, the statute makes him liable to creditors of the corporation for the full amount of unpaid calls on it, provided the debts were incurred by the corporation in transactions which were not ultra vires. It does not matter that the certificate of stock has not been issued to him. 

Allen v. Ryan 219 A.D. 634, affd. 246 N.Y. 609

Stock Corporation Law § 70. 

The liability of a stockholder to creditors for the amounts unpaid on his capital stock is joint and not several. He cannot contract with the corporation so as to relieve him from such liability. 

An action against a stockholder to recover upon unpaid subscriptions is barred, where over two years have expired since he has ceased to be a stockholder, or since the corporation has become hopelessly insolvent and has not and could not transact business and a receiver or trustce in bankruptcy has been appointed. 

Granger v. Allen 214 A. D. 367, affd. 244 N. Y. 587 

Schnitzler v. Tartell 130 Misc. 565, 224 N. Y. S. 339

Before a stockholder may be held liable for the corporate debt solely because he is a stockholder, the following must exist: (1) The creditor must first have obtained judgment against the corporation and execution must have been returned unsatisfied. (2) The stockholder must have been a stockholder when the debt was incurred. (3) The debt must have been payable within two years from the time it was contracted.

(4) The action against the corporation must have been started within two years after the amount claimed became due. 

Stock Corporation Law § 73 

Granger v. Allen 214 A. D. 367, affd. 244 N. Y. 587.

Where a laborer or employee of a corporation has a claim for payment for services, stockholders of domestic corporations are jointly and severally liable even though their stock be fully paid and nonassessable, provided the claimant within thirty days after work is done notifies the stockholder that should there be an execution against the corporation returned unsatisfied, he will hold the stockholder liable personally. The stockholder will be personally liable, provided that an action is begun against him within thirty days after the return of the unsatisfied execution. The following have been held proper claimants under this section: a civil engineer, newspaper reporter, bookkeeper, sales agent instructing customers in the use of articles sold, ball player. Lawyers, general managers with full control and officers of the corporation are not employees under this rule. 

Armstrong v. Dyer 268 N. Y. 671 

Evans v. Lawrence Stern & Co, 270 N. Y. 177

Stock Corporation Law § 71; Bristor v. Smith 158 N. Y. 157 

Bogardus v. Fitzpatrick 139 Misc. 533, 247 N. Y. S. 692.

A pledgee of stock is not liable as a stockholder. The pledgor is. 

Stock Corporation Law § 71; Bristor v. Smith 158 N. Y. 157. 

Transfer of Shares

An innocent purchaser for value of a certificate properly endorsed gets title as against one from whom that certificate may have previously been obtained by theft, fraud or duress or who may have lost that certificate. The certificate is treated as a negotiable document for the purpose of transfer. Thus a forged indorsement would not transfer title.

Stock Corporation Law §§ 166-169. 

Where a certificate is hypothecated to the plaintiff without indorsement, the plaintiff acquires an equitable lien and the owner may be compelled to complete the transfer by making the indorsement. 

Suchy v. Frankenberg 251 A. D. 349, 296 N. Y. S. 545.

If the stockholder accepts a stock certificate from the corporation with knowledge of a by-law printed on the face thereof requiring a stockholder to offer the stock to the corporation before selling it to others, he is estopped from questioning the validity of the by-law. The fact that he believed the corporation was in no financial condition to purchase the stock is immaterial. 

Hassel v. Pohle 214 A. D. 654, 212 N. Y. S. 561.

It is the duty of the transferor of stock to affix transfer tax stamps at the time of the transfer. Failure to do so means that the transferor may be barred from offering any proof relating to the transfer in any court in the state. This right to bar proof (1) may

PRIVATE CORPORATIONS 

149 be waived by the transferee by failing to plead it or by some other act showing a waiver. (2) It does not apply to proceedings to tax estates. 

Matter of Crump 289 N. Y. 287

Cooper v. Grosset 263 N. Y. 491. 

Meetings and Votes 

Notices of meetings may be signed by the president, or vice-president, or secretary, or assistant secretary and should contain the purpose and place of the meeting. They must be served in writing, personally or by mail, on each stockholder, no less than ten nor more than forty days before the meeting.

Stock Corporation Law § 45. 

A by-law to the effect that "no resolution of stockholders shall be adopted except by unanimous vote" is invalid, since it is inconsistent with the statute which in many instances fixes the required percentage necessary for approval, e.g.: Section 55 of the Stock Cor poration Law provides for the election of directors by a plurality vote of stockholders. A by-law requiring the unanimous vote of directors for a resolution is valid because the statute, though stating that directors may act by majority of a quorum, adds "except when otherwise required by law or the by-laws." 

General Corporation Law § 28 

Benintendi v. Kenton Hotel 181 Misc. 897,affd. 268 A. D. 857

Unless the certificate of incorporation or an amendment thereto provides otherwise, every shareholder of record is entitled to one vote for each share. The certificate, or an amendment thereto (not a by-law), may provide for cumulative voting for directors. Under this arrangement each stockholder is entitled to as many votes as shall equal the number of his shares multiplied by the number of directors to be elected and all the votes may be cast for a single director or distributed among as many as the voter sees fit. 

Where by unanimous vote of stockholders a resolution was adopted to amend the certificate to provide for cumulative voting for directors and the officers who were directed to file the amendment failed to do so, it was held that the rights of cumulative voting existed in the absence of prejudice to the rights of third parties. 

In re American Fibre Chair Seat Co. 265 N. Y. 416

General Corporation Law § 23; Stock Corporation Law § 49. 

A pledgor of stock who is the holder of record is prima facie entitled to vote. 

Elyea v. Lehigh Salt Mining Co. 169 N. Y. 29.

The inspectors of elections may keep the election open, within a reasonable discretion, as long as it is necessary to receive the vote of those present. An election is not vitiated because the polls were kept open after the time prescribed by the constitution and by-laws. 

Young v. Jebbelt 213 A. D. 774, 211 N. Y. S. 61.

Voting by Proxy

There may be voting by proxy at corporate meetings, except in religious corporations. An officer or clerk of a banking corporation cannot vote the share of a stockholder by proxy. The proxy, where allowed, must be in writing and may be good for any time specified. 

If no time is specified, the proxy is good for eleven months. But whether specified or not, it can always be revoked. The vote by proxy is as binding upon the stockholder as his own vote, except where the vote is cast in furtherance of a conspiracy or by collusion. 

Wellington v. Morris 132 Misc. 509, affd. 226 Á. D. 868

General Corporation Law § 19 

Voting Trust

A stockholder, by agreement in writing, may transfer his stock to a voting trustee, thus permitting the trustee to vote for him. The right to vote is thereby separated from the beneficial ownership of the stock. The right to vote is irrevocable for the definite period of the voting trust. A record of this voting agreement must be kept in the stock book of the corporation. The agreement must be for a period not exceeding ten years. There is no implied power in voting trustees to vote for the destruction or termination of the corporation but if a vote to sell the corporate assets were cast, the stockholder is required to make timely objection or his failure would be equivalent to a consent. Upon timely objection an appraisal of the stock may be had. 

Matter of Bacon 287 N. Y. 1

Stock Corporation Law §50; In re Morse 247 N. Y. 290. 

A voting trustee, unless specifically authorized, may not exercise his rights through another, but only in person. 

In re Green Bus Lines 166 Misc. 800, 2 N. Y. S. (2nd) 556. 

Directors and Officers

The management of the affairs of a corporation is vested in its board of directors as a board, and not in their individual capacity. 

Acting singly even all of the directors cannot bind the corporation. 

Unless a by-law otherwise provides, a majority of the board at a meeting duly assembled shall be necessary to constitute a quorum for the transaction of business and the act of a majority of the directors present as such a meeting shall be the act of the board. Each director is required to be a stockholder unless otherwise provided in the certificate of incorporation or in a by-law.* 

Knapp v. Rochester Dog Prot. Assn. 235 A.D. 436, 257 N.Y.S. 356 

In re Haecker 212 A.D. 167, 207 N.Y.S. 561

General Corporation Law § 27; Stock Corporation Law § 55 

The court will not regulate the conduct of directors in the reasonable performance of their duty, even though by their conduct they may render the corporation liable in damages. An agreement *In case of a conflict between the provisions of a by-law and the certificate of incorporation, the latter prevails. Davison v. Parke 285 N.Y. 500.

Clark v. Dodge 269 N. Y. 410; Fells v. Katz 256 N. Y. 67

The officers of a corporation and not the individual directors are treated as its agents and bind the corporation pursuant to the rules of agency.

Private instructions (and by-laws are that) do not limit the agent's authority as to third persons. Though a contract of employment for life, if authorized, will ordinarily be sustained, there is no implied authority in an officer to make a contract employing another for life under a general power to employ.

Heaman v. E. N. Rowell Co. 261 N. Y. 229

Directors and officers hold a position of trust and they are required to guard corporate property with the same degree of loyalty that men of average prudence apply to their private interests. For a violation of such duty resulting in a loss of corporate assets, they may be made to account to the corporation. This rule of liability is limited to fraudulent, dishonest or collusive acts and cannot be invoked for error of judgment or lack of efficiency.* 

Winters v. Anderson 242 A. D. 430, 275 N. Y. S. 373, 376.

If a business opportunity comes to such fiduciary which is in the line of the corporate activities and of advantage to it, the law will not allow him to divert the opportunity from the corporation and embrace it as his own. The corporation may impress the property which the fiduciary received together with all profits thereon, with a trust in its favor. The doctrine is not applicable if the opportunity is one which the corporation is financially unable to undertake. 

Blaustein v. Pan Ameruan 263 A. D. 97, affd. 293 N. Y. 281.

A director of a corporation whose business it is to buy securities of the corporation, does not act wrongfully if a purchase is made of stock in another corporation in which he or other directors are financially interested, provided the purchase is made solely for the benefit of the corporation and the director has not dealt with himself as an individual or in the character as trustee, director or of- Although a director who is about to buy stock from a stockholder is not permitted to practice active fraud upon the stockholder, there is doubt about the obligation of a director, before he makes the purchase, to disclose information he possesses. The weight of authority seems to be that he has no such obligation. See Fischer v. Guaranty Co., 259 A.D. 176, affd. 285 N.Y. 679.

Gerdes v. Reynolds 281 N. Y. 180.

Transactions between a director or officer and his corporation, or between boards having common members, for the sale or purchase of any property are regarded jealously by the law. The burden is upon those who would maintain the transaction to show that it was fairly and openly made for an adequate consideration and the corporation was adequately represented by other officers and direc tors. Should there be an increase in the capital stock authorized by stockholders, the directors and officers may, in the absence of fraud, issue stock to themselves. 

Chelrob Inc. v. Barrett 293 N. Y. 442, 461.

The directors have no right to lend the corporation's money to a stockholder. If it is done and a loss is suffered, the creditors can hold the directors who assent to the loan responsible for that amount. 

Flexner v. Babbit Inc. 290 N. Y. 604

Stock Corporation Law § 59 

The directors may lend money to the corporation if they honestly believe it can be made solvent. They may get an assignment of securities, the same as any other person. All that is needed is good faith. 

Converse v. Sharpe 161 N. Y. 571.

A corporation which shall have refused to pay an obligation when due, may not transfer any part of its property to its officers, directors or stockholders for the payment of any debt except for a cash consideration equivalent to the full value of the property. No transfer or any lien created or security given by the corporation when the corporation is insolvent or its insolvency is imminent, with the intent of giving a preference to one creditor over another is valid except as to rights acquired by a bona fide purchaser. But laborers' wages are preferred claims and are entitled to payment before any creditors.*

Stock Corporation Law § 15. 

The directors and officers are not entitled to any compensation for their work as such, unless provision is made for it before performance. However, when services are rendered by a director or officer which are outside the scope of ordinary duties of the office, compensation may be recovered as upon an implied contract if there was an understanding that he was to be paid for such services prior to the rendition of the service. Ordinarily, a decision of the parties as to the amount of compensation is final. A director of a corporation may be a director in other corporations.

Since the directors have to do the managing, every director has an absolute right to examine the corporation's books, even though it can be shown that the particular director was hostile to the corporation, and was engaged in competition with it and desired to harm it.

If the corporation divides its property among the shareholders, and the executions issued by the corporation's creditors against the corporation are returned unsatisfied, the creditors can follow the property into the hands of any of the stockholders, in the nature of a creditor's bill.

The attorney-general on behalf of the people, the corporation itself or a director, an existing creditor, receiver or trustee in bankruptcy, may bring an action against the directors to compel an accounting by them of their management and disposition of the property in their charge; to compel them to pay to the corporation the value of any property kept by them or transferred or lost through neglect; to enjoin a transfer of property when there is good reason to believe the transfer to be contrary to law. The attorney-general may also bring an action to suspend a director from exercising his office for an abuse of trust.

Upon dissolution of a corporation the directors are charged with the duty of winding up its affairs and for that purpose may sue and be sued. They are trustees first for the creditors and second for the stockholders, with full power to collect assets and pay debts.

Election of Directors

If directors are not elected on the day designated in the by-laws, the old directors are considered as remaining in office until successors have been elected. 

Gencrai Corporation Law § 28. 

If the date for the election of new directors has arrived, and the directors fail to call a meeting, any stockholder may call a meeting after a month has passed. He must serve notice at least two weeks before the meeting, personally or by mail, and he must publish a

notice of this meeting in a newspaper in the county once a week for two weeks immediately preceding the meeting. 

General Corporation Law § 29. 

Dividends

Directors may at their own discretion declare dividends but only out of surplus and never out of the capital fund. If they pay from capital they become personally liable to the corporation and its creditors. "Creditors" include those whose claims arose after the act. "Capital" means property capital. The appreciation in value of fixed assets though unrealized may be taken into consideration by directors in determining whether a surplus exists. Those directors whose names appear on the minutes as having been opposed to the declaration of dividends out of the capital; or who affirmatively show that they reasonably believed that such distribution would not impair the capital; or who were absent from the meeting at which the dividend was declared and communicated their dissent in writing to the secretary or caused the dissent to be entered upon the minutes, within a reasonable time after learning of the action, are not liable. 

Cox v. Leahy 209 A.D. 313, 204 N.Y.S. 741

Stock Corporation Law § 58; Randall v. Bailey 288 N. Y. 280 

The directors may add the surplus to the capital of the corporation and issue as dividend new shares to represent such additional capital. These new shares are known as stock dividends. If stock of another corporation be held, which constitutes a part of the surplus, it is legally distributed as a dividend, the same as if it were cash. 

Liebman v. Auto Strop Co. 241 N. Y. 427.

Courts will not interfere with the exercise of discretion as to declaration of dividends unless the bad faith of the directors is first shown. Thus, a contract engaging the directors unrestrictedly to declare dividends can have no legal force. 

Lindgrove v. Schluter & Co. 256 Ň. Y. 439.

When the corporation has spent money for improvements or when it has surplus profits equal to or greater than the amount of a planned dividend, it may borrow an equivalent sum for the purpose of dividends, if it has not ready funds sufficient to pay the dividend. 

Gilbert v. Prankard 204 A. D. 83, 198 N.Y.S. 25 

Bankers' Trust Co. v. Dietz 157 A. D. 594, 142 N. Y. S. 847.

Redress for Mismanagement 

A corporation may obtain restitution from directors who have misappropriated assets or acted negligently so as to inflict a loss upon the corporation. Relief is to be obtained in equity to compel an accounting, to compel restitution or the setting aside of wrongful transfers.

The right to bring an action based upon the misconduct or mismanagement of directors rests in the corporation. A stockholder may not maintain such an action unless:

PRIVATE CORPORATIONS 

155 (a) demand has been made upon the corporation to bring the action and it has refused. In such case the allegation of the demand and refusal is an essential averment in the complaint,* or (b) the control of the corporation is in the hands of directors whose acts are questioned so that a demand to bring the action would be futile. No allegation of demand and refusal is then necessary. (c) it is made to appear that the plaintiff stockholders were stockholders at the time of the transaction complained of or that their stock thereafter devolved upon them by operation of law.** 

Those bringing the action must own no less than 5% of the outstanding shares of any class or of voting trust certificates which are of a market value of at least $50,000. If that is not the case, the corporation may require a bond at any time before final judgment, for reasonable expense, including attorney's fees, for which it may be responsible in the action.

General Corporation Law §§ 61, 61a 

Jones v. Van Heusen 230 A. D. 694.

The action by a stockholder is maintained on behalf of himself and on behalf of other stockholders similarly situated. It is brought to enforce corporate rights and the shareholder can enforce such claims as the corporation itself could enforce. The judgment belongs to the corporation and the corporation must be a party and be before the court. Even if summary judgment dismissing the complaint was granted on motion of the corporation, the latter should be retained as a nominal party defendant*** 

Lyon v. Holton 286 N. Y. 70.

If an action, legal or equitable, is brought by or on behalf of a corporation against a present or former director, officer or stockholder and such action is for an accounting, or to procure a judgment because of fraud, or to recover a penalty or to enforce a common law or statutory liability, the statute of limitations is six years. 

If the action is for waste or for an injury to property or for an accounting in connection therewith, then the period is three years unless a different period is expressly provided by statute. 

Civil Practice Act. § 48. 

The misappropriation of corporate assets by an officer cannot be ratified by a vote or act of a majority of the stockholders. Acquiescence by all the stockholders may furnish a defense to an action by the corporation or a stockholder, but this acquiescence will not be *A stockholder may bring a derivative action against persons who are not directors, who have wronged the corporation, if those in control refuse to act.

Quintal v. Kellner 264 N. Y. 32.

Other creditors may come in and share in the management of the action, but until they do so the original plaintiff completely controls the action. He may compromise, abandon or discontinue at his pleasure. This rule applies both to creditors' representative actions and to stockholders' derivative suits. However, if a settlement is submitted for judicial approval, or is entered into during the trial, the court may require notice to all shareholders and an opportunity for them to be heard, before the final settlement is entered by the court. 

Officers and directors sued for misfeasance and nonfeasance, may not offset debts due them individually from the corporation, where the latter is insolvent. To permit this would in effect grant them a
