When plaintiffs in a derative suit, create a fund for the benefit of a corporation, they are entitled to their expenses and reasonable attorneys' and accountants' fees payable out of the fund. This does not include an allowance for personal efforts and for time taken from his personal business.

Neuberger v. Barrett 180 Misc. 222 Masholie v. Salvator 182 Misc. 523. 

The certificate or by-laws of a corporation or a resolution in a specific case, adopted by a majority vote of the outstanding shares. entitled to vote for directors may provide for indemnity to each present or former officer or director of it or to one who may have served at its request as a director or officer of another corporation in which it owns shares or of which it is a creditor, against his actual and necessary expenses in connection with a successful defense of a suit against him because he was a director. 

General Corporation Law § 27a. 

De Facto Corporations 

If three or more persons (1) in good faith attempt to organize a corporation, (2) under an existing law which authorizes incorporation and (3) they have acted as a corporation under this law, they are as a group regarded as a de facto corporation, even though there be defects in its organization. Its existence can be questioned only by the state in a quo warranto proceeding brought for that purpose. 

Munter v. Ideal Peerless Laundry 229 A. D. 56, 241 N. Y. S. 411.

A de facto corporation has a substantial legal existence as a corporate entity. It may take and convey property, can sue and be sued to the same extent as a de jure corporation. 

Sacks v. Anne Realty Co. 131 Misc. 117, 225 N. Y. S. 370.

A third person who dealt with them believing them to be a corporation can hold the members only as stockholders of a corpora-

PRIVATE CORPORATIONS 

157 tion and not as partners. By dealing with the association as a body corporate, he admits its legal existence as a corporation, and he is estopped from denying corporate existence. The de facto corporation cannot even if it so desires, deny its corporate existence. It is estopped from doing so. The proceeding taken to form a corporation and its attempted corporate acts are enough to hold it. 

Comm. Bank of Keokuk v. Pfeiffer 108 N.Y. 242 

Joint Stock Co. v. Natl. City Bank 210 A.D. 665, affd. 240 N.Y. 368

Those who were stockholders of record at the time the corporation was merely de facto and incurred liabilities and participated in its acts of user as a corporation, are liable as if the corporation de facto were a de jure corporation. 

Eaton v. Aspinwall 19 Ñ Y. 119.

A plaintiff sought to hold an individual, C, liable on a contract made between the plaintiff and the X corporation. His argument was as follows: A, B and C had contracted to form the X corporation and filed certificate. A and B were minors, and since the General Corporation Law requires that the incorporators be of full age, the certificate was void. Therefore, he said, Ĉ was liable. The court held the corporation to be de facto and C was therefore not individually liable. 

Foreign Corporations 

Foreign corporations may not maintain an action against a foreign corporation except in (1) actions to recover for breach of a contract made in New York; (2) actions involving property situated in New York when the contract was made; (3) actions to recover realty in the State of New York or a chattel which was replevied in this State; (4) actions where the cause of action arose within New York except where the purpose of the action affects the title to realty outside of New York, in which case the action cannot be maintained even though the cause of action arose within this State. (5) where a foreign corporation is doing business within this state.*

General Corporation Law § 225. 

Where a foreign corporation does a regular course of business in this State, it may sue à resident for breach of contract provided it had received a certificate from the Secretary of State permitting it to do business in New York, before the contract was entered into. 

This limitation does not apply to contracts made by a foreign corporation before it commenced doing business here though it subsequently did do such regular business. 

In re Scheftel's Estate 275 N. Y. 135. *This rule applies to non-residents as well. But a corporation located in New 

York and created by or under the laws of the United States, is not a foreign corporation.

As soon as it gets this certificate, the corporation can do business and sue on any contract made after it received the certificate. Neither the corporation doing business in New York, nor its assignee can sue on a contract made in this state before it got the certificate. But it can be sued on a contract (and in such action can put in a counter-claim) even if the contract had been made before it obtained the certificate. 

Stephenson v. Weltsee 223 A. D. 41, 227 N. Y. S. 230.

By "doing business" is meant a regular and systematic course. 

The following has been held not to be doing business in this state: 

The solicitation of orders in this State to a selling agent who sends the orders to the Home Office outside the State for approval; conducting research work and training employees in New York; acts done for the purpose of settling its affairs preparatory to becoming defunct; ownership of part of the capital stock of a different corporation which latter corporation is doing business in New York, and has its name listed in the telephone book, is not material as the two corporations are separate entities; maintaining an office in New 

York City, being listed in the telephone directory of New York City, with its name placed on its office door in New York City. 

International Fuel & Ice Co. v. Donner 242 N. Y. 224 

Spiegel v. Mitchell 125 Misc. 604, 211 N.Y.S. 495 

Brocia v. Franklin Plan Co. 235 A.D. 421, 257 N.Y.S. 167

Western Hair Goods Co. v. Haberkorn Co. 131 Misc. 930 

Lilenblum v. Wissotsky & Co. 213 A.D. 18, 209 N.Y.S. 704 

Hamlin v. G. E. Barrett & Co. Inc. 246 N. Y. 554

A complaint that shows upon its face that the plaintiff is a foreign corporation (other than a moneyed corporation) doing business in New York, trying to recover upon a contract made in New York, must allege that the plaintiff had obtained a certificate of doing business. If it fails to do so it may be dismissed for failure to state a cause for action. If the complaint does not state that it was doing business here, and it develops upon the trial that it was doing business here without authorization so to do, a motion by the defendant at the end of the plaintiff's case to dismiss the complaint, should be granted.

Western Felt v. Modern Carpet Co. 141 Misc. 495, 252 N. Y. S. 696. 

The foreign corporation may cease to do business in New York by filing with the Secretary of State, a statement in its corporate name, signed by its president, or vice-president, or secretary, or treasurer, or managing director, or attorney in fact, stating (1) the name of the corporation, (2) the state or country in which it was organized, (3) when it received authority to do business in New York, (4) that it consents that the Secretary of State shall receive process for the corporation in any claims against it which were created prior to the filing of the certificate of surrender. 

General Corporation Law § 216.

CRIMINAL LAW Crimes Are Statutory 

An act is deemed criminal or punishable only when so declared by statute. A crime is either a felony or a misdemeanor. A felony is a crime punishable by death or imprisonment in a state prison. 

Traffic infractions, vagrancy and disorderly conduct are not crimes. 

Penal Law, § 2; Code of Criminal Procedure §§ 887, 899 

People v. Legeri 239 A.D. 47, 266 N.Y.S. 86.

Venue in Criminal Cases 

A defendant in a criminal case is to be tried in the county in which the crime was committed. If a crime is committed partly in one county and partly in another or the acts or effects thereof constituting or necessary to the consummation of the crime, occur in two or more counties, the trial may take place in either county. 

Thus if A in County 1 is solicited by mail to remit money for the purchase of stock and the money is remitted and misappropriated in County 2 by X, X may be tried in either county. Likewise, where a forged check drawn on a bark in New York County was delivered in New Jersey to an innocent payee and was paid by the New York ties or within 500 yards thereof, jurisdiction is in either county. 

People v. Dryden 250 N. Y. 154; Code of Criminal Procedure § 134 

People v. Kastell 221 A. D. 135, affd. 250 N. Y. 518.

If a crime is committed on the boundary of two or more counties or within 500 yards thereof, jurisdiction is in either county. 

Code of Criminal Procedure § 135 

If a crime is committed in New York on a railway train, car, omnibus, truck, aeroplane or other common carrier, jurisdiction is in any county through which the train passes or has passed or is scheduled to pass in the course of that trip.

Code of Criminal Procedure § 137. 

Change of Venue 

A criminal action, prosecuted by indictment, may at any time before trial, on the application of the defendant to the Supreme Court at a Special Term in the district, be removed from the court in which it is pending to a term of the Supreme Court held in another county, on the ground that a fair and impartial trial cannot be had in the county or city where the indictment is pending. In each case it must be determined from the surrounding circumstances whether there is probable reason to believe that a fair and impartial trial cannot be had in the county where the same is laid. 

People v. Nathan 139 Misc. 345, 249 N. Y. S. 395

To enable the defendant to make the application, a judge of the Supreme Court may, in his descretion, upon good cause shown by 159

affidavit, make an order staying the trial of the indictment, until the application can be made and decided. 

Code of Criminal Procedure §§ 345, 346, 347 

People v. Becker 135 Misc. 471, 239 N. Y. S. 61.

The order denying a change of venue is not appealable. 

People v. Neutarz 235 A. D. 660, 255 N. Y. S. 214. 

Interstate Rendition (Extradition)

Whether or not a prisoner is a fugitive from justice is for the determination of the governor, whose granting of the warrant stands unless clearly shown to be without support in fact. The procedure when the legality of the detention is questioned is to sue out a writ of habeas corpus. The burden is upon the prisoner (relator) to show by conclusive evidence that he is not the fugitive. When the papers are in proper form and duly authenticated, the only evidence admissible before the court on the hearing is such as tends to prove that the relator is not the person who has been charged with a crime or it is conclusively established that he was not physically present in the demanding state at the time the crime is alleged to have been committed. 

People ex rel Higley v. Millspaw 281 N.Y. 441

Defenses to the indictment on the technical sufficiency of the indictment will not be inquired into on habeas corpus. 

People ex rel Higley v. Millspaw 281 N.Y. 441 

Infants and Crimes

An infant not yet 7 years of age is legally incapable of committing a crime. An infant between the ages of 7 and 16 who commits an act of omission which if committed by an adult would be punishable by imprisonment for a term less than life is not guilty of a crime but only of juvenile delinquency. It thus would follow that a homicide without deliberation or premeditation by an infant under 16 during the commission of an act which if done by an adult would be robbery, would not be a felony murder and therefore not a murder in the first degree. The acts of the infant which ordinarily would be an independent felony were only juvenile delinquency. 

People v. Murch 263 N. Y. 285; People v. Roper 259 N. Y. 170

Penal Law § 2186. 

Recent statutes (Code of Criminal Procedure Secs. 913e-913r) 

deal with criminal activities of minors between the ages of 16 and 19 years, who are not charged with a crime punishable by death and life imprisonment and who have not been previously convicted of a felony. Provision has been made to declare such youths "youthful offenders" and if this is done after examination of the youth, no further action is taken on the indictment or information. The determination is by the court without a jury. If the court does not determine that the defendant should be tried as a youthful offender, proceedings are continued on the indictment.

CRIMINAL LAW 

161 No statement, admission or confession made by the defendant to the court or to any officer thereof during the examination and investigation can ever be admissible as evidence against him though they may be taken into consideration at the time of sentence should the defendant be found guilty of a crime or adjudged a youthful offender.

Any person adjudged a youthful offender may be committed or sentence imposed or suspended, in which case he may be placed upon probation up to a period of three years during which two years more may be added. Commitment shall be to a religious, charitable or other reformative institution for a period not to exceed three years. No determination made under this amendment can operate as a disqualification subsequently to hold public office or as a forfeiture of any right or privilege and such defendant shall not be denominated a criminal and the determination is not deemed a conviction. Conspiracy

If two or more agree to commit a crime or to have a third party falsely indicted or arrested or to prevent one from exercising a lawful trade and one of them actually does an overt act toward the furtherance of this agreement, the parties to this agreement are guilty of a conspiracy.

If the crime agreed upon is a felony to be committed upon the person of another, or is arson or burglary there need be no overt act committed to constitute the crime a conspiracy. 

Penal Law §§ 580, 583; People v. Collins 234 N. Y. 355 

A conspiracy to commit a crime constitutes an independent crime complete in itself. It consists of a series of acts which constitute the misdemeanor, and the fact that the evidence discloses that the conspiracy was executed by the commission of a felony does not prevent a conviction for the crime of conspiracy. The conspiracy does not merge in the actual commission of the crime. 

People v. Tavormina 257 N. Y. 84, 92 Accomplices

An accomplice is one who can be found guilty of the crime in the same or different degree. Thus a police decoy cannot be an accomplice.

People v. Swift 277 N. Y. 618; People v. Blank 283 N. Y. 526 

A conviction cannot be had upon the testimony of an accomplice, unless he be corroborated by evidence from a source other than that of another accomplice, of some material fact tending to show not only that the crime has been committed, but that the defendant was implicated in its commission. It need not alone establish that the defendant committed the crime. 

People v. Mullens 292 N. Y. 408

The statute is not satisfied if the corroborative testimony tends only to establish the credibility of the accomplice; or that it merely

shows that the crime was committed in the fashion described by the accomplice. 

People v. Nitzberg 287 N.Y. 183

People v. Felber 264 A.D. 181. 

The presence of the defendant in the neighborhood of the crime at the time of its commission, together with a false denial of such presence there, are sufficient corroboration. But evidence of mere association of the defendant with the admitted perpetrators of the crime before its commission is insufficient. 

People v. Deitsch 237 N.Y. 300, 303 

People v. Crum 272 N.Y. 348; People v. Kress 284 N.Y. 452.

An exception exists where a defendant is indicted for criminally buying, receiving, concealing, or withholding stolen goods. In such cases conviction may be had on the uncorroborated testimony of the person selling, delivering, or offering the stolen goods, or of a person to whom the defendant has sold, offered, or delivered such goods. This is so even if the witness is an accomplice. 

Code of Criminal Procedure § 399; Penal Law §1308a. 

Accessories

There are no accessories before the fact in the case of felonies. 

They are considered principals. There may be an accessory after the fact in connection with a felony. Such accessory after the fact may be indicted, tried and convicted whether or not the principal is first convicted.

In the cases of misdemeanors all accessories whether before or after the fact are considered principals. 

Penal Law §§ 2, 1934 Foreign Representatives 

Ambassadors and other foreign Ministers accredited to the United States Government, together with their secretaries, messengers, families and servants are not liable to punishment in New York, but are to be sent back to their own country for trial and punishment. Attempts

An attempt is an act done with intent to commit a crime, but failing to effect the commission because of a physical situation. If 

G tries to burn a building and puts a light against the wall, he is guilty of an attempt to commit arson, even if the wall is fireproof and therefore will not burn. But if the reason for the failure to commit a crime is the lack of a legal element, there can be no attempt even though intent was present. Thus where a defendant had received property from the lawful owner in the belief that it was stolen, it was held that he could not be convicted of an attempt to receive stolen property because the stolen character of the property was an essential of the crime. 

Penal Law §§ 260, 2; People v. Jaffe, 185 N.Y. 497. 

If the act is merely in the way of preparation, or too remote to constitute the crime of attempt, the crime of attempt is not committed. There must be such nearness of accomplishment that in all

CRIMINAL LAW 

163 reasonable probability the crime itself would have been committed but for the interference or obstruction. In one case A, B and C planned to rob X. The three started out for the building in which they figured X to be. Three policemen followed and as they entered the building and before they saw X, they were arrested. They were held not guilty of attempted robbery, as the act did not come so near the commission of the crime of robbery that there was a reasonable likelihood of its accomplishment but for the interference. 

At the time of arrest the most that could be said was that the defendants were seeking an opportunity to commit a crime. 

People v. Rizzo 246 N.Y. 334. 

Effects of Intoxication 

An act committed by a person in a state of intoxication is not deemed less criminal because of the intoxication. Where, however, a particular or specific purpose, motive or intent is a necessary element to constitute a particular degree of crime, e.g., murder in the first degree, the jury should be permitted to consider the question of intoxication in determining the existence of such particular intent. The jury may find guilt of a lesser crime though voluntary intoxication does not call for an acquittal. 

People v. Koerber 244 N.Y. 147

Corpus Delicti 

In all cases the "body" of the crime charged must be proven. A defendant's confession is therefore not sufficient to warrant conviction without additional proof that the crime charged has actually been committed. In cases of murder or manslaughter, the body of the crime is divided into two parts, the death of the person and the cause of the death which must be through criminal agency, e.g., presence of wounds.

People v. Cuozzo 292 N.Y. 85 

Homicide Murder

There are two degrees of murder. In either of these there must be a design to kill, except in two instances. (1) When a persons kills while committing an independent felony alone or in association with others, e.g., larceny, robbery. In such cases the crime is murder in the first degree, even if the killing was never contemplated when the criminal started to commit the independent felony, or even if he struck his victim without intending to kill. Thus if D, while assaulting A, not intending to kill 

A, kills B who has rushed to the defense of A, D is guilty of murder in the first degree. The independent felony was the assault upon A. 

If D, however, assaults A not intending to kill A, but does kill A, it is not murder in the first degree since the assault upon the victim becomes a constituent part of the homicide and is merged. There is no independent felony. 

People v. Wagner 245 N.Y. 143; People v. Lazar 271 N.Y. 27.

If A, in prison for the commission of a felony, attempts to escape, the attempt is a felony. If he accidentally kills a keeper while thus attempting to escape, he is guilty of murder in the first degree, as he killed while committing an independent felony. 

People v. Weiner 248 N.Y. 118

If two or more are engaged in a felony and one is killed by his own act, there is not the killing of another and therefore the confederates are not guilty of a felony murder. 

People v. La Barbera 159 Misc. 177, 287 N.Y.S. 257 

If a killing occurs after the commission of a felony, even while making an escape from the scene of the felony, it would not be a killing during the commission of an independent felony. 

People v. Ryan 263 N.Y. 298 (2) The other instance occurs when a person recklessly disregards the life of others. If a man fires a gun into a crowd of persons, killing one, or wrecks a train and a passenger is killed, it is murder. 

There need be no intention to kill.

Penal Law § 1044; People v. Jernatowski 238 N.Y. 188 

If there is a design to kill plus a premeditation of an appreciable space of time, however short, it is murder in the first degree. If there is the design to kill, but no premeditation, it is murder in the second degree (except in the two instances mentioned). 

People v. Guadagnino 233 N.Y. 344

It thus follows that if the defendant inflicted the fatal wound in a sudden transport of passion, excited by what the victim had said, which for the time disturbed his reasoning powers and deprived him of the capacity of reflection, or while under the influence of some uncontrollable emotion, it is not murder in the first degree. 

People v. Caruso 246 N.Y. 437.

Where the indictment charges a killing during the commission of an independent felony, the court is not required to charge the law applicable to lesser degrees of homicide when the jury could not upon the evidence submitted under that indictment, properly find the elements which must be present where guilt of such lesser degrees of homicide exists. Where, however, a defendant was intoxicated or his mentality impaired as to call in question his ability to have formed an intent, or he is tried under an indictment upon a charge of murder in the first degree committed from a premeditated design to kill, the rule is that the court must charge upon the law applicable to other degrees of homicide, because of the facts as presented by the evidence may lead the jury to properly believe that all the elements of conviction existed with the absence of perhaps one essential, thus placing the conviction in a lesser degree of homicide. It may refuse to find an intent to effect death; there then could be a conviction only of manslaughter. 

People v. Seiler 246 N.Y. 262; People v. Cummings 274 N.Y. 336 

People v. Martone 256 N.Y. 395.

An indictment will lie against one who commits murder, even though death results more than a year and a day after the act. That period was the arbitrary span fixed by the common law, but there is

CRIMINAL LAW' 

165 no fixed limit in this state. The proximate relationship must, however, be established. 

People v. Brengard 265 N.Y. 100. Manslaughter

The next grade in homicide is manslaughter. The main difference between murder and manslaughter is that in the latter there is no design to kill (always remembering the above mentioned exceptions). There are two degrees of manslaughter. 

Manslaughter in the first degree occurs when a homicide is committed without a design to effect death, 1. While committing or attempting to commit a misdemeanor affecting the person or property of the victim or of another. If A without a design to effect death, kills B, while A is committing a civil trespass or other invasion of a private right, it is second degree manslaughter. Thus where a motorist operating an automobile while intoxicated (a misdemeanor) unintentionally struck and killed B whom he did not see until the moment of contact, a conviction of manslaughter in the first degree was held improper, as that misdemeanor did not affect the person or property of another, but was a crime against society alone. 

Penal Law §§ 1050, 1052; People v. Grieco 266 N.Y. 48 

2. In the heat of passion, but in a cruel or unusual manner or with a dangerous weapon. If the instrument used is not a dangerous weapon, e.g., chair, or a piece of wood, it is manslaughter in the second degree. 

People v. Caruso 249 N.Y. 302 

3. A wilful killing or aid in killing of an unborn quick child by one other than the mother is manslaughter in the first degree, unless done to save the woman's life.

Penal Law §1050 

The statute has arbitrarily declared certain acts which result in death to be manslaughter in the second degree: (1) A doctor who while drunk treats and kills a patient; (2) One who keeps gunpowder unlawfully, or keeps a dangerous animal, and death results; (3) One who overloads a vessel which transports passengers and death results; (4) A woman who deliberately produces a miscarriage upon herself and kills a quick child.

Penal Law § 1050, 1052 

Taking one's life is not a crime, but helping another to take his own life by giving advice or actual assistance is manslaughter in the first degree.

Penal Law § 2301, 2304 

A killing is excusable if committed by accident or misfortune in doing a lawful act by lawful means with ordinary caution, without unlawful intent. 

People v. Angelo 246 N.Y. 451.

Whenever intent becomes material-and it is material in cases of homicide the quality or persistence of the intent is for the jury. 

The jury is to be charged concerning the various degrees of murder and manslaughter. 

People v. Moran 246 N.Y. 100.

Attacking a Person - Assault 

This crime is divided into three degrees: 

First degree. There must be intent to kill or commit a felony upon the person or property with the use of poison or a dangerous weapon or any other means likely to produce death. The fact that the person attacked was not actually touched does not matter. 

There need be no battery, the assault being enough. So if A shoots at B with intent to kill, and misses, we have a case of assault in the first degree.

Penal Law § 240 

Second degree-If one intending to injure or commit a crime administers a drug to another; or willfully and wrongfully and intending to do so wounds or inflicts grievous bodily harm even without a weapon; or commits such assault with similar intention by the use of a weapon likely to produce grievous bodily harm without success; or intending to commit a felony, he assaults someone; or commits an assault to keep from being arrested, it is assault in the second degree. Intent to kill is not an element of this crime. 

Penal Law § 242 

People v. Wagner 245 N.Y. 43; People v. Katz 290 N.Y. 361.

Third degree. This constitutes all other assaults and is a misdemeanor. By a recent law it is third degree assault to drive, or allow another to drive one's car so negligently that a person is hurt. 

Penal Law § 244 

It has been held to be assault in the third degree to strike a person with an automobile while driving the car against the direction permitted by a traffic light.

Rape 

People v. Saroff 227 A.D. 114, 237 N.Y.S. 73.

Forcing a woman not one's wife to sexual intercouse, when by reason of unsoundness of mind or mental or physical weakness, or because her resistance has been overcome by force or fear of force or by drugs, she is unable to resist, constitutes the commission of the felony "rape, in the first degree."

Having intercourse with a girl who is under 18, and not one's own wife, she being willing, is second degree rape. A girl under 18 is incapable of giving consent to such intercourse. The fact that she appeared to be over 18, and said she was over 18, does not matter. 

The female, however, has no cause for action for damages, if she willingly and knowingly consorts.

Penal Law & 2010 

Barton v. Bee Line 238 A.D. 501, 265 N.Y.S. 284.

The female's testimony alone will not convict the defendant of rape. The material facts necessary to be established are (1) the

CRIMINAL LAW 

167 commission of the crime by someone and (2) the connection of the defendant with it. Corroboration of the fact of penetration may be proven by circumstantial evidence. Proof of opportunity to commit rape does not suffice as the necessary corroboration.* 

People v. Deitsch 237 N.Y. 300.

People v. Croes 285 N.Y. 279 

The rule that the female's evidence is not sufficient by itself does not apply to a case of attempted rape. 

People v. Brehm 218 A.D. 266, 218 N.Y.S. 469.

Seduction 

When an unmarried female over 18 agrees to sexual intercourse only because the man promised to marry her or convinced her he was married to her, the crime of rape is not committed because she allowed the intercourse. But it would constitute the crime of seduction, provided the female was of chaste character and virtuous. As in rape, the woman's testimony alone would need corroboration. The corroboration here would have to be as to the promise of marriage and the intercourse but not as to her chastity. 

Penal Law § 2175; People v. Nelson 153 N.Y. 90 

There can be no conviction for seduction if the complaining witness had actual knowledge that the defendant was a married man.

People v. Massaro 288 N. Y. 211 

If two years go by before an indictment is found against the defendant, the prosecution for seduction is barred. Should the man marry_the_woman involved, there cannot be any prosecution.

Penal Law § 2176. 

Bigamy 

A person having a husband or wife living, who marries another, is guilty of bigamy. The fact that he believed he was validly married to the second, or divorced from the first, whereas he was not (knowing, however, that his wife was alive), does not relieve him. 

The consort in the second marriage would also be guilty, if she knew that the man was entering into a marriage of a bigamous character.

Penal Law § 340. 

Robbery 

To constitute robbery in any degree, there must be (1) force or the causing of fear of force or of immediate injury to the person or to property, even in the slightest degree, of anyone present at the time, or of a member of his family. The force must be used either to take or retain possession. Thus using force to escape, after one has been caught pick-pocketing, is not robbery. (2) The property taken must be taken from one's person or in *Corroboration is required in cases involving rape, seduction, adultery abor tion, compulsory prostitution and compulsory marriage. Penal Law §§ 71, 103, 

1091, 1455, 2013, 2177, 2460

the presence of a person. Taking it from a room having no occupants is not robbery.

If the elements that make up robbery are present and more than one robber engage in the affair and are present, and by their presence or otherwise aid in causing fear or supplying the force, it is always robbery in the first degree. If one person alone robs, it is robbery in the first degree, if he is armed with a dangerous weapon or uses a motor vehicle to aid him, or actually injures someone present at the time of the robbery.

Penal Law § 2124. 

If violence is used, but no injury is done, and the lone robber has no dangerous weapon or motor vehicle, it is second degree robbery. 

Penal Law § 2124. 

A person who robs another under circumstances not amounting to robbery in the first or second degree is guilty of robbery in the third degree. Example: A takes personal property from X by means of "fear or injury in the future."

People v. Thompson 198 N.Y. 396; Penal Law § 2128. 

Extortion

Extortion is the obtaining of property with consent, by means of force, fear or under the color of official right. Where the intended victim pays money in apparent response to threats, but is really acting with the police to lay a trap for the accused, extortion is not committed, but it amounts to an attempt to commit extortion. 

People v. Gillette, 200 N.Y. 276.

The threats may be against the person or property of the one threatened or against his relatives, or they may be threats to accuse one of these of a crime or to expose a secret or kidnap any of them. 

Compelling the victim to sign, alter or destroy a paper which affects the legal rights of a party is extortion. 

Penal Law §§ 852, 853. 

Extortion is a felony, but if a police officer or one pretending to be one, unlawfully and maliciously and under the color of official authority detains another against his will, or injures him in his property or his rights, he is guilty of a misdemeanor. 

Penal Law §§ 854, 855. 

Robbery differs from extortion in that to constitute robbery the property must be taken against the will and without the consent of the possessor. In extortion consent is obtained. 

Penal Law §§ 850, 851 People v. Hagen 212 A.D. 879, 208 N.Y.S. 235. 

Larceny

Effective as of September 1, 1942, all distinctions differentiating one sort of theft from another (formerly common law larceny by asportation, by trick and device, obtaining property by false pretenses and embezzlement) were abolished. A larceny is now committed when a person with intent to deprive or defraud another of the use and benefit of property wrongfully takes, obtains or with-

CRIMINAL 

169 

LAW 

holds from the rightful possessor any money, personalty, things in action, evidence of debt, or contract.

Penal Law § 1290. 

Any person who, with intent to defraud, issues a check or draft for the payment of money either in his own behalf, as agent for another or as agent or officer of a corporation, knowing that the maker has not sufficient funds or credit with the drawee for the payment of such check or draft, is guilty of a misdemeanor. If money or property is obtained thereby, the drawer is guilty of larceny. The fact that the check was given for an indebtedness past due, is no defense. The refusal of payment by the drawee "for lack of funds" is prima facie evidence of intent to defraud, and of knowledge of the lack of funds or credit. The notice of protest is presumptive evidence of lack of funds or credit. Where there has been no notice of protest, a certificate under oath by any bank officer that there was a lack of funds or credit, is presumptive evidence. 

Penal Law § 1292a 

People v. Humphries 226 A.D. 500, 234 N.Y.S. 688.

The fact that the check was post-dated or that the recipient agreed to hold it for a time before presentment, is a defense. 

People v. Mazeloff, 229 A.D. 451; 242 N.Y.S. 623

People v. Will 289 N.Y. 413. 

If one finds and does not return an article when he knows who the owner is, he is guilty of larceny. 

Penal Law §§ 1290, 1300, 1302, 1303. 

It is not a defense to a criminal prosecution for larceny that the owner whose property was taken was a party to an illegal purpose. 

Tench v. Lawson 225 A.D. 198, 232 N.Y.S. 449.

Property to be the subject of larceny must be detectable or measurable by the senses or by some mechanical contrivance so far as its physical presence, quality or quantity are concerned. Thus a check, electricity and gas can be subjects of larceny. But the right to produce oil, or the good will of a business, cannot be the subject of larceny though they are personal property. 

Grand Larceny in the First Degree. If the market value of the property which is the subject of larceny is over $500, it is always larceny in the first degree, no matter in which one of the above mentioned ways it is obtained. If a negotiable instrument is stolen, its value is the amount which is still due on it. 

In amounts of $500 and less the property must be stolen or appropriated at night either from (a) the person of another or (b) from a dwelling house or railway car. In the case of (a) it may be of any value.

Penal Law § 1294. 

Second Degree. If property is taken from the person of another by day, it is larceny in the second degree if $500 or less. If taken in any way other than the above-mentioned ways, and is valued over $100, it is always larceny in the second degree, no matter when it is taken.

Penal Law § 1296.

Petit Larceny.--The first and second degrees of larceny are felonies. Any other larceny, like stealing a box of tooth-paste from a counter, or $100 or less from a dwelling house by day, is called petit larceny, and is a misdemeanor.

Penal Law § 1298. 

Burglary

There are three degrees in burglary. 

First Degree. All these elements must exist: (1) The act must take place at night (2) The burglar must break in by opening a closed door or closed window, or go through the chimney, or be let in by arrangement with someone inside. There is no requirement that violence must be shown, a latch lifted or a bolt drawn. Nor need a door be tightly closed. If so closed that some effort must be made to open it far enough to admit the body of the person or it is opened for that purpose, the element of breaking in is present. (3) He must "enter" by putting either a part of his body or an instrument inside to frighten the people in the house or in order to take something out. (4) The place entered must be a dwelling house in which there is a human being at the time. (5) The burglar must be armed with a dangerous weapon, no matter whether he has it when he gets to the house, or gets it inside; but if he has a confederate, or while committing a crime in the building or in escaping therefrom, he assaults someone, it would be an element which dispenses with the need of a dangerous weapon. (6) There must be intent to commit a crime at the time the entry is effected. What the burglar actually does when he gets inside is entirely immaterial.

Penal Law § 402; People v. Viola 264 A.D. 38. 

Second Degree.-If the entry took place in the daytime and the elements under subdivisions 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 were present, or if elements 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6 were present (5 was missing), it would be burglary in the second degree. 

Penal Law, § 403. 

Third Degree. If one breaks into any building not a dwelling house containing an occupant, with the intent to commit a crime; or if he enters a building when the door is open (so as not to constitute a "breaking in"), with no intent to commit a crime, but while inside he commits a crime and then opens the door which he had shut, in order to get out, he is guilty of burglary in the third degree. If the door had been open when he wanted to get out, it would not have been a breaking out, and so not burglary. 

Penal Law § 404. 

A building includes a railway car, vessel, house trailer, inclosed ginseng garden, booth, tent, shop, or other erection or enclosure. 

It does not include a gasoline pump, containting no storage compartment and separated by a driveway from a building. 

People v. Lamphere 219 A.D. 422, 219 N.Y.S. 390.
