Arson

This crime is a felony and is divided into three degrees. 

First degree.-It can be committed only at night. The building wilfully burnt must be a dwelling house which has a human being in it, whether the incendiary knows it or not, or it can be any other building not a dwelling house in which the incendiary knows there is a human being.

Penal Law § 221. 

The fact that the incendiary warns the occupants that he is going to set fire to the building is no defense to an indictment for arson in the first degree. 

Woodford v. People 62 N.Y. 117.

Second degree.-If the same conditions existed but the fire was wilfully started during the day instead of at night, it is arson in the second degree. But it is possible to have arson in the second degree even though the burning be at night. Such a case would be when the dwelling house or structure had no human being in it. 

It is arson in the second degree if a vehicle or structure is set on fire so as to defraud or prejudice the insurer thereof or of any article therein.

Penal Law § 222. 

Third degree. A wilful burning of any structure under circumstances not amounting to arson in the first or second degree, is arson in the third degree. For example, burning a structure with no human being in it during the day. 

Penal Law § 223. 

To constitute a burning there need not be a flame. Charring is enough. But the mere scorching or discoloration is not enough. Forgery

Copying the signature of another is not the only kind of forgery. 

Any material alteration of an instrument, or putting together different parts of genuine instruments, with intent to defraud, or knowingly disposing of a forged instrument all of these also are forgery. 

Suppose a paper is signed "John Brown." A man who did not sign that paper, but whose name happens to be John Brown, passes it off as his, after finding the paper. John Brown is a forger. 

Penal Law § 880, 883. 

First degree. If a person, intending to defraud, forges any instrument by which any right or interest in property is or purports to be affected, or the acknowledgment to such an instrument is so forged by him, he is guilty of forgery in the first degree. 

Penal Law § 884. 

If a notary public takes an acknowledgment of an instrument which may be recorded, and wilfully certifies falsely that it was executed by the parties, or that the execution was proved, he is guilty of forgery in the first degree.

Penal Law § 885. 

Second degree. If a person intending to defraud, forges or will-

ingly assists in the forging of the seal of this state, or of a court of record, or of a state officer, or of a corporation, or of any other state or county, or forges a record of any instrument or judgment or court decree, or a certified copy thereof, or an entry in the book of records or accounts of a state, city, village or town officer, or forges or makes or aids in making the plates for the forgery of any bank notes, or a stock certificate or instrument for the payment of money or transfer of title, or has in his possession or custody any materials, with intent that they be used in making a plate for forgery, he is guilty of forgery in the second degree.

Penal Law, § 887. 

Third degree.-An officer or employee of a corporation or partnership who falsifies or unlawfully alters or erases or destroys any writing of the firm, or any person intending and succeeding in injuring the good name of any person by altering or aiding in altering any written communication, is guilty of third degree forgery. 

If a person intending to defraud forges a ticket of a railroad or other public conveyance, or sells a forged ticket knowing it to be forged, he is guilty of third degree forgery. 

If one forges a postage or revenue stamp of the United States or of New York, or knowingly sells such a stamp, he is guilty of third degree forgery.

Penal Law § 889. 

Perjury

A person who even though he later proves to be an incompetent witness, wilfully and knowingly falsly swears or affirms under any of the following circumstances, is guilty of perjury. (1) In connection with any action or special proceeding, hearing, inquiry or any occasion in which an oath is required by law or necessary for the prosecution or defense. (2) Where the matters stated to be true are relied upon and affect the title to any real estate or personal property, including the assignment and satisfaction of a mortgage. (3) Where one has been designated as interpreter in a judicial action or proceeding, knowingly or wilfully falsely interprets evidence between a witness and the court. 

Penal Law §§ 1620, 1626. 

The false statement need not necessarily be given as a witness on the stand. It may be in a deposition, affidavit or other writing. 

To be perjury in the first degree, the perjury must be committed as to a material matter in connection with an action or proceeding or hearing involving the ends of public justice or when an oath or affirmation is required or may be lawfully administered. To be material, the matter must have some bearing on the main fact about which the person has testified. The fact that the ultimate decision was decided upon an entirely different point, about which this witness was asked nothing, does not mean that the false testimony given would not constitute perjury. His testimony need not

CRIMINAL LAW 

173 have affected it. The question of the materiality is for the jury. Perjury in the second degree is a misdemeanor and constitutes every other perjury not first degree perjury. Thus the matter testified to need not be material in this degree of perjury. 

People v. Samuels 284 N.Y. 410; Penal Law §§ 1620a, 1620b. 

If A induces or procures P to commit perjury in the first degree or second degree, he is guilty of subornation of perjury in the first degree or second degree respectively. If P should then not actually commit perjury, A would be guilty of attempted subornation. To have a case of subornation of perjury, perjury must have actually been committed. Note that if A attempts to have P say something under oath, which even if said would not be perjury, A is not guilty of even attempted subornation of perjury. 

People v. Teal, 196 N.Y. 372; Penal Law §§ 1632, 1632a. 

No civil action exists in favor of the defeated party to a litigation against a witness who gave material testimony on the trial, for his false swearing or his fraud in testifying. 

Morgan v. Morgan 129 Misc. 212, 221 N.Y.S. 117.

A conviction for perjury cannot be had upon the uncorroborated testimony of but one witness. If oral testimony is relied upon, at least two witnesses or one witness supported by corroborating circumstances, must be produced.

People v. Batt 165 Misc. 540, affd. 253 A.D. 718.

Damnum Absque Injuria 

DAMAGES 

Injuria Sine Damno

LTHOUGH IT IS the policy of the law to compensate as completely as possible one who has been damaged by another, not every damage is compensable. As a general proposition it may be stated that for the plaintiff to recover damages, there must have been a violation of some legal right to the plaintiff. The situation where the plaintiff is damaged but no legal right of his has been violated, is called a case of damnum absque injuria. Thus there can be no recovery for damage to property produced by vibrations from a nearby carefully operated railroad. 

Beardsley v. Kilmer 236 N.Y. 80

Frank v. City of New York 179 Misc. 895. 

In situations where a legal right of the plaintiff has been violated but there has been no damage, we have a case of injuria sine damno. 

In order to satisfy the theory that there must be a vindication of the rights of one whose rights have been violated, nominal damages are allowed. In one case the plaintiff leased land to the defendant, and the defendant under this lease was to improve the property. The improvements, however, were to be utilized solely for the benefit of the defendant. The defendant failed to make those improvements and the plaintiff exercised a right of re-entry under the terms of the lease, and then sued for damages. Upon the trial the plaintiff failed to show that he had suffered any damages because of the breach and he therefore was allowed no more than nominal damages. 

Chamberlain v. Parker 45 N.Y. 569.

A breach of contract to make a loan, standing by itself, involves no legal damages.

Avalon Construction Co. v. Kirsch Holding Co. 256 N.Y. 137 Mitigating the Damages 

The law imposes upon a party subjected to injury from a breach of contract, the active duty to make a reasonable effort to render the injury as light as possible. The failure of the claimant to make such reasonable effort to minimize the damages does not bar him entirely from recovery. It merely prevents the recovery of such damages as might have been avoided by reasonable effort on his part. 

Losei Realty Co. v. City of New York 254 N.Y. 41, 47 

Colonna v. State 232 A.D. 385, 249 N.Y.S. 578.

Contracts of Manufacture or Sale 

A party may recover for breach of contract such damages as would ordinarily and naturally flow from such breach. The damage must be proximate and must be capable of ascertainment. Profits which 174

DAMAGES 

175 the plaintiff would certainly have realized can be recovered. Where the profits are speculative, there can be no recovery. 

Ray Cons. Copper Co v. Amer. Eng. Co. Co. 123 Misc. 276, affd. 210 A.D. 831

If by reason of the breach of warranty of the seller the plaintiff buyer is obligated to defend against the action of a third person, to whom a resale was made, resales having been within the contemplation of the parties, the buyer may notify the seller of the pendency of the suit and may call upon him to defend him; if he fails to defend, then, if liable over, he is liable not only for the amount of damages recovered but for all reasonable and necessary expenses incurred in such defense. 

Lord & Taylor v. Yale 230 N.Y. 132.

The measure of damages for breach of warranty of condition or quality in the absence of special circumstances showing proximate damage of a greater amount where the full purchase price has been paid, is the difference between the actual value of the goods at the time of delivery to the buyer, and the value it would have had if it had been according to specifications. If the plaintiff has not paid the price, the unpaid portion may be offset against what the plaintiff would otherwise recover. This measure of damages is different from fraudulent misrepresentations inducing the making of the contract. There the measure of damages is merely indemnity, i.e., the difference between the value of the bargain which the plaintiff was induced to make and the consideration exacted as the price of the bargain. 

Sager v. Friedman 270 N.Y. 472 

Bond Electric Co. v. Gold Seal Co., 271 N.Y. 461.

Where a certain kind of seed was contracted for in order to raise crops and another kind delivered under circumstances constituting a breach of warranty, the damages would not be based merely upon a price paid for the seeds. They would be the value of a crop such as ordinarily would have been produced that year deducting the expense of raising the crop and the value of the crop actually raised. The nature of the proof required should consider the character of the season, the manner of cultivation, the condition of the ground, results obtained in the same vicinity where similar produce were planted under similar circumstances, the market value of the matured produce and the value of the crop raised from defective seed. 

White v. Miller 71 N.Y. 118.

Where the defendant wrongfully refuses to accept goods which were manufactured for him by the plaintiff at his request, the plaintiff can recover loss of profits plus the difference between the cost of manufacture and what the plaintiff realized upon the sale of the goods by him plus interest. 

Baxter v. Lustberg 205 A.D. 673, 200 N.Y.S. 125 

Hollwedel v. Duffy Mott Co., 263 N.Y. 95.

Where the plaintiff is entiled to recover a sum expressed in foreign money as damages for breach of contract or a tort, in determining the amount of the judgment expressed in our currency, the rate

of exchange prevailing at the date of the breach or of the commission of the tort is to be applied and not the rate as of the date of judgment. 

Kantor v. Aristo Hosiery Co. 222 A.D. 502, affd. 248 N.Y. 630.

Failure of Seller to Deliver Personalty 

A statement by one party prior to the date set forth for his performance, that he does not intend to go through with his part of the contract, is an anticipatory breach, provided the other party accepts the repudiation as final. As long as the plaintiff reasonably entertained hope of inducing the other party to complete his end of the contract, no anticipatory breach has occurred. The measure of damages is governed by what is the difference between the contract price and the market price at the time when the goods ought to have been delivered, or if no time was fixed, then at the time of the refusal and at the place of delivery. 

In the event of an anticipatory breach, the damages are based on the cost or value of performance at the time fixed by the contract for that performance, and not at the time of the breach. If the trial takes place before the scheduled date for performance, the jury estimates as nearly as it can the likely market price at the performance date. 

John Demon Co. v. Fed. S. Ref. Co. 215 A.D. 140, 213 N.Y.S. 106 

Goldfarb v, Campe Corp. 99 Misc. 475.

It is the general rule that a purchaser of goods who has contracted to resell them to his own customer, is, for a non-delivery by the original seller, entitled only to general damages for the reason that he might have replaced the undelivered goods and thereby satisfied his customer. Where, however, there were special circumstances made known to the seller at the making of the contract from which it might reasonably have been foreseen that a non-delivery would cause a breach of the buyer's contract with the customer, and the two contracts are in fact breached, the damages paid and expenses incurred by the buyer in satisfying the customer may be taken as the measure of the damages which the original seller must pay to the original buyer. The seller's liability to reimburse the buyer for losses substained is not conditional upon existence of a resale contract at the moment of the execution of the original contract; it may arise where the seller has knowledge that such a contract is in the contemplation of the buyer. 

On the other hand, mere knowledge that goods are purchased for resale in the ordinary course of business will not take the transaction out of the general rule. If besides notice of the contemplated resale the defendant also had notice that other goods could not be obtained to replace those not delivered, the profits of resale may be recovered; if there was no such notice it would be held that the loss of profits of resale was not within the contemplation of the parties. 

Czarnikow Rionda v. Fed. Sugar R. Co. 255 N.Y. 33. 1

DAMAGES 

177 If the contract is an installment contract, and one party falls behind in an installment, the whole contract can be treated as at an end if the breach goes to the essence and the injured party can sue for damages for the entire contract. If the breach does not go to the essence, the plaintiff can get only damages for the breach. He must go on with the rest of the contract. Each case is judged on its own circumstances. The mere failure of a seller to deliver an installment does not by itself permit a rescission of the whole contract. 

Janch v. Powertown Tire Co. 212 A.D. 326, 209 N.Y.S. 16

Personal Property Law § 126. 

It seems plain that if the buyer tells the seller he will not accept the remaining installments, the seller can sue at once. 

G. Bahnsen & Co., Inc. v. Aerst 235 N.Y. 426

Where the seller sends less than is required by the contract, the buyer may take the lesser amount at the contract price and sue for the breach of contract. The damages are the loss directly and naturally resulting because of the breach. 

Perkins v. Minford 235 N.Y. 301.

Upon a sale "f. o. b. point of shipment" title passes to the buyer at the moment of delivery to the carrier, unless there is a contrary intention. For failure to make delivery, the measure of damages is the difference between the contract price and the market value at the time and place of delivery in accordance with the terms of the contract, whether that be the place of delivery to the carrier or delivery at destination. 

Standard Casing Co. v. Cal. Casing Co. 233 N.Y. 413.

Unless there is something in a "c. i. f." contract to indicate the contrary, the seller completes his contract when he delivers the merchandise to the shipper, pays the freight to a point of destination, and forwards to the buyer the bill of lading, invoice, insurance policy and receipt showing payment of freight. When there is a breach of contract, by the seller's failure to make delivery, the measure of damages is the difference between the contract price and the market price at the time and place of delivery. 

Seaver v. Lindsay Light Co. 233 N.Y. 273.

If the delivery of goods is specified to be at a far distance, the buyer neither knows nor has means of knowledge that the contract has not been completed until he actually receives the goods or the bill of lading stating the amount shipped. The time as to when the damages are measured is in such a case shifted. It is now the date the buyer knew, or should have known, of the default and not at the place and time of delivery.* 

Perkins v. Minford 235 N.Y. 301.

Ordinarily in commercial contracts, time is the essence. But should the buyer waive prompt delivery, and agree to wait a while. *A wrongdoer or one who breaches a contract may not escape liability because there is no market value. In such cases the value to the owner is the valuation set, but sentimental values are eliminated. MacGregor v. Watts 254 A.D. 

904, 5 N.Y.S. (2d) 525.

1 the buyer cannot terminate the contract unless he gives the seller a further reasonable opportunity to perform. 

S.W. Bridges & Co., Inc. v. Barry 237 N.Y. 281.

If by the contract itself, the date of performance is fixed, failure to so perform is ground for rescission. If no time is fixed, performance must be completed within a reasonable time. What is a reasonable time is for the jury. 

John F. Trainor Co. v. G. Amsinck & Co. 236 N.Y. 392.

Breach of Contract of Employment 

The plaintiff is entitled to damages which will compensate him for the defendant's breach of contract. Prima facie the measure of such damages is the wage that would be payable during the remainder of the term. The actual damage is measured by the wage that would be payable during the remainder of the term reduced by the income which the discharged employee has earned, will earn, or could with reasonable diligence earn during the unexpired term. 

The uncertainties of human life may be taken into consideration in fixing the present worth of the obligation to pay money due at some time in the future, after the trial. The employee is only bound to use reasonable diligence to procure other employment of the same nature, in order to relieve the employer as much as possible from loss. He is not bound to look for or accept occupation of another kind. If he unreasonably rejects employment he will not be heard to say that the loss of wages from then on is the consequence of the earlier discharge. 

Hollwedel v. Duffy-Mott Co. 263 N.Y. 95 

McClelland v. Climax Hosiery Mills 252 N.Y. 347, 358 

Fuchs v. Koerner 107 N.Y. 529.

In one case the plaintiff employed the defendant and paid the defendant in advance. The defendant failed to render the services as required under the contract and the plaintiff sued for damages sustained by him because of the failure on the part of the defendant to render service. The defendant maintained that the limit of his liability was the amount he was paid under the contract, as that amount represented the plaintiff's valuation of the services. The court held that the plaintiff is entitled to recover whatever damages he can prove as flowing from the breach. The defendant, however, may keep the consideration already received because whenever a claim is made for damages for breach of contract there is an affirmation of the contract and it concedes the right of the defendant to retain whatever has been paid. 

Quinn v. Van Pelt 56 N.Y. 417.

A salesman, working on commission, who is wrongfully discharged, may recover damages for the remainder of the term, measured by the commissions which the plaintiff might have earned during the remainder of the term under reasonable probabilities, taking into consideration all the circumstances, including past success, prospective customers, and the sums he had expended in prep-

DAMAGES 

179 aration, which might have led to other sales or might have resulted only in future wasted effort. 

Prescott v. Buffalo Fire Appl. Co. 237 A.D. 198, affd. 262 N.Y. 475.

Breach of Building Contracts 

Where a builder has in good faith intended to comply with a con- . tract for erecting a building and has substantially complied with it, although there may be slight defects caused by inadvertence or unintentional omissions, he may recover the contract price less the damages, if any, caused by the defects. 

The burden of proof is on the contractor to show (1) That any defects or omission were unintentional and slight. (2) That they were made in good faith; and (3) The amount which should be deducted from the contract price.

A contractor, who in excavating, found the materials of the ground differed from the contract specifications, is entitled to recover the difference between the value of excavating the material shown in the contract and the value of excavating the materials found. 

Jackson v. State 210 A.D. 115 affd. 241 N.Y. 563.

Where the defendant breaches a contract for the erection of a house by the plaintiff, the plaintiff becomes entitled to the difference between the contract price and the actual cost of the building originally contracted for. This fits in with the rule of the measure of damages for a violation of an executory agreement, which is that the party who has been wrongfully deprived of profits of an executory contract, may recover the difference between the contract price and the amount it would have cost to perform. 

Industrial Eng. Co. v. Republic S. Co. 220 A.D. 178, 220 N. Y. 623 

Stearns v. Stollwerck Chocolate Co. 220 A.D. 221 N.Y.S. 512 

Breach of Contract for Sale of Realty

If a defendant is unable to deliver title in accordance with the contract, the plaintiff cannot have judgment for specific performance. When a vendor without fraud on his part is unable to convey a good title, and where the defect was unknown to him at the time the contract was made, the purchaser is entitled only to: (11) The return of payments made on account of the purchase price; (2) Interest upon such sum; (3) Reasonable expenses for examination of title and legal fees; (4) Nominal damages. 

Norris v. McMechen 135 Misc. 361, 238 N.Y.S. 181.

Special damages such as the amount of the bargain lost are allowed the plaintiff (a) If the seller arbitrarily refuses to perform; (b) Knowingly contracts beyond his power; (c) Has been guilty of fraud or bad faith. 

Bulkley v. Rouken Glen Inc. 222 A.D. 570, affd. 248 N.Y. 647.

Lessor and Lessee - Landlord and Tenant In the law of damages relating to lessor and lessee, the usual obligation to reduce damages does not apply where the action is one for rent under a contract of leasing. The absolute liability of the tenant to pay rent is not affected by the refusal on the part of the landlord to lease to a new tenant. Rent being a fixed compensation for a vested interest, it must be paid by the tenant. 

Sancourt Realty Co. v. Dowling 220 A.D. 660, 222 N.Y.S. 288.

Where a lessor refuses to deliver possession of the leased premises, the lessee is entitled to the difference between the rent reserved in the lease and the rental value of the premises. The latter is fixed by one qualified to testify as an expert upon rental values of the premises of the kind leased, in that general vicinity. 

A tenant who has been constructively evicted by superior title and who has not paid rent in advance, can recover only nominal damages. Where the breach of the covenant of quiet enjoyment results from the fraud of the landlord, the evicted tenant may recover the value of the unexpired term less rents received. 

Sears, Roebuck & Co. v. 9th Ave.-31st St. Co. 274 N.Y. 388, 403.

A lessee who is injured by a nuisance may recover the diminution in the usable value of the premises. The usable value is the use to the occupant and has no relation to the rental value as reserved in the lease before the injury and after its repair. 

Bly v. Edison Elec. Illum. Co., 97 N.Y.S. 592, affd. 188 N.Y. 582

In an action by a lessor against the lessee for failure to keep the premises in repair in accordance with the terms of an unexpired lease the proper measure of damages is the damage to the reversion and not the amount required to put the premises in repair. 

Where a landlord violates a covenant not to permit another business similar to that of the lessee to be conducted on the premises by another the proper measure of damages is the difference between the rental value of the demised premises with and without the other competing business for the time the breach lasted. 

Supreme Finance Co. v. Burnee Co. 146 Misc. 374, 262 N.Y.S. 147

Damage to Property Through Negligence 

Where personal property is damaged and not rendered wholly or practically worthless, the measure of damages is the difference between the value of the property before the injury, and its value in its injured condition immediately after the accident; an alternative method is the proof of the reasonable value of necessary repairs to restore it as nearly as possible to its original condition plus damages for loss of use during the time. The rule is subject to the limitations that the cost of repairs must be less than the diminution in market value because of the injury and no more than the value before the injury. Where the property injured is an automobile, the rule applies whether it be a commercial or pleasure car. 

Parilli v. B'klyn City R. Co. 236 A.D. 577, 260 N.Y.S. 60 

Gass v. Agate Ice Cream Co. 264 N.Y. 141.

DAMAGES 

181 If the property is so injured that repair will not restore it to a sound condition as where a violin was so injured that its tone value was permanently impaired the plaintiff may be allowed to recover the expense of restoration of the property to as near its former condition as possible, plus compensation for the loss of it during the period of disability, and in addition thereto, the difference in its value before the injury and after its repair. 

Howe v. Johnston 220 AD. 170, 221 N.Y.S. 516 

Schalscha v. Third Ave. R.R. Co. 19 Misc. 141, 43 N.Y.S. 251 

Dettman v. Burns Bros. 111 Misc. 189, 181 N.Y.S. 146.

In an action for damages for loss of a family photograph left with the defendant for enlargement, the measure is the value to the plaintiff, taking into consideration the cost of the picture lost and the probability of replacing it, without regard to sentimental value. 

Valentino v. Nasib Studio 136 Misc. 826, 242 N.Y.S. 277 

Where an article, like an automobile, is so wrecked so as to be worthless and entirely destroyed, the measure of damages would be the difference in value of the article before and after the accident. 

The right to recover for loss of use is limited to those cases in which the injury to the vehicle is not such as to render it beyond repair at a reasonable cost. The period allowed for loss of use is that time reasonably occupied in repairing the vehicle. Where the article has been totally destroyed, there should be no allowance for loss of use. 

The plaintiff may, however, collect for loss of use for the time elapsing between the date of the accident and the time within which he could reasonably purchase and get delivery of another substituting article.

Colonial Motor Co. v. N.Y.C.R. Co. 131 Misc. 891, 228 N.Y.S. 508. 

If the injury is not so great as to make the reparation or restoration of the property unreasonable or out of proportion to the condition and value thereof before the injury, the cost of repair, whether actually made or not, is competent evidence of the damage sustained. 

Weiner v. Liberty Bell Ins. Co. 137 Misc. 43, 243 N.Y.S. 54.

The diminution in the value of the land is the general rule for measuring damages in an action for injury to realty of a permanent character. If something be removed from the land, e.g.: a load of sand, the act might have no appreciable effect upon the value of the property, but the damages would be measured by the value of what was removed and the expense of repairs. 

Rensellaer C. M. Ins. Co. v. Rutland 243˜A.D. 642, affd. 268 N.Y.556 

Recovery for Personal Injuries

The general rule of damages except "lessor and lessee" applies particularly to cases where the plaintiff is injured through negligence of the defendant. The plaintiff must do everything reasonable to keep the damage as low as possible and he must not so act, or unreasonably refrain from acting, as to heap up the damages. 

If P is injured through the negligence of the defendant, he is bound to use ordinary care to cure and restore himself, in accord-

ance with the above rule. He cannot recklessly enhance his injury. 

He is not however, required to employ the very best doctors. If he innocently eats or exercises himself so as to retard his progress, the defendant remains liable although the mistake may have aggravated the injury. Where the original wrongdoer pays for all the damages and resultant damage, he becomes subrogated to a right of action of the injured party against the negligent physician for aggravation of the original injury and damages. The injured party may of course sue the original tortfeasor for the damage caused by his wrong, and the physician for his wrong. A pending action against the aggravator is not an election of remedies which should bar a subsequent recovery against the original wrong-doer for damages resulting from the original wrong. In any event, full payment from both for the combined injuries is not permissible. Should one of them be sued and a general release given in satisfaction, recovery is barred against the other for to permit further recovery would be giving double damages.

Parchefsky v. Kroll Brothers 267 N.Y. 410 

Wagner v. Mittendorf 232 N.Y. 481 

Mills v. Mclver 264 N.Y. 267.

The plaintiff is entitled to recover for all necessary expenses for nursing and medical aid, for pain, suffering, present and prospective, and for the deprivation of the use of any limb as a result of the injury and also pecuniary loss caused by inability to work. All these special damages must be alleged if they are to be recovered. 

Leeds v. Metropolitan Gas Light Co. 90 N.Y. 26.

Evidence of profits of business, which are uncertain and fluctuating in character, is not admissible to prove loss sustained by reason of personal injuries, but loss of services which have a certain and definite value may be proved. 

A plaintiff who was engaged in selling books for which sales he received a commission, was permitted to show what he received on his sales each year before the accident. The plaintiff's income was not from capital invested, but from personal skill and services. The same decision would be followed in cases where the plaintiffs were in the class of dentists, physicians, lawyers, whose earnings are the result of personal skill. Although each has a certain amount of capital investment yet the income is classed as personal earnings. 

Ehrgott v. Mayor 96 N.Y. 264.

If the work of the plaintiff can be done by an employee, the earnings cannot be shown as part of the damages. In one case the plaintiff was usually employed as a boatman, but prior to the accident he had rented a store and conducted a lunch and oyster business. 

Some of the time he employed two or three men. It was held that it was improper to show the profits of the business. 

Weir v. Union R. Co. 188 N.Y. 416 

Galanis v. Simon 222 A.D. 330, affd. 250 N.Y. 524.

A plaintiff was injured through the negligence of the defendant and as a result he was unable to fill contracts for the sale of his special variey of sweet corn. The business was specialized and de-

DAMAGES 

183 pended upon the plaintiff's personal effort. It was impossible to procure anybody else who could do the required work in time. The plaintiff was allowed to recover as part of his damages the difference between the amount received for the undelivered corn and the contract price. 

Steitz v. Gifford 280 N.Y. 15.

Where the plaintiff has worked for wages, he can recover such wages for the period he was rendered unable to work provided he was not paid the wages during his disability. 

Bethlehem Properties v. Patrick McGovern Inc. 291 N.Y.S. 217.

A parent of an infant who was physically injured through the negligence of the defendant, may recover an amount which the jury might fairly say, from the evidence, was sufficient to compensate him for the prospective loss of service of the injured infant during his minority, less the amount it would have cost to maintain the infant had he not been injured provided the parent alleges and proves some actual loss of the services of the child. He may also then recover all expenses actually and necessarily paid by him for medical treatment and care prior to the trial, but not the cost of prospective medical treatment and care. The latter can be recovered by the infant. 

Clarke v. Eighth Ave. R.R.Co. 238 N.Y. 246.

If the action is to recover for damages to his feelings for the abduction of a child the parent need not allege or prove loss of services as a condition of recovery. 

Pickle v. Page 252 N.Y. 474.

The negligent party is responsible for the proximate consequences of his act even though those consequences are more severe and aggravated because of the delicate health of the plaintiff than they would have been if the injured had been sound and well. 

McCahill v. N. Y. Transportation Co. 201 N.Y. 221

It is proper for one defendant to elicit the fact that the plaintiff has obtained a sum from another defendant in part payment for the injuries or damage caused the plaintiff for which he is suing, for the purpose of mitigating damages as against this defendant. 

Ammerman v. Utilities Oil Co. 222 A.D. 481, 226 N.Y.S. 673.

Death Actions 

Where recovery is had for the next of kin, the main elements to be considered are the age of the decedent, his health, habits, life expectancy, earning ability, prospect of increase, the number, age, sex and condition of dependents and his disposition to support them. 

Nothing is allowed for sentiment, grief or suffering. The precise question is: What were the probable chances of pecuniary benefit from the continuance in life of the decedent worth, under all circumstances? 

Dimitroff v. State 171 Misc. 635, 13 N.Y.S. (2nd) 458. 

Damages for Conversion

One whose property has been converted is entitled to recover the market value of the property converted at the time of the conversion

plus interest from that date, or the full amount received by the convertor for such property if that exceeds the market value. If, however, the convertor had to pay commissions to effect the sale of the converted goods at a higher price than the market value, the convertor must pay the amount for which the goods were sold, less these commissions, provided always that the net amount does not fall below the market value of the goods. 

Halladay v. McGraw 192 N.Y.S. 489.

Where household furniture and wearing apparel have been converted, the recovery is not based upon the market value. The owner should be allowed to recover the value to him, based upon price paid, date of purchase, use and all the circumstances and conditions, resulting from his being deprived of the property, not including any sentimental or fanciful value. 

Percy v. Bay Ridge Operating Co. 10 N.Y.S. (2nd) 549 

Lake v. Dye 232 N.Y. 209.

If the subject of the conversion is shares of stock of a fluctuating value, held for speculative purposes, the amount recoverable by the plaintiff is based upon the value of the stock at the time it reached its highest value within a reasonable time after the plaintiff learned of the conversion, within which he could have gone to the market and purchased it. 

Wright v. Bank of the Metropolis 110 N.Y. 237 

Mayer v. Monzo 221 N.Y. 442.

Where the articles converted are not readily salable as such, e.g., plates for illustrating a book published by the plaintiff, the actual value of the property to the person injured may be recovered, rather than the market value. Proof of replacement cost less depreciation is evidence of such value. 

Appleton v. Zeese-Wilkinson Co. 140 Misc. 653, 251 N.Y.S. 532

Spitefulness and high-handed conduct do not increase damages recoverable for conversion. The plaintiff can collect only the loss sustained.

Zeppitella v. Cappellino 199 N.Y.S. 273. 

Damages for Fraud and Deceit

The measure of damages in deceit is based upon the actual loss sustained as a direct result of the defendant's wrongful acts. 

The loss proximately caused by the fraud of the defendant is the difference between the price paid and the value of what was received when put to the use contemplated by the parties together with interest from the date of purchase. As long as the fraud continues to operate, the loss flowing naturally from the fraud may be regarded as its proximate result. If the plaintiff by false representations concerning the financial status of a corporation, whose bonds the defendants induced the plaintiff to buy for purpose of investment, suffers loss because of the financial debacle of that corporation, resulting from that poor financial status, the defendant is liable for that resultant loss even though at the time of the purchase the bonds may have been of value as represented, and even though

DAMAGES 

185 the plaintiff held on to the bonds through the period of the corporation's financial troubles. 

Hotaling v. A. B. Leasing Co. Inc. 247 N.Y. 84 

Reno v. Bull 226 N.Y. 546.

In one case the defendant induced the plaintiff by means of false statements, to buy stock at a high price. The plaintiff was allowed to keep the stock as he did not care to rescind the contract, and he was also allowed as damages the difference between the value of the stock that he received and the price he paid for them. 

Graetz v. Smith 125 Misc. 836, 211 N.Y.S. 577.

Profits which could have been made in dealings with third persons but for the fraud or deceit of the defendant, cannot be recovered even though the plaintiff can show that he had already made contracts which he could not carry out because of the defendant's fraud. 

Foster v. Di Palo 236 N.Y. 132.

In a recent case the defendant by false representations, induced the plaintiff to buy cider which proved to be of a poor quality. The plaintiff had meanwhile contracted to sell the cider to a third party and this contract fell through because of the poor quality of the cider. The plaintiff was not permitted to collect from the defendant the loss of profits. The direct result of the fraud as between the plaintiff and the defendant did not include this contract. 

Foster v. Di Palo 236 N.Y. 132.

Damages for Libel and Slander 

Punitive damages cannot be allowed, unless the plaintiff produces evidence affirmatively showing that the defendant had actual malice existing at the time that the tortious act was done, and which particular malice influenced the act. 

Corrigan v. Bobbs-Merrill Co. 228 N.Y. 58 

Krug v. Pitass 162 N.Y. 154.

In libel and slander cases where the plaintiff is a female, besides any direct pecuniary loss, she may have the jury consider as bearing upon the question of damage, a resulting change in her status. as a single woman, humiliation, disgrace, mental anguish, deprivation of a man's society and comfort. What these damages are or should be be must rest very largely in the discretion of the jury, but these are elements which they consider in arriving at the amount. 

Leventhal v. Liberman 262 N.Y. 209.

A passenger of a common carrier may recover damages for insulting and slanderous words used by its employees. The same rule obtains where the servant of an innkeeper offers insult to his guests or where the servants of a theatre owner insult one of the audience; also where the servants of a public bath house owner insult a patron. 

De Voy v. Irish World 208 A.D. 319, 203 N.Y.S. 369.

The jury may be permitted to consider in fixing the amount of the verdict, that the plaintiff has already recovered damages, or has agreed to receive compensation in connection with a libel of similar purport or effect as the libel for which the action has been brought.

The defendant may prove the absence of malice in mitigation of the verdict. He must show that he believed and had reason to believe the charge to be true when it was made. There are two ways of doing this: (1) By proving that he received such information from others as induced him to believe the charge to be true; (2) By showing the existence of facts within his knowledge calculated to produce such a belief. 

Varvaro v. Amer. Agriculturist 222 A.D. 213, 225 N.Y.S. 564

Civil Practice Act § 338a The Liquidated Damage Clause 

If at the time a contract is made, the parties agree on a lump sum as damages for a breach, the court will recognize this agreement, provided that the damages are impossible of ascertainment and not inserted in the contract as a penalty. If the amount agreed upon is out of proportion to the damages, the liquidated damage clause will not be enforced. In one case, the parties entered into a five-year lease with provisions that entitled the lessor to terminate the lease, if the lessee failed to pay the monthly installment of rent or vacated the premises before the end of the term, or violated one of the long list of covenants and regulations, many of which were of trivial nature, and there was also a provision for the forfeiture of a sum deposited with the lessor upon any breach. The court held that an agreement of such nature was void because it was in the nature of a penalty. 

884 West End Ave. Co. v. Pearlman 193 N.Y.S. 670, affd. 234 N.Y, 589 

J. & H. Garage v. H. Flow Co. 225 A.D. 65, affd. 251 N.Y. 553.

The liquidated damages clause must also deal with a definite degree of breach. So if S is under obligation to mow a lawn in a certain fashion, remove the rubbish, keep a fence in good repair, and make the tennis nets, an agreement by him to pay $50 for any breach would be considered a penalty and not liquidated damages for a definite breach. Therefore it would not be enforceable and there would have to be suit for damages done. The damage clause would play no part in the determination of the amount of damages. 

Hackenheimer v. Kurtzmann 235 N.Y. 57.

The tendency in doubtful cases is to construe the sum payable as a penalty rather than liquidated damages, even where the parties have styled it differently. 

Weinstein v. City of New York 264 A.D. 398, affd. 289 N.Y. 741

When Interest Is Recoverable 

The decisions are not clear upon the question of the allowance of interest to a successful claimant. Generally where damages can be ascertained by computation, interest is allowed from the time the money is due. This rather unsatisfactory rule has been clarified by decisions. 

Blackwell v. Finlay 233 N.Y. 361

Where a debtor is in default for non-payment of money due, or for failure to deliver property, or to pay for services rendered, we

DAMAGES 

187 have a clear case. Interest is recoverable from the time of the default until the obligation is fully discharged. From this it follows that in an action in conversion, interest is allowed on the fair value from the time of the conversion. 

If an action is based upon a breach of contract, expressed or implied, other than a contract to marry, interest is to be allowed upon the principal sum whether theretofore liquidated or unliquidated. 

Thus, interest is allowed when the amount recovered is the loss of profits sustained by the plaintiff because of the defendant's breach of contract of services to be rendered. If recovery is had upon a life insurance policy issued by a company doing business in New York, the plaintiff recovers interest from the date of the receipt by the company of the completed proof of death of the insured. 

Civil Practice Act §§ 480, 480a 

In some tort actions, e.g., assault and battery, slander, libel, seduction, false imprisonment, interest is not allowed except from the date of trial. În some, such as trespass and replevin, interest is always allowed. In some cases, such as injury to property through negligence, interest is allowed in the discretion of the jury. Where a verdict is secured for a sum parted with by reason of the defendant's misrepresentation, interest is allowed from the date the money was paid. 

Wilson v. City of Troy 135 N. Y. 96 

Hayes v. Island Park 146 Misc. 59, 260 N.Y.S. 574.

Interest is allowed by the trier of facts, by the jury or by the court if there is no jury. If no interest is added to a verdict where a litigant is entitled to interest as a matter of right, the interest cannot be added by the clerk when the judgment is filed, but the court may do so at a subsequent date. 

Klausner v. Queens Fur Dressing Co. 130 Misc. 579, 224 N.Y.S. 333 

Demms v. Blanchard 150 Misc. 867, 270 N.Y.S. 700.

A claim resting on a quantum meruit, draws interest to be computed from the time when the demand is made after the close of the services and the debtor is put in default. 

Blackwell v. Finlay 233 N.Y. 361.

After the rendition of a judgment for a sum of money by verdict, report or decision, interest begins to run upon the total amount awarded from the time of the rendition of the award. A judgment for alimony is a judgment similar to other money judgments, and interest on unpaid alimony is a proper charge even against the estate of a decedent. The running of interest on a judgment may be stopped by a tender or by payment of a special deposit into court. 

The rule applies where a party is restrained by injunction or attachment from making the payment. 

Moscow Fire Ins. Co. v. Heckscher 260 A.D. 646; affd. 285 N.Y. 674.

The statutory rate of interest allowed as charges or damages in the absence of any contract dealing with the situation, may be changed during the period between the maturity of an obligation and its payment. 

Metropolitan Sav. Bank v. Tuttle 290 N.Y. 497.

When Punitive Damages Are Recoverable 

Punitive or exemplary damages are penal in their nature despite the fact that the plaintiff is allowed to keep the damages. The purpose is to deter others from the commission of like acts. They are allowed in actions which show a reckless disregard toward the safety and rights of others. The fact that the defendant may have been punished in the criminal courts for the same act does not prevent the plaintiff from recovering punitive damages. 

Punitive damages are allowed in case of wanton or reckless acts amounting to assault, alienation of affections, battery, libel and false imprisonment, and in such cases the motive and conduct of the defendant may be considered by the jury for the purpose of assessment of damages. The award of only nominal damages is sufficient to carry with it even a larger sum of punitive damages. 

Powers v. Man. Ry 120 N.Y. 178 Buteau v. Naegli 215 N.Y.S. 823. 

Where a passenger is wrongfully expelled from a train, he may recover pecuniary loss, damages for injuries, for the annoyance, vexation, risk and indignity done him. 

Gillespie v. B'klyn Heights R.R. 178 N.Y. 347, 362

DOMESTIC RELATIONS Marriage 

OMMON LAW marriages entered into since April 29, 1933, are not valid in New York. No marriage relationship is recognized unless properly solemnized.

Domestic Relations Law § 11 

All marriage contracts are subject to certain legal obligations which cannot be contracted away, e.g., marital intercourse so that children may be born; support of wife and children. 

Miller v. Miller 132 Misc. 121, 228 N.Y.S. 657

The Husband's Responsibilities 

A husband is legally bound to support his wife in accordance with his means. This duty does not exist where the wife has herself breached her marital obligations or is committing adultery. This obligation to support when it does exist may be enforced in three ways: (1) in an acion for a decree of separation; (2) in a criminal proceeding charging him with being a disorderly person in that he has neglected to provide for her according to his means and she may become a public charge; (3) in an action to recover for necessaries furnished to the wife by another or by the wife herself if she has advanced her own money. 

Matter of Barc 177 Misc. 578, affd. 266 A.D. 677

The wife's wealth does not relieve the husband of any responsibility to support her or in determining in what manner he is to support her. A contract absolving the husband from the duty to support his wife is unenforceable. While agreements of separation are recognized, yet they are open to attack where their provisions are inadequate, inequitable, unjust, unconscionable or where the contract was improvidently entered into. 

Domestic Relations Law § 51 

Tirrel v. Tirrell, 232 N.Y. 224; Garlock v. Garlock 279 N.Y. 337 

Germer v. Germer 167 Misc. 882, 4 N.Y.S. (2d) 747.

The criminal proceeding will lie so long as the relation is not dissolved or limited by court decree, and this even though the husband himself might be entitled to a decree of separation. Even then the husband who in good faith is ready to support his wife in his home will not be declared disorderly because he refuses to maintain her separately.

Where the spouses are living together and the wife procures necessaries, in procuring them she acts as her husband's agent. If she abandons his home or refuses to cohabit, the agency is no longer presumed. Where credit for necessaries is given solely to the wife even though living with the husband, he is not liable therefor. The right to pledge her husband's credit does not exist if she receives 189

money from him sufficient to enable her to provide herself with necessaries. 

Kalb v. Anderson, 11 N.Y.S. (2d) 711.

A husband is liable for legal services rendered to his wife where such services are necessary for her protection in her subsisting marital rights. This includes legal services rendered in an action for separation brought against her or for the purpose of helping her in obtaining a separation decree, e.g., to find her husband who had left her without provision for her support. Likewise, legal services in defending husband's habeas corpus proceedings to obtain from her custody of a child; also in defending her against a charge of assault and grand larceny. 

McLaughlin v. McCauliss 146 Misc. 518, affd. 240 A.D. 964 

Elder v. Rosenwasser 238 N.Y. 427 

Lanyon Detective Agency v. Cochrane 240 N.Y. 274 

Turner v. Woolworth 221 N.Y. 425.

A husband may be held liable for a wife's reasonable funeral expenses but he is entitled to reimbursement from the wife's separate estate for such expenses, since her estate is primarily liable therefor.

Matter of Koretsky 180 Misc. 108 

A husband is not liable for any of his wife's debts incurred before the marriage with these exceptions: He may be held liable to the extent of any property which he received from her and he may be held responsible at the Court's discretion for expenses of any confinement and pregnancy caused by him out of wedlock. In fact the liability in the second case exists though there be no subsequent marriage.

Domestic Relations Law §§ 54, 120. 

A man takes his wife in her then existing state of health and assumes the cost of her medical care for an illness she had at the time of her marriage, after the marriage. 

Rademacher v. Torbensen 257 A.D. 91, 13 N.Y.S. (2nd) 124. 

Obligation to Support an Abandoned Wife

Where an abandoned wife uses her own money to support herself and her children she may recover the amount so expended, from her husband. This is so even if the money spent was the outcome of the wife's own labors. By analogy she is in the same position as a stranger who supplies necessities to abandoned children. 

She may, however, renounce her right to recovery, by word or act prior to the expenditures. 

Manufacturers Trust Co. v. Gray 278 N.Y. 380 

The Parent's Obligation

A father even though divorced is required to support minor children until they reach their maturity or are emancipated, unless there is a showing of their physical or mental disability in which case the liability continues. But although this is so, the child cannot buy necessaries and charge his father; nor can a stranger supply the infant with necessaries. It is only when the father has failed or

DOMESTIC RELATIONS 

191 neglected to support his child that the former is liable for the reasonable value of the necessaries supplied to the infant. The theory is that any person, even a divorced mother who supplies such necessaries is deemed to have conferred a benefit on the delinquent parent, for which the law raises an implied promise to pay on the part of the parent. Even where a divorce decree directs the father to support the child, the mother can recover for necessaries advanced in a separate action. She need not resort to a modification of the decree or to a contempt proceeding.* 

Domestic Relations Law § 120; Swanton v. Curley 273 N.Y. 325 

Laumeier v. Laumeier 237 N.Y. 357 

Halsted v. Halsted 228 A,D. 298, 239 N.Y.S. 422

Dumay v. Dumay 217 A.D. 773, (case 3) 

Though the wife obtains custody of their child by divorce decree, it is still the duty of the father to support the child. If he fails to support the child, he may be also convicted of being a disorderly person.

Code Criminal Procedure § 899. 

In this connection, it has been held that, though the mother is domiciled in a state which throws the burden of the support upon the custodial parent, if the father is domiciled in New York he may be held liable for the money advanced as reasonable support by the custodial mother. 

Whitton v. Schultz 265 A.D. 583.

A court of equity has jurisdiction to compel the support of a child only if the application is incidental to a matrimonial action. 

A separate proceeding by one parent to compel the other parent to support a child cannot be maintained. An exception exists where one parent controls a child's property and fails to make suitable provision therefrom for support.

Bedrick v. Bedrick 151 Misc. 4, affd. 241 A.D. 807. 

The estate of a deceased testator is not obligated to support infant orphans. And the will of the father may entirely cut off any and all of the infants. 

Rice v. Andrews 127 Misc. 826, 217 N.Y.S. 528.

Where the father is dead or incapable of supporting his child or cannot be found in the state, the mother is charged with its support according to her means. Where the child, however, has an estate from which the child can be supported, the estate must support both child and mother if the surrogate so direct. This is not so in the case of the father.

Domestic Relations Court Act § 101. 

Parent's Right to Earnings of Child 

The father is entitled to any money earned by the children if he gives thirty days' notice in writing to the employer. If the em- *The Statute of Limitations begins to run against one who has paid money for the necessaries of a child which the father should have advanced, from the time the advance is made in each expenditure and not from the time the obligation to support terminated. ployer despite the notice, pays the minor, he must make good to the parent all earnings subsequent to the notice.

Domestic Relations Law § 72 

The father is also entitled to compensation for loss of services arising from personal injuries to a child caused by the negligence of a defendant. The right to maintain an action of this character is based upon the relationship of master and servant. Under the common law the father originally had exclusive right to the services of his minor children. But a mother may, even during the lifetime of the father, bring an action for loss of services of an infant child where it was shown that she was practically the head of the family, paid the bills and by direction of the father was entitled to and did receive the earnings of the infant, she being responsible for his maintenance and support. 

Hagopian v. Samuelson 236 A.D. 491, 260 N.Y.S. 24

The parent is entitled to the services and earnings of a minor child while it is in the parent's custody or control and has not been emancipated. A parent may relinquish his rights or emancipate the child expressly or by implication. A minor, who with the consent and approval of his parents was receiving his own wages and paying his own way, was held to be emancipated. 

Crosby v. Crosby 230 A.D. 651, 246 N.Y.S. 384

Emancipation of a child* or failure to support him means the loss to the parent of the child's earnings and also the parent's right of action against a person whose wrongful act has injured the child. 

Cuming v. Brooklyn City R.R. Co. 109 N.Y. 95. 

A parent may not recover damages against an unemancipated minor child for his tort, but he may recover such damages from an emancipated child. 

LoGalbo v. LoGalbo, 138 Misc. 485, 246 N.Y.S. 565

If an infant is an employee, his parent's rights to wages are the same as those of the infant. 

Turner v. Kouwenhhoven 100 N.Y. 115, 119. 

Support of Illegitimate Children

Under the common law the putative father was under no legal liability to support his illegitimate offspring. By statute the court may by order specify the sum to be paid for support until the child reaches the age of sixteen, and may order payment of the necessary expenses incurred by the mother in connection with her pregnancy, confinement and recovery; for the funeral expenses if the child dies; for its support prior to the making of the order of filiation. No other amounts may be awarded. 

Prager v. Manowitz 243 A.D. 284, 276 N.Y.S. 875. *If an infant marries he is emancipated, and for all purposes of relationship between parent and child, the child is considered an adult. An emancipated child can recover from his father on a contract. Crosby v. Crosby 

230 A.D. 651, 246 N.Y.S. 384.

RELATIONS Support of Relatives 

The primary obligation for the support of a child rests upon the father. The obligation is placed upon the mother if the father is incapable of supporting the child or can not be found within the State. If the parents can not support the child and the grandparents are of sufficient means, the latter become obligated. After these come step-parents but before imposing the obligation upon the step+ parents to support a minor step-child, proof must be adduced establishing the fact that the step-parent had knowledge of the child's existence at the time he became a step-parent. 

Calhoun v. Calhoun 256 A.D. 672; Domestic Relations Court Act § 101 

Parents of a child born out of wedlock are liable for the necessary support and education of the child but the reverse is not true. Nor is there a legal obligation resting upon a brother to support an indigent sister.

Castellani v. Castellani 176 Misc. 763, affd. 263 A.D. 984 

No liability is to be imposed upon a minor child or grandchild for the support of a parent or grandparent unless the court expressly finds that the funds of the infant are in excess of the reasonable requirements of the infant, taking into account his maintenance, education, medical care and other factors applicable to his condition. 

If a child has been adopted and the adoptive parent becomes destitute, the natural parent need not provide for the child, though the child is likely to become a public charge and the parent is financially able. After adoption the natural parent has no obligations. 

Betz v. Horr 276 N.Y. 83

Code of Criminal Procedure § 914; Public Welfare Law §125. 

Adoption

Adoption was not recognized by the common law but it exists in this country solely by force of statutes. 

An adult unmarried person, or an adult husband together with his adult wife, may adopt anyone. A grandparent may adopt a grandchild. An adult spouse may adopt any child of the other. 

Upon adoption the natural parents of the adopted child lose all rights over him; as far as their rights and responsibilities are concerned, the child does not exist. But the child does inherit from both his natural parents, despite the adoption.

The adoptive parents become for all legal purposes, natural parents of the adopted child. They inherit from him and he from them. But he does not inherit from the collaterals of the adoptive parents. The latter's collaterals do inherit from him, as if he were a natural child of the adoptive parents. The only instance in which the adopted child is not deemed to be the child of the foster parents is where future estates may be cut off by such adoption. Where the passing by limitation over of real or personal property is dependent on a parent dying without heirs or children, it would be very easy for a person having no child to adopt one and thus cut off the contingent remainder. The statute was aimed at such a possibility. 

Domestic Relations Law 114; In re Horn's Will 256 N.Y. 294

Foster children and natural children of the adoptive parents have all the rights of fraternal relationship including the right of inheritance from each other. This right extends to the distributees of such children. The rule is, however, subject to the restrictions about cutting off remaindermen as stated in the preceding paragraph. 

Domestic Relations Law § 115. 

Note, however, that where a husband or wife adopts a natural child of the other spouse, such a child is for all legal purposes treated as a legitimate offspring of the marriage of its natural parent and its foster parent. 

In re Monroe 132 Misc. 279, 279 N.Y.S. 476

A non-resident may adopt a child who is a New York resident. 

In re Voluntary Adoption of Minor 130 Misc. 793, 226 N.Y.S. 445 

There are three methods in the Domestic Relations Law relating to abrogation of an adoption. The court issues a citation directed to the child, to the persons who were parties to the adoption proceedings and appoints a special guardian to protect the interests of the child. 

1. The first method is by a proceeding in which the foster parents, the persons adopted and those whose consent would be necessary to the original adoption, all agree to the abrogation. 

Domestic Relations Law § 116 

2. The second case deals with the case of a child taken from a charitable institution for adoption when the child or someone on behalf of the child, seeks the abrogation. The ground may be cruelty, misusage, failure or inability to support, maintain or educate the child, attempts to change the religion of the child, failure to safeguard its religion or other violations of duty. Consents are not necessary in this method. 

Domestic Relations Law § 117 

3. The third method provides for an application on the part of the foster parent because of the misconduct of the child. The court in this case gives due consideration to the interests of the child and the foster parents.

Domestic Relations Law § 118 

In re Souers 135 Misc. 521, 238 N.Y.S. 738.

The Surrogate may open, vacate or set aside an order of adoption for fraud, newly discovered evidence, or other sufficient cause. 

Where it was shown that an eleven-year-old girl, adopted at the age of six, was destructive and unruly, the court held that the interests of all required an abrogation of the adoption. 

Domestic Relations Law § 113 

In re Anonymous 157 Misc. 951, 285 N.Y.S. 827.

The Wife's Rights 

A wife can contract in her own name, and if she works she can keep all she earns. The husband cannot sue for what she earns. She can go into business with her husband as partner, and is liable to third parties just as a partner. But for work rendered by her for her husband in connection with his business which is not of extraordin-

DOMESTIC RELATIONS 

195 ary nature, she is not entitled to be paid as a matter of right. In a recent case a wife's services in managing her husband's rooming houses were not held of such character as to warrant a finding of an implied agreement to pay her compensation. 

Domestic Relations Law §§ 51, 60 

Martin v. Bronx County Trust Co. 237 A.D. 246, 260 N.Y.S. 344.

If a wife saves money from her weekly allowance, the amount so saved belongs to her husband unless given to her as a gift. 

Frick v. Cone 290 N.Y.S. 592, affd. 292, affd. 298 N.Y.S. 173

One spouse can sue the other spouse in tort. 

Domestic Relations Law § 57. 

Void Marriages 

(1) Marriages between ancestor and descendant, brother and sister, uncle and niece, or aunt and nephew, be they even of half blood, are void. The children are, however, legitimate. (2) A marriage is void if one of the parties is married at the time of the second marriage. Even though the polygamous marriage is contracted in a foreign jurisdiction where it is valid, it would be void in New York.

Domestic Relations Law § 6 

A court of another state lacks jurisdiction to declare the marriage relations of a citizen of this state dissolved, where the divorced citizen actually resides in New York during the divorce proceedings, makes no voluntary appearance in the other state's courts and receives no actual notice of such proceedings. Accordingly, that decree is no defense to a prosecution for bigamy.

A married B while B had a spouse (C) living. A did not know of the other living spouse. B obtained a divorce from C, thus making 

A and B competent to be husband and wife. Subsequent to the decree, A continued to live with B. B can have the marriage to A annulled, as the marriage was bigamous at its inception. 

Earle v. Earle 141 A.D. 611

The defendant in a successful divorce suit cannot remarry in New York without permission of the court. Power resides in the court, after the lapse of three years from the rendition of the decree, to modify the judgment upon proof of defendant's good conduct subsequent to the decree. The court cannot modify a decree nunc pro tunc, where the defendant married again after three years but without obtaining a modification. The defendant can marry in another state, because the provisions of the order of the courts forbidding the remarriage have no extraterritorial effect. The subsequent marriage of the guilty party in a sister state, if valid in that state, will be recognized here as a lawful marriage. 

Fisher v. Fisher 250 N.Y. 313; Merrick v. Merrick 266 N.Y. 120 *Whether a husband may be convicted for larceny from his wife is not altogether clear. The last expression at Special Term held that a wife could not commit larceny by appropriating her husband's property. See People ex ral Carr v. Martin 286 N.Y. 27; People v. Rapp 180 Misc. 839.

(3) A marriage in this state in which the male is under 16 or the female under 14 is prohibited.*

Domestic Relations Law § 15a 

In order to obtain an annulment decree from a New York court,. either of the following conditions must exist: (a) Both parties are resident of the state when the action is commenced. (b) Where the parties were married in New York and the plaintiff or defendant resided here when the action was commenced. (c) Where the marriage took place without the state and either party is a resident when the action is commenced and has been a New York resident one year continuously at any time before the action is commenced.

Civil Practice Act § 1165a Terminating a Valid Marital Status 

These cases fall into three classes: First, where the marital status automatically ends; Second: where the parties must complete a legal proceeding to end it but as to the parties, their obligations after the decree are such as if they had never been married; and 

Third, where they can end the marital status by legal proceedings, though it exists until the decree is entered. In the first class we have the case where a man is finally** sentenced in this or in another state to life imprisonment, e.g., "20 years to life;" or death. As soon as he is so sentenced the married state ends, in the same manner as if he had died. A pardon or parole does not restore the rights of a previous marriage. 

Jones v. Jones 249 A.D. 470, affd. 274 N.Y 574

In re Lindewall 287 N.Y. 347; Domestic Relations Law §§ 6, 58. 

In the second class we have these cases: (1) The 18-year Rule; (2) Lunacy at the time of marriage; (3) Impotency; (4) Duress; (5) Fraud. (1) The 18-Year Rule.-If the parties were New York residents and one of the parties was under 18 at the time of the marriage, that party or his parent, guardian or friend may sue for annulment. 

If the infant does not bring the action he must be made a party thereto. The granting of the annulment is in the discretion of the court but an appeal may be taken. The fact that the parents of the infant agreed to the marriage, or that the marriage took place in a state where a marriage by this infant under 18 would be valid, does not mean that in New York this party cannot annul the marriage. 

If there has been a cohabitation after the infant had reached 18, there can be no annulment on the ground of "under age.” 

Quinzi v. Quinzi 261 A.D. 929 *It has been held in a lower court decision that such marriage is voidable and not void. Anonymous v. Anonymous 176 Misc. 850 **See Matter of Bailey 291 N. The finality of the judgment was held not to be affected by the pendency of the appeal. See also Bond v.

Where a girl under eighteen compels a man to marry her because she is about to become the mother of his child, and her intention is simply to legitimatize the child and then dissolve the marriage, she will not be aided by the court. 

Smith v. Smith 129 Misc. 503, 221 N.Y.S. 672

Civil Practice Act § 1133. 

Since the laws of the place where the marriage takes place decide the validity of the marriage, if two non-residents marry in a jurisdiction where infants under 18 may marry, that marriage is valid and cannot be set aside even in New York. The case mentioned in the second preceding paragraph has reference to a situation where New York residents go to such jurisdiction only so as to avoid the marriage laws of New York. 

Simmons v. Simmons 208 A.D. 195, 203 N.Y.S. 215 (2) Lunacy. An action to annul a marriage on the ground that one of the parties was a lunatic at the time of the marriage may be maintained by a relative of the lunatic during the continued lunacy, or after his death in that condition, and during the life of the sane spouse. The action may also be maintained by the sane party during the continuance of the lunacy, provided the plaintiff did not know of the lunacy at the time of the marriage. 

Civil Practice Act § 1137 

(3) Impotency.-If one party to the marriage contract was impotent at the time of the marriage, and the impotency was incurable, an action to annul the marriage can be maintained by the other party. The action is to be brought within five years after marriage. 

If the defendant fails to plead the Statute of Limitations as a defense, the plaintiff is entitled to a decree, although the evidence shows that more than five years have elapsed since the marriage. 

Katz v. Katz 136 Misc. 377, 240 N.Y.S. 68. 'If the plaintiff is the impotent party, he must have been unaware of his incapacity at the marriage or unaware that it was incurable. 

Civil Practice Act § 1141 

(4) Duress.-If one of the parties was forced to marry under duress practiced by the other party to the marriage, the marriage contract may be set aside. The duress, if practiced by a third party is not sufficient ground for setting aside the marriage. (5) Fraud.-A marriage contract is voidable if the fraud practiced is so material, that had it not been practiced the party deceived would not have consented to the marriage, and if it be of such a nature as to deceive an ordinarily prudent person. 

Laage v. Laage 176 Misc. 190 

The following have been held to be cases of fraud permitting the annulment of a marriage: The defendant lied about or knowingly concealed that she was suffering from a disease which made her sterile; or that he was not addicted to drugs; or that defendant had a loathsome or dangerous disease, as syphilis, leprosy, or tuberculosis; or that he was subject to epilepsy, rendering cohabitation extremely dangerous, though the fact that a party was subject to epilepsy, or to fainting spells, has been held not to furnish ground

for an annulment; or concealed, on inquiry, previous unchastity; or held himself out as a person of good character, concealing from the plaintiff criminal activities in which he had been engaged; or falsely represented that the plaintiff was the father of the defendant's child; or stated that she was a widow whereas she was a divorcee; or was induced to enter into the marriage contract by a promise on the part of the defendant to join the plaintiff's religious faith, which promise the defendant had never intended to keep, and there had been no consummation of the marriage. *

Where plaintiff's consent to the marriage was obtained by the defendant's fraudulent representation that she had sufficient money to enable him to enter into a certain business enterprise, it could not be said as a matter of law that this was not a ground for annulment. The misrepresentation might be the essence of the contract.

Civil Practice Act § 1139; Blank v. Blank 109 N.Y. 91 

Lapides v. Lapides 254 N.Y. 73 

Williams v. Williams 11 N.Y.S. (2nd) 611 

Svenson v. Svenson 178 N.Y. 54.

Concealing characteristics, temper or lack of wealth, does not by itself justify annulment. It has also been held that a marriage would not be annuled because the parties were untruthful to each other in their mutual declarations of undying love for each other. But proof that the defendant never loved her and never intended to live with the plaintiff is ground for annulment though there was cohabitation during the honeymoon.** 

Shonfeld v. Shonfeld 260 N.Y. 477

Cohabitation, with knowledge of the fraud, constitutes a waiver, and the defrauded party is estopped from asserting the fraud. 

Watkins v. Watkins 197 A.D. 489, 189 N.Y.S. 860.

(3) Divorce. The statute permits one spouse to divorce the other and terminate the marriage relationship with certain limitations under conditions outlined in the discussion which follows. 

Under § 1147 of the Civil Practice Act, one of the parties to the marriage may procure a judgment in New York, divorcing the parties and dissolving the marriage by reason of the defendant's adultery, where one of the four following conditions exists. (a) Both parties were New York residents when the adultery was committed. (b) The parties were married in New York. (c) The plaintiff was a New York resident when the adultery was committed and when the action was commenced. (d) The adultery was committed in New York and the plaintiff was a New York resident when the action was commenced. 

There must be at least one credible witness to the adultery. A *The court will first make an interlocutory decree of dissolution to become final upon proper filing and compliance with the order.

confession by the wife is not sufficient. The evidence of a prostitute or of one whose testimony shows him to be shameless in sex matters should have corroboration. It seems that testimony of private detectives employed to check on the conduct of a spouse likewise needs corroboration. Triers of facts are justified in looking with suspicion upon such evidence.

Opportunity and inclination to adultery, e.g,. a woman and a man not her husband registered as man and wife at a hotel and stayed in the same room overnight, make out a sufficient case of adultery, and the testimony to this effect is enough without proof of the actual intercourse. 

Miller v. Miller 212 A.D. 114, 208 N.Y.S. 113.

In either of the following cases the plaintiff is not entitled to a divorce even though the adultery is established: (a) Where the offense was committed with the procurement or the connivance of the plaintiff. (b) Where the adultery has been forgiven by the plaintiff. Voluntary cohabitation with the knowledge of the adultery is equivalent to an affirmative forgiveness.

The knowledge which must exist must be sufficiently substantial upon which to base a belief, and usually there must be some legal proof of the commission of the offense before the condonation will be implied from cohabitation. (c) Where the action was not commenced within five years after the discovery by the plaintiff of the offense charged. (d) Where the plaintiff has also been guilty of adultery, so that the defendant would have been entitled, if innocent, to a divorce. 

Civil Practice Act § 1153. 

Suppose a plaintiff wife, in an action for divorce, had committed adultery in 1922. The action based on adultery on the part of the defendant husband was commenced by the plaintiff in 1928. The adultery of the wife had never been forgiven or condoned by the defendant husband. Is the adulterous act of 1922 (of over 5 years' standing) a defense to defeat the plaintiff's action? The court held that it was no defense, since the adulterous act of 1922 would not entitle the defendant to a divorce if innocent. 

Ryan v. Ryan 132 Misc. 339, 229 N.Y.S. 511.

Although adultery is a crime, the fact of adultery in a civil action may be proved by only fair preponderance of the evidence. 

Burgess v. Burgess 173 N.Y.S. 505.

The amount fixed by a court as alimony fixes the amount of the husband's liability for the support of his wife and children. Once the court has determined the extent of the liability, the decree becomes a complete bar to an action for necessaries purchased, or expenses incurred over and above the amount allowed as alimony. 

Thus there could be no recovery for an amount expended by the mother for an operation upon the child, when the sum so spent exceeded the amount fixed in the decree.

In determining the amount of alimony to be paid, the fortune of the husband together with his earning capacity are to be considered. 

The fact that he does not use his capabilities, does not limit the wife's recovery to a sum based only on the amount of property he has. If the husband will not exert himself, his capacity for earning must be estimated and added to his income.
