Counsel Fees Pendente Lite 

In an action for divorce, separation or annulment, the court, in its discretion, during the pendency thereof, from time to time may make and modify orders requiring the husband to pay counsel fees necessary to enable the wife to carry on or defend the action. The counsel fees to be awarded are those to be rendered in the future. 

Civil Practice Act § 1169. 

Where during the action counsel fees have been awarded the wife and the order therefor was filed, that allowance fixed the husband's liability for the expenses of the suit. The sole remedy to obtain compensation for extra labor is to move to increase the allowance. This, however, does not apply to legal services rendered for the purpose of enforcing the final judgment, e.g., an appeal. A common law action may be maintained. And it has been held that even after final judgment a court could allow counsel fees and disbursements to a wife compelled to defend an application to reduce alimony. 

Ehrlich v. McKee 170 Misc. 222, affd. 258 A.D. 715

Separation Agreements 

A husband and wife can make a valid contract for separation and support, provided that they are either living apart at the time they enter into the separation agreement or they intend to separate immediately after the signing of the agreement. An agreement to separate or to obtain or facilitate a divorce, as when the wife is promised a sum for getting a divorce, is invalid. 

La Montagne v. La Montagne 239 A.D. 352, affd. 264 N.Y. 552 

Matter of Rhinelander 290 N.Y. 31.

A valid separation agreement is binding upon the parties until it is set aside by the court, and the court has no power to fix by way of temporary alimony, a larger sum than that fixed in the agreement. But whatever effect the agreement may have upon the question of alimony, it does not oust the court of jurisdiction to entertain a separation action. Furthermore, if the husband has breached the agreement, the wife may maintain an action for separation if legal grounds exist, and in that event the court may determine de novo, the amount of alimony to which she may be entitled. 

Zysman v. Zysman 140 Misc. 617, 251 N.Y.S. 355 

Braunworth v. Braunworth 260 A.D. 113.

The provision for maintenance and support includes expenses for medical services for the wife. It does not fix a limit to expenses for a child, though the agreement states that it does. A child is never bound by the terms of a separation agreement, and his rights can be asserted separately. It thus differs from the rule where alimony is set by the court for support of the wife and children. 

D.M.E. v. D.D.E. 179 Misc. 406. 

The agreement can be set aside by an action in equity where it is shown that the provisions are inequitable, unjust or improvi-

205 dently entered into. And although resumed cohabitation does not ipso facto destroy the agreement, cohabitation with an intent to reconcile, does. 

Duoin v. Dubin 174 Misc. 952 

Hamlin v. Hamlin 129 Misc. 263, affd. 223 A.D. 810.

The agreement terminates upon the death of either spouse, but it may provide for a wife's allowance after the husband's death. A discharge in bankruptcy does not destroy the obligation to support. 

In re Herb's Estate 296 N.Y.S. 491 

D'Andria v. Hagerman 253 A. D. 518, affd. 278 N. Y. 630.

Where the agreement is not patently bad or in the absence of proof showing the invalidity of the agreement or the inadequacy of its provisions, the later enrichment of the husband is of no consequence, and the amounts set out in the separation agreement to be paid by the husband can not therefore be increased. Should the terms of the separation agreement later be incorporated in a divorce decree, the payments to be made may later be lowered by the court, because the court always retains jurisdiction to modify its decrees. 

Such modified decree is what the wife can enforce by matrimonial remedies, e.g., contempt, sequestration. The original contract stands and can be enforced as a contract. ** 

Goldman v. Goldman 282 N.Y. 296; Jackson v. Jackson 290 N.Y. 512.

It has been held that although the agreement calls for a lump sum settlement for the wife's future support, it can be disregarded in the event the proceeds of the settlement are exhausted though through extravagance, and the wife is liable to become a public charge. And if the lump sum payment under the contract was merely a purchase by the husband of a release from the wife of future support, it will be held a void contract and a violation of the statute which prohibits spouses from contracting to relieve the husband from his responsibility. Where, however, a lump sum agreement is entered into after the marriage relation was terminated by a decree of absolute divorce even if because of the husband's misconduct, it is valid. The wife's relief, if any, must come through an application to the court for a modification of the divorce decree. 

De Robertis v. De Robertis 261 A.D. 476

Action for Separation 

An action for separation may be maintained in either of the following cases: (1) Where both parties are New York residents when the action is commenced. (2) Where the marriage took place in New York, and either party is a resident at the time the action is commenced. (3) If the marriage took place without the State and either party is a New York resident when the action is commenced and has been for a year continuously at any time prior to the commencement of the action. It is not necessary that the year immediately precede the commencement of the action.

Residence, as here used, does not mean mere physical presence but is synonymous with domicile.

Civil Practice Act, § 1165a 

The action may be maintained by a duly authorized representative of an incompetent person. However, an action for divorce can not be maintained by, or on behalf of an incompetent. 

Mohrman v. Kob 291 N.Y. 181; Kaplan v. Kaplan 256 N.Y. 356.

The jurisdictional requirements above listed for actions for separation are the same as those required to maintain an action for annulment. 

The grounds for separation are: (1) Abandonment or desertion; (2) failure to support; (3) cruel and inhuman treatment; (4) conduct rendering cohabitation unsafe or improper. 

Abandonment contemplates the voluntary separation of one party from another without justification, with the intention of not returning. The intent is to be determined as of the time of departure. 

Pompilio v. Pompilio 129 Misc. 207, 221 N.Y.S. 594 

It is not necessary that the plaintiff allege and prove acts of violence to be entitled to a separation. Cruel and inhuman acts are sufficient. A continual ignoring by a husband of his wife, and his refusal to converse or communicate with her, constitute cruelty. 

Causing four unjustifiable arrests for non-support within eight months, was held to be cruel and inhuman treatment, giving the plaintiff the right to a judgment of separation. 

Bergman v. Bergman 138 Misc. 335, 245 N.Y.S. 439.

No judgment for a separation can be entered by the default of the defendant or by consent. The plaintiff in every case must pre-

DOMESTIC 

207 

RELATIONS 

sent his side to the court and the testimony should justify the decree. 

Greenfield v. Greenfield 215 A.D. 504, 213 N.Y.S. 643.

The judgment may separate the parties from bed and board forever or for a limited time. The court may award a decree of separation to a defendant husband for a period of years with leave to the plaintiff to again commence a proceeding placing the burden of proof upon the plaintiff to show that the causes for granting the decree to the husband no longer exist.

Goldsmith v. Goldsmith 151 Misc. 198, 270 N.Y.S. 47. 

A judgment of separation may be revoked by the court upon the joint application of the parties, and upon satisfactory evidence of reconciliation. No agreement of the parties affects the decree unless ratified and made effective by judicial sanction. It thus follows that a reconciliation and cohabitation subsequent to a separation judgment providing for alimony do not deprive the wife of the alimony under the decree should the parties again separate after the reconciliation. 

Schatzberg v. Schatzberg 229 A.D. 214, 241 N.Y.S. 684.

Where a wife has left her husband without justification, and he is ready to take her back, he is not liable even for necessaries furnished to her while she lived apart from him. If they are simply living apart, she has no authority to pledge the credit of her husband for necessaries, and the burden is upon the one seeking to hold the husband for necessaries furnished to the wife to show that the separation was due to the fault of the husband. 

McDermott v. Books 128 Misc. 17, 217 N.Y.S. 181.

If a separation action is decided in the husband's favor, it does not bar the granting of alimony to the wife in a subsequent divorce action, where she would otherwise be entitled thereto. 

Saltzman v. Saltzman 228 A.D. 788, 239 N.Y.S. 381.

The legal domicile of an infant whose mother has been divorced for her adultery is that of the father. On the father's death the infant's domicile becomes that of the mother. The fact that the mother has been divorced does not prevent her from applying for letters of guardianship over the infant, in the country of her domicile. 

In re Thorne 240 N.Y. 444.

Custody and Maintenance of Children 

Where a matrimonial action has been tried and the court for any reason other than lack of jurisdiction has refused relief, it may nevertheless render a judgment providing for the custody and maintenance of a child. This judgment may at any time be annulled or modified.

Civil Practice Act § 1170a. 

Defenses to Action for Separation 

A wife's refusal of sexual intercourse is a defense to her action to compel support despite an agreement not to consummate the mar-

riage until after a religious ceremony which the husband now refuses.

Mirizio v. Mirizio 242 N.Y. 74. 

A wife who deserts her husband, loses her right to support, but she may change her mind and come back, provided her desertion has not ripened into abandonment. Should the husband refuse to take her back, after she has in good faith offered to return, she may maintain a separation action. If her conduct amounts to an abandonment, the husband may maintain his action for a separation despite an offer on the part of the wife to return. Just what amounts to an abandonment depends on circumstances. Absence for over 5 years by the wife was not, as a matter of law, abandonment, when the wife had maintained a lawsuit, based upon reasonable grounds and with sincerity, and upon losing the lawsuit she in good faith, immediately offered to return to her husband. 

Bohmert v. Bohmert 241 N.Y. 446; Mirizio v. Mirizio 248 N.Y. 175

If the separation took place by consent, either one who has not wilfully repudiated or violated the marriage obligations, may terminate the separation by requesting in good faith a renewal of the marital relation and obligation. 

Solomon v. Solomon 290 N.Y. 337.

Cohabitation after acts of cruelty does not act as a condonation in the sense in which it would after an act of adultery. Endurance of kind treatment in an effort to overcome its practice does not condone a course of inhuman conduct. 

Fisher v. Fisher 223 A.D. 19, affd. 250 N.Y, 313.

Where the defendant's act on which the action for separation is based occurred more than ten years prior to the institution of the suit, the suit is barred by the Statute of Limitations. 

Guerin v. Guerin 127 Misc. 745, 217 N.Y.S. 1

The misconduct of the plaintiff is a defense to an action for separation and support. 

Civil Practice Act §1163. 

Counterclaims in Matrimonial Actions 

When an action for divorce, separation or annulment is brought, a cause for action for divorce, separation or annulment may be interposed by the defendant as a counterclaim in connection with the denials of the material allegations of the complaint. 

Civil Practice Act § 1168. 

That the adultery relied on did not occur until after the commencement of the separation action does not affect the defendant's right to counterclaim in divorce or to insert a supplemental answer. 

Weiss v. Weiss 135 Misc. 264, 238 N.Y.S. 36. 

Sequestration Proceedings

A matrimonial action is substantially a proceeding in rem, since its purpose is to alter the matrimonial status. Insofar as its purpose is to compel the defendant to furnish support it is a proceeding in personam.

Where a judgment has been rendered in this state in a matri-

DOMESTIC 

209 

RELATIONS 

monial action or a judgment has been rendered in another state for divorce upon the ground of adultery or for separation or annulment or support upon the grounds permitted in this state and there is a requirement in such judgment for the support of wife or child, the court in its discretion may direct that the husband give reasonable security for the payment of the sums required for that purpose. Where the judgment has been obtained in another state an action must have been brought in this state and judgment rendered therein before relief can be given. If the security is not given the court may cause the husband's personal property and the rents and profits of his real property to be sequestered and a receiver may be appointed. This may be applied to the payment of the sums of money specified to be paid and if it is insufficient, the court on the application of the receiver, may direct the property to be mortgaged or sold insofar as may be necessary to realize the necessary protection. 

If a matrimonial action is brought in this state and it appears that the defendant is not within the state or cannot be found nor that process can be personally served upon him, the court may, without notice, direct the sequestration of his property of any nature and appoint a receiver. The property sequestered and the income therefrom may be applied from time to time to the payment of such sums as the court may deem proper, for the purpose of supporting the wife, for her expenses in the action and for the education and maintenance of children. Here also if the sequestered property proves insufficient to pay the sums required, the court may direct the mortgage or sale of sufficient real estate to pay such sums. The wife may be the receiver. The court may also authorize the wife to use and keep free from any liability for rent, any property as a dwelling for herself and her children and may likewise turn over to her for her use and for the use of her children any chattels of her husband.

Civil Practice Act § 1170 et seq. 

To apply the remedy of sequestration, the matrimonial action must be then pending or presently begun. The proceeding is analogous to attachment where it appears that the defendant cannot be found within the State or is in hiding so that he cannot be personally served.

In one case a plaintiff obtained a sequestration order, though no action was pending and then without serving summons and complaint or obtaining an order for service by publication obtained an ex parte order for alimony and counsel fees to be paid out of the sequestered property. It was held that it could not be done. The sequestration order if not made in a pending action must be followed by publication commenced within a period provided by the Civil Practice Act where the order of attachment has been granted. 

Mathews v. Matthews 240 N.Y. 28 

Geary v. Geary 272 N.Y. 390.

Relief by way of sequestration can be obtained only against an existent property right. Accordingly a court cannot order a seques-

tration of a defendant's monthly earnings to become due. It can, however, order that distribution out of a trust fund be made to the receiver instead of to the husband's beneficiary. 

Patterson v. Patterson 251 A.D. 272, 296 N.Y.S. 311

Whedon v. Whedon 176 Misc: 504. 

Illegitimate Children

Such children are legitimatized if the parents marry at any time subsequently. But if any interest has been vested before this marriage, the legitimatized children cannot affect it in any way. 

Domestic Relations Law § 24. 

When the laws of a foreign jurisdiction provide that a child is legitimatized by the subsequent marriage of the parents within its jurisdiction, the status of legitimacy is recognized in this state and the child in entitled to inherit. Under no circumstances, however, will New York recognize a foreign statute which purports to legitimatize a child of a polygamous marriage. 

In re Bruington's Estate 160 Misc. 84, 289 N.Y.S. 725

EQUITY 

Decree in Equity

When a right to equitable relief exists at the commencement of the action, the extent of the relief actually given will be adapted to the situation at the time of the decree. Equity may give a personal judgment for a sum of money when that form of relief becomes necessary in order to prevent a failure of justice and when it is impracticable to grant the specific relief demanded. 

Satterlee v. Kobbe 173 N.Y. 91, 97 

Wappler v. Woodbury 246 N.Y. 152.

The Injunction and Equity Jurisdiction (a) Nuisances 

Though as a general rule, an owner is at liberty to use his property as he sees fit provided such use does not violate an ordinance or statute, he will not be permitted to make an unreasonable use of his premises to the material annoyance of his neighbor. 

Equity will enjoin a nuisance if the plaintiff can show that he is suffering special damage and that the remedy at law is inadequate. 

We shall observe that running through the entire scope of the jurisdiction of equity over the injunction is the thought that equity will intervene where it appears that damage will result which cannot in good justice' be measured in dollars and cents. 

A condition is a nuisance when it clearly appears that the rightful enjoyment of property is wrongfully materially lessened and the physical comfort of persons in their homes is materially interfered with thereby. Whether the particular use to which one put his property constitutes a nuisance or not is generally a question of fact, and depends upon whether such use is reasonable under all the surrounding circumstances. A condition which would cause little or no vexation in an industrial district might be extremely tantalizing to those living in a beautiful residential zone. Each case is unique. The inconvenience must not be fanciful, slight, or theoretical, but certain and substantial, and must interfere with the physical comfort of the ordinary reasonable person. 

Boye v. Donner-Hanna Coke Co. 236 A.D. 37, 258¯N.Y.S. 229 

McCarty v. Natural Carbonic Gas Co. 189 N.Y. 40. 

These are examples of nuisances: the erection of a "hot dog" stand in a beautiful residential section, the presence of which causes many to surround, overrun and litter the lawns of the plaintiff, and to park their cars along the street and disturb the rest and sleep of the plaintiff and other residents of the locality; the operation in a residential district of a boxing arena wherein boxing bouts are held one night a week, which draw crowds, autos and busses; the oper- 211

ation of a large bakery at night, creating noises which disturb the sleep of the neighborhood and cause actual discomfort to persons of ordinary sensibilities; contamination of the atmosphere by noxious odors, fumes and refuse from burning of garbage, if done frequently enough to cause discomfort and annoyance to those living in the neighborhood. The fact that an annoyance is intermittent and not constant does not affect the right of the plaintiff to protection. The right to an injunction will lie. The relief at law would be inadequate. 

Andrews v. Perry 127 Misc. 320; Dillon v. Cortland 224 A.D. 303

Russell v. Nostrand Club 240 N.Y. 681, Case 2 Nicoll v. Ossining 128 Misc. 848. 

If however, the protection of a legal right would do the plaintiff but comparatively little good and would produce great public or private hardship, equity will withhold its hand and remit the plaintiff to his remedies at law. Equity will balance conveniences. 

McCanh v. Chasm Power Co. 211 N.Y. 301.

The fact that the plaintiff purchased his own property long after the nuisance was present, and knew of its existence, does not affect the plaintiff's right to an injunction. 

Andrews v. Perry 127 Misc. 320, 216 N.Y.S. 537. 

(b) Compelling or Preventing Personal Service 

Equity will not, as a rule, compel personal service. In two kinds of cases equity may compel service, though personal. One is where not to do so would be aiding fraud, e.g.: Jones conveys a strip of land to a railroad, and the latter promises to build a station near his home and stop there every twelve hours. Should the railroad company refuse, equity would compel the railroad company to carry out its agreement. The second class of cases includes cases where the public is involved. If a railroad defendant promises to do something which would be of great benefit to the public, the other party to the contract can get equity to compel the defendant to perform. 

Equity will enjoin one whose services are unique, not easily replaced, or of special value, e.g., a great singer or very popular actor, from performing for anyone else during the period of his contract. 

The court will not compel performance of the contract for that would compel the defendant's personal service. Even though a negative covenant not to appear for anyone else may be lacking in the contract, such will be implied and enforced against the parties and against the threatening third parties. 

Rogers v. Comstock 225 A.D. 34, affd. 252 N.Y. 561 

Merl v. Janks 125 Misc. 318, 209 N.Y.S. 530.

A clause in a contract that for a breach of the negative covenant the plaintiff might obtain injunctive relief, is not conclusive upon the court. It is merely a concession that the parties recognized the defendant's service to be of a unique and exceptional character. 

Hammerstein v. Safronie, N.Y. Law Journ. July 19, 1928, p. 1734. 

An employee will be enjoined from disclosing trade secrets or con-

EQUITY 

213 fidential communications which he learned or obtained while in the employer's employ. 

(c) Labor Injunctions 

No person may be held in contempt for disobeying an injunction order in a case growing out of a labor dispute except by trial by jury to which the defendant shall be entitled as a matter of right, unless the contempt is committed in the presence of the court. 

Civil Practice Act § 882a. 

No court or judge has jurisdiction to issue any temporary or permanent injunction in a case growing out of a labor dispute except after hearing and finding the following facts: That unlawful acts, substantial and irreparable injury to complainant's property will follow and that greater injury will be inflicted upon complainant by the denial than by the granting of the order; that complainant has no adequate remedy at law; that the police have not protected or cannot protect complainant's property; that every reasonable effort has been made to settle the dispute by negotiation or mediation. If it is obvious that such effort would be an idle ceremony, it need not be alleged or proved as prerequisite to injunctive relief. 

May's Furs v. Bauer 282 N.Y. 331.

The order cannot prohibit employees from belonging to a union, from giving and getting information about the strike or assembling peacably or reasonably urging others to strike.

Every temporary injunction shall by its terms expire within a period of not more than 10 days unless the plaintiff is ready by the expiration of that time to proceed to trial. The permanent injunction shall remain in force only six months, but it may be extended for another six months after a hearing. 

Civil Practice Act §§ 876a. 

Notwithstanding these limitations upon the right to issue an injunction, the court may enjoin the breach of an agreement between the employer and employees. And where a union violates an agreement which precludes a strike, the court may give injunctive relief against the union upon general equitable principles, although the statutory conditions have not been met. 

Uneeda Credit Clothing Stores 14 N.Y.S. (2nd) 964 

Diamond Candle Co. v. Fratello 16 N.Y.S. (2nd) 346.

Where a business is run by the owner himself without employees or by partners who do all the work, an attempt to coerce the hiring of an employee is not a labor dispute. An injunction under the statute may be sought without reference to the special rules of labor cases. The same rule applies to activities of employees in charitable institutions. A business run as a corporation must comply with the statutory limitations and cannot be heard to say that the few people connected with it are members of a single family. 

Thompson v. Boekhout 273 N.Y. 390 

Jewish Hospital v. Doe 252 A.D. 581, 300 N.Y.S. 1111

Boro Park Poultry Market v. Heller 280 N.Y. 481 

Kershner v. Heller 258 A.D. 751, 14 N.Y.S. (2nd) 595.

The right to strike and picket is not limited to the original parties to the labor contract. A union may use those rights against establishments in the same industry where no grievance exists between employer and employee, but where the union insists that the same conditions of employment be maintained so that such employers and employees may not profit at the expense of those who maintain union standards. So too, union workers with proper regard for their self-interest, may refuse to work on non-union materials. 

Picketing of a retail establishment which resold for profit the product of a non-union manufacturer has also been held justified. This prevents the distribution of non-union goods. 

Mays Furs v. Bauer 278 N.Y. 331 

Goldfinger v. Feintuch 276 N.Y. 281. (d) Specific Performance

Equity when it has jurisdiction of the person, will compel specific performance of a contract, the subject matter of which is unique and not to be replaced by money and the remedy at law inadequate. In the following instances equity will grant specific performance: Since each piece of land is unique, equity may compel specific performance of an option or contract to buy and sell land; of a contract for the sale of shares of a close corporation where the value of the stock is not easily ascertainable or the stock not readily obtainable elsewhere; of a contract to leave property to a person by will who would be entitled to recover as a third party beneficiary; of a seller's agreement to make an advance on the purchaser's construction of a building. So also, equity may issue an injunction restraining one from leaving the jurisdiction with an unique chattel, which the plaintiff claims, e.g., an altar piece, a family heirloom, a painting by Titian. Although the technical right to specific performance is present the court may refuse it if to grant relief would be unfair or unconscionable. 

Butler v. Wright 186 N.Y. 259; Waddle v. Cabano 220 N.Y. 18 

Schaefer v. Thompson 237 N.Y. 55 

Spoolan Realty v. Haebler 147 Misc. 9, 262 N.Y.S. 197 

Thomas v. Hens 219 A.D. 627, 220 N.Y.S. 785.

Specific performance will not lie to compel the making of repairs under a covenant in a lease. 

Beck v. Allison 56 N.Y. 366.

Equity will compel a licensee, who received a free license to store material on the licensor's land to remove it on the day promised. 

A remedy at law would be inadequate, for it would give damages and not the land. 

Wheelock v. Noonan 108 N.Y. 179.

Equity will not enforce any contract where both parties are not bound. But let us take this case: A contract required to be in writing and orally agreed to by both parties and signed only by one, may be specifically enforceable if all the other elements necessary to give equity jurisdiction are there. The person who had not signed, by asking equity to give relief, had put himself under the

EQUITY 

215 jurisdiction of the court and subjected himself to its orders, and therefore there is mutuality.* 

Farago v. Burke 262 N.Y. 229.

The time that the parties need to be bound in order to have mutuality is when the decree is to be given. So if a vendor of realty did not have. title at the time he made the contract, he could still be compelled to convey if he had obtained the title before the decree was to be given. There was mutuality then. 

From the fact that one party to a contract is entitled to specific performance, it does not follow that the other contracting party has that right. For instance, though the assignee under a contract for the sale of realty may get specific performances if he is ready, willing and able to perform the terms of the contract as therein provided, the mere assignment of a bilateral executory contract may not be interpreted as a promise by the assignee to assume performance of the assignor's duties so as to be liable to be compelled to perform. The assignee is under no personal obligation because of the assignment, unless he has expressly or impliedly bound himself to perform. Where the assignee invokes the aid of the equity court against the original party to the contract, he impliedly binds himself to perform. 

Epstein v. Gluickin 233 N.Y. 490; Langel v. Betz 250 N.Y. 159.

Another instance occurs where there has been part performance of a contract for the conveyance of realty which contract does not satisfy the Statute of Frauds. Equity will, under certain circumstances, grant specific performance. It may thus happen that one party may have so acted in reliance upon the oral contract that failure to give him specific performance will create an irremediable injury, whereas the other contracting party may not be in this position. 

This would justify relief in equity for the former alone. 

Walter v. Hoffman 267 N.Y. 365.

It should be observed that the plaintiff seeking equity relief for part performance, must show the following: (1) the contract is definite as to parties, considerations, and the property involved; (2) the plaintiff must prove his case by a preponderance of the evidence; (3) his recovery must not be inequitable nor unjust; and (4) the performance must be referable unequivocally to the contract. 

Salem v. Kinney 127 Misc. 387, 215 N.Y.S. 553. 

Cf. Canute v. Minor 232 A.D. 325, affd. 258 N.Y. 558

If a party seeks specific performance in a situation when he knew it had become impossible at the time the action was begun, e.g.. the defendant had conveyed the land in dispute to another, equity has no jurisdiction and the plaintiff has only a legal remedy in a court of law. If however, the plaintiff, in ignorance of the truth, sought relief in good faith, then equity would assess damages. 

Saperstein v. Mechanics, etc. Bank 228 N.Y. 257.

Although equity will not ordinarily enforce a sale of land when *For a further discussion of "Mutuality" see supra, page 119.

there is an incumbrance or unmarketable title, it will do so if the vendee requests it. Of course there will be a decrease in price. It should be noted, however, that not every purchaser under a contract of sale of real property is entitled to specific performance with an abatement, if the facts are not as stated in the contract. This privilege applies if the deficiency is in the subject-matter of the contract. Thus, it would not apply if the seller misrepresented the income of the property. If the purchaser would not take the property as is, he could only sue for damages for breach of contract. 

Radel v. 134 W. 15th St. Bldg. Co. 222 A.D. 617, 226 N.Y.S. 560 

Chesebro v. Moers 233 N.Y. 75; Feldman v. Lisansky 239 N.Y. 81.

A delinquent plaintiff not guilty of bad faith, may have a specific performance decree if time is not of the essence of the agreement. 

A reasonable delay may be regarded as immaterial if no harm has been done and the positions of the parties have not changed. 

Mangaup Valley Co. v. Nyamco Associates 247 A.D. 694, 289 N.Y.S. 694. 

(e) Cloud Upon Title 

Equity will act to remove a cloud upon title if the deed is valid on its face and the defendant is not in possession. If the defendant is in possession, the plaintiff should use the remedy of ejectment, which would try the title. 

Equity will restrain a defendant from proceeding in an illegal action against the plaintiff's land, which action, if completed, will cast a cloud upon the plaintiff's title. 

De Witt v. Van Schoyk 110 N.Y. 7.

Equity will enjoin a continuous trespass and thus prevent a multiplicity of suits for the recovery of damages. (f) Encroachments

Where a structure enroaches upon land, the remedy by an action of ejectment is for practical purposes insufficient because the sheriff will hesitate to execute the judgment. The risks involved are too great. The statute now permits of an injunction directing the removal of the enroachment or an award of damages. or such other judgment as the facts may justify.

Real Property Law § 539. 

(g) Unfair Competition

One may not use even innocently, the advertised name, label designation or mark of another and thus give the public an impression that there is a connection between them. The use by a defendant of the trade name "Lois' Restaurant" was enjoined by a plaintiff who had commenced the use of the name "Louis' Restaurant," nine years earlier. 

Louis Restaurant v. Coffey 132 Misc.. 690, 230 N.Y.S. 82.

In one case the plaintiff used the name "Tecla" in a certain script. The defendant used the same name similarly written. The plaintiff sold jewelry, the defendant cosmetics. Although the parties were not competitors the defendant was enjoined from writing or printing the word "Tecla" on any advertising matter in the char-

EQUITY 

217 acteristic script as used by plaintiff. In another case a plaintiff, Tiffany & Company, organized in 1868 and engaged in the sale of jewelry, enjoined the defendant Tiffany Productions from using the name Tiffany with a picture of a diamond in connection with its motion picture business.*

Tecla Corp. v. Salon Tecla 249 N.Y. 157 

Tiffany & Co. v. Tiffany Productions 262 N.Y. 482 

Gotham Silk Hosiery Co. v. Reingold 223 A.D. 260, 228 N.Y.S. 9 

Albany Packing Co. v. Crispo 227 A.D. 591, affd. 253 N.Y. 607.

Words or phrases descriptive of an article cannot be exclusively appropriated by one unless so used that the word or phrase has come to mean that particular article which is his product. 

Even in cases where family names are involved, a person may not give his name to a corporation and thereby take from another his good will and rights which he has acquired by the use of such name, especially where the purpose is to mislead the public as to the identity of the establishments. 

Gabriel v. Niederstein 230 A.D. 716, 243 N.Y.S. 472 

Tecla Corp. v. Salon Tecla 249 N.Y. 157. If one party sends to the customers of a competitor false or misleading circulars or reading matter which would deceive the public and thus take away the competitor's business, the latter can successfully ask equity to enjoin the circularizing of the false material. 

Old Investors' Co. v. Jenkins 133 Misc. 213, affd. 225 A.D. 860.

Where the same trade-mark happens to be employed simultaneously by two manufacturers in different markets separate from each other, an innocent party who had in good faith employed the trademark as the first user in that jurisdiction and had built up a trade cannot be enjoined by one who had begun to use the mark in another jurisdiction at an earlier date.

United Drug Co. v. Rectanus Co. 248 U.S. 90. 

One who has sold the good-will of his business has no right to solicit trade from old customers, even though the absence of a covenant to refrain from competition may permit him to carry on a competing business. Former customers of the firm to which the seller belonged may of their own accord transfer their trade to him.** 

Tierney Sons v. Tierney Bros. 130 Misc. 428, 224 N.Y.S. 144. (h) Restrictive Covenants

Equity will enforce restrictive covenants. The law governing this subject may be summarized through the following examples: (1) X owns a whole block of lots. He prepares a building scheme, under which the tract is divided into lots for sale, by deeds containing uniform covenants restricting the use which the grantees may *For an additional list of cases and examples see Marolo Mills v. Marvel 

Mills 170 Misc. 770, affd. 258 A.D. 715. **The damages recoverable for such breach are limited strictly to losses which the buyer sustains, including loss of profits and diminution in value of the property purchased. Present v. Glazer 225 A.D. 23, 232 N.Y.S. 63.

make of their premises. X sells the lots to various buyers showing them the building plan, and each buyer covenants for himself, his heirs and his assigns, not to use the premises for anything but residences. These covenants for uniform developments "run with the land" and future grantees are bound by the covenants in the deeds. 

Rose v.Jasima 218 A.D. 646, 219 N.Y.Š. 222

Krekeler v. Aulbach 51 A.D. 591, affď. 169 N.Y. 372. 

The covenants are not only enforceable by X and his successors, but they are enforceable by any grantee as against any other, upon the theory that there is a mutuality of covenants and consideration which binds each and gives each the appropriate remedy. 

Besch v. Hyman 221 A.D. 238, 223 N.Y.S. 231. .(2) One person selling a tract of land may, for the benefit of his remaining land and also for the benefit of his grantees, impose any restrictions upon the land granted that he sees fit, which are not against public policy. These restrictions are enforceable in equity by the grantor or his assigns in favor of the property benefited and retained by the grantor against the property burdened. The restrictive covenants run with the land and bind subsequent purchasers. The fact that others have violated this restriction and that other actions have not been brought to enjoin and restrain such violations, is immaterial. 

McCain v. Aylesworth 128 Misc. 408, 219 N.Y.S. 59.

In the absence of actual notice before or at the time of his purchase or of other exceptional circumstances, an owner is only bound by restrictions if they appear in some deed of record in the conveyance to himself or to his direct predecessors in title. 

Buffalo Academy v. Boehm Bros. 267 N.Y. 242.

Where a covenant in a prior deed sought to establish a uniform front line for all adjacent houses, it was held that a subsequent purchaser of an adjacent lot took his lot subject to that restriction. One resident in a residential section, who projects his house farther into the street line than the adjacent houses, might be said to be put on notice of a restriction based on a general plan or easement of the neighbor. It is considered an exceptional circumstance. 

Holt v. Fleischman 75 A.D. 593, 78 N.Y.S. 647.

Where four lots in a residential section are sold with restrictive covenants binding heirs and assigns, and years later the neighborhood becomes a manufacturing district, a grantee of one of those lots who wants to change his house into a factory will not be enjoined at the suit of his neighbors nor the restrictive covenant enforced. The covenant has become of little value to the residential people, and equity will not enforce such a worthless covenant. The party aggrieved has his remedy at law. It seems, then, that in enforcing restrictive covenants equity will consider the balance of conveniences, and an injunction will be withheld when the injury is not serious or substantial, and the defendant would be subject to great inconvenience and loss in comparison to the inconvenience and loss which might be suffered by the plaintiff. 

Forstmann v. Joray 244 N.Y. 22; Amerman v. Deane 132 N.Y. 325.

219 A court of equity may, by injunction, prevent the defendant's lessee from using a building for a purpose which violates the restrictive covenants of the lease. 1 

Lyon v. Bethlehem Eng. Corp. 253 N.Y. 111.

A duty to speak does not arise except when the owner's property is being improved, or appropriated by another. One may not sit by passively and allow his property to be sold or conveyed, nor may he silently suffer it to be improved with the expensive structures and later receive the aid of equity. But, where the neighbor is buidir. structures on his property and there is no actual invasion of the plaintiff's property, there arises no duty to speak. 

Noble v. Echo Lake Tavern 142 Misc. 427, 254 N.Y.S. 662. (i) Crimes A court of equity will not undertake the prosecution, punishment or pardon of crimes, but the criminal nature of an act will not deprive equity of jurisdiction if it would otherwise attach. Thus jurisdiction exists to restrain pending or threatened criminal prosecution under an unconstitutional enactment, provided the prevention of such prosecution is essential to the safeguarding of rights and property, and jurisdiction also exists to restrain criminal acts. which threaten to destroy property rights. Accordingly, equity will restrain prosecution under an unconstitutional ordinance requiring a license for the keping of a house-trailer on one's own premises. 

Boxer v. Town of Harrison 175 Misc. 249.

There is now also the recognition that public health, morals, safety and the welfare of the community equally require protection from irreparable injury. Thus a complaint which sought an injunction against the practice of medicine by an unlicensed person without medical ability was held good despite the fact that the defendant could be punished criminally. The penalties were held to be inadequate to protect the public health against the danger. 

People v. Laman 277 N.Y. 368; I.R.T. v. Lavin 247 N. Y. 830. 

The violation of a city ordinance resulting in injury to him, may be enjoined at the instance of an individual. 

Bailer v. Ringe 255 A.D. 976, 8 N.Y.S. (2nd) 99. (j) Negotiable Documents

Equity takes jurisdiction to enjoin the transfer of unmatured negotiable instruments to the end that a defense of the maker may not be lost to him. Thus equity will act to enjoin the transfer of a usurious note in order to prevent its sale to a bank, which latter could and might collect despite the usury under Banking Law, § 108. 

Weissman v. Naitov 125 Misc. 647, 211 N.Y.S. 740. *The policy of New York to extend remedy by injunction may be observed from the fact that by statute the equitable jurisdiction has extended into many fields. The following, among others, may be enjoined: The unlawful exercise of corporate rights (Civil Practice Act § 1218); the unlawful practice of law (Civil Practice Act § 1221b); violations of rules and regulations respecting public markets and milk control and the Sanitary Code. For a more complete list see People v. Laman (supra).

(k) Matrimonial Disputes 

The commencement of divorce proceedings in another state by a spouse who, while a resident of this state, leaves for that other state for the purpose of the suit, may be enjoined, since a valid decree may be issued in that other jurisdiction without the presence of the marital status or of the petitioning spouse (defendant in the threatened action) therein. But this is not so as to a divorce sought in a foreign country, for the full faith and credit clause would not apply and such divorce would be wholly void. 

Oltarsh v. Oltarsh 181 Misc. 255 

Newman v. Newman 181 Misc. 256. 

Equitable Estoppel

The doctrine of equitable estoppel, or estoppel in pais, is that a party may be precluded by his acts and conduct from asserting a right to the detriment or prejudice of another party who, entitled to rely on such conduct, has acted upon it. 

Draper v. Oswego 190 N.Y. 12.

To estop the plaintiff, defendant must show (a) that there was actual fraud practiced by the plaintiff, relied upon by the defendant, or (b) that the plaintiff led the defendant into making an outlay in order to do the very thing to which the plaintiff now objects, by leading the defendant to assume that he had a right to do it, when the plaintiff knew that he had not. Where a riparian owner (plaintiff) saw the owner on the opposite side of a stream building a factory upon his own land and digging a ditch which theplaintiff knew would divert the water to a point below the plaintiff's land, the plaintiff's failure to object did not estop him from bringing an action to recover for the diversion. There was silence, but there must be a positive duty to speak, before a failure to do so can estop the owner. 

N.Y. Rubber Co. v. Rothery 107 N.Y. 310.

Where a defendant makes use of the statute of frauds to effectuate a fraudulent purpose, under circumstances where to permit a guilty defendant to rely upon that statute would be to help in the perpetration of the fraud, equity may forbid such misuse of the statute. 

Wagner v. Mfrs. Trust Co. 237 A.D. 175, affd. 261 N.Y. 699

Rescission of Contracts 

A person who is induced to make a contract by false representations has upon the discovery of the fraud, three remedies: (a) He may rescind and declare the contract void and then sue in a law action to recover back his consideration and damages.* He need neither allege nor prove that the alleged misrepresentations were knowingly made or made with fraudulent intent. It is sufficient if the representations were false, for the fraudulent intent or *By amendment, effective September 1, 1941, damages may be recovered in an action in rescission. Civil Practice Act § 112e.

EQUITY 

221 damages are important only in tort actions for deceit. The plaintiff must tender what he received, prior to suit unless what he has re- Iceived is of such a character that its return before the end of the suit would leave the defendant in as good a position as the return before suit would have done. In the latter case, tender at trial is sufficient. Thus where the injured party holds the note of the other party, he need not offer to restore before trial, since the note is a mere promise to pay and becomes valueless when the contract is voided. Likewise where a party has received only money which he will be entitled to in any event, he need not make offer of restitution. But where certificates of stock have been received, they must be tendered back.

E.T.C. Co. v. T.G. & T. Co. 271 N.Y. 124 

Goldfarb v. Wright 265 A.D. 738. (b) He may bring an action in equity to rescind and in that action have full relief. In this case the plaintiff need offer in his complaint to return what he has received and bring an action at law to recover damages sustained. This affirms the contract. 

Comm. C. Co. v. Third, etc. Garage 226 A.D. 235, 234 N.Y.S. 463

The representations to warrant rescission, must not be mere expressions of opinion or promissory in their nature. A representation that the premises are worth upwards of $7,000 is an expression of opinion; a representation that certain roads leading to the premises would be filled in is promissory. So, too, is the representation that the defendant would secure for the plaintiff a building loan mortgage to enable the latter to commence the erection of a building on the premises. 

Brang v. Stachnick 235 A.D. 591, affd. 261 N.Y. 614.

When an action is brought solely for rescission, the plaintiff must tender everything that he has received, including all profits realized from the articles obtained, e.g., dividends from stock. There cannot be partial rescission. If part of the goods received has been sold before the discovery of the grounds entitling him to rescission, the plaintiff may tender what remains immediately on the discovery of the grounds and tender a money allowance for what has been sold. 

Where, however, profits have been accepted with knowledge of the facts, he will be held to have waived the fraud and to have ratified his purchase. 

Friedman v. Richman 213 A.D. 467, affd. 215 N.Y. 576 

Marr v. Tumulty 256 N.Y. 15 

Brennan v. National 247 N.Y. 486.

An action to rescind a contract and recover the moneys paid is maintainable by one contracting party on account of a default in performance of an entire contract by the other party, although the latter in respect to minor provisions of this entire contract, may have performed. A plaintiff who has paid the entire price for a specific radio time and "spot" announcements, was said to be able to recover the entire price paid when it showed that the programs were shortened, and the announcements below the agreed number. 

Barney's Clothes v. W.B.O. Broadcasting Co. 165 Misc. 532, affd. 253 

A.D. 889

One who is induced by fraud to enter into a contract need not as a condition of rescission, restore what has been received, where the other party is indebted to him out of the same transaction in a larger amount. And where a settlement has been made and consideration given for a release, one seeking to set aside the release may retain the consideration if he would certainly be entitled to that sum whether or not he was successful in the present suit. 

Brennan v. National 221 A.D. 658, affd. 247 Ñ.Y. 486 

Kamerman v. Curtis 285 N.Y. 221.

Every contracting party has a right to rely on the express statement of an existing fact, the truth of which is known to the opposite party, and unknown to him, as the basis of a mutual engagement, and he is under no obligation to investigate and verify the statements to the truth of which the other party to the contract, with full means of knowledge, has deliberately pledged his faith. 

Rucksttuhl v. Healy 222 A.D. 152, 225 N.Y.S. 570.

A mistake not mutual but only on one side may be ground for rescinding a contract.* If the erroneous transaction was such as to involve the act of the plaintiff only and the effect of the transaction would be the unjust enrichment of the defendant, the plaintiff is entitled to have the transaction rescinded, although he was the only party mistaken. 

Rosenblum v. Manufacturers Trust Co. 270 N.Y. 79.

Equity takes jurisdiction in divorce and annulment cases since originally the jurisdiction was in the Court of Chancery. The Supreme Court received the jurisdiction as successor to the Chancellor. 

The courts have not common-law jurisdiction over the subject of divorce. 

Ryan v. Ryan 132 Misc. 339, 229 N.Y.S. 511

City of N. Y. v. Kaiser 125 Misc. 637, 210 N.Y.S. 598. 

Reformation of Contracts 

If there is a mistake of fact made by both sides, or a mistake of fact on one side and fraud by the other, equity can reform the contract to conform to the ideas both sides were supposed to have had. 

An action to reform a written agreement, rests upon the theory that the parties came to an understanding, but in reducing it to writing, through mutual mistake, or through mistake on one side and fraud on the other, omitted some provisions agreed upon or inserted something not agreed upon. The object of the action is to so change the instrument as written as to make it conform to the agreement as made, by inserting the provision omitted, or striking out the one inserted by mutual mistake. However, a judgment denying recovery in an action upon a written agreement shall not be deemed to bar an action to reform such agreement and to enforce it as reformed.

Civil Practice Act § 112d**. 

*As will appear in the next section this is not a ground for reforming a contract. Mutual mistake in the absence of fraud, must be found. **This comparatively new section does not abolish the doctrine of res judi

EQUITY 

223 1 A mistake on one side without fraud may be a ground for rescission or for refusing to enforce a specific provision, but it cannot be a ground for altering its terms. 

Curtis v. Albee 167 N.Y. 360 

Metzger v. Aetna Ins. Co. 227 N.Y. 411, 417.

Ordinary negligence of a plaintiff in failing to read an instrument is no defense to an action for reformation, unless it can be shown that the negligence was so gross as to amount to a violation of a positive legal duty. Thus, where an attorney drew a mortgage and made it payable in five instead of ten years as agreed between the parties, it was held that the mortgagor could have it reformed, despite the mortgagor's failure to read the instrument before he signed and the absence of artifice to prevent his reading it. 

Andrews v. Gillespie 47 N.Y. 487.

When a vendee agreed that the sale was subject to a lease held by X, who was in possession, and the scrivener omitted to mention X's lease, the vendor can get reformation of the agreemnt. The buyer cannot get damages because possession was refused him. There being no misrepresentation, rescission is not the action, but reformation. The mistake was one of fact, made by the scrivener. So where there has been no mistake in the agreement, but a mistake in reducing it to writing, an action may be maintained for reformation. 

Avery v. Equit. Life Assur. Co. 117 N.Y. 451 

Baird v. Erie R.R. Co. 210 N.Y. 225 

Unger v. Weisner 129 Misc. 363, 221 N.Y.S. 489.

Where the parties agreed upon a sale of stock at its actual value as shown by the books of the corporation, and in writing the contract the term "face value" was used upon the representation of one party that this meant actual value, reformation was held proper relief. 

It is no longer the law that relief is not available because of a mistake in law. An amendment effective April 29, 1942 (Civil Practice 

Act. Sec. 112B) provides that when relief against mistake in a transaction which occurrs after that date is sought in an action or proceeding, or by way of defense or counterclaim, it shall not be denied merely because the mistake is one of law rather than one of fact. This does not mean that relief will be granted in the same way as in cases of mistakes of fact. It permits the court to act in the appropriate case involving a mistake of law. Even under the old rule, payments of public money made by public officials under a mistake of law could be recovered back. 

N.Y.C. Employees v. Elliot 267 N.Y. 193

In cases where there has been a mistake of law on one side, and either positive fraud or unfair conduct though without evil intent on the other, equity will afford relief. The existence of a confidencata. It was intended to permit a litigant, mistaken in the form of remedy, to correct it and to obtain the proper remedy for his grievance. For example, should one be precluded from proving his facts because of the parol evidence rule he would not now be barred from another effort in an action to reform the agreement and enforce it as reformed Falkowski v. tial relationship such as husband and wife, or attorney and client, may found the basis of a charge of constructive fraud and the court may give equitable relief. 

Haviland v. Willets 141 N.Y. 35 

Jothann v. Irving Trust Co. 151 Misc. 107, affd. 243 A.D. 691.

Equity will not enforce or reform any contract if the petitioner was not absolutely fair and honest in his own dealings in the transaction. He must come into equity with clean hands.* Thus if A transfers property to X so as to keep it out of the hands of A's creditors and it is understood that the property is to be redelivered at the end of the year, A cannot get equity to compel a reconveyance to himself if X refuses. A was not fair and honest in his dealings. 

Knowlton v. Congress, etc. Spring Co. 57 N.Y. 518

Where a reformation of the instrument would operate to the actual prejudice of the intervening rights of bona fide purchasers or incumbrancers, a court of equity, as a general rule, will not exercise its jurisdiction. 

Burlingham v. Hanrahan 140 Misc. 512, 251 N.Y.S. 55.

Ordinarily a cause of action for reformation due to the mistake accrues when the mistake is made or the document executed, but this rule does not apply where there was an element of fraud or concealment of the error, e.g.: where the defendant has sole custody of the instrument. In the latter case the Statute of Limitations would begin to run from the discovery of the mistake. 

Metropolitan Life Ins. Co. v. Oseas 281 A.D. 768, affå. 289 N.Y. 731. 

Equity and Trusts

Accountings 

The general rule is that as to an existing trust the cestui que trust must sue in equity when he complains against the trustee concerning the performance of the trust. Equity will, however, impute an intention on the part of the trustees to carry out their obligations as trustees.

There are instances when a law action may also be maintained, e.g., where the breach of a specific covenant of the trust agreement resulted in the damages claimed. And where a trustee misappropriated trust funds he can be sued at law for conversion or in equity for an accounting.

Bank of N.Y. v. N. J. Title Co. 256 AD. 609 

Margulies v. Mfts. Trust Co. 148 Misc. 564, 266 N.Y.S. 157.

The basis for an equitable action for an accounting is the existence of a fiduciary or trust relation with reference to the subject matter of the controversy. A bare agency is not sufficient. It must appear that the person from whom the accounting is required has been intrusted with the custody and control of the property of another, with all the powers incident and necessary thereto, and in pursuance thereof has exercised such powers for the owner. No particular words are necessary to create the relation. 

Pelkey v. Pelkey 236 Á.D. 55, 258 N.Y.S. 562. *This doctrine applies to misconduct in regard to the particular transaction under consideration.

EQUITY 

225 Where one receives stolen goods knowing them to have been stolen, he holds the same ex maleficio for the benefit of the cestui que trust, despite the fact that the plaintiff owner has a remedy in conversion for the value of the merchandise at the time and place of conversion. The equity court has seen fit to give the benefit of its jurisdiction in such a situation and not to leave the plaintiff to a mere money judgment for the value. Thus, if the wrongdoer resells, the true owner is entitled to follow the res, if possible, and impress the trust; or if this cannot be done, he is entitled to an accounting of the profit made as well as to the value. 

Likewise, equity takes exclusive jurisdiction in actions for accounting where there are involved a trustee and cestui, guardian and ward, partners, joint adventurers where there is a relationship of trust and confidence, not generally, however, employee and employer. If the balance between the parties has been struck and the joint matter completely wound up, a court of law is competent to act. 

Sloane v. U.S. Syndicate 135 Misc. 365, 238 N.Y.S. 91.

Equity ordinarily will not aid a volunteer, e.g., one who has not given any consideration. An exception to this rule exists in the case of a completed trust. If a trust is completely created, equity will enforce it even at the instance of a volunteer. 

Equitable Conversion

A positive direction by a testator that his realty is to be converted into cash indicates that the conversion is to be made as of the time of the testator's death and the realty is treated as personalty for all purposes under the will. If, however, the conversion of the realty was directed in order to carry out a certain purpose, and the purpose could be carried out without affecting a conversion, or that purpose was illegal or unlawful, no conversion is effected. 

In re Hanis Will, 213 A.D. 487, affd. 242 N.Y. 536.

Also, where there is no imperative power of sale and the testator merely authorizes the trustees to sell in their discretion, the fund obtained upon sale and the realty until sale, retain the character of realty.

Where an equitable conversion is directed, the right of the life tenant to the income is the same as if the fund had come into existence immediately after the testator's death. The charges of carrying unproductive realty are not upon the life tenant until the sale. 

When there has been an equitable conversion, a partition action cannot be maintained. 

Allison v. Coffin 125 Misc. 615, 211 N.Y.S. 545. 

Conflicting Equities

If S contracts with B1 for the sale of a piece of land, and the former makes a similar contract with B2, B1 would prevail because his equity was prior to that of B2. The same rule would apply if a trustee of land contracted to convey it to a third party. The cestui would keep the land because his equity was a prior one.

But suppose that instead of contracting to sell to B2, S, actually sold the land to him. B2 gets a good title, for he was a bona fide purchaser for value and got the legal title rather than an equity. 

Whenever the legal title conflicts with the equitable, the legal prevails. 

But where the purchaser has paid no consideration or has actual or constructive notice of any outstanding equity, even though he receives legal title, he nevertheless takes subject to such equities. 

Jayne v. Cortland 107 A.D. 517, 95 N.Y.S. 227.

In New York the rule also is that a bona fide first mortgagee's rights take preference over the equitable rights of one who contracted to buy the land, even though the mortgage was made after the contract to convey. And this despite the fact that a mortgagee of realty does not have the legal title. 

X who owned lots 1, 2 and 3 gave a mortgage to Z on all three. 

X then sold lot 1 to A, 2 to B, both subject to the mortgage, and he kept lot 3. Z attempted to foreclose for non-payment. He cannot pick the lot to be foreclosed. The lot not sold (lot 3) must be first foreclosed. After that the lots must be foreclosed in the inverse order of their sale, i.e., lot 2 and then lot 1..

Laches and the Statute of Limitations A plaintiff who has been guilty of laches may be barred, even though the statutory period of limitations has not elapsed, and even though the defendant does not plead the laches of the plaintiff. 

The rule of laches is thus applied. If the plaintiff has negligently failed to press his claim in equity within a reasonable time and the delay has occasioned loss or hardship to the defendant or misled him to his injury, the plaintiff will be barred in equity, though the period allowed by the Statute of Limitations may not yet have ended. The hardship may consist of loss of evidence, change of title, intervention of equities, incurring expenses in improving the property which is the subject of a contract or sale, or a considerable rise in the value of the property. 

Feldman v. Metropolitan Life Ins. Co. 259 A.D. 123 

Seligson v. Weiss 222 A.D. 634, 227 N.Y.S. 338.

Where there is concurrent jurisdiction in law and equity, equity is bound by the Statute of Limitations of the law remedy. 

Minion v. Warner 238 N.Y. 413, 418.

INSURANCE 

Insurable Interest

LIFE INSURANCE policy upon the life of another is not valid, (1) unless obtained with the acquiescence of the person insured, and (2) unless there is an insurable interest in the person insured at the time the policy was issued. In order to collect on a fire, marine or personal property damage policy, there must be an insurable interest at the time the loss occurs. 

Miller v. Stuyvesant 131 Misc. 770, 227 N.Y.S. 324

The discussion of insurable interest must take into consideration a difference between life policies and other policies. (1) Life insurance policies.-Everyone has an insurable interest in his own life. The fact that one makes another the beneficiary is immaterial.

One spouse has an insurable interest in the other spouse. In this case and in the case of an employer taking out a life policy covering his employees collectively, and in the instance where a person is liable for the support of a child, a life policy may be obtained without the consent of the insured. 

Hilmes v. Gilman 138 N.Y. 369.

A relative has an insurable interest in the life of another relative, provided the person who takes the policy has a pecuniary interest in the life of the relative whose life is insured. 

One has an insurable interest in the life of a fiance or fiancee. 

Bogart v. Thompson 24 Misc. 581, 53 N.Y.S. 622 

A creditor has an insurable interest in a debtor's life, even after the Statute of Limitations has run against the debt, but the creditor's insurance must not be very disproportionate to the amount of the debt. Though there be payment of the debt by the debtor after his life has been insured, the policy remains in full force, and when the debtor dies the creditor can collect. He had an insurable interest when the policy was taken out. So also, if a wife takes out a policy on the life of her husband, she can collect on the policy after his death, even though they had divorced each other after the issuance of the policy. 

Reed v. Provident S. L. A. Soc'y 190 N.Y. 111.

Except in cases similar to the debtor-creditor relationship, there is no limit to the amount for which one can insure a life. (2) Fire insurance policies.-The owner of property has an insurable interest in his own property. So has a contractor building a house; also vested or contingent remaindermen; a contract vendor; contract vendee; carriers; bailees, who may recover as trustees for the bailor. If the policy covers property entrusted to the bailee, the customer bailor has a direct cause of action on the policy. 

Foley v. Mfr.'s Fire Ins. Co. 152 N.Y. 131 

Donavin v. Thurston 190 A.D. 48, 179 N.Y.S. 473 

Symmers v. Carroll 207 N.Y. 632 

Mord v. N. Y. Indem. Co. 216 A.D. 252, affd. 244 N.Y. 589 227

A mortgagee also has an insurable interest in the property of which he is the mortgagee, limited to the amount of the mortgage debt. A tenant, and one who is a remainderman (either vested or contingent), also has an insurable interest. 

Gen'l Ins. Co. v. Goldstein 182 Misc. 419 affd. 267 A.D. 898. 

Kent v. Aetna 84 A.D. 428, 82 N.Y.S. 817

Modern v. Concordia 131 Misc. 305. 

If one insures when he has no insurable interest, he gets nothing. 

If he gives notes for the premiums, the company cannot collect on the notes, because they were based on a void policy. 

Rights of Mortgagees and Conditional Vendors 

If the owner of goods is named as the insured and the policy states loss "payable to mortgagee," the latter is a mere nominee of the owner to receive the money. If the policy declares that it is issued to the owner and the mortgagee "as their interests may appear," the mortgagee is also covered and the insurance is for his benefit to the extent of his interest. A payment to the mortgagee under the policy would be payment pro tanto of the mortgage debt. 

The insurer is not subrogated to the rights of the mortgagee. A right of subrogation depends upon a clause to that effect being written into the policy. It is never read into it by implication. What has been stated here, applies to a conditional vendor as well. 

If a policy as above referred to, requires notice of intended cancellation to be given to the mortgagee, failure to give that notice results in the continued life of the policy. And if loss occurs and the mortgagee is paid because as to him there was no cancellation, that payment is on account of the debt, even though there may have been a cancellation as to the owner by giving proper notice to him. There having been no full cancellation of the policy, it remained alive and in the absence of a subrogation agreement, the insurer is not subrogated. 

Fields v. Western Millers' Ins. Co. 290 N.Y. 209 

Valued Policy

A valued policy is one in which a definite valuation is placed, by agreement, upon the subject-matter of the insurance and written in the face of the policy. Such valuation, in the absence of fraud or mistake, is conclusive upon the parties.

Thus, in case of a total loss under a valued policy, the amount recoverable is the amount of the policy, without regard to the depreciation or other elements entering into the market value of the loss. A loss is total only when the property has sustained such damage that repairs would not be reasonably practicable. 

Lee v. Hamilton 251 N.Y. 230. 

Statute of Frauds Assignments

A contract of insurance being a contract of indemnity, i.e., to pay on the happening of an event and not if another default, it is valid though not in writing.

A contract to assign or an assignment of a life, health, or acci-

INSURANCE 

229 dent insurance policy, or a promise to name a beneficiary of any such policy is subject to the Statute of Frauds. The presence or absence of consideration does not affect the rule. 

Personal Property Law § 31 The Binder 

A binder is intended to be superseded by a formal policy. It is a present contract of insurance issued to protect the assured temporarily while the insurer investigates the risk and finally determines whether or not to issue a permanent policy. It includes, however, all the obligations according to the terms of the policies in ordinary use by the insurer. If the form of the policy is fixed by the statute, then the statutory provisions are held to be included in the binder. 

Ell Dee Clothing Co. v. Marsh 247 N.Y. 392.

The Rider 

The indorsement or rider is part of the policy contract. Where the provisions of a policy are in conflict with the rider, the latter governs.

Mass Building Co. v. Rutley Const. Co. 159 Misc. 392, 287 N.Y.S. 662. 

Hostile and Friendly Fires

A fire which does not pass beyond the limits in which it is supposed to be confined, e.g., a stove or furnace, is called a friendly fire, and the insured is not entitled to recover for damages caused by the smoke or heat escaping from the proper confines of the fire. 

If the fire extends beyond the place in which it properly belongs, it is a hostile fire and the insured can collect for damages resulting even from a resulting explosion. 

Glen Nat'l Bank v. Auto Ins. Co. 249 A.D: 327, affd. 276 N.Y. 595.

Giambalvo v. Phoenix Ins. Co. 178 Misc. 887. 

Warranties, Representations and Conditions A warranty is a basic part of the insurance contract. A breach of warranty destroys the rights under the contract. A representation, if it is to avoid the policy, must concern itself with a material part of the policy. Since policies are written in the language of the insurer, all ambiguous and doubtful clauses will be construed against the insurer. The tendency is to construe a clause as a representation rather than a warranty, wherever possible.

By statute, all statements of the insured in life policies, unless put in by fraud, are representations and not warranties. So that to void the policy it must be a material part of the policy. The rule also applies to an application for reinstatement of a policy after a default in the payment of the premium. A material false statement in such application will as effectually void a policy as a similar statement in the original application.

Axelroad v. Metropolitan Life Ins. Co. 267 N.Y. 437 Insurance Law § 142. 

A statement by an applicant, even in good faith, that he was not suffering from cancer, when he was and died of that ailment, or a

negative answer to the question, "Have you consulted a physician within the last 10 years?" when he had been advised to stay at a hospital for two weeks and treatments were continued for two months, although not warranties, are material misrepresentations as a matter of law and void the policy. 

Eastern v. Travelers' 234 N.Y. 441 

Geer v. Union Mutual Ins. Co. 273 N.Y. 261

It has been held, however, that a question in the application "Have you ever consulted a physician?" following the question "Are you in good health?" may justly be taken by the insured to relate to a consultation concerning some ailment which pertained to her general good health and not to a temporary upset. It was not incumbent upon the insured, if then in good health, to recall visits for medical advice for such minor ills as constipation or common colds readily relieved by simple remedies. Where, however, the first question about health is "Have you ever consulted a physician?” and then follows a list of questions as to specific maladies, the question plainly indicates that the insurer wished to know the details of any professional treatment in order to decide whether it would issue a policy. A false answer in such case denying treatment for a specific ailment, e.g., discharge from ears, would void the policy. 

Equitable Life Assurance Soc'y v. Milman 291 N.Y. 90 

Nowak v. Brotherhood 226 A.D. 123, affd. 252 N.Y. 465 

Jenkins v. Hancock Mut. Life 257 N.Y. 289.

If a serious condition in the state of the applicant's health develops (e.g., the necessity of a major operation) after the application for insurance has been submitted, a failure to disclose the situation prior to the delivery of the policy constitutes a deliberate fraud and voids the policy, despite the fact that every statement in the application is true. 

Armand v. Met. Life Ins. 134 Misc. 357, 235 N.Y.S. 726.

A life, accident or health insurance policy and the papers attached are considered the entire contract. No unattached paper can be incorporated by reference, and the application for insurance is not admissible in evidence unless it is attached to the policy. 

Insurance Law § 142. 

When an insured receives a policy, it is his duty to read it and if an application incorporated therein does not contain answers to the questions asked by the medical examiner, it is his duty to have it corrected. A recovery by the insured is not permitted because the medical examiner or company's agent incorrectly recorded the applicant's answers or because the insured was unable to read or neglected to read the policy. This is a rule of substantive law. 

Minsky v. John Hancock Life Ins. 254 N.Y. 333. 

On the other hand, a defense that the insured made false statements inducing the issuance of the policy is no longer valid unless the statements were made a part of the policy, either by being attached to or indorsed upon the policy. Not constituting a defense, no evidence can be received of such material false statements if not a part of the policy.

Lampke v. Metropolitan Life Ins. Co. 279 N.Y. 157

231 The rule that the life policy consists only of the papers attached applies only to the original policy, and not to an application for reinstatement of a policy which had lapsed for nonpayment of premiums. In the latter instance, the insurer can defend on the ground of misrepresentation, even though the application for reinstatement was not attached. And where the insured signs the application for reinstatement without filling in the answers, but leaves the application to be filled in by the company's agent, the latter becomes the applicant's agent and the applicant is bound by the answers inserted. 

Insurance Law § 149 

N. Y. Life Ins. Co. v. Rosen 227 A.D. 79, affd. 225 N.Y. 567

Axelroad v. Metropolitan Life Ins. Co. 267 N.Y. 437 

Although the applicant's non-disclosure of a fact concerning which he has not been asked will ordinarily not void a fire or life policy, if the applicant is aware of the existence of some circumstances which he knows would influence the insurer in acting upon his application, good faith requires him to disclose that circumstance, though unasked. The failure on the part of an insurer to disclose the past record of its insured of an unfavorable nature would render a policy of reinsurance with another insurer, void. 

Sebring v. Fidelity Ins. Co. 255 N.Y. 382

The question of materiality of the representation is for the jurv. 

This is the test: If the underwriter, with full information, would have refused to accept the risk, then the concealment is material. 

The undisclosed fact need not be of such a nature as to have increased the risk or contributed to any loss or damage. In determining materiality evidence of the practice of the insurer with respect to the acceptance or rejection of similar risks is admissible. 

Sebring v. Fidelity Ins. Co. 255 N. Y. 382; Insurance Law § 149 (3) 

A case of breach of condition that would end the policy would be this: The policy provides that it will become void if the insured factory is left uninhabited for twenty days or more at a time. The owner departs for Washington on business, and the factory is shut down for a month. Later he returns, and from a cause in no way connected with its having been vacant, the factory burns down. The company need not pay the insurance. A material condition subsequent has been violated, and the fact that the breach was in no way connected with the loss is of no consequence. 

If the owner had leased it for three months, and the lessee, without the owner's knowledge, had permitted it to become vacant for a month, the policy would nevertheless be terminated. 

The standard fire policy in New York contains a clause that the insurer shall not be liable for loss while the hazard is increased by any means within the control or knowledge of the insured. This means that the company would not be liable for loss if occasioned while the increased hazard existed, even though the fire was not caused or affected by this new hazard. Once the hazard is removed, the liability of the insurer exists again. 

Taverna v. Pal. Ins. Co. 228 A.D. 33, 238 N.Y.S. 389

Filards v. Nat'l U. F. Ins. Co. 224 A.D. 136, 229 N.Y.S. 682

A policy that declares that it is to be void if the insurer die by his own hand becomes void if the insurer committed suicide. But if he were insane at the time he committed suicide, or killed himself accidentally, it would not be affected. Where the policy read, "The 

Company is not liable if the insured should die by anything taken or inhaled," and it appeared that gas had accidentally escaped in the room, which A inhaled causing his death, the court held that death was not caused by the inhaling of gas within the meaning of the policy. It was held that the policy contemplated a voluntary and intelligent act by the assured, not an involuntary and unconscious act.* 

Paul v. Travelers' Ins. Co. 112 N.Y. 472.

If a fire or accident policy has expired and loss has occurred, the insured cannot recover the premiums paid by him on the ground that the policy has all the time been invalid because of his breach of warranty, where no question of the validity of the policy had previously arisen. 

Misstatement of Age

If an insured misstates his age, in his life policy, in order to pay lower premiums, he would not get the full value, but only the amount owing the insured, based on the actual premiums paid, had the insured stated the correct age. A misstatement of age is not affected by the two-year incontestability clause, and all the insured collects is what he is rightfully entitled to. 

Murphy v. Trav. Ins. Co. 134 Misc. 238, 234 N.Y.S. 278.

If the insurer pays the amount of the policy to the named beneficiary who has not been guilty of fraud, without knowing the misstatement of age, it cannot thereafter recover any part of the sum paid. An insurer must investigate the facts upon which its liability depends before making payment. 

N.Y. Life Ins. Co. v. Veit 267 A.D. 695 Clause of Incontestability 

The insurance statute requires that life insurance policies shall contain a clause that the policy is to be incontestable after it has been in force during the lifetime of the insured for a period of two years from its date of issue except for nonpayment of premiums, and for violation of clauses relating to military or naval service. But a policy containing other clauses would be enforceable as written. 

Insurance Law § 155. 

*There is a presumption against suicide when there is evidence from which it may be inferred that the death was by violence and an inference must be drawn as to suicide or not. Thus a prima facie case of death by accident is made out by showing that the insured died because of monoxide poisoning at a time when the policy was in force. At this point the presumption is effective. When the insurer furnishes proof of suicide, the jury should decide from the evidence without regard to the presumption and on the whole case the burden to establish "accidental death" is upon the plaintiff, John v. Commercial Travelers' Assn. 256 A.D. 835, 9 N.Y.S. (2nd) *257. See also Wellisch v. John Hancock Ins. Co. 293 N.Y. 178.
