There have been variations of the required clause. Where the clause read "This policy shall be incontestable after it has been in force for a period of two years from its date of issue and the insured died before the two years expired, it was held that the insurer may still contest the policy, but within two years from the date of its issue. The policy continues in force for this purpose even after the death of the insured. It should be noted, however, that the time elapsing between the death of the assured and the appointment of a representative for the deceased against whom the insurer can commence an action, is not part of the two-year period. 

Jensen v. Met. Life Ins. Co. 251 N.Y. 336 

The contest on the part of the company must be begun by action or by the service of an answer when the company is sued. In one case the complaint was served on March 16, 1927; the non-contestability period expired April 1, 1927. The answer was served after

April 1, 1927, setting up a defense of fraud. It was held that the defense was inserted too late, as the contest takes its start when the insurer serves an answer disclaiming liability. The insured or beneficiary may not, however, manoeuvre the insurer out of his right. 

Thus where a plaintiff discontinues an action, the insurer may file its defense in a new action brought after the allowed period has expired. Likewise where the insurd is given an extension of time within which to serve his complaint, he cannot bar the insurer from serving an answer, because by reason of the stipulation the period within which to contest has passed. 

Wolpin v. Prudential Ins. Co. 223 A.D. 339, 228 N.Y.S. 78 

Killian v. Metropolitan Life Ins. Co. 251 N.Y. 44

Romano v. Metropolitan Life Ins. Co. 271 N.Y. 288. 

Proof of Loss

If the policy requires the assured to notify the insurer of any event against which the insurer insures within a specified time, such notice must be given if liability is to attach. Where, however, an insurer with full knowledge that proper notice has not been given, undertakes to defend the interests of the assured in a law suit, it is considered a waiver of the right to disclaim liability. 

If the insured agrees in writing to permit the insurer to defend subject to its right to disclaim, no waiver is spelled out. If, however, after the insurer has so acted as to have waived the breach, a subsequent signing of a non-waiver agreement by the insured is by itself, unsupported by consideration, unenforceable. 

269 Canal St. Corp. v. Zurich Gen. Acc. Co. 252 N.Y. 603 

Killeen v. Gen. Acc. etc. Co. 131 Misc. 691, affd. 224 A.D. 719 

Farrell v. Merchants' etc. Co. 203 A.D. 118, 196 N.Y.S. 383 

A requirement that "immediate" or "forthwith" notice be given means that the notice is to be given within a reasonable time, considering all the circumstances of the situation. A delay of 10 days was held, without a proper explanation, to be unreasonable as a matter of law. 

Greenwich Bank v. Hart Ins. Co. 222 A.D. 219, affd. 250 N.Y. 116 

Reena v. U.S. Cas. Co. 228 A.D. 108, affd. 256 N.Y. 537.

The liability of an insurance company to a mortgagee who is the beneficiary even by the words "loss, if any, payable to-as interest may appear" is different from its liability toward the owner with respect to presentation of proofs of loss, and the short period of limitations does not apply to a mortgagee. 

Miller v. Stuyvesant Îns. Co. 223 A.D. 6, 277 N.Y.S. 326. 

Waiver and Estoppel

If the agent of the insurer at the time the policy is issued, knows the true facts which are contrary to the statements included in the policy, the insurer is estopped from asserting such defense and the parol evidence rule does not prevent the introduction of oral evidence to establish the knowledge of the agent. To permit an insurer to accept payment of premiums on a policy which it knew when issued was void from its inception would constitute a fraud on the policyholder. The fact that the policy itself, for the first time, contained a provision to the effect that the agent could not bind the company by waiver, charged the insured with notice upon the acceptance of the policy that the agent could not thereafter waive a breach. It did not nullify a waiver or estoppel which had prior thereto come into effect. Of course, if the insured was aware of the fact that the agent did not have authority, before the policy was delivered, this warning extrinsic to the policy may be charged against the insured. The insurer is protected though the limitation is in the application for insurance.* 

Reznikoff v. Equitable Life Assurance Soc'y. 267 A.D. 785 

Bible v. John Hancock etc. Ins. Co. 256 N.Y. 458.

The extent of the agent's authority is not determined by his being called "general agent" or "special agent." The question is whether the particular act is within the scope of his actual or apparent authority. Where, however, the agent, who solicited the insurance, made out and had the application signed, received the policies from the insurer and delivered them to the insured, he was held to be an authorized agent, clothed with authority to waive a condition precedent. The knowledge of this agent is the knowledge of his principal, the insurer. 

Glagowski v. Erie etc. Ins. Co. 216 A.D. 654, 216 N.Y.S. 64 

McClelland v. Mut. Life Ins. Co. 217 N.Y. 336.

A false statement in a burglary policy that there had not been a prior burglary loss, is a breach of warranty, voiding the policy in the absence of a waiver. A delivery of a life insurance policy to one not in good health to the knowledge of the insurer, is a waiver. 

Drilling v. N. Y. Life Ins. Co. 234 N.Y. 234 

McClelland v. Mutual Life Ins. Co. 217 N.Y. 336.

The soliciting agent who is employed to secure insurance is usually regarded as the agent of the insured and not of the insurer. 

Robertson v. Globe Fire Ins. Co. 223 A.D. 296. 

*It would appear that the application itself is not admissible in evidence unless attached to the policy. See Insurance Law § 142. Also ante page 230 and dissenting opinion in Smith v. John Hancock Life Ins. Co. 260 A.D. 990.

INSURANCE 

235 If the insurer company by unfair conduct leads the insured to believe that a warranty relied upon is not a part of the contract, it would be estopped from alleging the breach of warranty.

There is no waiver of any breach if the knowledge of facts relied upon comes to a company representative who is not authorized to act for the insurer. Thus, even though the agent and doctor of the insurer knew that the insured fraudulently stated that he had never been in a hospital, the beneficiary cannot collect in an action on the policy. And even if the insured had informed the company's doctor that he recently had been sick and the agent deliberately kept that information from the company, the beneficiary cannot collect, even though he could not read or write English. 

Stanulevich v. St. Louis Life Assn. 228 N.Y. 586 

Grubick v. John Hancock etc. Co. 212 AD. 126, 208 N.Y.S. 279 

Malchak v. Met. Life Ins. Co. 134 Misc. 640, 236 N.Y.S. 300

Emanuele v. Met. Life Ins. Co. 137 Misc. 542. 

A statement by an applicant that he was in good health is a representation only that the applicant in good faith believed and was justified in believing that his health was not impaired. If he had had no symptoms of illness which would ordinarily act as a warning to laymen and believed that he was well, whereas he had a heart ailment, his statement that he was "in sound health" would not be ground for voiding the policy.

Sommer v. Guardian Life Ins. Co. 281 N.Y. 508. 

It has not been decided in this state whether evidence should be admissible, in an action to reform the contract of insurance, to show that the answers contained in the written statement were never given and that the defendant insurer, through its agents, took unfair advantage of the applicant's inability to read English. 

Kwiatkouski v. Brotherhood 243 N.Y. 394.

Where a policy of automobile insurance was entered into by mail, directly with the company's office, and the terms of the policy were stated in the letters, the insured is justified in taking the final policy without reading it, and in relying on the company not inserting representations which were not made. If these representations so inserted prove to be false, the company is estopped from urging a defense of misrepresentation based on its own wrong. 

Abell v. Cornwall Ind. Corp. 241 N.Y. 318.

Subrogation There is no subrogation under a life policy. The result is that if an insured is killed by A's negligence, the beneficiary gets the amount of the policy and the insurer company has no claim against the tort feasor. The estate of the insured can sue the tort-feasor in addition to collecting on the policy. 

An insurer who pays the claims of the insured under an accident or fire policy is entitled to be subrogated to the rights which the insured would have had against such third party for its default or wrongdoing. If the assured receives the damages from the wrongdoer before payment by the insurer, the amount so received will be applied pro tanto in discharge of the policy. The insurer can sue in

his own name and need not join the insured as a party. Where the insured sues the wrongdoer the subrogated insurer is a necessary party as a partial assignee and if not brought in by the plaintiff, may be brought in by the defendant. 

Sisson v. Hassett 155 Misc. 667, 280 N.Y.S. 148.

Upon payment of the entire loss to the insured, the insurer becomes the equitable owner of the proceeds the insured may recover from the wrongdoer. The insurer may sue the wrongdoer or may allow the legal owner to sue for its benefit, the legal owner becoming a trustee of the recovery. 

Herald Nathan Press v. Bourges 161 Misc. 208, 291 N.Y.S. 650.

The Appellate Term in New York City has held that where the insured settles with the tort-feasor after having been paid by the insurer under the policy, the insured is liable over to the insurer for the money received from the tort-feasor, in an action for money had and received, but that the right of subrogation was destroyed when without knowledge of the insurer's claim the tort-feasor obtained a release from the insured. 

Met, Cas. Ins. Co. v. Badler 132 Misc. 132, 229 N.Y.S. 81.

If the insured releases his claim against the tort-feasor before the insurer has made any payments, the right to subrogation is lost, and the insured cannot collect on his policy. 

Ocean Acc. etcL Co. v. Hooker 240 N.Ÿ. 37.

In one case the insured received $2,000 from his insurance company under a policy when a train destroyed his automobile. The railroad, not knowing of this policy, paid a sum to the insured in satisfaction of his claim for property damage and personal injuries. 

The court held that if the insured collected money in satisfaction of the damage for which the insurer had paid, he holds such money for the benefit of the insurer to the extent of the sum paid by the insurer to the insured. If the insurer desires to collect from the insured because its right of subrogation has been lost, it can do so by showing that it might have recovered against the tort-feasor and that the insurer has lost this because of the release. 

Hamilton Fire Ins. v. Greger 246 N.Y. 162.

Where a mortgagee takes out his own fire insurance or where he is covered by a policy taken out by the mortgagor with the usual mortgage clause, the mortgagee may recover in case of fire even though the property undestroyed is ample security for the debt. 

The insurer must also pay even if the mortgagor himself repairs the property and puts it back in as good condition as it was before the fire. The insurer's obligation is not affected by the acts of the mortgagor. The latter benefits by the payment as the insurance money reduces the amount of the mortgage debt. 

Savarese v. Ohio Farmers Ins. Co. 260 N.Y. 45.

Complete and Partial Destruction by Fire 

A fire which so damages a building that it cannot be repaired or rebuilt causes a loss to the owner of the entire value of the building, even though part of the building remains standing. That is as true

INSURANCE 

237 in a case where the state prohibits rebuilding or repair as it is where physical conditions make such rebuilding or repair impossible. 

Where a policy insures an owner against all loss or damage caused by fire, but reserves to the insurer an option to rebuild instead of paying the loss caused by the fire, the insurance company cannot avail itself of its option if the law prevents rebuilding, nor can the owner's loss or damage be measured by the cost of repairs which he is forbidden to make. In such circumstances the insurer must pay the full amount of the loss actually caused to the owner.' 

Midwood Sanatorium v. Firemen's Ins. Co. 261 N.Y. 381. 

Cancellation of Fire Policies* 

It is mandatory upon insurance companies, upon request of the assured and presentation of the policy, to cancel the policy and return the unearned premium. It is not essential that the presentation be made to the home office. If presented to a representative of the company it is sufficient. 

Crown Point Iron Co. v. Aetna Ins. Co. 127 N.Y. 608, 618.

Forfeiture of Life Policies 

The standard life policy requires the company to mail a notification to the insured of the amount of premiums due, where payable, and that the policy will be forfeited if the premium is not paid. The notice must be mailed not less than fifteen nor more than forty-five days before the premium is due. If the company does not do so it cannot declare the policy void for failure to pay the premium until one year after default. If the company does mail such a notice and the insured defaults, he is given two years' time to bring any suit under his now forfeited policy. This arrangement does not apply to policies payable in weekly or monthly installments. The insurer is not responsible for any miscarriage in the mail in giving the notice. 

Goeller v. 

Equitable L. Ass. Co. 251 A.D. 371, 296 N.Y.S. 854.

If there is a default, the insured can within three years after default reinstate the policy if the cash surrender value has not been paid provided he can give satisfactory evidence of insurability and he pays all premiums due, with interest at 6% compounded annually. 

Good health is not the only test of insurability. The insured's financial status or overinsurance may justify a refusal to reinstate the policy.

Insurance Law § 155i 

Kallman v. Equitable Life Assur. Co. 248 A.D. 146, affd. 272 N.Y. 648.

Where the insured maintains that the insurer was wrong in declaring a policy to be lapsed, he cannot rescind and recover back all premiums paid. His remedy is in equity to compel recognition of the policy. 

Gilbert v. N. Y. Life Ins. Co. 238 A.D. 544, 264 N.Y.S. 610.

Where by the request or authority of the insurer a premium pay- *Where there is no cancellation, an insurance policy which by its terms is to expire a certain day is in effect for the full day upon which it expires, unless a certain hour is fixed.

ment is sent by mail, the payment is deemed to have been made at the time of its deposit in the mail. 

Struhl v. Travelers' Ins. Co. 255 A.D. 527, affd. 281 N.Y. 584. 

Reforming a Policy

Policies are subject to reformation under the same circumstances as would be applicable in the case of any other contract. 

Schenectady Varnish v. Auto Ins. Co. 127 Misc. 751 217 N.Y.S. 504 

Paskie v. Con. P. Ins. Co. 223 A.D. 603, 229 N.Y.S. 121, 126.

There is no merit to the contention that by receiving and retaining the policy the assured waives any objection thereto. The court of equity has consistently refused to deprive the assured of relief when asking for reformation of an insurance policy when it was drawn by the insurer and contained terms other than were intended and agreed upon.

The Beneficiary and Creditors 

Where one effects insurance upon his own life for the benefit of another, the beneficiary takes as against the creditors of the insured, irrespective of who the beneficiary may be. If payments of premiums are made in fraud of creditors, the amount of premiums paid with interest thereon, enures to their benefit from the proceeds of the policy. The insurer is discharged of liability if it pays all to the beneficiary, unless before such payment the company shall have written notice from a creditor claiming a specific amount from the proceeds of the policy.

The beneficiary does not take over his own creditors, even if the beneficiary is the wife of the insured. A beneficiary, where the insured effects insurance upon his own life, takes free from creditors' claims except in an action to recover for necessaries, where an agreement relating to the proceeds of the policy to that effect has been left with the insurer.

Insurance Law § 166; Personal Property Law § 15 

Chatham Phoenix v. Crosney 251 N.Y. 189

Where A, having an insurable interest in the life of B, effects insurance upon B for A's own benefit, A takes over the creditors of B. 

But if it is the wife of the assured who effects such insurance, she takes over her own creditors as well. 

Levine v. Laurdan Management Co. 179 Misc. 241, affd. 266 A.D. 840.

The loan value of or dividends on a life policy are attachable where the insured has elected to receive them in cash. If they are to be applied to the payment of premium due or to obtain additional insurance, they are not attachable. 

Mfrs. Trust Co. v. Brain 177 Misc. 83, affd. 262 A.D. 989. 

Randik Realty Co. v. Moseyeff 147 Misc. 618, 263 N.Y.S. 440.

Periodic payments actually made under all annuity contracts to the one who paid the consideration are not subject to execution up to a joint total of $400 a month. The surplus beyond $400 monthly is liable for the claims of creditors in the same manner as other such property which cannot be reached by execution. 

Insurance Law § 166

239 If the beneficiary is to take only if he survives the insured, the proceeds of the policy go to the estate of the insured if the beneficiary predeceases the insured, If, however, the insured murdered the beneficiary, the estate of the latter would be entitled to the insurance moneys. If the beneficiary murders the insured, the estate of the latter collects the insurance money, provided that the policy was validly issued. If the policy was procured in furtherance of a conspiracy between assured and beneficiary to defraud the insurer, the policy is not valid, and the estate of the insured cannot take if the insured has been murdered by the beneficiary. It seems that where the policy has been validly issued and the assured has been murdered by the beneficiary, the estate of the insured can collect on the policy because of an implied intention read into the policy that, if the beneficiary cannot take, then the insurance should be paid to those who would take in the absence of a beneficiary. 

Goldstein v. N. Y. Life Ins. Co. 225 A.D. 642, 234 N.Y.S. 250

A wife who is the beneficiary under a policy insuring the life of her husband cannot make an irrevocable transfer of the policy while her husband is alive. She (and no one else) may recover the insurance money in spite of a previous assignment by her. Upon the death of her husband it is assignable without restriction and subject like other assets to seizure for the use of creditors. 

Jackson v. Tallmadge 214 N.Y.S. 528, affd. 246 N.Y. 133.

Change of Beneficiary 

The standard form of policy reserves to the insured the right to change his beneficiary upon his written request filed at the home office and provides that the change is not to be effective until the proper indorsement is made upon the policy. It has, however, been held that the change becomes effective without the company's indorsement, for the purpose of the insured cannot be defeated by the neglect of the company to perform a ministerial act. 

Lofaro v. John Hancock M. L. Co. 239 A.D. 54, affd. 272 N.Y. 627.

Where there is no reservation of a right in favor of the insured to change the beneficiary of a life insurance policy, the beneficiary has a present or vested right to receive, whenever the policy matures, whatever sum may become payable thereon in accordance with its terms. If therefore, while a policy is in force, the insured, insurer or both, without the consent or authorization of the beneficiary, take any action with respect to the policy that would defeat, impair, or materially change the rights of the beneficiary thereunder, such action is void as to the beneficiary. When there is a default in payment of the premium, there is no obligation on the part of the insurer to notify such beneficiary though the policy lapse as a result. 

Ruckenstein v. Metropolitan Life Ins. Co. 263 N.Y. 204.

Where the insured can change the beneficiary, the latter may maintain that such change was made under a mistake of fact. Even such beneficiary has a property right which can be asserted. 

Rosenblum v. Manfacturers Trust Co. 270 N.Y. 79

Davis v. Modern Industrial Bank 279 N.Y. 405.

A life insurance policy is a chose in action and an oral assignment accompanied by delivery is valid if established by sufficient evidence.

Considine v. Considine 255 A.D. 876. 

Accident Policies 

By statute, if a person insured against liability for causing damage to the person or property of another by means of his automobile, injures X or damages his property, X may recover against the insured if a judgment against the insured remains unsatisfied for 30 days after service of a copy of the judgment with notice of entry upon the insured or his attorney and the insurer. 

The amount of such recovery cannot exceed the coverage of the policy.

Insurance Law § 167. 

The insolvency or bankruptcy of the person insured does not relieve the insurance carrier.

If the injured party sues the insurer under § 167, the insurer may set up any defense that it could have set up against the insured. If, however, the defense asserted is that the insured had failed to give the insurer proper notice of the accident as specified in the insurance policy, the failure to do so shall not invalidate the claim if it can be shown that it could not have been reasonably possible to give notice on time and that it was given as soon as was reasonably possible. If the defense is that the insured had failed to cooperate with the insurer in the defense, the burden is upon the insurer to prove such facts.

Shalita v. American Motorists Ins. Co. 266 A.D. 131. 

A policy which omits to include § 167 of the Insurance Law or in any way attempts to limit it, is valid but is deemed to include that section without limitation. 

Bakker v. Aetna Life Ins. Co. 264 N.Y. 150.

Section 211a of the Civil Practice Act permits a joint tort-feasor who has paid a judgment recovered against him and others, to recover from the other joint-feasors their pro rata shares of such judgment. Let us suppose that A and B were joint tort-feasors. X sued both and recovered a judgment which A's insurer pays. By this payment A's insurer becomes subrogated to A's rights. May A's insurer recover the pro rata share from B under § 211a of the Civil Practice Act? The court held "No" on the ground that § 211a became law after § 167 of the Insurance Law and that it would be a forced construction to decide that § 167 of the Insurance Law applies to a right to maintain an action authorized by a subsequent enactment. 

By the same token a joint tort-feasor who pays the judgment, cannot obtain contribution from the insurer of the other tort-feasor. 

Metro'n Casualty v. Union Indemnity 141 Misc. 792, affd. 255 N.Y. 591

La Gumina v. Citizens Casualty Co. 180 Misc. 877, affd. 181 Misc. 180. 

*This cause of action against the insured is not assignable by the injured party. Jackson v. Citizens Casualty Co. 277 N.Y. 385.

INSURANCE 

241 The rule is settled in the law of insurance that the cause nearest the loss is to be considered and that distant causes are to be disregarded. Let us suppose that the plaintiff bank is insured by the defendant company against loss through larceny or theft only. A depositor of the plaintiff knowingly deposits to his own account a forged check wherein the maker is a fictitious person. Thus far the depositor is guilty of forgery. Then the depositor draws out some money against this check, the bank paying against uncollected funds. The depositor, having obtained money by false pretenses, is guilty of larceny. The loss thus sustained may be collected from the insurer, as the cause nearest the loss was the larceny. 

Trade Bank v. U. S. Fid. & G. Co. 223 A.D. 584, 229 N.Y.S. 92

It has been held that where one acts as aggressor in an attack, under circumstances which would render a homicide likely as the result of his own misconduct, death was not accidental within the meaning of a clause in a policy providing for payment in case of accidental death. Similarly one judicially executed for a crime or one who dies while jumping from a prison wall to escape does not die accidentally. 

Manno v. Met. Life Ins. Co. 139 Misc. 848, 249 N.Y.S. 471

Udisky v. Met. Life Ins. Co. 264 A.D. 890. 

The Co-Insurance Clause 

Since most fire insurance policies carry an 80% co-insurance clause, such clause will be used to explain its working. Under a coinsurance clause the insured is obligated to carry insurance to an amount equal to 80% of the value of the insured property. 

Let us assume the value of the insured property to be $10,000. 

The 80% clause of course requires that $8,000 insurance be carried. Should the insured carry only $6,000 and the fire loss amount to $4,000, the insured can get only 75% of his loss since the insurance carried was only 75% of what the co-insurance clause required him to carry. Putting it in a different way, the insured gets only that percentage of his loss which the amount of insurance carried bears to the amount which should have been carried.

Statute of Frauds

EASES OR assignments of leases which are to run for a period of more than a year from the time the term commences must be in writing and subscribed by the party to be charged or his agent, authorized in writing. It thus differs from a contract of employment, which must be in writing if it is not to terminate within a year from the making of the contract. An oral lease of premises for a year or less containing an option for an extension for an additional three years is not within the statute, as it is possible for the lease to terminate at the end of the definite period agreed upon. 

Real Property Law § 242, 259; Ward v. Hasbrouck 169 N.Y. 407 

Courts v. Golden 257 A.D. 31.

The fact that the oral lease agreement is voidable does not excuse the lessee from paying the reasonable value for the use and occupation of the premises. 

Real Property Law § 220. 

If the unexpired term of a lease does not exceed one year, parol evidence is admissible to prove an agreement for its surrender. 

Gorlin v. Hrvatsky 126 Misc. 570, 214 N.Y.S. 45.

Duty of Lessor to Repair 

In the absence of fraud or a covenant, a lessor does not represent that the premises are tenantable and that they may be used for the purpose for which they are apparently intended. 

Welson v. Neujan Bldg. Co. 264 N.Y. 303.

The person in possession and control of premises is bound to take reasonable care to keep the common halls and stairways reasonably safe for passage of tenants and those lawfully using the same even though there be no lease. The degree of care owed to a guest and family of a tenant is the same as that which the landlord owes his tenant. This duty cannot be delegated and the one in control is not relieved by having an independent contractor do the work. 

Schabel v. Onseyga Realty 233 A.D. 208, 251 N.Y.S. 280 

Russo v. Watson 249 A.D. 782, 292 N.Y.S. 249.

The statute requires that a multiple dwelling* be kept by a landlord reasonably safe for intended and reasonably anticipated uses. 

This includes a duty to keep a proper light burning in the public hallways near the stairs, upon the entrance door, and upon the second floor above the entrance floor of said house, every night from sunset to sunrise throughout the year; to keep in such condition, among other things walls, ceilings, water equipment, piping, toilets, flushometers, faucets (but not wash-tub cover or clothes drier).

Before liability for injury to person or property can attach, it must *A multiple dwelling is defined as a building occupied by three or more families living independently of each other. 242

243 be shown that the landlord had actual or constructive notice of the defect. The fact that the Multiple Dwelling Law places the burden on the owner to keep the premises in good repair does not give a lessee the right to enforce the obligation in the absence of a covenant to make such repairs. The municipal authorities are those who may require compliance. On the other hand where there is an agreement between a lessor and lessee, the latter being in full possession, by which the former undertakes to make repairs, no liability is created in tort against the lessor in favor of a person injured by its breach.

Fleming v. Oppel 254 A.D. 740 (Case 1) 

Ocean Acc, etc. Co. v. Hooker 240 N.Y. 37 

Boylan v. 1986 Grand Ave. Co. 169 Misc. 881, 8 N.Y.S. (2nd) 200 

Emigrant Bank v. 108 W. 49th St. Co. 255 A.D. 570, affd. 280 N.Y. 791. 

Lefkowitz v. Greenwich Savings Bank 293 N. Y.

A lease of the entire premises does not relieve the owner of his liability to keep in good repair those portions of the multiple dwelling as provided by the Multiple Dwelling Law. An essential element of liability under the statute is notice of the defect to the owner. Actual notice to the tenant of the entire premises given by a plaintiff is not actual notice to the owner, for the tenant is not the agent of the owner. If the dangerous condition is long continued in a portion used in common by the tenant and others, and the premises are available for examination by the owner as well as the lessee, there may in that fact be found constructive notice to the owner. Whether there is constructive notice to the owner where the latter has no right to inspect, is still undecided. 

Weiner v. Leroco Realty Co. 279 N.Y. 127 

Tkach v. Montefiore Hospital 289 N.Y. 387 

Becker v. Mftrs. Trust Co. 262 A.D. 525.

Where a vendor and not the vendee had notice of a defective condition of a ceiling in a multiple dwelling apartment, and had ample opportunity to remedy the defect, it was held that the vendor was had no knowledge of such defect, it was held that the vendor was liable for injuries to the tenant resulting from the fall of a portion of the ceiling, before the new owner had reasonable opportunity to discover the condition and make repairs.* 

Pharm v. Lituchy, 170 Misc. 221, affd. 283 N.Y. 130.

A clause providing that the lessor of realty should not be liable for negligence in the operation or maintenance of the realty, of himself or agents is void as against public policy. This applies to active and passive negligence.

Real Property Law § 234 

Int. Underwear Co. v. B'klyn Trust Co. 287 N.Y. 589.

The fact that a tenant remains in an apartment having a defective ceiling for a long period does not, as a matter of law, make the tenant guilty of contributory negligence. It is a question of fact for the jury. 

Eckert v. Reichardt 243 N.Y. 72. *Whatever is dangerous to human life or detrimental to health, is in contemplation of the Multiple Dwelling Law, a nuisance.

Where the Multiple Dwelling Law has no application, e.g.: a private dwelling, a lessor is not liable in tort for personal injuries resulting from defects of the premises, after the lessee has taken possession. This rule applies even if the lessor has agreed to make repairs. The liability in that event would be on the covenant. There are however, certain exceptions to the rule. If unsuitable premises are leased and they are to be used by the public; if the deception of the lessor prevents the lessee from learning of hidden defects, the lessor may be held liable. 

Junkerman v. Tilyou Realty Co. 213 N.Y. 404

Duty of Lessee to Repair 

A covenant requiring a tenant to make "all repairs," requires the tenant merely to make all ordinary repairs, not structural changes; and the further requirement that the tenant would comply with all ordinances and municipal regulations, does not cast upon the tenant the obligation of compliance with the orders of the building department where a structural change would be required. 

140 West 34th St. Co. v. Davis 158 Misc. 470, 285 N.Y.S. 957. 

Constructive Eviction

A tenant may plead constructive eviction where, through the landlord's acts, he has been substantially deprived of the beneficial enjoyment of the demised premises. The eviction cannot be predicated on acts or conduct, however wrongful or distressing, unless committed, encouraged or connived at by the landlord. He is not responsible for the conduct of other tenants acting within their rights in their own apartments. Redress may be secured, not against his landlord, but against the offending tenant in the other premises. For even where the landlord might have the right to terminate the lease because of a tenant's noisy and boisterous conduct, his failure to exercise such a privilege would not necessarily support the claim of constructive eviction. 

Tudor City v. Perkett 143 Misc. 209, 256 N.Y.S. 395.

Where there is a constructive eviction the lessee may terminate the lease, provided he speedily vacates the premises after the commencement of the causes constituting such constructive eviction. 

Eviction as a defense to a claim for rent does not depend upon a covenant for quiet enjoyment, either express or implied. The obligation of payment is suspended because there is a failure of the consideration. 

City of N. Y. v. Cokenes 229 A.D. 695, 242 N.Y.S. 374.

The rule that the tenant must vacate speedily before he can assert the defense of constructive eviction, does not apply where the tenant holds a lease in a tenement house and the premises are in disrepair. It is the landlord's statutory duty to repair. 

3175 Holding Co. v. Schmidt 150 Misc. 853, 270 N.Y.S. 663.

Where noises and leaks amount to a constructive eviction, a tenant remaining in the premises is not absolved from paying rent because a clause in the lease provides he is to live rent free in the 1

LANDLORD AND 

245 TENAN'T case of noise and leaks. The court will construe the clause as a penalty. The tenant will be limited to an action for damages on the covenant. Rent falling due while the tenant is in possession, must be paid. 

19 John St. Corp v. M'Namara 136 Misc. 844, 242 N.Y.S. 407.

Since in the absence of fraud or a covenant a lessor does not represent that the premises are tenantable and usable for the purposes for which they are intended, the lessee has no cause of action when he vacates because of deterioration of the premises. The lease merely is at an end. Should the lease cover the situation by its terms these terms would control. 

Altz v. Lieberson 233 N.Y. 16 

Mulligan v. Fioravera 228 A.D. 270, affå. 255 N.Y. 559.

Grounds for terminating the lease or constructive eviction are, among others: numerous bedbugs which cannot be gotten rid of; failure to furnish heat during the cold weather, the means of furnishing such heat being in the landlord's control; failure to provide elevator service seriously interfering with the use of the premises; destruction by the elements; use of machinery which caused great vibrations; presence of offensive odors not there_to_the_lessee's knowledge when the lease was made. What is and what is not a good cause is in most cases a question of fact. 

Bliss v. Clark 104 Misc. 543, 172 N.Y.S. 112 

Read v. Levy 101 Misc. 547, 167 N.Y.S. 568 

Ess-Eff Realty Co. v. Buttenheim 125 N.Y.S. 401 

Fleckner v. Douglas 136 Misc. 57, 239 N.Y.S. 121.

Where a lease restricts and limits the use of premises to a specified purpose which thereafter becomes unlawful, the subject matter of the contract is destroyed and the lease is terminated. A change in the law which merely restricts but does not wholly prohibit the conduct of the hess, does not release the tenant. 

Byrnes v. Balcom 265 A.D. 268, affd. 290 N.Y. 730. 

Partial Eviction

Where there has been an actual eviction from a part of the demised premises by an act of the landlord, the entire rent which becomes due during the eviction is suspended until full possession is restored. The tenant need not vacate the premises. The landlord is not permitted to apportion his own wrong. If the eviction is the act of a stranger by force of paramount title, the rent is apportioned and recovery permitted only for the value of the premises retained. 

Fifth Ave. Bldg. Co. v. Kernschan 221 N.Y. 370 

Friedman v. Garage D. Corp. 130 Misc. 266, 223 N.Y.S. 839.

Payment of rent by the tenant after an original partial eviction is not a waiver of a continued eviction and the tenant can set up the defense of eviction to an action for rent for the following months. 

Kusche v. Sabin 6 N.Y.S. (2nd) 771. 

If by reason of the eviction the tenant vacates the premises he is entitled to recover the proportionate share of the rent paid in advance, on the ground of failure of consideration. Retention of possession to the end of the term prevents any such recovery. 

Kennedy v. Peterart Realty Co. 171 Misc. 351

The tenant, in cases of partial eviction, is not entitled to damages. If the tenant pays the rent, or admits liability for it, he may claim damages. He may also assert his rights for the eviction at any time and not pay rent thereafter. 

Davis v. Schatzen 124 Misc. 170, 207 N.Y.S. 217 

524 West End Ave. v. Rawak 125 Misc. 862, 212 N.Y.S. 287 

Peerless v. Halbreich 125 Misc. 889, 213 N.Y.S. 49 

Macomber v. Clark 152 Misc. 360, 273 N.Y.S. 314.

These are examples of a partial eviction: an arbitrary refusal to give the tenant the key; the lack of use of a lavatory; an actual ouster by a landloard of a tenant from space in a rented garage which can be occupied by six automobiles, regardless of the size of the garage; interfering with a tenant's occupation of premises by the landlord's entry upon the demised premises without permission from the tenant, in order to install a new hot water system. 

City of N. Y. v. Pike Realty Co. 247 N.Y. 245 

Kermacoe v. McKenna 132 Misc. 293, 229 N.Y.S. 498.

Covenant of Quiet Enjoyment 

The lessor, in making a lease, impliedly affirms that he has such title as to enable him to give an unencumbered lease for the term therein stated. If the lease contains a covenant of quiet enjoyment, the possession of the lessee is not to be disturbed by a superior title during the term of the lease. This is not dependent upon the continued title of the lessor, or upon subsequent payments of mortgages which were or became liens upon the premises. Neither the beginning of an action to foreclose a mortgage superior to the lease, in which action he is made a defendant, nor the appointment of a receiver in foreclosure proceedings, nor the entry of a judgment of foreclosure and sale, constitutes an eviction. The sale may never occur or the amount due on the mortgage may be paid. When the sale actually takes place the tenant is constructively evicted. Where the tenant is ousted, he may recover from the original lessor for the breach of the covenant.* 

Ganz v. Clark 252 N.Y. 92

Metropolitan Life Ins. Co. v. Childs 230 N.Y. 285 

Destruction of Premises

Upon the destruction or injury of the leased premises by the elements or other cause, so that they become untenantable, neither the tenant nor the laidlord need rebuild, in the absence of a writing requiring it to be done. The tenant, if the destruction or injury was not caused by his negligence, may declare the lease at an end provided he moves, and he is not liable to pay rent for the time subsequent to the surrender. Any rent paid in advance or which may have accrued, shall be adjusted to the date of such surrender. 

Real Property Law § 227 

The landlord, in the absence of a covenant to rebuild, cannot enter upon the premises to do repair work, but if the tenant makes no *For the measure of damages recoverable for breach of the covenant of quiet enjoyment see, supra, chapter on Damages, at page 180.

Assignments and Subleases If the lessee transfers the whole or a specific part of the leasehold estate for the residue of the term, it is an "assignment." A transfer of the whole or a specific part of the leasehold for a part of the term, is a "sublease.' 

A sublease of the entire premises which sublease expires before the original lease, even as little as one day, absolves the subtenant of liability for rent to the overlandlord. The liability of an assignee grows out of privity of estate only. This means that the landlord is entitled to proceed for the rent reserved in his lease against the assignee, even though a different rent has been contracted for by the assignee. The liability ceases when the privity ceases, and each successive assignee is liable for such breaches of covenant as occur while there is privity of estate between him and the lessor. The covenant to pay runs with the land. The privity of estate is not terminable by an abandonment of the premises but by the surrender with consent or by further assignment to another. To hold an assignee of a lease after he has given it up or vacated, there must exist an express promise to pay.

Bradbury Homes v. John's Doughnut Shops 270 N.Y.S. 592 Sandford v. Ambassador Restaurant 139 Misc. 3 New Amsterdam Cas. Co. v. Nat. Union F. Ins. Co. 266 N.Y. 254 

Hart v. Socony Vacuum Co. 291 N.Y. 13

If the lease requires that the permission of the landlord be obtained before the tenant may sublease, and the tenant subleases without that permission, the landlord is considered to have waived that provision of the lease by accepting the rent from the new tenant with knowledge of the sublease. But should the new tenant fail to pay rent, the original lessee is liable, for nothing short of a novation will transfer the lease to the new tenant. 

If the landlord gives his written consent to an assignment, the covenant against assignment in the lease is cancelled and the assignee can then assign without permission. The original tenant still remains liable. Where the assignee assumes the obligations of the lease, the original tenant stands in the position of a surety. 

Costallat v. Diamond 226 A.D. 755, 234 Ñ.Y.S. 152 

Lynch v. Joseph 228 A.D. 367, 240 N.Y.S. 176

Durand v. Lipman 165 Misc. 615. 

Gillette Bros. v. Aristocrat Restaurant 239 N.Y. 87.

A lessee who assigns his lease and is obliged to pay the landlord

for the default of the assignee acquires a cause for action against the assignee, not by virtue of a privity of contract or estate, as neither exists, but merely for the reason that the lessee is a surety and the assignee is the principal obligor. Where, however, the assignee has assigned to a subsequent assignee, and the lessee is obliged to pay for the default of this subsequent assignee, the lessee can recover only from the subsequent assignee and not from the first assignee, for there is no longer any surety agreement between the lessee and the first assignee and there never was privity of contract or estate. The principal obligor is the second assignee. 

Schlessel v. Sherman 130 Misc. 633, 224 N.Y.S. 593

Where a sub-tenant remained in possession without permission of the landlord after the expiration of the lease of the original tenant, it was held that the landlord could hold the original tenant as a holdover. 

Meyerowitz v. Horowitz 129 Misc. 215, 220 N.Y.S. 681

On the sale of leasehold interest the vendor must show: (1) that he owns the lease; (2) that he has authority to sell it; (3) that the original lessor had power to create the term. 

If the lessee buys the building in which the leased premises are, the lease automatically ends, even if the tenant buyer resells at once. 

Reckoning Time in Lease 

A lease to end on a stated date, expires at noon of that day. A lease to a stated date expires at midnight of the day previous. 

Big Four Realty Co. v. Belnord 141 Misc. 472, affd. 235 A.D. 672. 

Holdover Tenants

A tenancy at will or by sufferance can be terminated by thirty days' notice in writing served on the tenant personally or by delivering the notice to one of suitable age and discretion upon the premises, or if one cannot be found, by affixing the notice to the door. 

After thirty days the landlord may reenter, maintain ejectment or remove the tenant by summary process.

Real Property Law § 228; Bastedo v. Levan 171 Misc. 140 

A monthly tenant cannot be removed as a holdover in the City of New York unless at least 30 days before the expiration of the term the landlord serves upon the tenant a written notice of his election to terminate the tenancy and that unless the tenant moves he will commence summary proceedings. There is no reciprocal obligation on a tenant. He may surrender possession at the end of any month without notice to the landlord. But if the premises are outside of the City of New York, such tenancy may be terminated by the landlord notifying the other at least one month before the expiration of the election to terminate. In this case the tenant has a reciprocal obligation.*

Real Property Law §§ 232a; 232b; Andriola v. Naber 181 Misc. 764 

*The service of the notice in the City of New York must be served in the manner a precept in a summary proceeding must be served. Outside the City of New York it is not the rule. There it would be enough to slide it under the door of the apartment. Angell v. McInerney 182 Misc. 412.

If a tenant of indefinite tenancy, i.e., not a lessee for a term, says that he will leave on a certain date and he does not, he must pay double the amount of the rental for the period during which he holds over. (If sickness was the cause of the holding over, the rule does not apply.) If a lessee for a definite tenancy of a year or more, holds over, the landlord can assume that the lease which just terminated is renewed for another year upon the terms of the original lease so far as they are appliable to the new relation. The law as to holding over by a tenant does not apply to holding over by a licensee.*

In order to give the landlord a right to consider a tenant a holdover under an implied lease, there must be an actual retention of possession of the premises by the tenant, as against the landlord, so that the tenant would by virtue of his possession become a trespasser. 

Merely leaving property on the leased premises after the expiration of the lease may or may not entitle the landlord to treat the tenancy as a holdover liable for another year's rent. The determination is one of fact. Not only the value of the goods which are left over by the tenant must be considered, but the ratio of that value to the amount of rent is also material. If a tenant for a year or years, in possession of a store, should leave his entire stock and fixtures after the expiration of the lease, the court would be required, as a matter of law, to hold that he had retained actual possession and that the landlord would elect to hold the tenant for another year. 

If the tenant merely leaves litter, filth and worthless articles which tenants are accustomed to leave behind them, there is no such holding over which can permit the landlord to consider the tenant liable under an implied lease. 

Canfield v. Harrison 222 A.D. 326, affd. 248 N.Y. 541.

Should a tenant for such a fixed term state that he wished to remain as a monthly tenant, mere silence on the part of the landlord after receiving such notice, would not suffice to establish that a month-to-month agreement was created. 

Thiot Realty Co. v. Rosen 176 Misc. 109

If a tenant vacates the premises and the landlord comes into possession, the relationship of landlord and tenant ends. A reletting by a landlord after abandonment by the tenant works a surrender and acceptance by operation of law, in the absence of consent to such reletting. Where the lease permits the landlord to relet for the remainder of the term, the landlord must not relet for a longer period. If he does relet for a longer period, there is a surrender and acceptance. 

Bonsignore v. Koondel 134 Misc. 344, 235 N.Y.S. 453

Under a lease giving the tenant a privilege of renewing on the same terms and conditions and not requiring a notice of election to renew, the tenant's mere remaining in possession and the landlord's failure to object for a length of time after the expiration of of the lease (in one case five months was held to be a sufficient period, although no rent was due till then) are equivalent to an exercise of the privilege to renew. 

Fritz v. City of New York, 125 Misc. 296, 210 N.Y.S. 717

Upon the termination of the tenancy the landlord is entitled to receive full and complete possession of the demised premises from the tenant. If there be an undertenant in possession, the tenant must get him out, else his possession will be regarded the possession of the tenant and the latter may be considered a holdover tenant. 

Goodwin v. Humbert 216 A.D. 295, 215 N.Y.S. 20

When a lease is made to two or more tenants jointly, with covenants for renewal of the privilege of an additional term, it cannot be exercised by one of them without the other. 

Goldberg v. Himlyn 121 Misc. 580, 201 N.Y.S. 837

If a summons to recover title or possession to the property occupied by the tenant is served on the tenant by a person other than the landlord, he must forthwith notify the landlord. If he fails to do so, he forfeits three years' rental to the landlord. 

Real Property Law § 225. 

There can be no recovery for use and occupation unless it is shown by the plaintiff that the conventional relation of landlord and tenant existed between the parties. There must have existed some contract, express or implied, to pay for the use and occupation. Thus, in one recent case, the defendant was not required to pay rent in the following circumstances. He entered into possession of the property as a purchaser at a defective sale under a mortgage foreclosure. 

By stipulation the sale was set aside and a second sale took place. 

The suit was for use and occupation of the premises by the defendant between the first and second sales.

If a lease requires a tenant to pay all taxes assessed against the demised premises during the term when due, it is construed to mean that the tenant must pay all such taxes assessed during the term, even those payable at a date after the expiration of the term.

Automatic Renewal Clause

If a lease provides that it is automatically renewed for a specified term unless the tenant gives notice of his intention to quite at some stated date, such provision is not operative unless the lessor gives the tenant written notice served personally or by registered mail, at least fifteen and not more than thirty days previous to the time specified for the furnishing of the notice by the tenant, calling the attention of the tenant to the existence of the provision. If it is not given, the lessor is deprived of the right to avail himself of the automatic renewal clause. The tenant by remaining in the premises

Wood Co. v. Horgan 291 N.Y. 422

J. H. Holding Co. v. Wooten 291 N.Y. 427 Eviction by Summary Proceedings* 

When a lease expires because of a conditional limitation, the landlord may remove the tenant by summary proceedings. If the lease ends because of a condition subsequent, the landlord must proceed in eject to remove the tenant. 

There is much confusion in the cases where the inquiry is whether the language of a particular lease operates as a conditional limitation or condition subsequent. If the term has expired and the tenant is a holdover, the tenant may be removed by summary proceedings. Likewise where a lease provides for its termination by a sale of the premises at the option of the landlord and upon giving of notice. The test of a conditional limitation is whether the lease evinces a clear intention that an event, though its occurrence is optional with the landlord, shall, when it transpires, end the lease as if by its terms it had been limited to that time. Thus, summary proceedings may be maintained under the following clause after notice given: "If default be made in the payment of rent.........the landlord may, if he so elects........terminate this lease by giving the tenant 5 days' notice in writing of his intention to do so and this lease and the term thereof shall expire and come to an end on the day fixed in such notice as if said date were the date originally fixed in the lease for the expiration thereof." And where a lease read that "an adjudication that the lessee is bankrupt shall ipso facto terminate this lease" it was held that the clause was a conditional limitation. Since in this instance the termination did not depend upon an election on the part of the landlord, there was an automatic termination. 

Murray Realty Co. v. Regal Shoe Co. 265 N.Y. 332 

Paul v. Levine 137 Misc. 82, 242 N.Y.S. 729 

Reisberg v. Ownitt 133 Misc. 156, 231 N.Y.S. 42 

Ross v. Aaront 147 Misc. 44, 263 N.Y.S. 474.

Radlog Realty Co. v. Geiger 254 A.D. 352, 5 N.Y.S. (2nd) 82.

A landlord need not give his lessee possession. The lessee must get that for himself. And the lessee cannot bring dispossess proceedings. Only the landlord can do that. All the lessee can do is to bring ejectment. If a landlord commencès summary proceedings by service of a precept and petition, the lease is at an end not upon the making of the final order but from the time the warrant for the removal of the tenant is issued, or upon the voluntary removal of the tenant and the resumption of possession by the landlord. When the original lease is ended by the dispossess proceedings, all underleases fall with it. N. Y. Ry Co. v. Savoy Associates 239 A.D. 504, 268 N.Y.S. 181

The landlord cannot claim any more rent. All he can claim are damages for breach of lease. Even though the lease contains a clause that the landlord may relet as the agent of the tenant, it means that the reletting shall be evidence of the damages sustained by the breach of the lease resulting in the eviction by summary proceedings. 

There is no right belonging to the landlord to sue every month for loss of rental. The claim, as a subject of suit, exists at the termination of the time mentioned in the lease.

Disposition of Security Furnished by Tenant 

Whenever money shall be deposited on a contract for the use or rental of realty as security for performance of the contract or to be applied to payments upon such lease when due, such money with interest accruing if any, until repaid or so applied, shall continue to be the money of the person making the deposit and shall be treated as a trust fund in the possession of the person with whom such deposit shall be made and shall not be mingled with other funds or become an asset of such trustee. Any provision of such contract, for a term not exceeding two years, whereby a person who so deposits money waives any provision of this section, is void. If this trust fund is commingled with other funds of the landlord, a conversion is committted and suit may be brought to recover the deposit, immediately upon such conversion. 

2710-8th Ave. Inc. v. Forman 180 Misc. 376. 

Real Property Law § 233.

After a landlord evicts a tenant by summary proceedings, he cannot retain a deposit, though the terms of the lease state that he has a right to retain the deposit in case of a breach of the covenants. 

The damages for the breach are the amount unpaid at the time the summary proceedings were had. These damages are absolutely fixed by the lease, and no other damagés accrue after the summary proceedings, for these proceedings terminate the lease. 

Bloomberg v. F.G.W. Const. Co. 144 Misc. 17, 257 N.Y.S. 657

An assignment of a lease does not include the security deposited by the tenant thereunder, unless it is specifically included in the assignment.

Nature of a Mortgage

A 

MORTGAGES 

MORTGAGE is personal property. It is a mere security for a personal indebtedness created by the bond and is an incumbrance upon land. Regardless of who has possession, title is in the mortgagor. But if the mortgagor has surrendered possession to the mortgagee, the former cannot maintain ejectment to oust the latter, but he must resort to an action in equity to redeem.*

Real Property Law § 249 

Becker v. McCrea 193 N.Y. 423

An agreement to resell the same property for the same price, made at the same time as the contract of sale and between the same parties, operates in law to create a mortgage. 

Lipe v. Beech-Nut Packing Co. 243 A.D. 433, 277 N.Y.S. 832.

A mortgage has its inception when first it is delivered to somebody with the intention of having it become a binding lien, upon which the one to whom it is delivered could sue in case the conditions of the mortgage were not performed. Where A gives to B a mortgage for 3 years, in the amount of $800, the intention of the parties being that B is to assign that mortgage to X for $600, which sum B is to return to A, the mortgage has its inception, not when A delivered it to B, but when B delivered it to X. Therefore the mortgage is usurious and is void. 

The failure on the part of the owner of the mortgage to record it does not affect its validity. It is good against all but subsequent lienors who act in good faith without knowledge of the unrecorded mortgage.

Real Property Law § 291 Ochenowsky v. Dunaj 137 Misc. 674, affd. 232 A.D. 441 

An instrument purporting to be a mortgage, which is left blank as to the name of the mortgagee, is absolutely void. However, if authority is expressly granted to fill in blank spaces left in a mortgage, or if the granting of such authority is by a legitimate factual inference, the mortgagor in respect to innocent third parties may be bound by the words inserted. 

Hulbert v. Walker 258 N.Y. 8

A contract to give a mortgage, or to cause another to give it, is a contract for a transfer of an interest in realty, which must be in writing. 

When the owner of a senior (prior) mortgage is seeking to enforce collection by a foreclosure, the holder of a junior mortgage may compel an assignment of the senior mortgage to him, provided he first tenders the amount due, with interest and costs. 

In re Ryan 216 A.D. 619, 215 N.Y.S. 571. *In so far as a real estate mortgage covers personal property, it is a chattel mortgage. Prudential Ins. Co. v. McGoldrick 256 A.D. 205, affd. 281 N.Y. 595. 255

Where a second mortgagee pays city taxes for the owner of the property, he is not the owner of the rights of the city so as to have a lien prior to the first mortgagee in the amount so paid. The taxes were not the first mortgagee's debt and he is not affected by the payment. 

Lawyers T & G. Co. v. Claren 237 A.D. 188, 260 N.Y.S. 847.

The lien of a mortgage is upon the entire property, and when a portion is taken in condemnation proceedings and an award made, the lien attaches to the award. The mortgagee may satisfy the entire amount of his lien from the award. 

In re Houghton & Olmstead Avenues 266 N.Y. 26. 

Mortgage to Secure Future Advances 

Mortgages given to secure future advances are a recognized form of security. The question arises whether the security of the mortgage is effective from the date of each particular advance or whether there is a lien when the agreement for further advances is made. 

This is the rule: Where the mortgagee has bound himself to make advances, such advances when made relate back, and the mortgage is a valid lien for advances made against subsequent incumbrancers having notice of the mortgage. Where there is no obligation on the mortgagee, but such advances are optional with him, and he has actual notice of a subsequent incumbrance or conveyance of the mortgaged premises before any advances are made, the lien is not good as against a subsequent incumbrancer.

Rights of Mortgage Holder 

The holder of a bond and mortgage has two remedies: one at law to recover a judgment on the bond and the other in equity to foreclose. Upon conveyance "subject" to the mortgage, the premises become the primary fund for the payment of the debt as between the grantor and grantee, but the right of the creditor (mortgagee) to resort to the bond for collection of the debt is not affected by the conveyance. Of course, if the obligor on the bond pays the debt, he may proceed against the land for his indemnity. The original obligor, not the vendee, remains personally liable on the bond. An extension of the time of payment operates to discharge the mortgagor to the extent of the value of the land. 

Seaman's Bank v. Smadbeck 293 N.Y. 91.

If, however, the vendee assumes the payment of the mortgage, the vendee becomes, as between the parties, the principal debtor, and the grantor or vendor becomes a surety for payment of the mortgage indebtedness. It therefore follows, in accordance with the rule of suretyship, that if a holder of a bond and mortgage, which contains a clause that the "whole of the principal sum shall become due after default in payment of interest," extends the time of payment to a grantee who has assumed that mortgage, the grantor is discharged. 

The same result follows if the holder releases the grantee. 

Carpenter v. Hogan 182 Misc. 103

Payment of a Mortgage

Not always does the payment of a mortgage destroy this lien for equity preserves the lien for the security of the payor. An equitable assignment arises by subrogation. Of course one who has no interest in paying it is merely a meddler and in the absence of an assignment will not be protected by equity. Fixtures A mortgage containing provisions that it covers fixtures attached or to be attached to the building does not include fixtures that did not exist at the time of the execution of the mortgage and which were attached thereto later under a conditional sales contract.* 

Perfect Lighting v. Grubar Realty 228 A.D. 141 239 N.Y.S. 286.

Merger of the Fee and the Equity It is the general rule at law that if the ownership of the equity of redemption and of the mortgaged premises coincide in the same person, without the consent of the mortgagor, the mortgage debt is extinguished. The merger will operate even though one of the estates be held in trust and the other benficially, by the same person; or if both the estates were held by the same person in different trusts. 

The doctrine of merger has never been favored in equity and the estates will be held separate when justice requires it and when such was the intention of the parties. The intent of the holder of the two estates will be gathered from the situation and will govern the effect which a merger of the title would have upon his interest. 

Equity will prevent a merger whenever it will result in injury or an injustice to the owner and in the absence of some intervening right or equity in a third person, estates may be treated as merged or not, as is deemed fit.

Dunkum v. Maceck Building Co. 256 N.Y. 275. 

Where a mortgagee acquires the equity of redemption or fee from the mortgagor or a subsequent owner with the consent of the mortgagor, the mortgage and bond are paid to the extent of the then value of the property conveyed.** If there is a definite intent that the lien should not merge with the fee, and the value of the land at the time of conveyance does not equal the lien, the balance of the debt can be collected, first by foreclosure of the surviving mortgage lien. When that remedy is exhausted, by suit on the bond. 

Central Hanover Bk. v. Roslyn Estates 266 A. D. 244, affd. 293 N.Y. 680.

An equitable estate would merge in the legal title subsequently acquired by cestui que trust. In equity, the rule would be modified by the intent of the parties and the requirements of justice so that *See infra, page 294 for detailed discussion of fixtures attached to realty. **The same principle applies to personal property.

the equitable estate if necessary might be kept in existence. 

Burton v. Klein 135 Misc. 571, 239 N.Y.S. 103.

Where an owner of mortgaged land inherits the mortgage he has a reasonable time to decide whether the merger shall occur. He is not required to act before he knows what the situation is. Less than 60 days' delay in manifesting intention whether or not the merger should result is not unreasonable. 

Tharburn v. Wende 235 A.D. 424, affd. 260 N.Y. 554

Foreclosure of Mortgages 

The foreclosure of the mortgage is the legal process for realizing upon the lien. In early common-law days title to land mortgaged vested in the mortgagee. Chancery courts developed the doctrine that the mortgagor has an equity of redemption which would not be destroyed except by foreclosure in an equity proceeding in rem. In such proceeding, no judgment in personam for any part of the mortgage debt could be entered. Such relief could be obtained in a common law action on the mortgagor's bond. In this state title continues in the mortgagor and the alternative remedies persist unless restrained by statute. Resort to both at the same time is restrained by the statute unless leave of the court is obtained. But in an action to foreclose a mortgage upon realty or any interest therein, a deficiency judgment may be obtained, subject to statutory regulations. The present statute limits the deficiency to the extent of the difference in value between the debt plus interest and costs, and the market value of the property, or sale price, whichever is higher. Statutory enactments effective during this present "emergency" have definitely restricted foreclosure activities* on realty *See sections 1077 et seq. of the Civil Practice Act for the restrictions allowable in foreclosure proceedings with respect to mortgages executed before July 1st, 1932. A moratorium for owners for the emergency period has been provided for, conditioned upon the payment of taxes, interest, and carrying charges and an annual payment of 1% of the principal due from July 1, 1942 through June 30, 1944 and 2% thereafter. Although a default in the terms of the mortgage does not allow for a foreclosure if these mentioned charges are met, yet if upon application to the court it is determined that the property has produced a surplus for twelve months prior to the application, the court must order all the surplus paid to the mortgage. If the order is not obeyed, the applicant may foreclose. The court is permitted, however, to allow part of the surplus to be retained if it is needed to meet prospective expenses or carrying charges. If the owner fails to keep or refuses to make available for inspection the data as to income and expense the court may allow a foreclosure action. 

Though ordinarily the application is to be made on the basis of the preceding calendar year and notice thereof served before March 15 next, the court for cause may entertain an application on any other consecutive twelve month basis, in which case notice must be served on or before the 15th of the third month following the end of the period. T.G. & Tr. Co. v. Foxvale Realty Co. 

287 N.Y. 147; East River Savings Bank v. Lash Realty Co. 178 Misc. 103; 

Matter of Mtge Co. (Ohlbaum) 263 A.D. 627, affd. 289 Ň.Y. 686.

The interest rate upon a loan originally contracted for simultaneously with a mortgage upon realty, dated prior to July 1, 1932 and secured solely by such mortgage, can not be increased during the emergency period, just because the loan may have matured. Met. Savings Bank v. Tuttle 290 N.Y. 497. 

The 1945 Legislature may increase the allowed 2% amortization.

Civil Practice Act § 1077h Receivers in Foreclosures 

Ordinarily, prior to judgment in the foreclosure action, the only remedy of the mortgagee for possession, and through it for the rents, is by the appointment of a receiver, unless consent to take possession has been given by the mortgagor. Even though the terms of a mortgage permit the holder in an action to foreclose, to have a receiver appointed for the premises if the owner fails to maintain the premises in reasonably good repair, the court will not appoint a receiver unless it can be shown that the failure to repair impaired the security. Where there is no such clause in the mortgage, the court under its equity powers, in a proper case, may appoint a receiver to maintain and preserve the property. 

L. I. Bond and M. Co. v. Brown 171 Misc. 15, 11 N.Y.S. (2nd) 793

N.Y. Title & Mortgage Co. v. Polk Arms 262 N.Y. 21 

Where the mortgagor is not in posession during the foreclosure of all or part of the premises and they are occupied by others not having title, a receiver may be appointed in a proper case to take possession, collect the rents, and apply them to the payment of the carrying charges. If only the mortgagor is in possession, no receiver may be appointed since the mortgagee, merely by virtue of a mortgage pending its foreclosure, has no right of possession and he does not acquire such rights except in a proper .case where the right grows out of facts extrinsic to the mortgage contract or where there is a clause in the mortgage expressly giving him that right. If the mortgage gives only the right to appoint a receiver of the "rents and profits," a receiver cannot be appointed of premises occupied by the mortgagor alone, for there are no such rents and profits when the mortgagor rightfully occupies the premises as his residence. 

Holmes v. Gravenhorst 263 N.Y. 148 

City of Long Beach v. Gold 171 Misc. 658, 14 N.Y.S. (2nd) 269 *But cf. Domus Realty Co. v. 3440 Realty Co. 179 Misc. 749, affd. 266 A.D. 

725 where the ignorance as to the period of grace resulted in late sending of the required instalment. The court held a swift foreclosure unconscionable and denied plaintiff's motion for summary judgment.

When a receiver of the rents is appointed in a foreclosure action under the mortgage, he does not stand in the shoes of the owner; he has the rights of the mortgagee under the mortgage. He cannot sue a tenant for rent unless the tenant attorns to him. Upon failure to attorn, the receiver may apply to the court which appointed him, to fix the reasonable value of the use and occupation of the premises. 

Then suit may be brought for the fair and reasonable value of the use and occupation. 

An assignee of future rents has no precedence over a receiver's right thereto. "Assignment of rents clause" in a mortgage is not an absolute assignment, but only further security. Under such clause a mortgagee may have the rents by possessing himself of them with the consent of the owner or by application to the court in legal proceedings through the appointment of a receiver. Where the assignment of rents clause gives the mortgagee a right of entry upon default, then upon demand and refusal, the assignment of rents may become absolute. An entry by the mortgagee is a trespass, if without the owner's consent or without court authorization. 

Dime Savings Bank v. Altman 275 N.Y. 62

The receiver has a right both to the rents that become due after his appointment and to those that have accrued prior thereto, but which have not been paid. A receiver appointed in an action to foreclose a junior mortgage may keep and apply to that mortgage the rents actually collected as against a receiver subsequently appointed in an action to foreclose a senior mortgage.

Monica Realty Co. v. 122 Fifth Ave. Co. 264 N.Y. 52

The expenses of a receiver appointed at the instance of the plaintiff mortgagee in a foreclosure action, are chargeable only to the fund collected. If the receiver spends any more than he has collected, he cannot charge the expenses to the plaintiff. 

Handman v. Madonick 235 A. D. 47, 256 N.Y.S. 188

A receiver may not incur any indebtedness which exceeds the sum he collects, nor may he spend money for any purpose other than the physical preservation of the property, unless authorized.

If no motion for a deficiency judgment is made as herein prescribed, the proceeds of the sale are deemed to be in full satisfaction of the mortgage debt, and no right to recover any deficiency exists. MUNICIPAL CORPORATIONS* The Legislature and the Municipality THE 

HE AUTHORITY of the Legislature over the boundaries of subdivisions of the state is absolute. It may consolidate, add to, or take from the territory of a municipality or district, without the consent of the municipality or district affected. The fact that persons and property in the territory annexed may be subject to taxation to pay bonds and obligations theretofore voted, without having had any voice in creating the liability, does not render the act or annexation void. 

Adriaansen v Bd. of Education, 222 A. D. 320, affd. 248 N. Y. 542

The right to levy and collect taxes is a power delegated to the municipality by the Legislature. The municipality has no power to grant exemptions from taxation, nor to make any contract looking to that result.

Torts 

Troy Union R. Co. v. Troy, 227 A. D. 351, affd. 253 N. Y. 597

A municipal corporation possesses two kinds of powers, one "governmental and public" and the other "private." In the exercise of the latter power a municipality is liable for its torts. When acting as a political division of the state, it is not liable for its torts. It is difficult to determine when a city is acting in one capacity, and when in the other. The distinctions are not clear. 

The following activities have been held to be governmental, and no liability exists in the performance of those activities: the exercise of the duties of policemen and firemen; regulation of traffic lights;** of inspectors of election; the care and erection of buildings and apparatus used solely for governmental purposes, e.g., a court house, city hall, prisons, workhouse, and their appurtenances; furnishing water for fire purposes; the approval or disapproval of plans for the construction of buildings; lighting of streets. 

Oeters v. City of New York, 270 N. Y. 364 

Parsons v. City of New York, 248 A. D. 825, affd. 273 N. Y. 547 

Schlicher v. Schlicher, 175 Misc. 696, affd. 264 A. D. 763 

Finkelstein v. City of New York, 183 A. D. 539, 169 N. Y. S. 718 

Wilcox v. City of Rochester, 190 N. Y. 137 

Boutet v. City of New York, 199 A. D. 835, 192 N. Y. S. 608 

O'Brien v. Saratoga Springs, 131 Misc. 728, affd. 224 A. By statute, every municipality is liable for the negligence of an appointee of the municipality who operates a municipally owned vehicle or facility of transportation* upon the public highway anywhere in the state, in the discharge of a statutory duty imposed on the municipality, provided the appointee was within the scope of his employment at the time. Under the same circumstances it is obligated to save harmless the employee in such operations. A similar dual liability is placed upon a municipality for the negligence of its policemen and firemen in the operation of a vehicle upon a public highway anywhere in the city during the performance of their duties. This liability exists even though the operator was performing a government duty. Thus, although the extinguishment of fires is a governmental function in connection with which a municipality incurs no liability for inadequacy in equipment or for negligence of its employees, a plaintiff injured by the negligent operation of an engine responding to a fire alarm may recover against the city.

The municipality must save such physician or dentist harmless for damages for per- *A horse has been held to be a "facility of transportation" under the statute so that a city was held liable for damages caused by a carelessly watched runaway police-horse. General Municipal Law, § 50d. 

Attempts have been made to distinguish between public and private powers. When the power exercised has relation to public purposes and is for the public good, it is to be classified as governmental in its nature. When it relates to the accomplishment of private corporate purposes, in which the public is only indirectly concerned, it is private in its nature. 

If a municipality delegates a governmental function to a private corporation, this latter corporation is not immune from liability for wrongs committed during the performance of these acts. 

Condition Precedent to Suit

Before one can maintain his action against a muncipality for personal injuries, he must comply with certain statutory requirements which include usually, service upon a designated official of intent to sue to be given with a period stated in the City Charter. Physical or mental inability to prepare this notice may be ground for the allowance of additional time. Whether the ability is present in the plaintiff, is a question of fact for the jury. 

Clawson v. City of Ithaca, 214 A. D. 333, 212 N. Y. 433.

The strict requirements of the statute are not enforced against an immature infant of approximately ten years or less. They are enforced against an infant of riper years, of ordinary physical and mental capacity. Between these two periods lies a middle period where the infant may or may not be held to the provisions of the statute, as the jury may determine. But it is the age and capacity of the infant, rather than the conduct of its parents or guardians which control. 

Russo v. City of New York, 258 N. Y. 344.

A plaintiff cannot escape the consequences of a failure to file the notice of claim upon the theory that the injuries were the result of nuisance and not of negligence.

Bowers v. S. Glens Falls 286 N. Y. 616. 

Liability of Boards of Education for Torts 

Boards of Education in cities having at least 1,000,000 inhabitants are in the first instance liable for injuries caused by the negligence of its teaching staff and must also save harmless such employees in the event one of them is made to pay for his negligence while acting within the scope of his employment. In cities having a population under 1,000,000, there is no direct liability against the Board, but its liability is only that of indemnification. 

Education Law §§ 569a, 881a 

Reeder v. Board of Education, 290 N. Y. 829.

A Board of Education is always liable for its own negligence and for acts of negligence committed by its agents or employees in the management of its property to the extent of funds vested in it by statute or which it is empowered to raise by local taxation. Accord-

ingly, recovery was allowed where a child ran into an open elevator shaft of the school, while at play; where no ordinary protection was put on a brick side wall in a school gymnasium during a violent game; where a buzz-saw was not protected by a guard; where the driver of a school bus was negligent. 

Garber v. Central School District, 251 4. D. 44, 295 N. Y. S. 850 

Bradley v. Board of Education, 274 N. Y. 473 

Herman v. Board of Education 234 N. Y. 196. 

Care of Streets

It is the primary duty of the municipality to maintain its streets in reasonably safe condition and this is so, even though there be an ordinance requiring the owner of an abutting building to keep the sidewalk in repair. It is only when the condition which caused the accident has been created by the owner; or where the manner in which the sidewalk is used produces the defective condition; or where the owner fails to maintain in a reasonably safe condition a sidewalk which is constructed in a special manner so as to give him a special benefit, that he may be held responsible.
