Thus an owner of premises adjoining a street would be liable to a pedestrian who was injured by the opening of a cellar door in the street without warning, where the owner had control of the cellar. And where a sidewalk is used as a driveway for vehicles, the special use carries with it the duty not to permit the use to create conditions in the driveway unsafe for the passing of pedestrians. 

McEvoy v. City of New York 266 A. D. 445, affd. 292 N. Y. 654

Nicklesburg v. City of New York 263 A. D. 625 Pensa v. Raleight Hall 243 A. D. 816. 

A municipality is not liable for any defects in the highway of a trivial nature such as slight depressions made by constant use. 

Moore v. City of Lockport 228 A. D. 162 

Boyne v. City of Buffalo 269 N. Y. 657.

Where a municipality maintains a sufficiently wide highway in good condition, it is not responsible for accidents caused to or by people who leave the traveled portion of the highway. 

Horton v. City of N. Y., 213 A. D. 172, 210 N. Y. S. 433 

Pensa v. Raleigh Hall, 243 A. D. 816, 278 N. Y. S. 380 

Moore v. City of Lockport, 228 A. D. 162, 239 N. Y. S. 190 

Boyne v. City of Buffalo, 269 N. Y. 657.

The cases in which liability of a municipal corporation has been sustained, for damages caused by the acts of a third party in a public street, performed with the permission of the municipal corporation, may be divided into two groups. In the first group fall those cases in which the municipal corporation has joined in the creation of a nuisance by its attempted authorization of an act which is unlawful, regardless of the manner of its performance, or an act, which though otherwise lawful, has a natural tendency to create such danger of injury to person or property that it might properly be found a nuisance either as matter of fact or matter of law. In such cases, liability may be sustained even though the damages were in fact caused by the negligence of the person who received the permit, and the municipal corporation had not notice or knowledge of 1

MUNICIPAL CORPORATIONS 

269 such negligence. There the primary wrong was permission to create a nuisance, which the municipal corporation had no power to authorize, and all the damages may be regarded as the consequences of that primary wrong.

In the second group fall those cases in which the municipal corporation granted a permit for work in its streets which was lawful, when authorized by the municipal corporation, and by its nature created no unreasonable danger of injury to person or property; but which became a nuisance thereafter or otherwise caused injury to person or property through the negligent manner in which the work was performed, and the city had knowledge or was charged with notice of the existence of the dangerous condition or of the negligent manner in which the work was performed. There the municipal corporation commits no wrong in granting the permit, and it is not responsible for the negligent acts of the person who has received the permit. It is responsible for its own negligence in the maintenance of the street after it has notice of the existence of a danger therein. 

Whittaker v. Franklinville, 265 N. Y. 11 

Ehret v. Village of Scarsdale, 269 N. Y. 198.

This duty of the municipality cannot be shifted except by the legislature. Thus, a city may be liable for damages caused by a defective bridge substituted for a sidewalk over which people walk, or for damages caused by a defective shed under which they walk, which shed was put up during the erection of a building, provided, of course, the city had actual or constructive notice of the defects. 

If a shed, inappropriate for carrying material, had stored upon it tons of bricks, making it unsafe for pedestrians, and this condition had existed for months, during which time inspectors were at the permission, they become responsible for its condition.* 

Metzroth v. City of New York, 241 N. Y. 470.

A town is not liable for damages sustained by reason of a defective sidewalk, unless it was constructed or maintained by the town or its superintendent of highways. The rule is different insofar as cities and villages are concerned. When a sidewalk is built without permission, they become responsible for its condition". 

Rupert v. Town of West Seneca 293 N. Y. 421. 

Contracts 

A municipality can make contracts subject to its charter provisions, and it can be held liable for any breach. The purpose of these contracts made by the city must be municipal. Municipal purposes are such purposes as are public in character, for the common good and welfare of the municipality, e.g., to furnish free band concerts, free recreation piers, free colleges; celebrations of the city's anniversary; aid of the poor as a class; auditing city's books; care of highways, docks and bridges; construction of sewers, airports; care of 

There is no rule that a hole in a public thoroughfare must be of any particular depth before its existence can fix liability against anyone. The question is one for the jury. Wilson v. Jaybro Realty Co. 289 N. Y. 410.

parks,etc. The Legislature can determine what is and what is not a municipal purpose, but its determination is subject to review by the courts. It follows from the above that the plea of ultra vires is available to a municipality. 

Schieffelin v. Hylan 236 N.Y. 254 

Hesse v. Roth, 224 A. D. 344, affd. 249 N. Y. 436 

Troy Union R. Co. v. Troy, 227 A. D. 351, affd. 253 N. Y. 597

It is illegal for a municipal corporation to sell water to persons for consumption outside of its city limits except by authority of the Legislature. The mere illegality of the act, however, does not give a taxpayer the right to enjoin the city, unless the taxpayer can show that the illegal acts are injurious or dangerous to the public interest. 

Western N. Y. Water Co. v. City of Buffalo, 242 N. Y. 202.

Once the city makes a contract for a stipulated sum it cannot pay the other party a greater sum, even if such sum was promised during the performance of the work. 

Suppose several municipalities are co-operating for a number of years in a public project (as building a highway) on which a large amount of money has already been spent. One of the municipalities cannot withdraw on the ground that its representatives made a mistake of judgment when they started the project. 

An employee of a city cannot contract with the city, even though the employee gains no benefit therefrom. 

There is no right to assume that the agent of a municipality is acting within the scope of his authority. Those dealing with him are to ascertain the nature and extent of this authority to contract. 

The mere acceptance of benefits by the city under the contract made without authority does not estop a municipal corporation from challenging the validity of the contract. 

Seif v. City of Long Beach 286 N.Y. 382 

Pierce v. Board of Education, 125 Misc. 589, affd. 216 A. D. 787.

A municipality cannot be authorized by the Legislature to pay the expenses of a police officer in successfully defending himself in a criminal action based on acts committed by him as police officer. 

It is not for a city purpose but would be a gift. 

Schieffelin v. Henry, 123 Misc. 792, affd. 211 A. D. 850. 

A city has the right to pay or compromise claims in contract or tort, equitably or morally payable by the city though the same be not legally binding on it. 

Blazejewski v. Ecket 166 Misc. 716, 3 N.Y.S. (2nd) 87

PARTNERSHIP When a Partnership Exists 

IF

A RECEIVES a share of the profits of a business, he is prima facie a partner. But this is rebutted if it was (1) in payment of a debt owed to A; or (2) A's wages; or (3) rent to A, who was a landlord.

Partnership Law, § 11 

In re Rosenberg's Will, 213 A. D. 167, 209 N. Y. S. 315 

Soane v. U. S. Syndicate, 135 Misc. 365, 238 N. Y. S. 91.

If A had invested money in the firm and had risked losing it in whole or in part, and was to share in any profits, and in addition had a right to participate in the management of the firm, there would be present the elements of the existence of a partnership. 

They would not be conclusive, however. The surrounding circumstances and the intention would have much to do with the determination.

If A lends B certain machines to use in B's factory, for which A is to get one-fifth of the profits, A is not therefore a partner. But if he had loaned money to B, for which he was to receive one-fifth of the profits, and had the option of allowing his money to stay in the business or drawing it out, he would be a partner. There was a community of profits and a specific interest therein. 

A may be partner for all legal purposes, even though he may not have invested any money. He may be a partner by estoppel. Instances of a partner by estoppel would be: (1) A falsely states that he is Z's partner. L hearing A, extends credit to Z. L can hold A as Z's partner for the purpose of this debt, and A would be estopped from denying the partnership. (2) The same result would follow if Z told people that A was his partner, and A, knowing of those statements, deliberately failed to deny them. L, lending money to Z on the supposition that he was 

A's partner, could hold A as a partner. 

A partnership is not like a corporation, which is a legal entity having certain rights and subject to definite liabilities. It has no independent existence. It has a name by which individuals conduct a joint business, and in which their accounts as such are kept, and through which certain established equitable rights in marshaling assets are acquired. However, the persons contracting with a partnership, deal with the partners collectively. For example, A and B as partners were insured under a contract with the X Insurance Company. B sold his interest to C and the insurer was not notified. 

A claim under the policy then arose. The partnership of A and C was not permitted to recover since the original partnership of A and B no longer existed despite A's presence in both. The contract 271

of insurance was between the insurer and the now terminated partnership. 

Ardolino v. Ierna, 225 A. D. 439, 233 N. Y. S. 477 

Matter of Peck, 206 N. Y. 55. 

Partners as Agents of Each Other

A partner is the agent of every other partner carrying on the business. If a partnership does an act which is apparently partnership business, the partnership is bound, even though the partner had no authority thus to act for the partnership, unless the person with whom the partner dealt knew that there was no authority. So a partner can borrow money in the partnership name. Also, an admission made by a partner concerning partnership affairs, within the apparent scope of authority, is evidence against the partnership. 

If the act done by the partner was not apparently partnership business and unauthorized, the partnership is not bound. Acts which are not apparently part of the partnership business, are (a) an unauthorized assignment of the partnership property in trust for creditors; (b) confession of a judgment against the partnership; (c) submission of a partnership claim to a referee or arbitrators; (d) binding the firm by a contract of suretyship for the accommodation of a stranger; (e) any act which would make it impossible to further carry on the partnership business.

Parnership Law § 20 

If the title to realty is in the partnership's name, any partner may convey the property if the partner so conveying could be reckoned as acting as the partnership's agent. If the buyer is not a bona fide purchaser and the partner who sells it is trying to defraud the partnership, the partnership can recover the property. 

Partnership Law, § 21. 

The partnership can acquire any estate in realty and it can as well convey in the partnership name. 

Partnership Law, §§ 12, 51. 

The Partnership and its Creditors

Parties are liable jointly with respect to partnership contract obligations. The liability in tort or for breach of trust by a partner, is joint and several. The liability of the partnership is as extensive as that of the partner committing the tort. 

Partnership Law, §§ 24, 25, 26. 

A partner has an equal right with his partner to use for partnership purposes all partnership property. This right to specific partnership property is not subject to attachments or execution, if one partner should happen to be liable for his individual debt. But the partner-debtor's intangible interest in the property can be levied on in such a case. The intangible interest consists of his share in the profits and surplus.

Partnership Law, § 51. 

Since partners are jointly liable in contracts, all are necessary par-

PARTNERSHIP 

273 ties in an action. But should a non-joinder not be objected to and the plaintiff proceed to judgment against those partners named, the plaintiff may still sue the omitted partner since the debt is not merged in the judgment. But while the plaintiff is required to name every partner as a defendant, he is not required to serve more than one. If one or more, but not all, are served, any judgment obtained would be enforceable against the individual property, real and personal, of those served and the partnership real and personal property of those named as defendants. If execution should be returned unsatisfied, the plaintiff may still proceed against the other partners who were not yet served and the judgment would charge their separate property with the sum remaining unpaid upon the original judgment. Since partners are jointly and severally liable for a partnership tort, all are proper but not necessary parties. Service on less than all the partners would permit execution against the jointly owned property and against all the property of those served.

Civil Practice Act §§ 1197, 1199, 229a 

If the partnership itself is the debtor, then the specific property can be levied upon.

Where the obligation is joint and not joint and several and a partner dies, it is necessary to allege and prove inability to collect from the surviving joint debtors before liability can be enforced against the estate of the deceased. 

Georgian Press v. Hill 180 Misc. 548, affd. 181 Misc. 464. 

Suppose there are creditors of both the partnership and the individual members. Can the creditors of the partnership issue execution against the property of individual members? First, partnership creditors must issue execution against partnership property and individual claimants against individual property. If one group, for instance, the creditors of the partnership, is not satisfied, it can issue execution against the property of the individual members if there be any individual property left over. But an attachment was allowed to stand in an action on a partnership debt against the separate property of an absconding partner. 

Patrikes v. J. C. H. Service Stations 180 Misc. 917, affd. 180 Misc 927. 

Gomez v. Vasquez 177 Misc. 874.

Individual contract claims against a deceased partner's estate cannot be preferred over tort claims against the estate or against the partnership. All share pro rata. 

In re Seybel's Will, 124 Misc. 297, 207 N. Y. S. 765.

A conveyance of partnership property or the incurring of a partnership obligation where the partnership will be thereby rendered insolvent, is fraudulent as to partnership creditors, if (a) made to a partner or (b) to one not a partner, without fair consideration to the partnership.

Debtor & Creditor Law, § 277. 

Rights of Partners as Among Themselves Where several persons agree on terms of a partnership to begin at a future date, and in order to be ready to transact business on the

day in question they proceed with the plans necessary for that purpose, the partners who have been authorized to incur liabilities or expend money in making such preparations may bring an action for an accounting against the other members of the partnership and obtain judgment for the proportionate share the other members of the partnership must pay. 

Sivin v. Jones, 236 A. D. 483, 260 N. Y. S. 91. (1) Suppose a partner lends money to the partnership over and above the amount he is required to contribute. Even if no mention is made of payment of interest, it is implied that the partner is to get interest from the date of the advance. 

Partnership Law, § 40. 

(2) A partner is not entitled to special compensation for services though they may be extraordinary unless there was an agreement to pay for these services at the time they were rendered, or unless the services were performed under an employment or special agency altogether distinct from the powers and duties as a partner. 

Levy v. Leavitt, 257 N. Y. 461. (3) Neither joint participants nor partners can sue each other at law for anything relating to the concerns of the joint enterprise, until after a settlement and balance struck and an express promise to pay, i.e., only after there has been an account stated between them. Before such account stated, the partners should seek their remedy in an accounting in equity. 

Perlman v. Perlman 139 Misc. 396, 247 N. Y. S. 453.

Where one partner fraudulently misrepresents the value of certain stock to the other and induces him to purchase the stock from him at a high price, an action for damages in deceit should be brought in a law court. It is not an equity action but rather one for fraud, for it had nothing to do with the partnership. 

Langford v. Lalalle, 136 Misc. 62, 239 N. Y. S. 107 

Ludlum v. Wagner, 212 A. D. 779, 209 N. Y. S. 540 

Arona v. Fraser, 125 Misc. 333, 209 N. Y. S. 756. (4) If one partner sells any partnership property, he hold the amount received for the partnership. Every partner is a strict fiduciary toward the other. 

Greenslete v. Ferguson, 191 A. D. 745, 182 N. Y. S. 198.

When A, who held a lease in his own name for himself and B as a joint adventurer, obtained a renewal of that lease before its expiration without B's knowledge, it was held that B was entitled to an interest in the new lease, as A was a trustee for B. The fact that the new lease covered the adjoining premises together with the original premises, was held immaterial. 

Meinhard v. Salmon, 249 N. Y. 458.

A partner who is expelled has a pecuniary interest in every existing incomplete contract, in the trade-name and in the then existing assets. Such contracts as are taken in that trade-name after the expulsion, become a subject-matter of accounting. 

Helfenbaum v. Mish, 248 A. D. 900, 290 N. Y. S. 708.

When a partnership for a fixed term is continued after that term without any express agreement, the rights and duties of the part-

PARTNERSHIP 

275 ners remain the same as they were at the termination, so far as is consistent with the new partnership at will. 

Partnership Law, § 45. 

Dissolution of the Partnership

A partnership is dissolved by the death, determination and act, or bankruptcy of one of the partners, or by agreement of the partners, or by termination of the definite term or particular undertaking specified in the agreement. No one can be forced to continue as a partner against his will. He may be liable to the other partner for breach of contract and an accounting. Separate actions may be brought for each form of relief. 

Partnership Law, § 62; Burnstine v. Geist 257 A. D. 792. 

Upon the death of a partner, title to firm assets passes to the surviving members. The representative of the deceased has only an equitable interest in the distribution of any surplus remaining after the payment of the firm debts. They obtain no right to interfere with the administration of the partnership. The surviving partners are considered as trustees for the estate of the deceased, but they may complete a pending transaction to prevent a large loss, or make a profit which otherwise would not be made. Money may be borrowed to prevent a ruinous liquidation. 

Losch v. Marcin, 251 N. Y. 402

In re Kalik 178 Misc 607. 

If the surviving partner fails to account and continues the business, he must account to the representatives of the decedent, not only for the value of his share at the date of his death, but also for profits earned which may be attributed to that value. All losses are to be borne by the surviving partner. 

Cahill v. Haff, 248 N. Y. 377; Partnership Law, § 73.

Although ordinarily no partner is entitled to any compensation for acting in the partnership business, a surviving partner is entitled to reasonable compensation for his services in winding up the partnership affairs.

Partnership Law, § 40. 

Suppose a partner transfers his interest in the partnership, consisting of his share of the profits and surplus, to another person. 

This transfer does not, of itself, dissolve the partnership. Nevertheless, the assignee cannot participate in the partnership's affairs or management or even inspect the partnership's books as a partner. 

All that he is entitled to is the assignor's share of the profits. Of course if the remaining partners decide to dissolve, they can do so. 

The assignee can then require an account of all the accounts since the last accounting.

Partnership Law, § 53. 

All third parties who had extended credit to the partnership after the dissolution, but knew of the fact of its existence but not of its dissolution (and the dissolution had not been advertised in a paper of general circulation), can hold the individual partners liable. 

If a partner is declared a lunatic in a judicial proceeding, or in

any other way is declared insane, so that it is not reasonably practicable to carry on the business with him, any other partner can apply to the court for a decree of dissolution. 

If the dissolution was caused by death, bankruptcy or any act of a partner, a partner who had incurred any liability while acting for the partnership, without knowledge of the dissolution, can get from each partner his share of the liability. 

It is a general rule that books should be kept open for the inspection of any partner at all times, even after dissolution. But this right in the partnership books may be transferred by a retiring partner like his right to any other bit of property, by express or implied agreement. 

Sanderson v. Cooke, 256 N. Y. 73. 

The Retiring Partner

When the fact of retirement is published in the newspapers by a retiring partner, he is not liable to any who may become future creditors of the partnership. Future creditors here include even past customers, but who have heretofore been dealing on a cash basis. 

But such publication is not enough to keep him from being liable to those who have in the past extended credit, who have not read the notice and who continue to give the partnership credit. The retiring partner should have given these creditors actual notice. The notice must be received.

If the retiring partner has been a silent one, he need give no notice to anyone, for since no one was supposed to know that he was a partner, no one gave the partnership credit because of him. 

Is a retiring partner liable for partnership debts contracted before he left? Yes, even as to the customers that get notice, but only as a guarantor of collection. The creditors must exhaust their remedies against the partnership first. The same rule applies to the case where a partner dies. His estate is liable as a surety, and if the creditor fails to collect his debt against the survivor he can resort to an equity action against the representative of the deceased partner. 

If one member of a partnership sells the entire assets of the firm to a corporation of which he is the principal stockholder, and for a non-existing debt, the sale will be set aside at the instance of the other partner, and it is such a fraud as would justify a dissolution. 

Where, upon the dissolution of a firm, one of the copartners purchases and succeeds to the business, the exclusive right to use trademarks belonging to the firm passes to this purchaser, although no express mention is made of them in the deed or assignment. 

Merry v. Hoopes, 111 N. Y. 415. 

The Incoming Partner

An incoming partner is liable for debts contracted by the partnership before he became a partner. But his liability is to be satisfied out of partnership property. He cannot be held responsible for these debts as he can for those that are contracted after he became a partner.

Partnership Law, § 28.

PARTNERSHIP 

277 Limited Partnership Suppose A wants to be a partner in the X Radio Company, but he wants to be liable for not more than the amount of capital invested by him, and not be personally liable beyond that amount, as other general partners are. What must be done to effect such a result? He must invest money or goods (services alone will not do). 

A certificate sworn to by the general partners, as well as by the special partner, must be filed in the office of the County Clerk in the county where the partnership's principal place of business is located. The certificate must state the name and address of the firm, and the names and addresses of each partner, the contribution of the limited partner, the nature and life of the partnership. After being filed, the certificate must be published in two of the county's newspapers once a week for six consecutive weeks. If a false statement is put in the certificate, the special partner becomes liable as a general partner.

Partnership Law, § 90. 

The name of a special partner cannot be used in the firm name. 

If it is used with his permission, the special partner becomes a general one.

The general partners control and manage the business, but the special partner may transact business with the partnership, and in all such transactions he is treated as if he were a general creditor. 

Though claims of creditors have priority over those of special partners, the claims of the latter have priority over claims of general partners. 

Partnership Law, §§ 98, 99, 103, 112.

The special partner cannot withdraw any money he originally put in, unless the filed certificate so provides. If he withdraws any such amount, he is liable as a general partner to the extent of the amount so withdrawn until he returns it. 

If a special partner withdraws his contribution from the partnership at a time when the partnership is insolvent, the special partner can be made to respond to the extent of his withdrawal after the legal remedies against the firm have been exhausted. 

The special partner may also be so charged, even though at the time of his withdrawal there are sufficient assets left with the general partners to discharge the then outstanding liabilities, if before satisfaction of such liabilities the firm becomes insolvent. The contribution withdrawn is treated as a fund to be used for the discharge of liabilities existing when the special partner withdraws. 

Partnership Law, § 105; Kittredge v. Langley, 252 N. Y. 405.

A special partner can assign his interest. The assignee gets the assignor's right in the income and a right to dissolution. If the other partners agree to substitute him for the other, he may become a full-fledged special partner. 

Partnership Law, § 108.

REAL PROPERTY 

Tenure

ITIZENS and aliens are empowered to take, hold, transmit and dispose of New York realty. The heirs and devises of aliens take in the same manner as citizens. Control of property, real and personal of alien enemies is now left solely to the Federal government. 

Real Property Law § 10. 

A sale to a lunatic is void, unless it is for his benefit, made in good faith, and the seller cannot be put in status quo. Deeds of minors and of persons not adjudged insane, e.g., a person confined under summary commitment, are voidable. Once a person has been adjudged insane or a committee appointed to take care of the property of the incompetent, his subsequent deed is void. A deed of an insane person before officially so found is not even voidable as against a bona fide purchaser for value without notice of the incompetency. Should an infant desire to sell realty and give a perfectly valid deed, he can apply to the Supreme Court for permission. 

Real Property Law, § 11; Finch v. Goldstein, 245 N. Y. 300 

Goldberg v. McCord 251 N Y. 28

Before a deed becomes effective as a grant there must be delivery and acceptance, with the mutual intent that title pass. The recording of the deed raises a rebuttable presumption of delivery. 

Buszozak v. Wolo, 125 Misc. 546 affd. 220 Ñ. Y. S. 921. 

Estates 

A "fee" implies a proprietary ownership and is the greatest interest in real estate. A fee is conditional if it is limited upon the happening of some event of such character that it may never happen. 

Fee tails do not exist in New York. Therefore, a conveyance to 

A and the heirs of his body gives A absolute title (fee simple). If land is conveyed to A and the heirs of his body, remainder to B and his heirs (a common-law fee tail, with a fee simple remainder), what does B get if a fee tail is now equal to a fee simple? If A dies without issue, B gets the fee. 

Real Property Law, § 32. 

The rule in Shelley's case is also abolished: So A to B for life, remainder to his heirs, gives B a life estate and his heirs take a vested remainder. B has not a fee simple, for the life estate is not merged. 

A life tenant may so enjoy the estate that the land shall pass to the remaindermen as nearly as practicable unimpaired in its nature. 

He may only do what is required for the general use and enjoyment of the estate as he received it. He may not make structural changes or improvements, or destroy existing buildings even to erect better ones, for this would be a material change and would render it im- 278

REAL 

PROPERTY 

possible for the life tenant to restore the same premises substantially, at the end of the term. 

In re Edgar's Will, 282 N. Y. S. 795.

While the common-law rule that incumbrances on real property at the time of the death of the owner should be paid out of the personal estate of the late owner, has been modified to the extent that mortgages must be satisfied by the heir or devisee out of his own property without resorting to the administrator or executor, the common-rule still remains that taxes due at the time of the owner's death must be paid out of the late owner's personal estate. Taxes assessed upon the productive premises during a life tenancy must be paid by the life tenant. If he fails to pay these taxes, the remainderman may pay and recover a judgment in damages and, if necessary, sell out the estate on execution, or else have a receiver appointed of the rents and profits, sufficient to satisfy the judgment or to discharge the taxes in arrears. The remainderman is also entitled to priority of payment in a life tenant's estate for the payment of taxes which it was the duty of the life tenant to pay. Where the property is unproductive, the burden of taxation should be borne by the remainderman. 

Keeley v. Clark, 125 Misc. 541, 211 N. Y. S. 391 

In re Hone's Estate, 152 Misc. 221, 274 N. Y. S. 101 

In re Harris' Estate, 61 Misc. 793, 293 N. Y. S. 250.

There cannot be created a remainder on any estate per autre vie unless this remainder is in fee. This applies to personalty also. 

Real Property Law, § 44. 

Estates for years are chattels real and are charged with any judgment docketed against the lessee. The interest in the lease is also subject to sale under execution. If the unexpired term is five years or more, it must be sold on execution the same as realty; if the unexpired term is less than five years, it is sold as personalty. 

Henderson v. Tomb 169 Misc. 737

Estates at will or sufferance are chattel interests, but they cannot be subject to sale on execution.

Real Property Law, § 33. 

A lease is personal property and the right to renew a lease is personal property. A mortgage upon it is a personal property mortgage. 

First Trust & Dep. Co. v. Hurwitz, 249 A. D. 285, 292 N. Y. S. 206.

Vested and Contingent Estates 

The statute permits remainders, both vested and contingent. 

They are descendible, devisable and alienable, even though subject to defeat by the remainderman's death before the life tenant. This applies to personalty as well as to realty. The attitude of the law is to favor vesting of estates. 

Moore v, Littel, 41 N. Y. 66.

A remainder is vested if there is a person living who would take at once, if one who then had the estate (less than a fee) died. But if the person or event upon which it is to take effect is not existent or is uncertain, as the case may be, it is contingent. The law recog-

nizes three varieties of remainders: (1) Absolutely vested remainders in which the taking by a specified person is directed without any limitation whatever, e.g., to A for life, with remainder to B; (2) Remainders vested subject to being divested, e.g., to A for life with remainder to B if B survives A, otherwise to C; or to A for life, with remainder to B if C dies without issue, otherwise to the issue of C; (3) Contingent remainders, where the gift is to a person who may answer a certain description at some future time, e.g., to A for life, remainder to the issue of B, who is then childless. 

In re Terwilliger's Will 135 Misc. 170, affd. 230 A.D. 763 

Real Property Law, § 40 

In re De Puy's Will, 194 A. D. 796, 185 N. Y. S. 817.

In one case X was given a life estate and upon the death of X the estate was to go to the children of X, and in case X should die without issue, then to F. F predeceased X, who left no issue. It was held that F's interest went to his heirs. The remainder, though strictly a contingent one, descended by virtue of the statute. The court refused to imply a condition that F should also be living at the death of X. 

Hennessy v. Patterson, 85 N. Y. 91 

Guaranty Trust Co. v. Curry, 134 Misc. 99, 234 N. Y. S. 329.

Upon the death of one seized of real property the title to such real property vests in the devisee by virtue of the will itself. 

Milliner v. Morris, 219 A. D. 425, 219 N. Y. S. 166.

A direction in a will to convert realty into personalty and to divide and pay it over at a future time, imports an intention of the testator to postpone the date of vesting until the time of payment.

Thus, "a devise to A for life, and if he has issue, in fee; in the event of A's death without issue, the realty is to be sold and the proceeds divided among testator's next of kin according to laws of distribution," gives no gift to the next of kin, but the vesting is postponed. 

In re Potter's Estate, 167 Misc. 848 affd. 255 A. D. 823. Easements

An easement is a form of servitude, a right which one parcel (the servient estate) yields up to another parcel (the dominant estate). 

The dominant and servient estates need not be contiguous. It is created (1) by deed or (2) adverse use, open and notorious, for the prescriptive period. It is an incorporeal hereditament and being an estate or interest in real property, it cannot be created by a parol agreement. 

Rochester Post Adv. Co. v. Smithers, 224 A. D. 435, 231 N. Y. S. 315 

Ehrle v. Sutton Place Apts., 137 Misc. 122, affd. 231 A. D. 712.

An "easement in gross" is a mere personal interest in the realty of another. The principal distinction between an easement proper, that is, an easement appurtenant and a right in gross is found in the fact that in the first there is, and in the second there is not, a dominánt tenement. Whether easements in gross are assignable or inheritable is a moot question. Whether an easement is one appurtenant or in gross is to be determined by the nature of the right and

REAL PROPERTY 

281 the intention of the parties in creating it*. The surrounding circumstances are of importance in determining that intention. As a rule of construction, courts favor the appurtenant easement. An easement or servitude created by a deed is never presumed to be personal or in gross when it can be fairly construed to be appurtenant to some other estate; and when the reservation naturally operates to enhance the value of the other adjacent land of the grantor it is a strong circumstance to indicate that it was intended to be appurtenant to the estate and not merely personal to the grantor. 

Saratoga, etc., Corp. v. Pratt, 227 N. Y. 429, 442 

Weigold v. Bates 144 Misc. 395, 258 N.Y.S. 695

A right of way by prescription cannot be acquired to wander generally and at random over the property of another. Such right can only be acquired by use of a definite and well defined route, not necessarily, however, certain definite tracks. 

Olofson v. Malpede 127 Misc. 813, 216 N. Y. S. 695. 

If a party claiming the easement shows an open and uninterrupted enjoyment for the prescriptive period, one must prove that such use was licensed or permitted, or that it was restrained or limited in point of time in order to defeat the claim. 

Niesz v. Spencer, 213 A. D. 476, 211 N. Y. S. 3.

If one sells a part of his land, he does not automatically have any easement over the sold portion. If he had wanted to keep an easement, he should have reserved it at the time of sale. But this reservation could not have been made for any one but for himself and his land, or for one to whom he later sold his dominant estate. The conveyor impliedly grants all those apparent and visible easements which at the time of the grant were used by the owner for the benefit of the part granted. 

Scrum v. Davis, 141 Misc. 46, affd. 235 A. D. 879.

Suppose X and Y are tenants in common of Lot 1. Y floods the lot for thirty years, the flooding being the result of Y's placing a dam in a bordering stream. Y sells the dam and the machinery near to it to A. Lot 1 is sold to B. Can B prevent A's flooding the lot? 

Yes; A has not gained any prescriptive right because his grantor used the land for more than fifteen years, because one tenant in common cannot create an easement in land held in common. 

Crippen v. Morss, 49 N. Y. 63.

If an easement is created by grant, mere non-user of the easement by the grantee for any length of time does not destroy the easement. 

It may be lost by a definite unequivocal act of abandonment for 15 years continuously or an actual adverse user for that period. 

Scrum v. Davis, 141 Misc. 46, affd. 235 A. D. 879 

O'Neill v. O'Hare, 254 N. Y. 186. *In Weigold v. Bates 144 Misc. 395, an easement in gross was held to be neither assignable nor inheritable. The court in Antonopulos v. Postal Telegraph Co. 

261 A. D. 564, affd 287 N. Y. 712 suggested the contrary, basing its comment on an interpretation of the facts in Wilson v. Ford, 209 N. Y. 186, where what seemed to be an easement in gross was held to be assignable and inheritable. 

Yet in Saratoga v. Pratt, 227 N. Y. at page 444, the court in passing speaks of the "rule of non-assignability of easements in gross."

To establish an abandonment there must be a definite unequivocal act showing a clear purport to abandon. 

Easement by Necessity 

If a grantor conveys a portion of his property to another, keeping other land to which he has no access except by passing over the land conveyed, an easement is reserved by implication. Actual necessity for an easement must exist. Mere convenience will not suffice. The necessity speaks as of the date of the conveyance and not as of some later point of time. Once the grantor acquires another right of way, the easement by necessity is lost. 

Smith v. N. Y. Central R. Co., 235 A. D. 262, 257 N. Y. S. 313.

The way permitted under a right of way by necessity is the route which is most reasonable and most convenient. No subsequent grantee is exempt from the easement of the right of way by necessity which might be reasonably determined upon as the most con- Ivenient under all the circumstances. 

Falcone v. Benjamin, 129 Misc. 143, 221 N. Y. S. 190.

Covenants Running with the Land 

For a covenant to run with the land, it must appear (1) that the grantor and grantee intended that it should so run; (2) the covenant must concern the land involved; (3) there must be privity of estate between the promisee or the party claiming the benefit of the covenant and the right to enforce it, and the promisor or party who rests under its burden. Thus where A and B, adjoining land owners, contract for A to build a party wall and B to pay part of its cost, there is no covenant running with the land. The party who was to build and the one who was to pay were expressly designated and it is merely a personal obligation. If, however, each had conferred upon the other the authority to build such wall and dedicated to that use a portion of each of their lots, with an agreement that if either build, the other might use it by paying his share of the expense, we have a covenant running with the land. The agreement was prospective and its purpose imposed upon the land the burden of a future wall.

Neponsit P. O. Assn v Emigrant Industrial Bank 278 N.Y. 248 

A railroad grantee in a deed covenanted to pay for any damages caused by sparks or cinders from the railroad, to the ice in the lake of the grantor, his heirs or assigns. It was held to run with the land. 

Morgan Lake v. N.Y., N.H. & H.R. 262 N. Y. 234

A covenant running with the land will enure to the benefit of the grantor and his heirs and assigns, even though the original agreement did not mention "assigns" or the original parties. 

Real Property Law, § 257. 

St. Regis v. Powers 219 A. D. 321. 

Dedication of Highways 

Before there can be a dedication of a street or highway by a private owner to the public, the owner must show by act or declaration a deliberate, unequivocal and decisive intention to perma-

REAL PROPERTY 

283 nently abandon his property to the specific public use. To constitute acceptance there must be (1) a user by the public, (2) the tract must be kept in repair, and (3) taken in charge by the public. 

People v. Sutherand, 252 N. Y. 86 

Scarborough Properties v. Briarcliff, 278 N. Y. 370.

In one case, a so-called street was used for 10 years, was policed by a city policeman, a gas main was laid therein, street lamps were installed, a sign posts erected. The court held that there was not sufficient adoption by the public authorities to impose expenses of a city "street" upon the public. 

Matter of Wallace Ave., 222 N. Y. 139 

Lynbrook Homes v. Frey, 217 A. D. 164, 216 N. Y. S. 351. 

The Profit

An easement is a right to do something on the land of another. 

A profit is a right to take something from the land of another. 

A profit, and an easement, are both lost by unity of seisin. When a dominant and a servient estate become merged in a single owner, an easement of profit is extinguished upon the theory of merger. 

Let us suppose that A owns Lot 1 and X owns Lot 2. A has an easement or profit in X's land, Lot 1 being the dominant and Lot 2 the servient. A buys Lot 2 and he immediately sells the lot to 

Smith. A although he still owns Lot 1, has lost his easement or profit in Lot 2, for once the same person owns the dominant and servient estates, any easement or profit is ended. 

Lathrop v. Lytle, 84 Misc. 161, 145 N. Y. S. 906. 

A profit is also lost if the dominant estate is split up among several new owners or the servient burden is increased because of an act of the dominant tenant. If the servient estate is split into parts, the dominant estate is required to take a proportionate share from each of the new servient parts, unless the product to be taken is practically entirely in one particular part of the servient estate. In such a case the dominant party may take all from that part. So if 

A has a profit to get coal from B's land, and one-half of B's land is sold to Z, should Z's part contain all of the coal, A is not limited to one-half from Z, but can get the whole share from him. 

The License 

A license in respect to real property is an authority, revocable at the will of the licensor, to do particular acts upon the land of the licensor, which would amount to a trespass without such permission. It may be given orally or in writing. 

Meers v. Munsch, 217 A. D. 541, 217 N. Y. S. 256.

If A, the licensor, barred up the road which the licensee, B, had made at great expense to the latter and had used for a long period, even forty years, B could have no recourse against A. 

A theatre ticket is a mere token or evidence of a license. Another case is where A allows B to open a road on A's land. 

Harris v. Jack Theatre, 139 Misc. 111, 246 N. Y. S. 396.

A mere license creates no right in the licensor's property and it will not be protected by an injunction.

The exception to the rule that licenses are revocable at will is the license coupled with an interest. C sells hay to J, and J is to come and get it. When J comes, C will not let him on his land. J still has a license, for the license J has is one coupled with an interest, and it is irrevocable. This applies to personalty as well. 

Adverse Possession and Prescription 

Six elements together constitute an effective adverse possession of land. The possession must be (1) hostile, (2) actual, not constructive, (3) exclusive, (4) under a claim of right, (5) it must be known by the person against whom the adverse user is claimed, or it must be so visible, open, or notorious that the knowledge of such use or claim will be presumed, (6) it must be continuous for at least 15 years.

Civil Practice Act, § 35. 

When property of the state or of a city is inalienable, title cannot be obtained by adverse possession. 

City of New York v. Wilson, 278 N. Y. 86.

Although adverse possession and prescription are not the same thing, the former referring to a certain kind of possession of land which ripens into an actual title, and prescription resting upon the presumption after the required lapse ripens into a title, the 15 year period as the prescription period applies to both. The user and adverse user are the same in both cases. But because of the inherent abstract nature of rights acquired by prescription, any change therein will disrupt the running of the period of limitation. Adverse user of land, on the other hand, despite diversity of use, will not be thus affected. 

Klin So. v. N.Y. Rapid Transit Co. 271 N.Y. 376

One in possession without title of any kind is not in adverse possession if during the period of possession negotiations were carried on in which it was sought to determine the question of right to possession. But where A, through mistake or inadvertance, possesses, uses or improves the land of B as owners are accustomed to, such possession has been said to be hostile and under claim of right. B is charged with notice by the physical fact alone. 

Smith v. Egan, 225 A. D. 586, 233 N. Y. S. 582 

Hintley v. State, 234 N. Y. 309.

Open and notorious use for the prescriptive period throws upon the owner of the used premises the burden of showing that the user was not under a claim of right. 

Olofson v. Malpede, 127 Misc. 813, 216 N. Y. S. 695.

Where the occupant, or those under whom he claims, enters into possession under a claim of title, based upon a written instrument or upon the decree or judgment of a competent court, and there has been a continued occupation and possession of the premises for fifteen years under the same claim, the premises are deemed to have been held adversely, by statute. Where the land is a tract divided into lots, the possession of one lot is not deemed the possession of any other lot.

Civil Practice Act, § 37.

REAL PROPERTY 

285 By "possession," as used in the preceding paragraph, we mean either (1) where the land has been usually cultivated or improved, (2) where it has been protected by a substantial enclosure, or (3) where it has been used for the supply of fuel or of fencing timber. 

Civil Practice Act, § 38. 

Where there has been a continued occupation under a claim of title, not founded upon a written instrument, the premises actually, occupied, and no others, are deemed to have been held adversely. 

Civil Practice Act, § 39. 

The possession by a tenant is deemed to be the possession of the landlord until the expiration of 15 years after the termination of the tenancy. Where there has been no written lease the landlord's possession ceases 15 years after the last payment of rent. This rule exists notwithstanding that the tenant has acquired another title or has claimed to hold adversely to his landlord during that period. 

Civil Practice Act, § 41. 

By "possession," when the claim is not founded upon a written instrument, we mean either of the following, and no others: (1)

Where the land has been usually cultivated or improved; (2) where it has been protected by a substantial enclosure. 

Where premises have been bounded by a fence for upwards of the prescriptive period, the law presumes that the fence is the true boundary, and will not disturb this line, even where it does not correspond with the line of the premises as shown upon the map according to which they were conveyed. 

McMahon v. Morse, 135 Misc. 233, 237 N. Y. S. 361.

Tenants in Common and Joint Tenants Every estate granted or devised to two or more, unless expressly declared to be a joint tenancy, is a tenancy in common. But if these grantees or devisees are executors or trustees in their representative capacities, it is a joint tenancy, though not so stipulated. This applies to personalty as well.

Real Property Law, § 66. 

In re Deming's Will, 106 Misc. 133, 174 N. Y. S. 172.

The essence of a joint tenancy is that the joint tenants take and ' hold as though they together constituted one person. The four unities of (1) time that they acquired their interests at the same moment (2) title-that they acquired their interest by the same deed or will, (3) interest-that each has an interest identical with the interest of each of the other co-tenants, and (4) possessionthat each be entitled to the common possession of the entire property, must all exist. A tenancy in common requires only the unity of possession. 

Moore Lumber Co. v. Behrman, 144 Misc. 291, 259 N. Y. S. 248.

A tenant in common may convey his rights, and the conveyee becomes a tenant in common just as the conveyor was. If a joint tenant conveys his share, the conveyee becomes a tenant in common with the remaining joint tenants of that part conveyed to him. 

If a joint tenant dies, his interest goes to the surviving joint tenants until one is left, and the latter takes all. This is not the case

among tenants in common. There is no survivorship rule applicable to them. : An individual tenant in common may occupy the property without incurring liability for rent or for use and occupation, so long as he does not exclude other cotenants from the exercise of similar rights. But the rent of all strangers living on the land is to be divided equally among all the tenants in common. 

In re Limberg's Estate, 281 N. Y. 463.

One tenant in common, however, cannot bind the other tenants in common by leasing property, unless authorized to act for them. 

Early v. Robinson, 128 Misc. 184, 218 N. Y. S. 55.

One claiming as a joint tenant or tenant in common even though not in actual possession, may maintain a suit for partition* in which all questions of title affecting the entire property may be tried. Ejectment is no longer the sole remedy. Should it be impossible to subdivide the land, e.g., because of the structures on it, he can ask to have the land sold and the proceeds divided. 

Fisher v. Lister, 130 Misc. 1; Civil Practice Act, § 1016. 

A co-tenant against whom a partition action has been brought is entitled to credit for improvements and repairs when he has acted in good faith and there has been a substantial benefit to the premises. The co-tenant is not allowed credit for any improvements and repairs made after the commencement of the partition action. Moreover, the tenant in common possessing the premises can be compelled to account for the use, rentals, occupation, crops and avails of the premises from and after the date of the commencement of the action for partition. Of course, the tenant in common who simply occupies the premises himself cannot be charged with rent for his own occupancy, unless he has agreed to pay rental or has ousted or denied the rights of his co-tenant as regards the use of the premises. 

The expenses of the land must be borne by those tenants in common who use the land. 

Eldridge v. Wolf 129 Misc. 617, 221 N.Y.S. 508

Tenants by the Entirety If an estate is conveyed in one grant to a husband and wife without any words of exception, a tenancy by the entirety is created. So if Mr. Jones and Mr. Smith owned Greenacre as tenants in common, and Mr. Smith conveyed his rights to Mrs. Jones, Mr. and Mrs. 

Jones are tenants in common and not tenants by the entirety, because they were not grantees in one grant. Also, if conveyance was made to "Fred Beyer and Mary Beyer, his wife, share and share alike," they would not be tenants by the entirety, as there were clear words of exception taking the grant out of the rule. Likewise a tenancy by the entirety can never be created by descent. 

Hill v. Gross 226 A.D. 621, affd. 253 N.Y. 55 

Miner v Brown, 133 N. Y. 308. *The right to an action for partition continues as long as common ownership exists and is therefore not barred by any statute of limitations. Eaton v. Eaton, 170 Misc. 71, 9 N. Y. S. (2nd) 476.

REAL PROPERTY 

287 If H deeds his realty to himself and wife, a tenancy by the entirety is created, even though there was not apparently one grant. 

The husband's original estate is considered lost in the new estate, and unity of title, interest and time is thus spelled out. 

Boehringer v. Schmid, 133 Misc. 236, affd. 254 N. Y. 355. 

Coon v. Campbell, 240 N. Y. S. 772.

The interest acquired by husband and wife as vendees under a contract of sale has been held to be that of tenants by entirety. 

Sasso v. Meachem Realty Co., 242 A. D. 853, 275 N. Y. S. 230.

A conveyance to two who are about to marry creates a tenancy in common.

When realty is conveyed to a husband and wife and a third person, the husband and wife have one moiety as tenants by the entirety and the third person is a tenant in common with them of the other. 

Bartholomew v. Marshall, 257 A. D. 1060.

In the construction of the deed the real but unexpressed intention of the grantor does not count. The husband and wife will take by the entirety, even though the grantor did not know that they were husband and wife, and even though the deed did not describe them as husband and wife. And if the conveyance is made to "H. and D., husband and wife as tenants of the entirety," they do not take as such if they actually are not husband and wife, because a tenancy of the entirety can exist only where there is a valid marital relation. They take as tenants in common, unless the conveyance shows an intention to create what amounts to a joint tenancy. Thus, where a deed ran to "Michael Cowley and Matilda

Cowley, his wife,........survivor to take the fee," and they were not husband and wife, it was held that a joint tenancy was created. 

Gaza v. Gaza, 247 A. D. 837, affd. 272 N. Y. 617 

Bambauer v Schleider, 176 A. D. 562, 163 N. Y. S. 186 

Armondi v. Dunham 221 A.D. 679, affd. 248 N.Y. 603

Where the purpose of the parties to take as tenants by the entirety has been defeated by the fact that the parties could not contract a valid marriage, then a court of equity, in a partition action, may take into account the amounts invested in the property by the respective tenants in common, in determining the shares thereof to which they are entitled. 

Perrin v. Harrington, 146 A. D. 292, 130 N. Y. S. 944.

The fee in a tenancy by the entirety is an indivisible one and is vested in both husband and wife. On the death of one, the fee vests entirely in the other, not because the survivor acquired any additional rights (as in the case in survivorship under a joint tenancy), but because the survivor was the representative of the single ownership. 

Matter of Klatzl 216 N. Y. 83 

Armondi v. Dunham, 128 Misc. 881, affd. 248 N. Y. 603.

One tenant by the entirety may not, in the absence of any legal consent of the other, subject the property to an easement in the nature of a right of way. 

Grassi v Loweth, 130 Misc. 861, 225 N. Y. S. 91.

A tenant by the entirety in possession cannot acquire a co-tenant's interest by purchase at a tax sale, because it is the duty of a co-tenant to pay taxes thereon. 

Either the husband or the wife can convey his or her own interest to a third person and such a third person becomes a tenant in common with the other tenant by the entirety, subject to such other tenant's right of survivorship; and an action of ejectment may be maintained by the third party to recover possession of his interest in the premises thus acquired. Where an interest is purchased at an execution sale under a judgment held against one tenant by the entirety, the purchaser is in the same position as one who has bought at a voluntary conveyance. 

Finnegan v. Humes, 252 A. D. 385, affd. 277 N. Y. 682.

A tenant by the entirety may also mortgage his or her interest. A purchaser on the foreclosure sale would get all provided the mortgagor survives the other spouse. If the mortgagor is not the survivor, the mortgagee cannot get any part, for on the death of one tenant the other gets the fee, so that there is nothing left for strangers. If both tenants jointly and severally execute a bond and mortgage the death of one does not affect the liability of his estate upon such obligation. 

Misiaszek v, Roberts, 211 A. D. 417, 207 N. Y. S. 621. 

First Natl. Bank v. Goodman, 173 Misc. 562.

Neither spouse in a tenancy by the entirety can maintain an action to partition the fee. A conveyance, however, of the share of the rents or profits of either is valid. The parties are tenants in common of the use or rental value and each is entitled to one half of the rent. 

In re Strong's Will, 171 Misc. 445, 12 N. Y. S. (2nd) 544

Cornell v. Golder 179 Misc. 757 

If both convey the fee, the husband and wife are tenants in common of the proceeds, including the bond and mortgage which may be taken as part of the purchase price. There is no estate by entirety in personal property. Where, however, the husband has obtained the entire sales price, the wife may bring an equity action for an accounting. 1 Villone v. Villone, 135 Misc, 512, affd. 228 A. D. 884 

In re Blumenthal's Estate, 236 N. Y. 448.

Upon the annulment of the marriage, or divorce of the parties, the tenancy by the entirety becomes a tenancy in common with equal shares, and it does not matter that prior to the dissolution one had paid all the consideration for the premises.* 

Carpenter v. Carpenter, 130 Misc. 701, 225 Ñ. Y. S. 426. 

Conditions and Limitations

The differences between a condition and a limitation are these. In order to defeat the estate in the case of a condition there must be an entry; whereas to defeat the estate of a limitation there need be no *Since dower rights and rights of curtesy arising after August 31, 1930, have been abolished in New York, the discussion of these subjects is omitted.

REAL PROPERTY 

289 act by anyone. The happening of the event is, in itself, the sign of the end of the estate. In addition, at the entry, in the case of a condition, the estate goes back to the grantor or his heirs, as part of the old estate; in the case of the termination by limitation, a new estate is created in favor of a stranger. 

Lyon v Hersey, 103 N. Y. 264.

We can now see how these differences affect various situations. A conveys to B and his heirs, with a condition that if there is a default in the performance of any covenants the land is to revert to the grantor. In this grant upon a condition subsequent, the grantee takes a determinable fee, and not a title in fee simple absolute. The grantor retains nothing execpt the right to take advantage of the breach; it is not an estate or even an interest in real property. 

The right in the grantor is not assignable or devisable. Upon the death of the grantor, his heirs succeed to his rights of reentry for condition broken by force of representation, and not by descent. 

Calvary Presby. Church v. Putnam, 221 A. D. 502, affd. 249 N. Y. 111 

Upington v Corrigan, 151 N. Y. 143.

A conveyance on condition subsequent, followed by another conveyance of a part of the same premises from the original grantor to a third party, destroys the condition in the first deed and precludes recovery for breach by the heir of the original grantor. 

Nichols v. N. Y. & Erie R. R. Co., 12 N. Y. 121 

People v Wainwright, 237 N. Y. 407 

Tinkham v. Erie R. R. Co., 53 Barb. 393.

A deed conveying realty on the condition that the property is always used for the worship of God according to the doctrines of the Presbyterian Church, with right to reenter for breach of condition, creates, as we have seen, a fee with possibility of reverter for condition broken.

Although the grantor cannot assign his right of reentry to a stranger, he or his heirs can put an end to his own right of reentry by a release or a deed to the grantee, before breach, or by an attempted conveyance to any other person. The waiver binds the unborn heirs also. 

Trustees of Calvary Presb. Church v. Putnam, 249 N. Y. 111.

If a grantee is unable to perform the condition because of an interfering act of God, the fulfillment of the condition is excused and the estate becomes absolute in the grantee or his heirs at law, unless there exists a covenant to the contrary. 

Condition subsequent are not favored in the law, and are construed strictly because they tend to destroy estates. 

The bringing of an action of ejectment is sufficient to constitute an entry. It need not be a forceful entry. 

City of N. Y. v. Coney Is. Fire Dept., 170 Misc. 787, affd. 285 N.Y. 535.

It is now necessary to notice this case: A to B and his heirs so long as the monument stands. This is not, as in the former case, a condition subsequent. It is a state of being which is part and parcel of the description of the actual life of the estate. It is a "limitation." 

Therefore A has no right of entry for condition broken, but a possi- 1

bility of reverter. When the monument no longer stands, title automatically goes back, and no entry is necessary. The happening of the event limits the estate and it ends. So, A to B and his heirs until 

X returns from Rome-or until Danville is incorporated into a village, are also examples of estates on limitation.

A reversion does not arise by a conveyance, but arises by operation of law. It is something left in the grantor after the deed to property has been delivered by him, with only possession by him postponed until the happening of an event contemplated by the parties. Any separate agreement by the grantee to reconvey upon the happening of that event is mere surplusage. 

Second R. P. Church v. Trustees, 127 Misc. 498, affd. 220 A. D 244 

The Statute of Frauds

A contract for the sale of any interest in realty or for the leasing for more than one year of any interest in realty must be evidenced by a writing expressing the consideration, and subscribed by the party to be charged or by his lawful agent thereunto authorized in writing. The memorandum must state the entire contract with enough definiteness so that its substance will appear. 

Real Property Law, § 259. 

Where a material element of what was to be done was left open for future negotiations, it was held that the agreement was not specifically enforceable as there was no compliance with the Statute of Frauds. In this case the memorandum of sale stated "Price $32,000, payable $12,000 cash and the balance on first mortgage for five years. Sum to be paid on signing of contract, March 26, 1915 to be agreed upon." The memorandum omitted the amount to be paid on the signing of the contract. 

Ansorge v. Kane, 244 N. Y. 395; Real Property Law, § 259.

If interest is mentioned but not the rate, and the date of maturity of the mortgage is not mentioned at all, the law implies interest at the rate of 6 per cent, and that the mortgage is payable in demand. 

But if the writing says, “terms of interest and date of maturity of mortgage to be arranged on closing of title," there is no compliance with the Statute of Frauds, as a material element was left open for future negotiations.

And a memorandum is insufficient if it does not state who both contracting parties are. 

Drake v. Sop, 131 Misc. 573, 227 N. Y. S. 576 

Lerand Corp. v. Meltzer, 267 N. Y. 343.

If the contract is not in writing, it is voidable at the election of the parties sought to be charged. Mere payment of the price in a "sale" of realty is not enough. In such cases the vendee has his action at law to recover the purchase price of such part as he has paid.

Where there have been clear, definite acts of part performance of an oral agreement to convey, which are in part performance of a complete agreement, the oral agreement to convey realty will be enforced. Where the plaintiff collected the rents, paid the taxes and

REAL PROPERTY 

291 insurance, and had actual possession of the premises, it was held that there was sufficient part performance to take the case out of the Statute of Frauds. Where possession by the buyer has been long continued and the buyer's alterations have made it impossible for the seller to regain exactly what he gave the buyer, equity will enforce the contract, though the alterations improved the property. 

Whitaker v. Westberg, 124 Misc. 556, affd. 215 A. D. 785 

Zim v. Cohen, 221 Ă. D. 341, 233 N. Y. S. 424 

Sleeth v Sampson, 237 N. Y. 69; Walter v. Hoffman, 267 N. Y. 365 ·

Where land is purchased in breach of a contract with the money of one but in the name of another; where a confidential relationship exists and the confidence has been abused; where there was, at the time of making the contract, a preconceived intent to violate itthese and similar acts are such as will induce a court of equity to intervene. It is not the contract, which is void under the Statute of Frauds, but the fraud, whether actual or constructive, or the equivalent, which brings injury to the victim and which is not remediable at law and may result in such part performance as will induce a court of equity to protect the innocent party. 

Zelzer v. Yorkville Park Co. 141 Misc. 190, 252 N.Y.S. 626

Where a vendee has made payments as part performance, and the contract to convey is not carried out because of a default on the part of the vendor, the vendee has a lien upon the property to the amount of his payments. 

Giarrantano v. McIllwain 215 A.D. 644, 214 N.Y.S. 582 

Vendors and Vendees

Any contract for the purchase and sale or exchange of realty is to be interpreted, unless the contract expressly provides otherwise, as including an agreement that the parties shall have these rights and duties: (a) When neither the legal title nor possession of the subject matter has been transferred to the purchaser, if all or a material part thereof is destroyed without fault of the purchaser or is taken by eminent domain, the seller cannot enforce the contract, and the buyer is entitled to recover any portion of the price that he has paid; but the vendor shall not be deprived of any right to recover damages against the purchaser for any breach of contract by the buyer prior to the destruction or taking. If an immaterial part is destroyed without fault of the purchaser or is taken by eminent domain, neither the seller nor buyer is thereby deprived of the right to enforce the contract, but there shall be, to the extent of the destruction or taking, an abatement of the price. (b) When either the legal title or possession of the subject matter of the contract has been transferred to the purchaser, if all or any part thereof is destroyed without fault of the seller or is taken by eminent domain, the purchaser is not thereby relieved from duty to pay the price, nor is he entitled to recover any part that he has paid; but the buyer is not deprived of any right to recover damages against the seller for any breach of contract by the vendor prior to the destruction or taking.

Real Property Law, § 240a.

A vendee in an ordinary contract for the purchase of realty at a foreclosure sale is not entitled to an apportionment of accrued interest not due and payable, under a mortgage subject to which he takes title, or to a tax allowance which has not yet become a lien, unless otherwise provided for in the contract. 

Al-Dit Realty v. Hefferan 225 A.D. 567, 233 N.Y.S. 588

If a contract involving the sale of realty provides for the passing of title upon a certain day, that does not result in making that date the essence of the contract. If upon the day set, performance cannot be effected by a party, that party has a reasonable time after that to perform. Where, however, a clear and unequivocal notice or statement setting a fixed time exists, that time is of the essence. 

Ballen v Potter, 251 N. Y. 224.

Where a contract vendee is given possession before the passage of title, and it later is found that the vendor cannot deliver a marketable title, the vendee must pay or quit possession. The remedy of the vendor, upon refusal to vacate, is ejectment. 

Ballard v. Knapp, 152 Misc. 215, 273 N. Y. S. 25.

The Conveyance 

The part of a deed containing the names of the parties, the granting or operative words, the quantity of the estate transferred by the use of the word "heirs," the description and designation of encumbrances, is called the "premises." The clause starting "To have and to hold" is known as the habendum clause. If the grant as contained in the habendum clause is repugnant to the premises, the latter prevails. Thus if there be a grant to one and to his heirs and the habendum clause gave it to him for life, effect would be denied to the latter clause. 

Bannin v. Peck 266 A. D. 209, affd. 291 N.Y. 717.

A promise or warranty in a deed or conveyance delivered in such form that it can be recorded, is not to be denied effect because of the absence of consideration, if no consideration was intended. 

Real Property Law, § 283. 

If an owner of land unequivocally delivers a deed to A, with directions to give it to T upon the owner's death, the grantee receives title upon the final delivery, and this title is deemed to have vested as of the time of the first delivery to A. The actual change of ownership occurs at the time of the owner's death. If, however, the owner retains control of the deed and does not unconditionally deliver it to A, but keeps the right to recall the same, the owner does not dispose of his property by such an instrument. 

Allen v Leet, 127 Misc. 652, 217 N. Y. S. 274 

Gridley v. Home Ins. Co. 226 A.D. 596, affd. 254 N.Y. 635

Suppose Y is in possession and claims to be the owner. R says that he is the owner. A conveyance or mortgage by R is not void for the reason that at the time of delivery the realty was in the actual possession of one claiming under a title adverse to that of R, the grantor. The grantee may maintain an action to recover possession in his own name.

Real Property Law, § 260; Civil Practice Act § 994.

REAL PROPERTY 

293 The tenants of a grantor are protected as against the grantee as to all payments made by them to the grantor before they received notice of the grant.

Real Property Law, § 248. 

Conveyances of land made with intent to hinder, delay or defraud creditors (intent is always a question of fact) are void as against them, their heirs, representatives or assigns, but if the grantee is a bona fide purchaser for value, he is protected as against creditors. 

Real Property Law, §§ 263, 266. 

A conveyance bounded by or on a stream will be recorded, in the absence of stipulations to the contrary, as running to the center of the stream. When lands are described in a grant as being bounded by a tidal river the title ends at the high water mark. 

Smith v. Bartlett, 180 N. Y. 360 

City of New York v. Wilson, 278 N. Y. 86.

Effect of Death Before Title Passes 

A contract for the sale of realty immediately vests in the purchaser the equitable title while the vendor remains seized in the land for the benefit of the purchaser, holding the legal title only as security for the remainder of the purchase price. Upon the death of the vendor his interest in the money payable under the contract, passes as personal property. The legal title vests in his heirs who may be compelled to execute the conveyance in accordance with the contract.

Crippen v. Spies 255 A.D. 411, 7 N.Y.S. (2nd) 704 

Recording the Conveyance

A conveyance not recorded is void as against a subsequent purchaser in good faith and for consideration, from the same vendor, his heirs or devisees, whose conveyance is first duly recorded. To prevail under an unrecorded deed, it must be shown that the later record purchaser took with notice, actual or constructive. Possession is constructive notice. 

Page v. Warring, 76 N. Y. 463; Hood v. Webster, 271 N. Y. 57

The principle of constructive notice does not apply to unimproved land or unfurnished dwelling houses. The possession must be actual, open and inconsistent with the title of the apparent record owner. 

Schenectady Sav. Bank v. Wertheim, 237 A. D. 311, affd. 263 N. Y. 585

A purchaser is not chargeable with constructive notice of a recorded mortgage, which was not indexed under the proper block number because of an error in the description. If he had no knowledge of the encumbrance when he bought, he obtained a title superior to that of the mortgagee and he can convey such title even though he and the later grantee know of the mortgage at the time of the latter sale.

O'Neill v Lola Realty Co. 264 A. D. 60. 

Fixtures Certain chattels have (1) such a determinable character as movables that they remain personalty after their annexation to realty in-

dependently of any agreement between the owners of the chattel and realty, e.g., gas ranges attached by a coupling to the gas service pipe. 

Madfes v. Beverly Development Co., 251 N. Y. 12.

Therefore the reservation of title by a conditional vendor of such articles would not be void even against a purchaser of the realty for value and without notice. The vendor's rights are determined by 

Sections 65 and 66 of the Personal Property Law (see p. 303), and a mortgagee of real property would not upon foreclosure obtain such personalty though the conditional sales contract was not filed prior to the recording of the mortgage. If, however, the mortgage contained a clause under which personal property as well as fixtures were covered, then even personal property in this first class would belong to a purchaser at a foreclosure sale where the conditional sales contract was not filed before the mortgage was recorded, pur suant to Sections 65 and 66 of the Personal Property Law. 

Cohen v. 1165 Fulton Ave. Corp. 215 N. Y. 24 (2) Other chattels, notwithstanding any agreement, become realty when attached, e.g., bricks, stone, plaster. Here the chattel is so annexed to the realty that it cannot be removed without practically being destroyed. The filing of a conditional sales contract, would not protect the conditional vendor against a subsequent mortgagee. (3) There are some chattels that are in a middle class. The controlling elements are the character and purpose of the annexation and the intent with which it is made. In the requirements of an intention to make an article a permanent part of the realty, it is sufficient that it be contemplated that the article shall remain where fastened until worn out. Thus seats in a theatre were held to be part of the realty. 

Pike v. Naylow Securities Co. 140 Misc. 734, 251 N.Y.S. 659

Any agreement declaring articles of the third class personalty, and reserving title in the vendor until full payment, is not binding as against a bona fide purchaser for value of the realty, without notice of the contract of sale of the fixtures. If the goods are so attached, a reservation of title to said property by the seller is void as against a bona fide purchaser who had no notice of the conditional seller's title. The conditional seller should have filed the condiditional contract in the office where a deed of the realty would be recorded to affect such realty. This is not pursuant to Sections 65 and 66, but pursuant to Section 67 of the Personal Property Law. 

One who purchases the property at a foreclosure sale, without knowledge of the conditional sale of the article so attached to the realty, is considered such bona fide purchaser as to take title to the article if the conditional sale contract has not been filed in the proper office. 

Kohler Co. v. Brasun, 249 N. Y. 224 

Madfes v. Beverly, 251 N. Y. 12 

East N. Y. Elec. Co. v. Petmalane 243 N¸Y. 477

Suppose that X tore down Banton's fences, intending to replace them after his work was completed. Before he does so, Banton sells
