PROPERTY 

the land. The buyer gets the fences, for the fences were intended to be kept as part of the realty when X tore them down. 

Where the agreement between a landlord and his tenant declares that title to fixtures after they are affixed to the realty is to remain in the tenant, the fixtures can be removed by the tenant during the term. But that part of the tenant's fixtures which is not removed at the expiration of the term of the lease or upon surrender of possession of the land to which they are attached vests in the landlord. 

Talbot v Cruger, 151 N. Y. 117.

The tenant can remove from the premises whatever he erects for the purpose of carrying on trade, even though affixed to that land. 

Crater's Wharf v. Valvoline Oil Co. 196 N.Y.S. 815

Accretions and Avulsions When one's property is increased by the gradual action of the elements, as the receding of a lake or river, the added land belongs to the owner of the old land. The increase must be gradual. The added land is subject to the same liens and mortgages as the old property, of which it has become a part. 

If the part of the land becomes submerged by reason of avulsion the owner does not lose title to the land so submerged. He can even after the submersion, put up a sea wall and thus make use of the land again. 

Schwartzstein v. Bathing Park, 203 A. D. 700, 197 N. Y. S. 490 

City of N. Y. v. Realty Associates, 256 N. Y. 217. 

Party Walls

A party wall is for the common benefit of contiguous properties. 

Neither party may subject it to a use whereby it ceases to be continuously available for enjoyment by the other. 

The owners of a party wall have title to the soil up to the dividing line which is the center of the wall. This title is qualified by an easement which each owner has in the half standing on his neighbor's land of supporting his building by means of a common wall. 

This right exists as long as the wall continues to be sufficient for the purpose. When the wall must be repaired in orded to be used for the purpose of support, either may call upon the other to contribute towards rebuilding the wall; and in case of his default, to build it himself and call upon the other owner to contribute his one-half of the expense. Upon the complete demolition of the wall by the owners of the property, the easment is lost and is not revived by the erection of new buildings. 

Varriale v. B'klyn Edison Co., 252 N. Y. 222 

Partride v. Gilbert 15 N.Y. 601 

357 E. 76th St, Co. v Knickerbocker Ice Co., 263 N. Y. 63

One owner is not liable to the other for damages resulting to the other owner because of an unforseseen accident, e.g., a storm, while the wall is being rebuilt. 

Either party, may, at his own risk, increase the height of a party wall when it can be done without injury to the adjoining building and the wall is able to bear the addition. The addition must be

solid, without windows, though the court has hinted that circumstances may alter the requirement concerning windows. 

Brooks v. Curtis 50 N.Y. 639 

Varriale v. B'klyn Edison Co. 252 N.Y. 222 Emblements

If a life tenant plants crops and dies before the crops can be gathered, the representatives of the deceased life tenant get the crops when they are ready, because growing crops, which are the result of husbandry, are personalty. Any regular annual growth belongs to the remainderman. Annual growth is considered realty. 

Matter of Chamberlain, 140 N. Y. 390.

But a lessee for a term can take nothing from the land after the expiration of the lease, not even the results of husbandry. He knew when his term was over, and he should have acted accordingly. 

Reeder v. Sayre, 70 N. Y. 185.

Suppose A contracts with B in relation to the sale of growing timber. Is it a sale of realty or personalty? If A was to sell the timber "cut down and delivered as cordwood," it is a contract for the sale of personalty. If, however, title was to pass before the severance, the sale would be one of realty. 

Killmore v. Howlett, 48 N. Y. 569.

Surface and Underground Waters 

Surface waters include water spread over the surface of land or gathering into natural depressions or into swamps, or percolating the soil beneath the surface if flowing in no definite channel. 

An adjacent owner of real estate is not required to take care of the surface water coming on to his land from the lands of another. 

He may not, it is true, gather this water and cast it upon adjoining premises by drains or ditches, but in good faith and for the purpose of improving the land, the lower proprietor may deal with his land no matter what may be the consequences with reference to gathering or setting back surface waters upon the land of his neighbor from whose lands the surface waters flow. 

Barclay v. Wilcox, 86 N. Y. 140; Bennett v. Cupina, 253 N. Y. 436 

Vanderville v Taylor, 65 N. Y. 341.

It should be noted, however, that the appropriation of underground water must be for purposes connected with ordinary use or improvement of the plaintiff's land, and if the use of such underground water is excessive and interferes seriously with a natural surface stream on adjoining land, the plaintiff may be enjoined. 

Smith v. City of B’klyn., 160 N. Y. 357 

Forbell v. City of New York, 104 N. Y. 522. 

Riparian Rights

A riparian owner is one who owns the land contiguous to a natural water-course. The ownership extends to the high water mark. Riparian rights which are rights of navigation, boating, fishing and the like, are incidental to this ownership and can be severed from land, by grant, condemnation, relinquishment or prescription. 

Onondaga v. Crown Mills 132 Misc. 848 230 N. Y. S. 691 

Water Power Comm. v Niagara Power Co. 262 A. D. 463.

REAL PROPERTY 

297 A riparian owner in a non-navigable fresh water stream is entitled to have the water that passes his land free from pollution and undiminished in quantity, except as may be occasioned by the reasonable use of the stream by other like proprietors. Although the riparian owner owns no part of the stream, he may withdraw water from it and cause it to flow unnaturally through his land, provided he causes it, in its substantial volume and quality to return to the stream. 

Fulton v. Rockwood, 238 N. Y. 109 

Squaw Island F.T.Co. v. Buffalo 273 N.Y. 119

The riparian rights cannot be taken from the owner by the state without a just compensation. But the state may authorize the construction of bridges, piers, wharves, etc., in navigable* rivers, for the purpose of navigation and commerce, even though they cut the access of the riparian owners to the channels; and, in such cases, no compensation need be given. 

In re West 205th Street, 240 N. Y. 68.

If, however, the state diverts the water of a river into a channel wholly distinct and apart from the river itself, in order to improve navigation in that channel and not in the river, the state must pay compensation to the riparian owners. 

West Shore R. R. Co. v State, 216 A D. 603, 215 N. Y. S 684

A riparian owner has no right to divert waters of a navigable river, and he cannot acquire title to the land under the water by filling it up.

The riparian owner has right of access to the channel or to the navigable part of the river for navigation, fishing and other uses commonly belonging to a riparian owner. He can make a pier for his own use or for that of the public. 

The purchaser of land bordering an artificial lake or pond, created by a dam, acquires no riparian rights. 

The general character of a stream with reference to its navigability is not changed by the fact that at a particular place it is not, in fact, navigable for a short distance. 

People v. N.Y. & O.P. Co. 219 A. D. 114, 219 N.Y. S. 497. *A stream is regarded as "navigable" which affords a channel for useful commerce. The mode of use is immaterial. It may be by steamboat, sailing vessel or flatboat. People ex rel Erie v. State Tax Commission 266 A. D. 452.

 The Statute of Frauds 

A contract to sell, or for the sale of personal property, of the value of fifty dollars or more, is within the Statute of Frauds and is not enforceable by an action unless (1) The buyer shall accept part of goods contracted for and actually receive the same, or (2) The buyer shall give something to bind the contract or make part payment, or (3) Some note or memorandum in writing be signed by the party to be charged or his agent in his behalf, or (4) Goods are to be manufactured especially for the buyer and are not suitable for sale in the ordinary course of the seller's business.

Personal Property Law, § 85. 

The rule is not affected by the fact that the goods are not yet in existence or are to be delivered at some future date. Certificates of stock are held to be "goods." 

Agar v. Orda, 264 N. Y. 248.

Where many items are bought at one time, the total reaching $50, but the price of each individual item being under $50, the statute applies if the purchases are part of one contract. Whether it is only one contract is a question of fact. (1) Receipt and Acceptance.-To take the case out of the Statute of Frauds under this subdivision, there must be an affirmative act of delivery by the seller and an affirmative assent by the buyer to become the owner of the goods evidenced by an actual receipt and acceptance. Delivery to the buyer without the buyer's knowledge or receipt for the purpose of examination does not take the case out of the Statute. A mere retention for even an unreasonable time for such purpose, although a sufficient acceptance to bar a rejection of the goods later, because of a breach of warranty (see page 314), is not a sufficient acceptance to take it out of the statute. A very long detention might be such an affirmative acceptance, but how much is necessary is really a question of fact. 

Maher v. Randolph, 275 N. Y. 80; Young v. Ingalsbe, 208 N. Y. 503

A delivery to the carrier is not an acceptance by the buyer, even if the buyer had designated the carrier to receive the goods. The agency at most is for receipt and carriage only, (2) Part Payment. This payment may be in any amount and need not necessarily be by means of money. Goods or services will suffice. 

(3) The Memorandum.—The memorandum must specify the subject-matter and contain every essential term of the agreement, 298

such as the consideration, the terms, and names of the parties, even though an agent sign. It need not be a formal document. It may consist of letters, telegrams or notations, provided that when considered together, all the necessary elements of a contract are found. 

Byrne v. McDonough, 114 Misc. 529, affd. 198 A. D. 908 

Stone v. Browning, 68 N. Y. 598 

Irumor Co. v. Rodewald, 253 N. Y. 472. 

In one case, the memorandum read, "Received from C. A. Haas, $25 as deposit on property (describing the property). Price $25,000, payable as follows: $2,500 on signing of contract, $9,500 on taking title, and balance first mortgage for five years standing. Contract to be for four months." This was signed by the defendant seller. 

Actually, Haas was not the purchaser, but merely the broker for an undisclosed principal. The court held that the memorandum was insufficient. A memorandum does not fail of its effect if one described as principal is in truth only an agent, for the authority of the agent may be shown by parol, and the principal for whom he acts, may sue and be sued as if his name had been disclosed. It is essential, however, that the agent shall bind himself as principal, if the writing does not identify the principal. The memorandum may be adequate, though the agent is described as agent, provided the form of the contract purports to bind him personally. The memorandum is inadequate where by its terms the principal is not identified, and the agent, though his name is on the paper, is not there as a contracting party. Though this case dealt with realty it would not have been decided otherwise were personalty involved. 

If the parol agreement fixed no time for delivery, the memorandum is sufficient even if that item is omitted. The law supplies the missing term and requires delivery within a reasonable time. 

If, on the other hand, the time was fixed by the parties, the memorandum is insufficient if it does not mention the time for delivery. 

Berman v. Hirsh, 240 N. Y. 209.

The signature may be placed on any part of the memorandum. 

A name which is written or printed is not a signature unless inserted or adopted with an intent, actual or apparent, to authenticate the writing. A signature is adequate if the party to be charged writes "O. K." in the margin or on the top, and adds thereto his name in full or his initials. The delivery of a paper containing the order of goods written under the printed name of the seller, i.e., under his letterhead, has been held to be an acceptance of the contract, and the printed name in the letterhead held to be a signature. 

Where, however, in this latter case, there was a line for a signature next to the word "accepted" at the bottom of the page, the court held that this showed an intention on the part of the seller not to have the printed name in the letterhead constitute the signature, but that a later acceptance was necessary for the formation of the contract. 

Mesibov v. Cohen, 245 N. Y. 305.

If a contract was required to be in writing, an alleged, oral extension of that contract will not be enforced, unless the party claiming

the benefit of the oral extension could have performed within the original time set, but refrained from doing so in reliance upon the alleged extension. In the latter instance, the other party is estopped from setting up the defense of the Statute of Frauds. 

Davison v. Weston, 209 A. D. 514, affd, 240 N. Y. 705.

Where a plaintiff accepts delivery of the subject matter of the sale and an oral agreement is made simultaneously, by which the seller agrees that if the plaintiff should thereafter become dissatisfied the seller would on demand take it back at the contract price, the oral agreement is without the statute, since it is not a contract for sale, but a provision for the rescission of the entire contract. 

Johnston v. Trask 116 N.Y. 136 (4) Special Goods.-This section operates not only in favor of the seller, but also in favor of the buyer so that if the seller or buyer breaches an oral contract to sell goods not suitable for sale in the ordinary course of the seller's business, the other party may recover in an action for breach of contract.

Indian Limestone Co. v. Bernstein 263 A.D. 312 

Fraudulent Transfers

Every conveyance or mortgage made and every obligation incurred by a person who is or will be thereby rendered insolvent is fraudulent as to creditors without regard to his actual intent if the conveyance is made or the obligation is incurred without a fair consideration. A person is insolvent when the present fair salable value of his assets is less that the amount that will be required to pay his probable liability on his existing debts as they become absolute and matured. The return of execution unsatisfied is prima facie evidence of insolvency. A creditor is a person having any claim, matured or unmatured, liquidated or unliquidated, fixed or contingent.

Where there is actual intent to defraud creditors, a mortgage may be set aside regardless of the adequacy of the consideration or solvency of the debtor. 

Scholtz v. Yastizemski, 247 A. D. 823, 286 N. Y. S. 694

A person who has a tort claim against the transferor at the time the transfer is made is considered a creditor under this section, so that if the claimant obtains a judgment for the tort subsequent to the transfer, he may maintain his action to set aside a fraudulent transfer. The rule applies to a fraudulent transfer of realty as well. 

Debtor and Creditor Law, §§ 271, 273 

Leefer v. Murphy, 149 Misc. 455, 267 N. Y. S. 701.

Where a conveyance is fraudulent as to a creditor whose claim has matured, he may, as against any person except an innocent purchaser for value or his assignee, (a) have the conveyance set aside to the extent necessary to satisfy his claim; (b) disregard the conveyance and attach or levy execution upon the property conveyed. 

If the creditor's claim has not yet matured, the court may (a) restrain the defendant from disposing of his property; (b) appoint a receiver of the property; (c) set aside the conveyance; (d) make

any order which the circumstances require. In neither of these situations is a judgment essential before the creditor can act. 

Amer. Surety Co. v. Conner, 251 N. Y. 1.

In his action to set aside an alleged fraudulent transfer, the plaintiff must specify the property claimed to have been fraudulently conveyed and the time when the transfers were made. 

Herring v. Curtiss, 140 Misc. 857, 252 N. Y. S. 106

If a transfer is made to a bona fide purchaser for value, he is protected despite the intentions of the transferor.

Personal Property Law, § 40. 

Bulk Sales

We discuss now the case where otherwise than in the ordinary prosecution of a business, all or part of a stock in trade or fixtures alone of a fixed place of business are sold or mortgaged in bulk, e.g., when separating, counting or measuring do not take place, but the mass is sold as one, or when a part of the stock of merchandise in bulk or the merchandise together with the fixtures are mortgaged. 

Such sale or mortgage is void as against creditors of the seller whether the claims have matured or not. He can prevent this by (a) delivering to the transferee at least 10 days before the sale a full inventory, showing as far as possible the cost to the seller of each item; the inventory is to be retained by the transferee for at least 90 days, during which time it is to be open for inspection by creditors, and (b) by the transferee at least 10 days before taking possession or paying, notifying personally or by registered mail every creditor found on the list of creditors to be furnished by the transferor or known to the transferee, of the proposed sale, price and terms. Where a seller makes an affidavit to the effect that he has no creditors and a careful inquiry by the buyer discloses none, and he has no knowledge of any, he need not further comply with the provisions of the statute. 

Himmelstein v. Bach, 261 A. D. 57 

Marcus v. Knitzer, 168 Misc. 9, 4 N. Y. S. (2nd) 308.

Where a transferee does not conform to the above, he becomes upon the application of a creditor of the transferor, a receiver for the creditors for all that has come into his possession. 

Feldstein v. Fusco, 238 N. Y. 58

Personal Property Law § 44; Lien Law § 230a 

Atamian v. O'Leary, 154 Misc. 757, 278 N. Y. S. 218.

When an action is brought under § 44 of the Personal Property Law (Bulk Sales Act), the plaintiffs need not allege that they are judgment creditors. Any creditor of a seller, whether his claim has been put in judgment or not, may sue under the act. This does not apply to contingent claim creditors. The nature of their claim, however, must be set forth. The creditor has no right of action for personal judgment against the transferee. The remedy is by a creditor's action. The sale may be set aside. 

Phoenix Indem. Co. v. Alpine Cream Co. 151 Misc. 447, 270 N.Y.S. 519 

Willi v. Lyons, 131 Misc. 73, 226 N. Y. S. 283.

The action may be maintained by the trustee in bankruptcy who represents the creditors of the seller. 

Mott v Reeves, 125 Misc. 511, affď. 246 N. Y. 567.

The transfer by a partner to his copartner of his interest in a copartnership does not come within the Bulk Sales Law; nor does the transfer of furniture and fixtures of a hotel. 

Citizen's Trust Co. v. Merselis 271 N. Y. 539. 

Stewart v. Sulger, 174 A. D. 838, 161 N. Y. S. 489

Conditional Sales* 

Whenever the owner of personal property contracts to sell it, the purchase price to be paid in the future, the vendee to have possession but the title remaining in the vendor, there is a conditional sale. If the conditional vendor of property not attached to realty desires to protect his title, he must record the conditional sale in the county in which the vendee resides within 10 days after the making of the conditional sale. Otherwise the sale will not be effective as against a later bona fide purchaser from the conditional vendee who bought for value without notice of the conditional sale, or as against one who has actually levied on the chattel, or as against a trustee in bankruptcy of the vendee. Notice of the conditional bill of sale given to the sheriff prior to the levy is notice to the creditor and has the effect of filing. 

Baker v Hull, 250 N. Y. 484

Personal Property Law, §§ 64, 65, 66 

Edwards v. Walker, 163 Misc. 96, affd. 255 A. D. 248.

Any waiver of a statutory requirement, whereby the vendee consents to any modification of the provisions of the statute, in the contract, is invalid. Where, however, a new contract arises for a new consideration passing between the parties, the modification agreed upon outside the instrument itself will be enforced. 

Fisher v Stewart, 132 Misc. 225, 228 N. Y. S. 549.

Despite the fact that title may not yet have passed, the vendor in a conditional sales agreement may sue for the price if there is a default in the payment of an installment. 

In an action to obtain possession of a chattel under a conditional sales contract, the proper remedy is replevin. 

Marcus v. Sherr, 132 Misc. 734, 230 N. Y. S. 425.

The general rule is that upon a sale of personal property at auction, the property must be at hand and within the view of those attending. This rule is not so absolute as to admit of no exception. 

The exceptions depend upon considerations of policy and fairness in view of circumstances. The thing sold may be too bulky to be brought within the view of the bidders. However, when for some special reason the chattel to be sold is not to be present in the auction room, and its nature is such that inspection by the bidder *For a further discussion, see supra "Fixtures" on pages 293-4. This discussion deals with group (1) of that section, i.e., chattels which are not so attached to realty that they obviously retain a classification of personalty.

can have any possible utility, the notice of sale must state the place where the chattel is located and give opportunity to view it.* 

Manhattan Taxi Corp v Checker C. M. Corp., 253 N. Y. 455. 

Chattel Mortgages

Every chattel mortgage, not accompanied by an immediate delivery, and actual and continuous change of possession of the chattel mortgaged, is absolutely void against creditors of the mortgagor and subsequent bona fide purchasers and mortgagees, unless the mortgage is duly filed. If the mortgagee has unreasonably delayed the filing of his mortgage, he cannot, as against creditors at large, save the mortgage by filing it prior to the acquisition of a lien by such creditors. These creditors do not need to be judgmentcreditors. It should thus be noted that there is a decided difference in the law as respects creditors where a conditional sale is involved and where a chattel mortgage is involved. 

Baker v Hull, 250 N. Y. 484; Lien Law, § 230.

Either the mortgagor or mortgagee may sue and recover against one who has negligently damaged the mortgaged chattel. Recovery by one is a bar to a suit by the other. 

Stewart Motor Trucks v. N. Y. City 158 Misc. 738, 287 N.Y.S. 881

A chattel mortgage executed by a resident of another state and within 30 days next preceding the expiration of three years from the date of the original filing and within 30 days from the expiration of each additional year thereafter. If this is not done, the protection of the lien is lost as against creditors of the mortgagor. 

Lien Law § 235. 

Mortgages pledging subsequently acquired property will be enforced in equity as between mortgagor and mortgagee as agreements to give liens, and also as against purchasers with notice. They will not be enforced as against attaching or execution creditors. 

Diana Paper Co. v. Wheeler-Green 228 A.D. 577240 py 5 108.

A chattel mortgage executed by a resident of another state and there recorded properly, protects the mortgagee and a sale by the mortgagor to a third party in New York does not pass good title unless the third party can show apparent authority to deal with the mortgaged property as his own. Possession alone is not such apparent authority. 

Farnham v. Eichin, 230 A. D. 639, 246 N. Y. S. 133.

Passing of Title** 

Where goods are destroyed en route it becomes necessary to determine the owner of the title as that person must usually bear the loss. Where creditor's attach goods in the possession of a debtor, the latter's lack of title to such goods vitally affects the creditor. *For a detailed discussion of the procedure upon default by the conditional vendee see Laufer v. Burghard, 146 Misc. 39, 261 N. Y. S. 364. **A transaction for the passing of title is not governed by the Sales Act unless the consideration (the price) is to be payable in personal property. If services are to be rendered for food, there is no sale of the food under the Act. Haag v. Klee, 162 Misc. 250, 293 N. Y. S. 266.

As a general rule the title passes from the seller to buyer at the time the parties intend to have it pass. The following rules will be helpful in determining the time of passage of title where the intentions are unexpressed or ambiguous. 

(1) Future and Unascertained Goods.-Under the Sales Act the buyer of future goods, e.g., crops to be grown, cannot get title from the time of the bargain, but gets only a contract right. Title to future or unascertained goods passes (a) when the goods come into existence, and (b) they are in a deliverable state, and appropriated to the contract by either party with the assent of the other. Such assent may be inferred from express words or circumstances.

Where the seller delivers goods to the carrier for transmission to the buyer, the presumption exists that the seller has appropriated the goods to the contract. 

Personal Property Law § 68, Subd. 3; § 100, Subd. 4 

These rules cover C. O. D. transactions. Delivery of the goods to the carrier for transmission to the buyer effects the passing of title even though the purchaser is required to pay before he can obtain possession or inspect the goods. 

Where an article of personalty is to be built and paid for in installments, title to as much as is completed does not pass either upon completion or upon payment of the installment. The payment and its receipt are not considered the assent. 

Andrews v. Durant, 11 N. Y. 35.

In one case the buyer ordered goods which were to be packed and delivered to him. The goods were packed properly, and before shipment the buyer asked the seller to hold the goods for further instructions. Title passed upon the notification, since the goods had been properly appropriated to the contract and the buyer had assented.

Taylor v. Kurzrok 214 A.D. 308, 222 N.Y.S. 133 

(2) Fungible Goods.-Where a quantity of a specific mass is contracted for, e.g., 1,000 bushels of wheat from a heap, the buyer becomes a tenant in common with the owner of such proportionate share as the amount bought bears to the amount in the heap. If, before delivery, a large part of the heap is stolen or burnt, the buyer is responsible for his proportionate share of the loss, as he was a tenant in common with the owner of a proportionate share. This is called a contract to sell an undivided share of fungible goods. 

Personal Property Law, §§ 87, 98; Kimberly v. Patchin, 19 N. Y. 330. 

(3) Sale of Specific Goods.-Where goods are specific or ascertained at the time the contract for sale is entered into and the goods are in a deliverable state at that time, the presumption is that title was intended to pass at the making of the contract. Where something remains to be done for the purpose of putting the goods in a deliverable state, the title does not pass until that is done. 

Personal Property Law, § 99; § 100, Rules 1, 2.

The expenses incurred in putting the goods in a deliverable state are borne by the seller in the absence of a contrary agreement. 

Personal Property Law, § 124, Subd. 3. 

It makes no difference that the buyer is to pay at a later date or is to get the goods later. So if a buyer enters a store and orders a coat which is ready for delivery, the buyer would stand the loss should the store and coat burn that night. There was (a) an unconditional contract (b) to sell specific goods and (c) the goods were in a deliverable state, i.e., in such a condition that the buyer would be bound to accept the goods under the contract. If the coat had lacked buttons, or trimmings, or needed alteration, title would not have passed until those things had been taken care of. 

Proctor & Gamble Co. v. Peters, 233 N. Y. 97

Personal Property Law, § 100. 

(4) Sale or Return.-If goods are sent "on sale or return," title passes at once. If the buyer sends back the goods within the time fixed in the contract, or, if no time has been fixed, within a reasonable time, the title reverts to the seller. 

Personal Property Law, § 100, Rule 3, Subd. 1. 

The buyer pays the freight where nothing in the contract covers the point. Therefore, a return to a railroad depot for shipment to the seller is not sufficient to revest title. 

Lyon v. Motley 9 Misc. 500, 30 N.Y.S. 218 (5) Sale on Approval.-Where a party is permitted to take possession of specific goods with the right to determine within a period whether he is to become the owner, the arrangement is termed a sale on approval. Title passes only when the buyer shows that he accepts the goods, either by saying so or by retaining the goods beyond a reasonable time. What is "reasonable" is a question of fact. 

But a retention and use for sixteen months was held more than a reasonable time as a matter of law. 

Brown v. Potolski, 221 A. D. 299, 223 N. Y. S. 71

Personal Property Law, §100, Rule 3, Subd. 4. 

A sale by the possessor to a third party is deemed an approval and title will be considered as having passed. 

In the absence of any contrary arrangement, the seller must bear the expense of the return. The prospective buyer need only notify the seller of his dissatisfaction. (6) F. O. B. Contracts. The letters F. O. B. mean "free on board." The seller is to deliver the goods free of expense to the buyer to the place named after the F.O.B. Thus if goods are shipped "F.O.B. New York," the seller pays for packing, freight and other charges until the goods reach New York.

Title passes when the goods arrive at the place stated after the 

F. O. B. If goods are sold "F. O. B. New York," by a seller in New

York to a buyer in Cleveland, title passes when the goods are delivered to the carrier in New York. The fact that the consignee has the privilege of inspection does not affect the above rules. 

Rosenberg Bros. v. Buffum, 234 N. Y. 338 

Standard Casing Co. v. California Casing, 233 N. Y. 413. 

Porter v. Penn. R. Co., 217 A. D. 49, 215 N. Y. S. 727.

(7) C. I. F. Contracts.-These letters stand for "cost, insurance and freight." A c. i. f. sale means that the agreed price includes the cost of goods at the point of shipment plus insurance and freight to the point stated after the c. i. f. 

In a c. i. f. contract the seller completes his contract and the risk is on the buyer after the seller delivers the merchandise called for to the shipper directed to the point of destination, pays the freight threon to such point and sends the bill of lading with the insurance policy to the buyer. If goods are lost in transit, the buyer must look to the insurance for indemnity. 

Seaver v. Lindsay Light Co., 233 N. Y. 273.

In a recent case the contract declared itself to be a "c. i. f." contract. However, the insurance was "for the account of the seller." 

Payment was declared to be "net cash against shipping documents upon arrival," manifesting an agreement that if the steamer did not arrive no payments were to be made and indicating that risk was on the seller. It was held that although the letters c. i. f. in the contract created an inference that the instrument was in fact a c. i. f. contract, the express terms of the contract were, however, utterly inconsistent with such inference. The express terms must prevail, and the letters c. i. f. must be limited and applied to the price and not to the passing of title. 

Cundill v. Milhauser, 257 N. Y. 416.

If the seller, instead of shipping the goods direct to the buyer as required, sends them to a third party together with some goods for this third party, title does not pass to the buyer on delivery to the carrier. To pass the title the goods must be consigned to the buyer. (8) Custom and Usage.—If there is any particular usage of trade in vogue, that, unless the parties clearly intend the contrary, governs the transaction, and the title rests as the usage dictates. 

Of course, the contract may declare where the risk is to be. The above rules apply when the contract does not so state. (9) Delivery to Carrier.-If the contract requires delivery to a particular place in order to pass title, title cannot pass until the goods are delivered there. But if there is no such stipulation, the place where the goods happen to be at the time of the sale is the place of delivery. If a third party is then in possession, that party must acknowledge that he holds them for the buyer before title passes. 

Taylor v. Kurzrok, 214 A. D. 308, 212 N. Y. S. 133.

If no delivery to a particular place is required for passage of title, title passes to the buyer on the delivery to the carrier of the goods in a deliverable state. Risk of loss from that moment is on the buyer. The risk would remain on the seller only if the carrier happened to be the particular agent of the seller. 

A sells goods to B‍and ships them by a common carrier to B, payment to be made upon delivery. Through the negligence of the carrier, B obtains possession of the goods without paying them the money and sells them to C, a bona fide purchaser for value without

notice. Neither A nor the carrier can recover the goods from C. 

Upon the delivery of the goods to the carrier, B had obtained title, subject to A's rights. These rights A lost when a bona fide purchaser for value without notice obtained the goods. 

Penn. R. R. v. Bank of U. S., 214 A. D. 410, 212 N. Y. S. 437. 

Risk of Loss

The risk of accidental damage or loss is upon the party having title when the damage or loss occurs, except in these instances: (1) When the seller takes the bill of lading to his own order. In such a case, if but for the fact that the seller so made out the bill of lading, title would have been in the buyer, the risk of loss is on the buyer. Title is in the seller for purposes of security only. The seller may still sue for the price. 

Personal Property Law, § 101. 

(2) Where delivery has been delayed through the fault of one of the parties and loss resulted therefrom, the risk of loss is on the party causing the delay, regardless of where the title might be. 

Personal Property Law, § 103. 

(3) If the goods are sent to the buyer under circumstances where it is usual to insure the goods, and the goods are not insured, nor the buyer notified of it in time to obtain his own insurance, risk of loss during transit is on the seller, even though the buyer has title. 

Miller v. N. Y. C. R. R., 205 A. D. 663, 200 N. Y. S. 287. 

Bill of Lading

The bill of lading serves three distinct functions: First, as a receipt for the goods; second, a contract for their carriage; and third, documentary evidence of title to the goods. As a receipt, it recites the place and date of shipment, describes the goods as to quantity, weight, dimensions, identification marks, and condition, quality and value. As a contract, it names the contracting parties which includes the consignee, fixes the route, destination, and freight rate or charges, and stipulates the rights of and obligations assumed by the parties. 

Schwalb v. Erie R. Co., 161 Misc. 743, 293 N. Y. S. 842.

Where a seller, upon delivery of the goods to the carrier for shipment has the latter issue a straight bill of lading to the buyer as consignee, a presumption is created that there was an unconditional appropriation of the goods to the contract. If the seller names himself as a consignee, the carrier is considered a bailee for the seller. 

Personal Property Law, § 226, Rule 101, Subd. 2. 

Suppose a document of title states that the goods are deliverable to the order of X. The document thus is apparently negotiable. 

Even if it is stamped "non-negotiable," the stamp does not change the negotiability; it remains negotiable. But if à common carrier had so stamped such a document of title, it would be protected if it delivered the goods without taking up the document and the document came into the hands of a holder in due course. 

If the document was not stamped and the instrument was passed

on to a holder in due course, the carrier would have to make good any loss such holder suffered because of its failure to take up the bill on delivery of the goods. 

N. Y. C. R. Co. v. Fed. Sugar Ref. Co., 235 N. Y. 182.

Sometimes negotiable bills of lading are issued in sets by the carrier. Suppose that a bona fide purchaser buys one of these sets. The goods having already been delivered to the owner, the carrier is unable to deliver to the bona fide purchaser. The carrier is liable for the damages suffered by the bona fide purchaser unless the duplicate bill was plainly marked as a duplicate. 

If one other than the person holding a bill of lading claims ownership of the goods, the carrier has a reasonable time within which to ascertain the validity of the claim. 

Of course, if the bill of lading is non-negotiable, its endorsement gives the transferee only those rights which the transferor had. If the transferee wants full protection against any creditors of the transferor, he must notify the carrier that he is the transferee, for until such notice the creditors can attach the goods. 

If a draft is sent with a bill of lading and it is payable within three days after sight, the buyer must pay the draft before he can get the bill of lading. If it is payable more than three days after sight acceptance is enough. 

Express Warranties

Warranties are express or implied. An express warranty is (1) an affirmation of fact or promise relating to the goods (2) the natural tendency of which induced the purchase, and (3) the buyer must purchase in reliance upon the affirmation or promise.

Personal Property Law, § 93. 

A statement than an article is "very fair," "excellent," or "wellmade," or "unbeatable," or of a "true and actual value," is not a warranty; it is just selling talk. A statement declaring what is the "book value" for corporate stock is a statement of present fact. 

O'Hara v. Derschug, 241 A. D. 513, 272 N. Y. S. 189.

If the seller expressly or impliedly, even though in good faith warrants the goods and title has not yet passed, this warranty may be considered a condition, and a breach of it permits a refusal on the part of the buyer to go on with the contract. 

Personal Property Law, § 92. 

But suppose the goods are sold and the satisfaction of buyer is one of the conditions necessary. The rule here is that the buyer cannot unreasonably reject the goods where the personal taste of the buyer is not involved. Such cases include articles worked on by mechanics, builders and unskilled labor. But if the personal taste of the buyer is involved (as in a contract to paint a picture), the buyer must really be satisfied. If he is not genuinely satisfied, he may reject the article ordered. This is a rule of contracts. 

Duplex Safety Boiler Co. v. Garden, 101 N. Y. 387 

Crawford v. Mail & Exp. Pub. Co., 163 N. Y. 404.

Where a seller's letter accompanying an invoice stated that the seller expected the goods to arrive in April, such statement was interpreted to be only a statement of mere expectancy and not a warranty. 

Eitington-Schild Co. v. Friedman 213 A.D. 663, 211 N.Y.S. 208 

Implied Warranties

In addition to express warranties, the law will imply certain warranties unless the contrary is declared in the contract of purchase. 

An express refusal to make any warranties with respect to an article sold, which refusal is contained in a written instrument of sale, precludes the buyer from claiming under the warranties which the Personal Property Law implies, or from claiming an alleged breach of parol warranty, or a sale by sample. 

Sayeg v. Gloria Light Co., 236 A. D. 761, 259 N. Y. S. 492

Personal Property Law, § 152; Lumbrazo v. Woodruff, 256 N. Y. 92. 

A refusal to warrant does not relieve from liability the maker of a fraudulent representation or relieve the seller from the duty of delivering the article contracted for in merchantable condition. 

Stroock v. Lichtenthal, 224 A. D. 19, 229 N. Y. S. 371 

Abel v. Paterno, 245 A. D. 285, 281 N. Y. S. 58.

Except in the case of a sale by a sheriff, mortgagee, or one selling by virtue of an open agency, the seller impliedly warrants (1) That he has a right to sell the goods or that he will have such good title at the time when the property is to pass. (2) That the goods are free from incumbrances. (3) That the goods correspond with the description given or with the sample. (4) That the goods are fit for the purpose for which they are bought provided the buyer makes known to the seller, expressly or impliedly, the purpose for which the goods are bought and the buyer has relied on the seller's judgment in buying. If the buyer had examined the goods and should have discovered the defect, there is no warranty.* 

Spotless Co. v. Comm. Trust Co., 215 A. D. 412, 214 N. Y. S. 10 

Hoisting Engines Sales Co. v. Hart, 237 N. Y. 30

Personal Property Law, §§ 94, 95, 96. 

The purchase of food ordinarily used for human consumption in and of itself impliedly informs the seller of the purpose for which the purchase is made. The purchase without any other circumstances is evidence of the buyer's reliance on the seller's judgment. The mere purchase by a customer from a retail dealer of an article, the use of which is ordinarily known, does by implication make known to the vendor the purpose for which the article is required There exists a warranty of fitness. This warranty does not exist between the wholesaler and retail purchaser. There is not any privity of *The burden of showing that he has made known his purpose and that he has relied upon the seller, is on him who claims the existence of an implied warranty.

contract between the wholesaler (or manufacturer) and the purchaser from the retailer.* 

Rinaldi v. Mohican Co., 225 N. Y. 70 

Temple v. Keeler 238 N.Y. 344 

Chysky v. Drake Bros. Co., Inc., 235 N. Y. 568.

Where the wife is the purchaser of food the cause of action for breach of warranty is hers alone and the husband has no cause for action for loss of services arising from a breach of warranty. 

Giminez v. Gt. Atlantic & Pacific Tea Co. 264 N.Y. 390

In the case of a contract to sell or the sale of a specific article under a patent or trade name, e.g., a "No. 52 Thermo-Oil Heating 

Equipment, manufactured by Kellog Mfg. Co.," or a "Delco Oil 

Burner" or "Velvet," a pipe tobacco, there is no implied warranty as to its fitness for any particular purpose although such goods must be of merchantable quality.

Personal Property Law, § 96 

Barcham v. Kane, 228 A. D. 396, 240 N. Y. S. 123 

Foley v. Liggett, 136 Misc. 468, affd. 232 A. D. 822.

The fact, however, that an article sold happens to have a trade name does not exclude all warranties. Where a buyer in purchasing trade-marked oil relied upon the seller's representation that the oil was what the buyer's particular machinery required, and not upon the trade name, it was held that the representation constituted a warranty. 

Sachter v. Gulf Refining Co., 203 N. Y. S. 769. (5) Where the goods are bought by description from a seller who deals in goods of that description (whether he be the grower or manufacturer or not), there is an implied warranty that the goods shall be of merchantable quality.

Personal Property Law, § 96, Subd. 2. 

Where a purchaser asked the retailer for a loaf of "Ward's Bread" and was given a loaf wrapped in a sealed package as it came from the Ward Baking Company, the baker, the court held that recovery could not be based on the imputation of reliance upon the seller for damages resulting from the presence of a pin in that bread under Section 96, subdivision 1, of the Personal Property Law, since it was bought under a trade name; but since the buyer was entitled to goods of merchantable quality under subdivision 2 of that section, recovery was allowed on the latter section. Loaves containing pins are not of merchantable quality. 

Ryan v. Progressive Stores, 255 N. Y. 388. (6) That the goods have no latent defect. But if the buyer ought to have seen patent defects, there is no such warranty. (7) Where there is a contract to sell or a sale by sample, there is an implied warranty that the bulk shall correspond with the sample, and if the seller is a dealer in that kind of goods, that the goods shall not have any latent defects rendering them unmerchantable. *See infra, page 339 for a discussion of Torts arising from sales.

Rights and Remedies of the Unpaid Seller* 

(1) The Unpaid Seller's Lien.-Such seller may exercise a right of lien if he has possession and (a) the price is past due, or (b) the buyer has become insolvent. The insolvency of the buyer does not work a rescission. He may tender full payment before the rescission is declared and obtain the goods. By "insolvent" is not meant "bankrupt" but rather an inability to meet payments properly required of him.

Personal Property Law, §§ 134, 135, 136, 137. 

The lien is lost when the unpaid seller delivers the goods to a carrier for transmission to the buyer without taking a bill of lading to his own order or without retaining the bill of lading to the buyer's order, or when the buyer lawfully obtains possession or when the seller does any other act waiving the lien. 

Tuthill v. Skidmore, 124 N. Y. 148. (2) Stoppage in Transit.-A seller may stop the goods in transit and retake possession if (a) the buyer has become involent and (b) he has not yet obtained possession.

Whether the goods have been delivered to the carrier and title passed do not matter, so long as the buyer or his agent has not possession. Notification to hold the goods given to the carrier under circumstances which give it reasonable opportunity to retain the goods, is sufficient. Failure to hold the goods after proper notice attaches liability for their value. The carrier, however, may refuse to deliver to the seller until expenses are paid and outstanding bills of lading returned.

Personal Property Law, §§ 139, 140. 

It is not always easy to determine whether transit has ended. The transfer of an order bill of lading to an innocent purchaser for value has been held to destroy the right to stop in transit. 

Personal Property Law, § 143. 

If a portion of the goods has been delivered to the buyer, the right to stop the balance remains provided the part delivery was not made under such circumstances as to show an intention to give possession. (3) Right of the Seller to Resell.-A seller who has asserted a lien or who has retaken possession during transit may resell the goods without liability in three circumstances. (a) Where the goods are perishable (b) When the contract by its terms permits a resale. (c) Where the buyer has been in default for an unreasonable time.

Notice of the resale need not be given to the buyer. The failure to give notice is only evidence upon the question as to whether or not the resale took place within a reasonable time after the buyer's default under subdivision (c). 

D'Aprile v. Turner Looker Co., 239 N. Y. 427. *A seller need not take advantage of an anticipatory breach. If he refuses to do so, the contract stands for the benefit of both parties so that even the defaulting vendee may demand performance despite the earlier repudiation.

The resale may be by either public or private sale. The seller need exercise only due diligence and good faith to obtain the best price. (4) Seller's Right to Rescind.-The unpaid seller may rescind the contract of sale on the same grounds that any party may rescind a contract, e.g., duress, fraud in the inception, etc. In addition, the seller may rescind for failure on the part of the buyer to pay. 

When the latter ground is the basis for the rescission, one of the following must exist before the rescission is effective as such: (a) The default must exist for an unreasonable time, the seller must have possession, and the seller must have manifested his intention to rescind. The act evidencing the intention need not be communicated to the buyer, but the giving or failure to give notice is relevant in any issue involving the question of the buyer's default for an unreasonable time.

Personal Property Law, § 142. 

(b) The buyer has repudiated the contract or manifested his inability to perform, or has committed a material breach. In each such instance it is essential that the possession be in the seller. Furthermore, notice of rescission must be given to the buyer. 

Personal Property Law, § 146. 

The right to sue for damages exists as well as the right to rescind where a breach occurs. The seller may elect either. 

When the seller sells as lienor under Section 141 (supra, subheading 3) he acts as agent for the buyer and he is required to deduct the sum realized from the damages he may have sustained. Nevertheless, if the resale brings more than the contract price, the defaulting buyer is not entitled to the excess. When the resale takes place after a rescission under Section 142, the sale is for the seller's account since title is now revested in him. 

Henderson Tire Co. v. Wilson 235 N. Y. 489. (5) Action for the Price.-Subject to two exceptions, a seller cannot maintain an action for the price unless title is in the buyer. (a) Where the contract requires payment on a day certain, an action for the price may be maintained though title has not passed. 

Even in this case if the seller at any time before judgment has manifested an inability to perform, it is a defense of the buyer. (b) Where the goods cannot be readily resold for a reasonable price, an action for the price may be maintained although title has not passed, provided a tender was made, the buyer refused to accept and the buyer was notified that the seller was holding the goods as bailee for the buyer.

Personal Property Law, § 144 

Murray v. Ridgewood 132 Misc. 414, affd. 251 N. Y. 558 

Glass Co. v. Misroch, 239 N. Y. 475. (6) Damages for Non-Acceptance. This phase has previously been mentioned, but it is worth while to summarize the rules. 

Where the buyer refuses delivery, he is liable for any loss sustained and for reasonable charges for the care of goods. Where there is an available market, the measure of damages in the absence of a show-

ing of special proximate damages, is the difference between the contract price and the market price at the time and place of delivery, or if no time has been fixed, at the time of the refusal to accept.* 

If the article is to be manufactured and while in the process the seller is told by the buyer that no acceptance will be made, it is the duty of the seller to cease work. Where the breach occurs before any work has been done, the recovery is the difference between the contract price and the cost of manufacture.**

Personal Property Law, §§ 132, 145; Todd v. Gamble, 148 N. Y. 382. 

Rights and Remedies of the Buyer 

(1) Breach of Warranty.-In order to succeed on the theory of an implied warranty other than those implied by law from the very fact of the sale, e.g., title in the seller, the buyer must establish two things: (a) That he made known to the seller the particular purpose for which he wanted the article, and (b) That he relied on the seller's skill and judgment that the article would serve that purpose. *** 

Bowser v. McCormack, 230 A. D. 303, 243 N. Y. S. 442.

Where there has been a breach of warranty, the buyer (a) may accept or keep the goods and set up against the seller the breach by way of recoupment in dimunition or extinction of the price; (b) he may accept or keep the goods and sue for damages for breach of warranty; (c) he may refuse to accept the goods if title has not passed, and sue for damages for breach of warranty. The buyer has a reasonable time after receipt to examine and determine whether he will reject; (d) he may rescind the contract. If title has passed and the buyer later discovers the breach, he may refuse to accept the goods. If they have been received, they may be returned. Damages may be recovered by virtue of Civil Practice Act, § 112e which permits a recovery of damages in a rescission action. It is to be observed that a notice of breach of warranty to fasten liability upon the seller must be given within a reasonable time after the buyer knows, or ought to know, of such breach. In the case of rescission the notice is to be given within a reasonable time of the breach. 

What is a reasonable time is determined by all the circumstances. 

If the buyer does not learn of the breach for a long time it may be that he retains only his right to sue for damages. 

Apex Chemical Co. v. Compton, 171 N. Y. S. 60 

Donovan v. Aeolian Co., 270 N. Y. 267. *If it appears to the court that the ownership of any goods will depend upon the outcome of a pending action, and neither party is willing to accept them as his property, the court on the application of either party may order the sale of the goods. Upon such sale a party to the action may purchase the goods. 

Civil Practice Act, § 979a. 

**For a further discussion of "Damages," see ante, page 176. ***The doctrine of a seller's liability for breach of warranty extends to the container as well as to the contents. They are both part of the sale. Haller v. 

Rudmann, 249 A. D., 831, 292 N. Y. S. 138.

Where defects were discovered three days after receipt and notice thereof given five weeks later together with a notice of rescission, it was held that both the right to sue for damages and to rescind was lost. 

Milz v. Bloomfield 146 Misc. 649 

Silberman v. Engel 125 Misc. 816.

The buyer has lost his right to take advantage of the breach of warranty if he failed to give notice to the seller within a reasonable time after he learned of the breach and continued to use the article for a long time thereafter. 

Ellis v. Allen, 125 Misc. 841, 211 N. Y. S. 488.

If part of the goods was sold before the discovery of the breach, there can be no rescission since it is impossible to put the parties in status quo. Nor can there be a rescission if buyer knew of the breach of warranty when he accepted the goods. Where a buyer bought a used piano under a justifiable belief that it was new and used it for two years, rescission was held not to lie upon the then discovery of the facts. The property could not be returned in substantially as good condition as when bought and the demand came after a reasonable time. 

Donovan v. Aeolian Co., 270 N. Y. 267 

Peterson v. Guarino, 221 A. D. 146, 223 N. Y. S. 107.

Acceptance does not waive any rights one may have because of the other party's breach of warranty.

Personal Property Law, § 130 

Should the seller refuse to take back the goods, the buyer can hold the goods as bailee with a lien for the purchase money. The buyer may exercise a right of resale in the same way as the seller when the latter has a right to resell. (See supra, pages 311-2) The sale must take place within a reasonable time as the seller cannot be held liable for charges for a longer period. 

Jones v. Healy, 237 A. D. 264, 261 N. Y. S. 464 

C. D. Brown v. Darling, 238 A. D. 487, 264 N. Y. S. 792.

The acceptance of an instalment of the merchandise does not preclude the purchaser from asserting that the undelivered balance is defective. The retention of the goods received, without comment as to their defective condition, does not impose any liability upon the defendant to take the balance of the merchandise, if it did not satisfy the requirements of the contract.* 

Foster v. Fox, 124 Misc. 740, 209 N. Y. S. 230.

Damages arising from the use of the article after the discovery of the breach cannot be recovered. 

Standard Oil Co. v. Boyle, 237 A. D. 471, 261 N. Y. S. 512.

X, a wholesaler, sells goods to A, a retailer, and it is within the contemplation of the parties that goods are being bought for the purpose of specific resales. The goods are warranted to be of a certain quality. A sells the goods to Y and Z, giving the same warranties to them as X gave to him. It is then found that the goods were *For the damages for breach of warranty, see ante page 175 Chapter on Damages.

of an inferior quality. Y and Z bring suit against A for breach of warranty. The court held that A can recover from X for breach of the similar warranty as well as the cost of defending suits brought against him by the third parties arising out of the resale. The expenses incurred for the defenses are to be pleaded as specific damages.

Lamborn v. Czarnikow-Rionda Co. 221 A. D. 737, 225 N. Y. S. 228. 

(2) Delivery of Wrong Quantity.-Where too little is delivered, the buyer may reject the delivery. Rejection includes notification of the fact to the seller, but not redelivery to him. But if the buyer accepts what has been sent, knowing it to be less than the amount ordered and that the rest is not forthcoming, he pays the proportionate contract price.

If the buyer has disposed of the goods before he knows that the seller does not intend to perform his contract in full, the buyer need pay only the reasonable value of the goods disposed of. 

Where too much is delivered, the buyer can reject the delivery or take out the correct amount, or accept all, in which case he pays at the contract rate.

If the goods delivered contain both the kind of material ordered and kind not ordered, he may reject all or accept what he ordered. 

Where there has been a defective delivery and the position of the buyer has not been affected to his detriment, the seller may correct the delivery within the contract period and meet the contract's terms. (3) Refusal or Failure to Deliver.-If title has passed, but the seller wrongfully will not ship the goods, the buyer can sue in conversion, and get the market value of the goods at the time of the conversion. If stocks are the subject of sale, he gets the highest market value within a reasonable time after knowledge of the conversion.

Personal Property Law § 147; Mayer v. Monzo 221 N.Y. 442 

Where title has not passed, there is no conversion and the buyer can sue for damages. The measure of damages is the difference between the contract price and the market value at the time and place they ought to have been delivered. If no time for delivery was fixed, then at the time of the refusal to deliver. If there is no market value at the place of delivery, the value of the goods at the time fixed for delivery is to be shown by the best evidence possible. A neighboring market value would be competent evidence, making due allowance for the cost of transportation between points. 

Schopflacher v. Zimmerman 240 N.Y. 507 (4) Right to Inspect. It is the general rule that title to future goods does not pass until the buyer has had a chance to inspect them unless the seller has been authorized to appropriate the goods to the contract before delivery in which case the authorization is equivalent to a waiver of the right to inspect. When there has been no such authorization title does not pass if the buyer refuses to inspect the goods and accepts them. Should the goods be rejected be-

cause of the seller's refusal to permit examination, title does not pass, although the goods do comply with the contract. 

Personal Property Law, § 128, Subd. 2 

Glass Co. v. Misroch, 239 N. Y. 475 

Beals v. Hirsch, 214 A. D. 86, affd. 242 N. Y. 529.

Where the contract requires delivery to the buyer's place, the opportunity to inspect is a condition precedent to the passing of title. 

Where title has passed before delivery to the buyer and upon inspection he discovers that the goods do not conform to the contract, he may revest title in the seller by giving prompt notice of rejection. 

Unless otherwise previously agreed, there is no right to examine in a C.O.D. transaction. Where the buyer must pay before inspection, he is entitled to recover the payment made, if on inspection the goods do not comply with the contract. The action is one for money had and received. 

Liebovitz v. Rosenberg, 213 A. D. 143, 210 N. Y. S. 145.

Entire and Divisible Contracts of Sale 

A contract is entire when the parties intend that the promise by one party is conditional upon entire performance of his part by the other. It is severable when the part to be performed by one consists of several distinct and separate items, and the price to be paid by the other is apportioned to each item, or left to be implied by law. 

Portfolio v. Rubin, 233 N. Y. 439.

Where there is a contract to sell goods to be delivered in stated installments, which are to be separately paid for, and the seller makes defective deliveries in respect of one or more installments, or the buyer neglects or refuses to take delivery of or pay for one or more installments, it depends in each case on the terms of the contract and the circumstances of the case whether the breach of contract is so material as to justify the injured party in refusing to proceed further and sue for damages for breach of the entire contract, or whether the breach is severable, giving rise to a claim for compensation, but not to a right to treat the whole contract as broken. 

Personal Property Law, § 126.

SURETYSHIP 

Nature of the Guaranty

A surety is one who undertakes to answer for the debt or default of another. His liability arises as soon as D's debt is due. 

A guarantor of payment is one who undertakes unconditionally that the debtor will pay. His liability arises as soon as D defaults. 

No notice of default need be given to the guarantor of payment. 

In re Simmons' Will, 213 A. D. 32, 209 N. Y. S. 724.

A guarantor of collection undertakes to pay if D does not and cannot be made to pay. His liability arises after C has obtained a judgment against D and execution has been returned unsatisfied. 

He must get notice of D's default within a reasonable time after the default. In addition, an unreasonable delay by C in enforcing his legal remedies will release the guarantor of collection. 

Even in the absence of collusion a judgment against D entered by consent or upon default is only prima facie evidence against S, and the latter may establish affirmatively that D was not liable. 

Brescia Const. Co. v. Walart C. Co., 245 A. D. 105, 281 N. Y. S. 43.

An agreement to act as surety for the benefit of a particular C is a "special guaranty" limited to this C. C cannot assign his rights so that S would be bound to the assignee. If, however, a cause of action has once arisen against S in favor of C, C may assign this cause of action.

Very often the nature of the guaranty contemplates a continual relationship between C and D for which S expresses his intention to stand good. A letter sent by S to C stating, "I will be responsible for what stock M. E. McKee (D) has had or may want hereafter to the amount of $500," was held to contemplate a continuous business and a standing credit up to $500.

Likewise, "I hereby guarantee the account of Ira Margolies up to $500." The guaranty continues until notice of its withdrawal. It is to be observed that where an existing obligation of D is renewed by C on the strength of a new guaranty by S and S guarantees "the claim now existing or which may hereafter arise including rcnewals," S remains liable until the amount is paid even though there be renewals after S revokes his guaranty. 

Corn Exchange Bank v. Gifford, 268 Ñ. Y. 153 

Gates v. McKee, 13 N. Y. 232 

Levy v. Margolies, 152 Misc. 367, 273 N. Y. S. 327.

With every sale by C to D, there arises a distinct and separate unilateral contract. The offer by S may be withdrawn before any specific sale has been made. *In this discussion "S" represents the surety or guarantor, "D" the debtor, and "C" the creditor. 317

Guaranties have been divided into two classes. The first is where the entire consideration passes wholly at one time; the other where it passes at different times and is separable or divisible. The former are not revocable by the guarantor and are not affected by his death. The latter, on the contrary, may be revoked as to subsequent transactions by the guarantor upon notice to that effect and are determined by his death. It is wholly irrelevant whether or not the other parties acquire notice of the death. 

Amer. Chain Co. v. Arrow Grip Co., 134 Misc. 321, 235 N. Y. S. 228.

The Formation of the Relationship 

The same qualifications necessary to allow one to be a party to an ordinary contract exist in the contract of suretyship. The privity, of course, exists between C and S, and not between D and S. A promise to guarantee the account of another, like every promise requires the support of consideration paid or promised, in order that an enforceable contract may have been formed. 

Witshafd v. Brody, 257 N. Y. 97.

Where a contract of guaranty is entered into concurrently with the principal obligation, a consideration which supports the principal contract supports the subsidiary one. 

Jonas v. Michlin 220 A.D. 649, 222 N.Y.S. 442

Where a guaranty of payment is made subsequent to the creation of the debt between D and C, the consideration of the original extension of credit to D will not support the guaranty, as it is a past consideration. Thus, if D already owes C $1,000, and then S writes "I will personally guarantee the payment of the amount of $1,000 owing by D to C," S cannot be held to the written promise, in the absence of consideration.* 

Sun Oil Co. v. Heller, 248 N. Y. 28.

No notice of acceptance by C is needed to complete the contract. 

S's offer to be a surety is turned into a contract when C acts on it by advancing money to D or in any other way agreed upon. Of course, if S stipulates that he is to receive notice of acceptance before his liability is to attach, that notice must first be given. 

The Statute of Frauds 

Every undertaking of a surety or guarantor must be evidenced by a memorandum in writing. This defense of the Statute of Frauds, to avail the defendant, must be pleaded. It is an affirmative defense. 

The memorandum must contain all the substantial and material terms of the contract including the consideration. 

Standard Oil Co. v. Koch 260 N.Y. 150

The promise of the surety, in order to come within the statute, must be made to C. A promise by S to D that he will pay D's debt is not within the statute, because it is a contract of indemnity. Contracts of indemnity need not be in writing. 

Block v. Greenfield 137 Misc. 573, 143 N.Y.S. 117 *See ante page 117 as to the effect of past consideration under the 1941 amendment,

SURETY SHIP 

319 Note that in order for a contract of suretyship to exist, there must be an obligation which runs from D to C, and for which obligation S agrees to stand good. One who undertakes to pay for something which is given to D, is not a surety, because no credit was ever extended to D and D undertook no obligation. There was, therefore, no debt owing by D for which one could be surety. This promise to pay is not within the Statute of Frauds. The same result would follow if S and D jointly promised to pay for what C gave D. The obligations of S and D would both be original obligations. 

Maddock v. Root 150 N.Y. 561

Kennedy v. Dzengielowski 131 Misc. 635, affc. N.Y. 520 

Defenses of the Surety 

(1) Payment. If D's debt is paid or a tender is made, or D defeats C in C's suit for the debt alleged to be due, that absolutely frees S. It is a defense of payment. S, however, is not relieved of liability on account of a debt of D upon the latter's discharge in bankruptcy, even though C accepted the part payment allotted him in the bankruptcy proceedings. 

Union Trust Co. v. Willsea 275 N.Y. 164 (2) Fraud and Duress.-Where C, by actual or passive fraud induces D to enter into a valid contract, and S, in ignorance of this fraud, agrees to be surety for D, S is liable so long as D permits his contract with C to stand, even though he originally was entirely ignorant of the fraud, and D deliberately refused to use his defense.

If C gets S to be a surety and C knows something about D, e.g.: acts of embezzlement or of moral delinquency, which if known to S would deter S from becoming a surety, C's concealment of these facts discharges S of liability. 

Phillips v. U.S.F. & G.Co. 200 A.D. 208, affd. 234 N.Y. 618

If the obligation of D was obtained under duress, S can set up that defense against C, even though D does not. In this respect it differs from the rule in cases of fraud. 

Osborn v. Robbins 36 N.Y. 365 

(3) Illegality of Contract.-If the contract between C and D is illegal or contrary to public policy, the suretyship obligation is void.

In this connection it should be noted that S cannot interpose as a defense the claim that the transaction between D and C was usurious. This defense can be asserted only by the borrower. 

Sturman v. Lomor Realty 148 Misc. 277, 265 N.Y.S. 564

Faber v. Siegel 158 Misc. 722, 286 N.Y.S. 974 (4) Alteration of Original Contract.-Alteration of the contract between C and D releases S. If S had issued a bond to C covering D in his employment as bookkeeper, his promotion to job of teller would discharge S. The same result would follow if a contract, between C and D involving 1000 feet of lumber were changed to 1200 feet; or if a bank (S) guaranteed payment by D for "dried grapes" and the bill of landing called for "raisins," S would be justified in

refusing to pay. Although both articles may be subject to the same influences, the subject-matter is apparently different, and this appears to be material enough to discharge S. The increase or decrease of the risk is not important. The contract of a surety is strictissimi juris and is not to be extended beyond the express terms. 

This rule of strictissimi juris applies to the application of the contract rather than to its interpretation. 

Herskovitz Fur Co. v. Hollander 138 Misc. 456, affd. 257 N.Y. 606 

Bank of Italy v. Merchants' Nat'l Bank 236 N.Y. 106.

Where, however, the contract itself is not changed, but C has remitted or agreed to remit part of the performance due from D without changing its character e.g: by lessening the amount of rent to be paid under a guaranteed lease, or by providing for a lower rate of interest, S is not thereby discharged. A lowering of the interest rate together with a change of installment payments from semi-annually to quarter-annually would release the surety 

Becker v. Faber 280 N.Y. 146 

Greenwich Bank v. Eckford Realty Co. 268 A.D. 195

Where the surety has so acted as to consent, even orally, to a change in the original obligation, he will not be relieved. 

M. M. Metal Product Corp. v. April 251 N.Y. 146 

(5) Extension of Time.-A binding agreement by C without the consent of S, to give D additional time releases S.* Whether or not 

S is damaged is immaterial. But if C so agreed to extend time and reserved his rights against S, S is not discharged. If S is made to pay, he can then sue D and get back his money, for D would not have the defense against S that he would have against C. 

Nat'l Park Bank v. Koehler 204 N.Y. 174

Payment by D of part of the payment then due to C for a promise to extend time, does not release S because there was no valid consideration for the extension agreement. 

Dussault v. Wellman 130 Misc. 614, 224 N.Y.S. 321 (6) Refusal to Proceed to Collect Debt.-Failure by C to sue D then solvent, does not discharge S even though D later becomes insolvent unless during solvency S expressly gave C a clear and explicit request to C to sue D on the latter's default and C refused.** 

Pain v. Packard 13 John. 174 

Nat'l. Sav. Bank v. Fermac Co. 241 A.D. 204, affd. 266 N.Y. 443 *Under the statute, a mere agreement in writing between the creditor and debtor to extend payment to a definite or determinable future time is enforceable without consideration. But note that a surety is not released because of the statutory extension of time to pay the mortgage principal of mortgages executed before July 1, 1932.

The general rule is that the receipt of interest in advance upon a note is prima facie evidence of a binding contract to forbear and delay the time of payment for the time for which interest has been paid. In the absence of any rebutting evidence, it is conclusive. N.Y. Life Ins. Co. v. Casey, 178 N.Y. 381. **The obligation of C to proceed diligently against collateral or against D when called upon, does not extend to a negotiable document. Thus, å known accommodation maker, primarily liable with the real maker, was not permitted to set up an equitable defense that the holder did not, upon default, sell the collateral. Citizens Natl. Bank v. Parkinson 266 A. D. 1055.
