321 (7) Release of Security.-Suppose that C, holding D's property as security, releases some of it without getting other property substituted. S is discharged pro tanto. If C releases half the security S is discharged to that extent. The same result would follow if there is a release by C of one of a group of sureties; the remaining sureties are released to the extent that such released surety would have been liable to contribute to his cosureties. 

Newburger v. Lubell 266 N.Y. 4 (8) Personal Defenses.-Should D have a defense against C which is personal to D, S cannot avail himself of it. Examples of such defenses are: D's incapacity to contract; D's discharge in bankruptcy barring suit by C against him; completion of a composition agreement with creditors. Failure of consideration from C to D is a defense to S.

Klipstein v. Lipschitz 130 Misc. 291, 223 Ñ.Y.S. 822 

Forsythe v. U.S. Fidelity 130 Misc. 569, 24 N.Y.S. 330 

If after C has executed his part of the contract with D, S dies, his estate is responsible as a surety. 

A judgment which has been obtained against D is not even evidence against S unless the latter had notice of the suit and an opportunity to defend. The exception is where the covenant is to indemnify against the consequences of a suit. 

Adams v. U.S.F. & G.Co. 239 A.D. 525, affd. 264 N. Y. 550 (9) Statute of Limitations.-The statute runs in favor of a surety from the time his liability becomes fixed. Any payment by D which extends the statute against himself does not affect S. The converse, that a payment by S does not extend the statute against D, is also true. 

People's Trust Co. v. O'Neil 273 N.Y. 312

It is also true that where there are two sureties in whose favor the statute has run, a payment by one will not affect the other. But if the statute had run in favor of one, and the other still bound had paid, he could get contribution in equity from the one in whose favor the statute had run, because the right to contribution does not arise until the payment is made. 

Hard v. Mingle 206 N.Y. 179, 184 

Rights of the Surety (1) Contribution.-To apply the doctrine of contribution, the sureties must be bound to the same principal and for the same engagement, although not necessarily in the same instrument. 

Indemnity Co. v. Amer. Surety Co. 239 A.D. 522, 268 N.Y.S. 203

Suppose S1, S2 and S3 are co-sureties on D's debt for $3,000. On 

D's default the creditor can sue any one of the three sureties for the whole $3,000. The one who pays can then collect $1,000 from each of the other two, for each was responsible for one-third, they being three equal co-sureties.

It is entirely immaterial whether they knew of each other when they became sureties; when they find out, they can get contribution. 

Suppose, however, that S1 was a surety for $1,000, S2 for $2,000

and S3 for $3,000. SI's share should therefore be one-sixth. All that 

S1 pays above one-sixth he can get from S2 and S3, they paying twosixths and three-sixths respectively. But his right to contribution arises after he has paid more than his pro rata share. Therefore the 

Statute of Limitations as to his right of contribution begins to run when payment of more than his share is made. 

Suppose S2 became bankrupt after S1 paid the whole debt, each owing one-third. Does S3 have to pay one-half to S1 or only his original one-third share? In equity, S3 would have to pay one-half. 

Insolvent co-sureties are not counted in contribution. In law, S3 would have to pay only one-third. 

Where several makers share in the consideration on a joint and several note, one maker is entitled to contribution from the others, but in the case of a note given where one signs as a borrower and the others co-makers, without receiving any of the proceeds, they are merely sureties for the borrower. 

Salzberg v. Deutsch 150 Misc. 870, 270 N.Y.S. 595 

Where one of two sureties is a defendant he may bring in the other as an additional party defendant since he may be entitled to contribution. (2) Subrogation. If S pays to C the entire unpaid balance of D's debt in full, S is entitled to all the rights of C against D, and he can proceed against D. This is the right of subrogation. If C held any securities, S can get them, or their value if C lost them. Actual payment, and not liability to pay, confers the right of subrogation. 

American Surety Co. v. Gerold 7 N.Y.S. (2nd) 447 

American Surety v. Palmer 240 N.Y. 63

The doctrine of subrogation is of equitable and not contractual origin. Though it is invoked to obtain substantial justice in compelling the person primarily liable to pay his debt, it cannot be invoked against one whose equities are equal to or greater than those of the party seeking to be subrogated. Thus, a surety of a surety, though compelled to pay the creditor, is not entitled to be substituted in place of the creditor in order to enforce payment against the principal debtor, if the latter has paid his immediate surety. 

Bell v. Greenwood 229 A.D. 550, 242 N.Y.S. 149

It should be noted that the surety is subrogated only to those rights and remedies of which the creditor might have availed himself for the collection of that debt. He is not subrogated to the rights of the creditor wholly disconnected with the debt. 

American Surety Co. v. Islip 268 A.D. 92 

(3) Indemnity. In addition to rights of subrogration, S has a right to indemnity after he pays D's debt in whole or in part. The fact that C could not sue D because of any defense D had against C, or because of a release, does not mean that S loses indemnity rights. 

Since a surety's cause of action against the principal for reimbursement does not arise until the surety pays the principal's debt, a surety in a suit against him by the creditor is not entitled to join the principal debtor as a co-defendant, for if the joinder were per-

SURETY SHIP 

323 mitted, the surety might thus recover indemnity from the debtor without paying the judgment against himself. 

Scripture v. Buckley 137 Misc, 155, 241 N.Y.S. 635

Suppose D defaults on a $5,000 debt. S settles for $3,000, and then sues for the whole $5,000. His rights being indemnity rights, he can recover only what he paid out-$3,000. (4) Marshalling Assets.-The rule with respect to marshalling of assets has been defined as one "which courts of equity sometimes invoke to compel creditor who has the right to take his debt out of either of two funds to resort to that one of them which will not interfere with or defeat the rights of another creditor who has recourse to only one of these funds." 

In re Van Zandt's Estate 142 Misc. 663, 255 N.Y.S. 359

Suppose D and S both give securities as collateral. D defaults and 

C sells S's securities. C is liable in conversion, for knowing that the securities were not the debtor's, C should have used D's first. 

This equitable doctrine of marshalling assets is seen in the following case. T owns two lots. He mortgages lots 1 and 2 to E and places an additional mortgage on lot 1, with F as the mortgagee. 

There is a default in payment and E tries to foreclose on lot 1, rather than on lot 2. B can ask equity to compel E to exhaust the remedy against lot 2 on which he alone held the mortgage. F is to be protected. 

Farmer's Loan & Trust Co. v. Kip 192 N.Y. 285 

Ingalls v. Morgan 10 N.Y. 178 

Diamond v. Tau Holding Corp. 131 Misc. 446, 226 N.Y.S. 129

TORTS 

Who Are Liable for Their Torts-Exceptions

All persons including corporations are liable for their torts. 

There are, however, certain definite limitations to this rule which we shall first consider. (a) Insane Persons.-An insane person is liable for his torts, except that whenever malice is a necessary constituent of the tort for which an insane person is sued, the insane person is not liable. 

Williams v. Hays 143 N.Y. 442 (b) Infants.*-When an infant is of such tender years as to lack the experience which would enable him to realize the presence of a threatening danger, the infant is said to be non sui jūris, and as a matter of law cannot be guilty of contributory negligence. Consequently an infant is not guilty of contributory negligence if he has exercised the degree of care which may reasonably be expected from a child of like age, intelligence and experience. The cases seem to hold that an infant under four is in all cases non sui juris as a matter of law. An infant, five weeks over four was held presumably non sui juris. There is a rebuttable presumption that a child of twelve or over is presumed to be sui juris and that a child less than twelve is non sui juris. It is the duty of an infant to exercise a degree of care commensurate with his age and capacity. With the approach of maturity a greater degree of care may be expected. 

Gloshinsky v. Bergen Milk Co. 279 N.Y. 54 

Jacobs v. Koehler 208 N. Y. 416; Day v. Johnson 265 A.D. 383 

Meyer v. Inguangiato 258 A.D. 331, 10 N.Y.S. (2nd) 672

The negligence of his parents or other custodian, is not to be imputed to the child in an action brought by the latter for personal injuries.

Domestic Relations Law § 73 

If an infant deceives an adult into making a contract with him, the adult cannot maintain an action in deceit if the gist of the damages in the action is a breach of the contract made with the infant. To hold an infant for tort of this nature, the tort must be a positive wrong itself. The test is, Can the infant be held liable without directly enforcing his contract? If so, he is liable for the tort.

An unemancipated infant has no cause of action in tort for unintentional personal injury against his parents, but he may maintain a tort action against a grandparent. A parent has no cause for action in tort for personal injuries against an unemancipated minor child, but each has cause of action against the other if the child is emancipated. A responsible parent is not immune to suit where there is *For a discussion of Infant as trespassers, see infra page 334. 324

325 injury to the infant's property. An infant of sixteen has been held liable for a tort committed against her younger brother. 

Rozell v. Rozell 281 N.Y. 106; Cannon v. Cannon 287 N.Y. 425 

Sorrentino v. Sorrentino 248 N.Y. 626

Lo Galbo v. Lo Galbo 138 Misc. 485, 246 N.Y.S. 565 

(c) Parents.-There is no liability on the part of a parent, as such, for the tort of a child. There are situations in which the parent may be held liable to the stranger. (1) Where the parent is negligent in intrusting to the child an instrument which, because of its nature or purpose, is so dangerous as to constitute in the hands of a child, an unreasonable risk to others. (2) Where the parent is negligent in intrusting to the child an instrument not inherently dangerous, but which is likely to become dangerous because of the known propensities of the child. (3) Where the parent fails to reasonably restrain the child from vicious conduct, when the parent knows of the child's propensities toward such conduct.* 

Steinberg v. Cauchois 249 A.D. 518, 293 N.Y.S. 147 (d) Sovereign Powers.-Sovereign powers, such as the State and 

Federal government, cannot be sued in tort without their consent. 

The State of New York by statute has waived immunity from liability for the tort caused by the malfeasance or negligence of its officers or employees. The claim in tort must be filed with the clerk of the court and served upon the attorney general within 90 days after the accrual of the claim. If the claimant files a written notice of intention to sue within 90 days, the claim may be filed within 2 years after the accrual of tht claim. 

Court of Claims Act §§ 8, 11, 12 

The state is liable for damages suffered from defects in state highways from May 1st to November 15th in any year.

Highway Law § 58 

The Court of Claims cannot entertain a suit by the state against an individual, but it may entertain the state's counterclaim against the plaintiff and grant affirmative judgment based upon it. 

Gross v. State 243 N.Y. 629

Frequently the State assumes to act through a corporation organized for the purpose of carrying out a government function. In that case the State assumes responsibility for the act of such agent. Thus the State may create a state system of parks and thereby subject itself to liability for negligence of its officers and employees; or, with like liability, it may provide for the imprisonment of young delinquents and commit their custody to an authorized institution for the purpose. The agent doing a wrong cannot hide behind immunity because it it doing governmental work. Since the state as prin- 

A father's action for loss of services is to be construed as an action for personal injury and is barred if not commenced within 3 years after it has oc curred. No period is tolled because of the infancy of the child. Constantinides v. Manhattan Transit Co. 264 A.D. 147.

cipal has waived immunity, the agent cannot be in a better position. And where, instead of acting directly through such corporations the state delegates the governmental power to an independent entity not acting as agent of the state, e:g: a school board or a corporation to take care of delinquent children, there is no authority for making claim against the state, but the agency exercising the delegated authority must respond to the injured for its own actionable conduct.

Panteas v. Saratoga Springs Authority 255 A‚D 426 Bloom v. Jewish Board of Guardians 286 N.Y. 349 

(e) Institutions.-Hospitals and universities, whether public or private,* are not liable to any beneficiary or patient for the negligence on the part of doctors, nurses, dentists or teachers. If a patient is injured because of the negligence of a nurse in-using a caustic solution instead of the anaesthetic called for by the attending physician, the hospital is not liable for the tort. If a student is hurt through negligence of the teacher, the college is not liable. These employees are not regarded as servants and the doctrine of respondeat superior does not apply. The institution undertakes to supply others who will act on their own responsibility. Its only duty is to select functionaries with due care. ** 

Grawunder v. Beth Israel Hospital 242 A.D. 56, affå. 266 N.Y. 605 

Mills v. New York Hospital 242 A.D. 245, affd. 270 N.Y. 594 

Hamburger v. Cornell University 240 N.Y. 328

An institution is liable for its own negligence and the negligence of its agents acting in an administrative capacity. Thus a hospital is liable when a patient being driven in an ambulance is injured because of the fault of the driver. This would be true though the driver was a doctor.

Sheehan v. N. Country Community Hospital 273 N.Y. 163 

The rule with respect to institutions must not be confused with the rule applicable to persons who commit torts in the execution of gratuitous acts. The rule stated in the preceding paragraph is limited to institutions.*** One who assumes to act, even though gratuitously, becomes subject to the duty of acting carefully if he acts at all. Marks v. Nambil Realty Co. 245 N.Y. 256 Joint Tort Feasors 

Two persons cannot be sued as joint tort-feasors where it is alleged that one defendant caused death by its negligent maintenance of a fence, an act alleged in the complaint as an independent and exclusive act of negligence, and that another defendant caused death by a later negligent surgical treatment, also set forth as an independent and disconnected act. Where, however, the complaint alleges that the acts of two defendant railroads, together with the act of another defendant, all contributed to the damaged condition of goods on arrival at their destination, these defendants are properly joined. 

Adler v. Blau 241 N. Y. 7; Kalm v. Westmoreland 129 Misc. 238.

Where wrongdoers have not acted in concert, and the act or neglect of each results in damage, the liability of the wrongdoers is several. So where several parties polluted a stream, each one separately from his own premises and independently of each other, each owner is liable separately for the injury done by his own acts. 

Chipman v. Palmer 77 N.Y. 51

If the plaintiff releases one of several joint tort-feasors, they all are released automatically, unless (1) the plaintiff, in releasing the one, expressly reserved his right to sue the others (the release in such case is really an agreement with him not to sue him); (2) or unless it can be shown that for some reason the release is void. A discharge in bankruptcy of one tort-feasor is no defense in an action against the other. 

Gilbert v. Finch 173 N. Y. 455; Findlay v. Findlay 178 Misc. 855 

MccNamara v. Eastman Kodak Co. 232 N.Y. 18 

Poswick v. Cutten 258 A.D. 218, affd. 283 N.Y. 660

A jury cannot apportion the liability for damages caused by joint tort-feasors. If a jury should bring back a verdict against defendant 

X for $4,500.00 and against the joint defendant Y for $500.00, the court, even in the absence of the jury, can be asked to have the verdict read as a verdict for $4,500.00—the larger, not the combined amount against X and Y. 

Farber v. Demino 254 N.Y. 363

No judgment over may be awarded in favor of one joint tortfeasor against another where the negligent act of the party seeking such indemnity concurred in the wrong which caused the damage. 

Unless it is first established that the party against whom the indemnity is sought was primarily liable and the party seeking indemnity free from negligent participation, there is no recovery over.** 

Smith v. 167th St. Corp. 264 A. D. 570. *A gratuitous promisor who wholly omits to perform his promise is not liable, notwithstanding the promisee may have sustained damage. Responsibility attaches only when an attempt to perform is made and there is misfeasance. 

Comfort v. McCorkle 149 Misc. 826, 268 N.Y.S. 192. 

**This statement does not refer to the right of contribution under Section 

211a of the Civil Practice Act.

Proximate Cause 

Before any recovery for a tort can be had, there must be (1) a violation by the defendant of a right belonging to the plaintiff, and (2) this violation must be a proximate cause of the injuries sustained. If no hazard to the plaintiff was apparent to the eye of ordinary vigilance, an act seemingly innocent and harmless, with reference to the plaintiff, does not become a tort though it happened to be a wrong with reference to one other than the plaintiff. Thus if 

A jostles B, in a large crowd, and as a result of this jostling a bomb carried by C, standing in the crowd, is dropped injuring X fifty feet away, X has no claim against A. The "eye of vigilance" could not perceive the damage. Where, however, A drives at a reckless speed through a crowded street, the eye of vigilance perceives the risk of damage, and though the force set in motion should pursue an unexpected path, A would be liable. Likewise, if A shoots in a place where people are likely to be present, he is liable for injuries sustained by one unexpectedly being hit. The act of the defendant may be one of commission, or it may be the omission of an obligation or duty which the defendant has left undischarged and which he owed the plaintiff.

Scott v. Del Lack. W. R. Co. 222 A.D. 409, 226 N.Y.S. 287 

O'Neill v. City of Port Jervis 253 N. Y. 423 

Palsgraf v. Long Island R. R. Co. 248 N.Y. 339

The determination of proximate cause is not to be made after the occurrence. The real point is whether men of average prudence and ordinary care would have anticipated the accident under the cir cumstances. The determination is left to the jury. The law does not impose a duty to guard against that which does not naturally suggest itself to a careful and prudent man as something which should be guarded against and which is very unlikely to occur. In one case, the plaintiff guest, sitting in the lobby of the defendant's hotel, was hurt when a 200-pound lamp fell upon him when another guest tilted his chair against the lamp. The defendant was held not negligent for its failure to have the lamp securely fastened to the floor and to anticipate the misuse by a guest of an article of common use. 

It was not shown that the lamp would have fallen with slight contact. But where the defendant negligently leaves stones in a public highway he is held to a duty to reasonably foresee that a passing automobile may strike a stone on the slant and cause it to fly through the air and hurt someone. 

Payne v. City of New York 277 N.Y. 393 

McKinney v. N. Y. Consol. R. Co. 230 N.Y. 194 

Polsey v. Waldorf-Astoria 220 A.D. 613, 222 N.Y.S. 273 cf. Halpin v. New York Railways 276 N.Y. 545

In one case, the defendant, in violation of a city ordinance, stored some boxes of nitro-glycerine caps upon public land. The containers were not marked. Two boys stole a box and then invited a third boy to come along. While carrying the box, it exploded and killed the third boy. It was held that the accident was not the proximate

TORTS 

329 result of leaving the boxes on the highway, and that new and unexpected causes intervened before the explosion. The chain of causation was broken. 

Perry v. Rochester Lime Co. 219 N.Y. 60 

Babcock v. Fitzpatrick 248 N.Y. 608

Where the plaintiff while eating pie in a restaurant, saw roaches imbedded in the bottom crust of the pie and became very ill, he was permitted to recover when the jury found that the physical injuries were the natural and proximate result of the restaurateur's negligence. 

Carroll v. N.Y. Pie Baking Co. 215 A.D. 240, 213 N.Y.S. 553

Under ordinary circumstances no one is chargeable with damages because he had not anticipated the commission of a crime by some third party. Even where bonds of a corporation, signed in blank by duly authorized officers, were stolen from the corporation by vant who had access to them, and sold to innocent purchasers, no recovery has been permitted against the corporation for its failure to safeguard the public from the hazard of being defrauded in such manner. 

Benenson v. Natl. Surety Co. 260 N.Y. 299

Where a trespasser does an act causing damage which would not be the proximate result of the act if he were not a trespasser, he is nevertheless liable. The intrusion is at the peril of the intruder. 

Van Alstyne v. Rochester Tel. Co. 163 Misc. 258, 296 N.Y.S. 726

Proximate Cause Without Liability 

(a) Inevitability of Damage-One is not responsible if the same harm would have resulted if all due care had been exercised, even though the one who caused the damage happened to have been negligent. Thus where a car skids and hits the barrier along the edge of the road, should the impact break the barrier and the car fall down an embankment, the owner cannot collect from the state if it can be shown that a barrier which was perfect in construction and quality would likewise have been broken. The state need not place a barrier along the road strong enough to support a car which crashes against it. If the barrier was obviously decayed and known to be so, the failure to replace it indicated an indifference toward the public's protection. This failure would be actionable negligence. The court has stated in such case that a sound barrier might or might not have averted the accident. 

Countrymen v. State 277 N.Y. 586 

(b) Contributory Negligence. If the plaintiff has been guilty of contributory negligence, no matter how slight, he cannot recover from the defendant for the latter's negligence. But there is no such thing as contributory negligence in vacuo. The contributory negligence, in order to defeat the plaintiff's claim, must be negligence that actually contributes to the accident. 

Parillo v. Friss 129 Misc. 340, 221 N.Y.S. 418

This rule does not apply where the fault of one is purely constructive or vicarious. Indemnification will be allowed in favor of

the constructive tort-feasor and against the one whose fault is actual or personal. So where a master has been held in damages for the fault of his servant, the master may obtain judgment over against the servant. A municipality held because of a defect in the street, responsibility for which is imposed by statute upon an abutting owner, may recover against the latter.

Iroquois Gas Co. v. Intl. Ry. 240 A.D. 432, 270 N.Y.S. 197 

There is libality incurred by a defendant who creates a nuisance which causes damage which could have been averted only if the plaintiff had deprived himself of natural and appropriate privileges. Thus, if an owner of land casts noisome smells into the plaintiff's house, he cannot be heard to say that the plaintiff could have shut them out by closing doors and windows. This must not be taken to mean that in any action based on the nuisance of the defendant, the contributory negligence of the plaintiff is no defense. 

When a nuisance has its origin in negligence, one may not avert the consequences of his contributory negligence by affixing to the negligence of the wrongdoer the label of nuisance. Unless there be the deprivation of natural and appropriate rights, where the substance of the wrong is negligence, the plaintiff, though pleading nuisance, is under a duty to show care proportioned to the danger. If the danger is seen, there must be an effort to avoid it. If unseen it becomes a question whether under the circumstances the average person would perceive the danger and escape it. 

MccFarlane v. City of Niagara Falls 247 N.Y. 340

There are some circumstances in which the fact that the plaintiff was guilty of contributory negligence will not aid the defendant to defeat recovery by the plaintiff. Subdivisions (c) and (d) which follow are examples. (c) Doctrine of the Last Clear Chance.—This doctrine is brought out clearly in a recent case: The plaintiff was running diagonally across the street, the defendant chauffeur had a clear view of the plaintiff for at least 100 feet, but made no attempt to check or stop his car. Although the plaintiff was clearly negligent, he was allowed to recover, for the exercise of a reasonable amount of care by the defendant chauffeur under these circumstances would have avoided the accident.

Kunze v. Pictorial Review Co. 246 N. Y. 600 

If the plaintiff has put himself in a dangerous position negligently, even though the defendant is negligent in not seeing him, there is concurrent negligence, and the doctrine of the last clear chance does not apply. The doctrine, therefore, is never wakened into action unless and until there is brought home to the defendant to be charged with liability, a knowledge that another is in a state of present peril, in which event there must be reasonable effort to counteract the peril and avert its consequences. 

Woloszyowski v. N.Y. Central 254 N.Y. 206 

Wright v. Union Ry. Co. 224 A.D. 55, affd. 250 N.Y. 526 (d) Violation of a Prohibitory Statute.-An example will make

TORTS 

331 clear this subdivision. The Statute (Labor Law § 146) provides that no child under 16 shall operate an elevator. If a child so employed under that age is injured in the course of his work, the contributory negligence of the child could not defeat a recovery. 

Karpeles v. Heine 227 N.Y. 74 (e) Assumption of Risk.-Where the plaintiff has assumed the risk of harm through the acts or omissions of the defendant, a plaintiff cannot recover though he has been free from contributory negligence. In this type of case the defendant really cannot be considered to have been negligent. To invoke the doctrine of assumption of risk there must be an appreciation of the danger by the plaintiff. 

McEvoy v. City of New York 266 A. D. 445, affd. 292 N. Y. 654.

Invitees, Business Visitors, Licensees and Trespassers 

One in possession of premises is bound to use reasonable care and prudence, commensurate with the hazard to be apprehended, to keep his premises in such a condition that those who enter therein at his invitation, whether adults or infants, shall not unnecessarily or unreasonably be exposed to an unusual danger of which he knows or ought to know. He is not however an insurer of the safety of those whom he invites to visit his property. 

DiBiase v. Ewart 228 A.D. 407, affd. 255 N.Y. 620

Whenever a person enters upon the premises of another for a purpose connected with the business of the occupant of the premises, the person entering is a business visitor and is to be regarded as an invitee in so far as liability for injury is concerned. Thus the owner of a place of entertainment is charged with an affirmative positive obligation to know that the premises are safe for public use. Mere lack of knowledge of a defective condition is no excuse. 

When people accept his invitation and pay an admission fee, they have a right to assume he has furnished a safe place. A visitor to a sick patient in a hospital is ordinarily considered the latter's invitee. 

Greenfield v. Hospital Assn. 258 A.D. 352, 16 N.Y.S. (2nd) 729 

Riehl v. West Farms Co. 162 Misc. 47, 293 N.Y.S. 360 

Meiers v. Koch Brewery 229 N.Y. 10 

Heffron v. N.Y.C. & H. R. R. Co. 223 N.Y. 473 

Haefeli v. Woodrich Eng. Co. 255 N.Y. 442

If one has not been invited, but his presence upon the premises has not been forbidden by the owner, he is at most a licensee, who must take the premises as he found them. The owner's duty would be to abstain from acts which would amount to affirmative negligence. If an injury is sustained by reason of a mere defect in the premises, the owner is not liable. Mere darkness in a hallway at 9 in the morning, cannot be held an affirmative act of negligence so as to permit a bare licensee to recover for an injury suffered because of the lack of light. Where, however, there is a statutory duty in connection with the maintenance of premises, the owner owes even a licensee an observance of this duty. Thus when a peddler, who

visited the defendant's premises daily with the owner's knowledge to sell food to the employees, was injured by falling into an elevator shaft maintained in violation of the Labor Law, he was entitled to the benefit of the protection of the statute. 

Jolles v. 3720 Co. 163 Misc. 51, 296 N.Y.S. 354 

Stacy v. Shapiro 212 A.D. 723, 209 N.Y.S. 305

There is no duty owing to the trespasser except to abstain from intentional, reckless and wanton injury unless he maintains some hidden engine of destruction, such as spring guns or kindred devices upon his property. 

Mendelowitz v. Ñeisner 258 N.Y. 181

In determining the liability of a defendant to the plaintiff, one must consider the relationship of one to the other. The plaintiff may be a trespasser toward X, yet not toward the defendant. In one case, the plaintiff was riding on the rear end of a truck without permission of the owner. The truck collided with a trolley. It was held that the plaintiff was a trespasser as to the owner of the truck and the owner owed him only the duty of refraining from doing wilful or wanton injury. Whether the plaintiff was rightfully on the truck did not concern the car company. He was legally on the thoroughfare and the trolley company owed him the duty of exercising reasonable care. 

North v. David Donaldson Co., Inc. 131 Misc. 170, 226 N.Y.S. 382

The fact that the plaintiff operates an auto bus for the carriage of passengers, without lawful authority so to act as a carrier, does not make the auto bus a trespasser upon the public highway, and he can recover for damages to his bus, caused by negligence on the part of the defendant, unless such use caused the accident, for the plaintiff had the right to drive his bus on the street. Defendant railroad would be liable to a trespasser walking on its tracks, if it was negligent after his presence has been discovered. 

Aspinall v. City of New York 246 N.Y. 644 

Capitula v. N.Y.C.R.R. Co. 210 N.Y.S. 651, affð. 241 N.Y. 614

The rule of immunity of an owner of land for damages suffered by a trespasser, has not been extended to cases where the injured was a trespasser upon the land of a person other than the wrongdoer. Thus where a boy was injured by hot water expelled from a pipe which projected from the defendant's building and over adjoining premises, the defendant was not relieved from liability solely by the fact that the injured boy was then a trespasser on adjoining land. And where a defendant commits a wrongful act outside of his own premises, the effect of which is to injure a trespasser on his premises, there is liability. A trespasser in a house belonging to the defendant may have assumed the risk that the defendant's use of its land might endanger persons thereon. He did not assume the risk that such danger would arise from a condition existing several hundred feet away in the public street, heedlessly created by the defendant or any other person. 

Ehret v. Village of Scarsdale 269 N.Y. 198 

Wilson v. American Bridge Co. 74 A.D. 596

TORT S 333 Long continued acquiescence in a use by an owner does not become an invitation, so as to change the owner's responsibility from that owing to a trespasser of licensee to that owing an invitee. 

Panunzio v. New York 266 A.D. 9 Duty to Infants 

The obligation to infants is different from what it is to adults where the injury occurs off the premises of the defendant. Recognition must be taken of the fact that proclivities of children may draw them to dangerous objects. Thus it was held to be a negligent act permitting recovery, where an infant put his hand in an unguarded, uncovered kettle of hot tar on a street. The reason was that the defendant was negligent in keeping inherently dangerous articles near a place easily accessible to children. The defendant was bound to anticipate the possibilities of such results. 

Long v. City of Dunkirk 260 N.Y. 599 

Tierney v. N.Y. Dugan Bros. 288 N.Y. 16 

Ferrari v. N.Y. Central 244 A.D. 182, affd. 250 N.Y. 527

If the infant is a trespasser and comes in contact with a dangerous article, there is no recovery. And the rule applies though the object be near a public highway. If an infant plaintiff, playing on the defendant's lot, picks up some film left by the defendant, the defendant is not responsible for personal injuries to the plaintiff, which injuries result when this film is accidentally ignited by the plaintiff. These pieces of film were not inherently dangerous, but only became so when an entirely distinct act- the ignition-was effected.* 

Keenan v. Lawyers Mtge, Co. 254 A.D. 348, affd. 280 N.Y. 525

Beickert v. G. M. Laboratories 242 N.Y. 168 

O'Callaghan v. Commonwealth Eng. Corp. 247 N.Y. 127

Duties to The Public 

(a) Buildings. It is the duty of the duty of the owner of a building, abutting upon a public street, to maintain it in such condition that it does not become dangerous to the traveling public. 

He who maintains the building may be charged with knowledge of defects causing damage to the public, which reasonable inspection would disclose. This duty may be suspended by leasing the property to a tenant with exclusive possession. However, if he has covenanted with the tenant to make repairs or has reserved the right of entry for inspection and repair, he is liable to the passerby. This liability is not in contract since that runs only to the tenant. Note that a *Despite the expressions in the text that there is no liability to an infant trespasser, there is some justification in believing that there might be liability to an infant trespasser if all of these conditions exist: a very dangerous article is kept on the defendant's premises, near a highway, on which premises children have been accustomed to play and which article is easily accessible and the article is not used in connection with the defendant's business. This conclusion is gathered from an expression in Morse v. Buffalo Tank Company (280 

N.Y. at page 116) and considered together with the case of Travell v. Banneman 174 N.Y. 47 and Flaherty v. Metro 202 A.D. 583, affd. 235 N.Y. 605.

For discussion of cases involving infants, see Jaffy v. N. Y. Central 118 Misc. 147.

guest of the tenant in exclusive possession, cannot recover from the landlord for injuries sustained because of the covenant to repair. 

The reason a passer-by is in a different position under the covenant to repair is that the landlord's original duty to the public to maintain the structure in a safe condition and his retention of power to perform the duty, combine to make him liable. 

Appel v. Muller 262 N.Y. 278

Ford v. Grand Union Co. 268 N.Y. 243 

If a lessor rents the premises for a public use to which he knows they are unsuited, he remains liable for injuries resulting even from defects existing when the lessee took complete and exclusive possession. Thus a lessor was held liable for injuries resulting from a defect in a dock leased by him when he knew its unsuitability therefor; from a defective grand stand in a leased athletic park under similar condition; from a defective toboggan slide; from a defective boardwalk in an amusement park. 

Campbell v. Elsie S. Holding Co. 251 N.Y. 446

The owner of property not inherently dangerous, who does not knowingly permit others to put the property to a dangerous use, is not subject to any absolute duty to prevent unauthorized persons from putting it to a dangerous use.

Ford v. Grand Union Co. 268 N.Y. 243 

(b) Care of land.-The common law rule is that one is free to leave unmarked or unfenced the boundaries of his land. A person entering without permission is a trespasser. But where one maintains a dangerous condition so close to the public highway that a passerby may, by slight deviation, enter upon such land and suffer injury, liability is cast upon the person in control of the land. 

Bennett v. Mount Vernon 243 A.D. 119, 276 N.Y.S. 205 (c) Domestic Animals.-An owner of a domestic animal is not liable ipso facto for an injury caused by a bite of that animal. To attach liability it must be shown that the owner knew of the vicious propensities of the animals, or that with the exercise of due care the owner would have had such knowledge. Where, however, the animal attacked the plaintiff while trespassing on the latter's land, the plaintiff needn't prove the animal was vicious to the knowledge of the plaintiff. 

Muller v. McKesson 73 N.Y. 195 

Warsevecz v. Millo 258 A. D. 846, 15 N.Y.S. (2nd) 687. 

(d) Violation of Ordinances.-Where a statute imposes a duty for a special class not measured by the usual norm of what a reasonable prudent man would do under the same circumstances, rather than a standard of care, the duty is absolute. Proof of a disregard of that duty, e.g., to equip machinery at factories creating dust, with hoods and pipes to an exhaust fan (Labor Law § 299); to place lights on a vehicle at night; to muzzle a dog, establishes negligence as a matter of law. Similarly the violation of the Labor 

Law by the illegal employment in a business or service, of an infant under 16 is per se prima facie evidence of negligence if the infant is hurt. The usual standard of care is superseded by the standard en-

TORTS 

335 acted by the legislature. Lateral support of an adjacent building while shoring up land in the City of New York, is such statutory obligation, that its deprivation results in absolute liability, irrespective of negligence. The same thing is true when an action is based on a violation of the Farm and Market Law, i.e., sale of adulterated food. When, however, the statute defines in the interest of the general public, the degree of care which shall be exercised under specified circumstances, rather than specific duties toward a special class, a failure to comply with the requirements of an ordinance or statute is evidence of negligence and establishes liability only if there is a logical connection between the proven neglect of statutory duty and the alleged negligence. Therefore, the violation of an ordinance which prohibits swimming in a specified channel; the operation of a motor vehicle while under the age provided for drivers; the storing of gasoline without the required license; disregard of the statutory rule that pedestrians shall keep to the left of the center line of a highway, are all just evidences of negligence. 

Schmidt v. Merchants' Despatch Co. 270 N.Y. 287 

Walker v. Bradt 225 A.D. 415, 233 N.Y.S. 388 

Homin v. Cleveland & W. Corp. 281 N.Y. 484 

Friedman v. Beck 250 A.D. 87, 293 N.Y.S. 649 

Corbett v. Scott 243 N. Y. 66 

Morse v. Buffalo Tank Corp. 280 N.Y. 110 

Tecla v. Ellman 280 N.Y. 124; Warney v. Bd. of Education 290 N.Y. 329 

Kennet v. Sossnitz 260 A. D. 759. affd. 286 N. Y. 649.

In applying the principle to the case of domestic animals, the following case may be mentioned: An ordinance of the city states that a horse is not to be left unbridled or without having the wheels of the wagon to which it is harnessed tied together. It would be evidence of negligence if a horse were left unattended or untied. If such horse stepped upon the sidewalk and bit the plaintiff, the plaintiff can recover, in the absence of contributory negligence, upon the theory of the defendant's negligence. 

Turner v. Craighead 155 N.Y. 631; Brown v. Shyne 242 N.Y. 176 

Koffler v. Amer. Ry Express 126 Misc. 838, 214 N.Y.S. 787 

Words Negligently Spoken

In some cases, words negligently spoken may justify recovery for proximate damage caused by faith in their accurancy. A bailee negligently misstating to his bailor where his goods are stored, knowing that the inquiry is made for insurance purposes, is liable for resulting loss. A public weigher hired by the seller to weigh goods, realizing that the buyer would rely on his statement in payment therefor, was held liable for erroneous statements concerning the weight. One who recommended a surgeon as skillful knowing the contrary to be the fact, is liable in tort. The liability in such cases arises only when there is a duty, if one speaks at all, to give correct information. There must be (1) knowledge, or its equivalent, that the information is desired for a stated purpose; (2) that the information will be acted upon; (3) that the injury will follow if the information is false; (4) the relationship between the par-

ties must be such that, in morals and good conscience, the one has the right to rely upon the other for the information; and (5) the informant has a duty to give it due care. 

Intern. Prod. Co. v. Erie R. Co. 244 N.Y. 331 

Glanzer v. Shepard 233 N.Y. 236 

Doyle v. Chatham & Phenix Bank 253 N.Y. 369 

Cestone v. Harkavy 243 A.D. 732, 277 N.Y.S. 438

It thus follows that if public accountants prepare a balance sheet for a client which in the usual course of business will be exhibited to unidentified creditors as the basis of financial dealings, they are not liable in negligence if the balance sheet was negligently drawn up causing a creditor to lose money because of advances made to the client in reliance upon the false balance sheet. The service of the accountants was primarily for the benefit of the client as a conventional instrumentality for use in the development of the business and only collaterally for the use of those to whom the client might later exhibit it. If the accountants certify as a fact true to their knowledge, that a balance sheet was in accordance with the books of account whereas it was false, they are not exonerated. Likewise a refusal to see the obvious or gross failure to investigate the doubtful, may furnish evidence leading to an inference of fraud. 

Ultramares Corp. v. Touche 255 N.Y. 170

State Street Trust Co. v. Ernst 278 N.Y. 104 

If a merchant inquires of a bank as to the account of the bank's customer, the bank has the duty to speak carefully when the inquiry imported the merchant's purpose to rely upon such information. 

Anchor Lumber Co. v. Mfrs. Trust Co. 272 N.Y.S. 610

Words Maliciously Spoken 

A lawful act done solely out of malice, to injure another, may be actionable. And where one maliciously circulates false information resulting in intentional injury to another, he has committed a tort. 

Raschid v. New Syndicate Co. 265 N.Y. 1

Malicious Interference with Contracts 

One who having knowledge of an existing valid contract between others, intentionally, knowingly, and with reasonable justification or excuse, induces one of the parties to the contract to breach it to the damage of the other party, is liable in an action to recover the damages suffered. Such interference constitutes a legal wrong. 

Hornstein v. Podwitz 254 N.Y. 443

This rule has not been extended to contracts to marry nor to advice given by a parent to an infant child to disaffirm a contract. 

The exceptions are dictated by public policy. 

Ryther v. Lefferts 232 A.D. 552, 250 N.Y.S. 699 

Lee v. Silver 262 A. D. 149, affd. 287 N. Y. 575.

Where a third party by means of false statements and unfair means induces a party to a contract to exercise his privilege of cancelling it and cancellation would not have otherwise resulted, the third party is answerable in damages.

Gen. Outdoor Adv. Co. v. Hamilton 154 Misc. 871, 278 N.Y.S. 226

TORTS 

337 There is also a cause of action where a party would have received a contract but for the malicious, fraudulent and deceitful acts of the defendant.

Keviczky v. Lorber 290 N.Y. 297 Limitations to Rule of Proximate Cause 

(1) Injuries from Fright.—A plaintiff cannot recover for fright and the injuries and mental anguish directly resulting therefrom caused by the defendant's negligence, unless there has been physical contact with the person of the plaintiff. If the fright is preceded, accompanied or followed by actual physical molestation, even in the slightest degree, the plaintiff can recover for the battery as well as for the mental anguish. There can be recovery for mental anguish and subsequent physical suffering without there having been a battery, when the damage and injuries are caused deliberately and not through mere negligence.

Mitchell v. Rochester Ry. Čo. 151 N.Y. 107 

O'Brien v. Moss 220 A.D. 464, 221 N.Y.S. 621 

Beck v. Libraro 220 A.D. 547, 221 N.Y.S. 737

A defendant who has maliciously and wilfully libeled the plaintiff will be held liable for mental suffering caused thereby, as an element of special damage.

Garrison v. Sun Print. & Pub, Ass'n 207 N.Y. 1 

The tendency of the courts is to get away from the ruling that there can be no recovery for fright and the resulting injuries and mental anguish. The courts have allowed the "physical contact" to be asserted through any of the senses, e.g., touch, feeling, smell, or sight. Thus, where a plaintiff receiving his laundry package from the defendant saw a dead mouse therein and became ill as a result thereof, a motion by the defendant to dismiss the complaint on these facts was denied.* 

Gregory v. Wallabout Laundry, N.Y. Law Jrl. May 5, 1927 

Carroll v. N.Y. Pie Baking Co. 215 A.D. 240, 213 N.Y.S. 553 

Sider v. Reid Ice Cream Co. 125 Misc. 835, 211 N.Y.S. 582

The Appellate Division further extended the rule and held for the plaintiff where he fractured his leg while trying to avoid the horses of the defendant which had been permitted to run away. 

Maloney v. Knickerbocker Ice Co. 229 A.D. 317, 241 N.Y.S. 160 

(2) Prenatal Injuries.-A prenatal injury suffered by a child after his mother is injured by negligence cannot be the basis of an action in his behalf, as he has no legal personality for the purpose of such action at the date of the accident. From this it follows that a father may not enforce a claim for loss of services because of the child's injuries. 

Drobner v. Peters 232 N.Y. 220 

In re Roberts' Estate 158 Misc. 698, 286 N.Y.S. 476 (3) Fires.-The courts have arbitrarily ruled that where a fire is negligently started by defendant, the only proximate damage is that *It has also been said that the recovery is not for damages resulting from fright but for damages resulting from nausea and disgust.

which results to a plaintiff whose property catches fire directly from the premises on which the fire started. If other lands intervening catch fire and the plaintiff's premises are therefore affected, there is no liability. 

Hoffman v. King 160 N.Y. 618

If the fire which was negligently started on the defendant's land proceeds by sparks or flames across the intervening land, nothing upon which is ignited, directly upon plaintiff's buildings or premises not contiguous to defendant's premises and ignites a building, the defendant would be liable as the damage would be considered proximate without a fire on intervening land. 

Homac Corp. v. Sun Oil Co. 258 N.Y. 462 

(4) Railroads. At common law no owner was obligated to fence his property against trespassing cattle, and if one's cattle strayed upon the plaintiff's land, he became liable for the damage. 

By statute an owner of adjoining lands must maintain a just and equitable portion of the division fence. 

In the same way every railroad corporation, by statute, is required to erect and maintain fences on the sides of its roads sufficient to prevent cattle, horses, sheep and hogs, from going upon its road from adjacent lands. If such fences are not kept in good repair, the railroad corporation is liable for all damages done by its agents, engines or cars to the animals that stray upon the property. This liability is absolute. The contributory negligence on the part of the plaintiff is immaterial if the fences are not maintained as the statute requires. 

Tator v. Rutland R. Co. 130 Misc. 904, 225 N.Y.S. 731

Railroad Law § 52 

The liability is limited only to damage to the animals which may be hurt by its agents, engines or cars. If a horse falls from an embankment upon the property of the railroad because the fence was defective, and is killed by the fall, the railroad company is not liable. 

Smack v. N.Y. Cent, R. Co. 223 A.D. 192, 227 N.Y.S. 739

In this connection it should be noted that the statute provides that no person other than those connected with or employed upon the railroad shall walk upon or along its track or tracks, except where the same shall be laid across or along streets or highways, in which case he shall not walk upon the track unless necessary to cross the same. Thus a woman struck by a locomotive while walking on a track, though with the company's acquiescence, was held a trespasser for whose death the company was not liable in the absence of proof of wantonness and recklessness in the operation of the locomotive. 

Gleason v. Central New Eng. Ry. 261 N.Y. 333

Nuisances 

Nuisance consists of the wrongful maintenance of the thing itself, resulting in damage, irrespective of whether the operation was careful or careless; while in negligence, it is the careless operation of

TORTS 

339 the thing whereby others are damaged. Therefore, that the defendant exercised due care in maintaining an absolute nuisance would be no defense, while that it was lawfully maintained would be. 

That the defendant observed due care would be a defense in an action predicated upon negligence, but that he was lawfully authorized to operate the thing would be no defense. Where a nuisance arises from negligence, contributory negligence is a defense. 

Clover v. Holbrook 189 A.D. 328, 178 N.Y.S. 517

Morse v. Buffalo Tank Corp. 280 N.Y. 110 

If no license has been issued then an obstruction in the public way is an absolute nuisance, whereas if a permit has been issued, but the privilege to obstruct the public way is exercised in an improper manner, then the resulting nuisance is of a kind which arises out of negligence. 

Delaney v. Philbern Realty Co. 280 N.Y. 461 

Torts Arising from Sales

A purchaser from a retailer has no cause of action based on breach of warranty against the manufacturer, because there is no privity of contract between them. Rights in an action based on breach of warranty are limited to claims against the retailer. In such cases if injury results to a purchaser the latter may maintain an action on contract for damages for personal injuries for its breach, as the injury is a natural and necessary result of breach of warranty. 

Even if death results from the injuries, the executor or administrator may maintain the action.*

Greco v. S.S. Kresge Co. 277 N.Y. 26 

Weiner v. Mager 167 Misc. 338, 3 N.Y.S. (2nd) 918

Subsequent users have claims in tort against the manufacturer for negligence. The rule is that where a manufacturer supplies an article or preparation for immediate use in its existing state, which would be dangerous if defective and used as intended, the manufacturer is liable for injuries to person or property received by one who uses the same in an ordinary, expected manner, if the danger is not patent, nor discoverable by reasonable inspection, not known and no warning given.

Noone v. Perlberg Inc. 268 A.D. 149 

In one case a motor car company sent one of its cars with a defective wheel to an independent distributor. The plaintiff who had bought the car from the distributor, was thereby hurt.The court held the defendant manufacturer liable in negligence for placing a dangerous instrumentality in a position where it was reasonably certain to cause damage. A manufacturer of pop bottles, selling them to bottlers was held liable for injuries resulting from an explosion, where a bottle was defective and inspection thereof inad- *An action for personal injuries based on breach of warranty is governed by the 3-year Statute of Limitations. Schleck v. N.Y. Dugan Bros. 175 Misc. 182. 

The liability of the retailer to the consumer is the proximate result of the manufacturer's negligence and the retailer can recover from the manufacturer on his own contract if he has paid the judgment against him,

equate. A manufacturer of ladders was held liable when a ladder collapsed because it had been made of decayed wood. 

MacPherson v. Buick Motor Co. 217 N.Y. 382 Genesee Co. v. L. Sonnenborn Sons 263 N.Y. 463 

Smith v. Peerless Glass Co. 259 N.Y. 292 

Whiting v. Chesebro 264' A.D. 935

The principle here enunciated has been applied where a manufacturer has placed upon the market prepared foodstuffs in sealed packages for human consumption or for external use, when the normal use would result with reasonable certainty in personal harm to the user of the article if not properly made. Thus, a manufacturer was held liable for permitting a nail to remain in a piece of bread injuring the mouth of the plaintiff; for permitting dead animal matter to be ground in pipe tobacco contained and sold in a sealed can. 

Cohen v. Dugan Bros. 132 Misc. 896, mod 227 A.D. 714 

Foley v. Liggett & Myers 136 Misc. 468, affd. 232 A.D. 822

A manufacturer of a mattress which had been sold with sharp points of metal which had injured the plaintiff who had bought from a retailer, when he lay upon the mattress, was held not liable because a mattress was not a thing inherently or imminently dangerous, which if imperfectly constructed is reasonably certain to injure the user, any more than would a suit of clothes which might contain a needle which might prick the plaintiff. A manufacturer was held not liable to a purchaser of shoes for injuries occurring when a heel broke, causing her to lose her balance and fall down stairs. The same ruling was applied to a manufacturer of a can and key; and to a cigarette manufacturer when a cigarette contained a piece of steel blade.* 

Sherwood v. Lax 145 Misc. 578, affd. 238 A.D. 799 

Jaronier v. Hasselbarth 223 A.D. 182, 228 N.Y.S. 302 

Boyd v. American Can Co. 249 A.D. 644, affd. 274 N.Y. 526 

Block v. Liggett 162 Misc. 325, 296 N.Y.S. 922

The retailer, though generally liable for breach of warranty and not in tort, may in some instances be held in tort. Thus if a vendor holds himself out to his customer as being the manufacturer, he takes on a manufacturer's liability. If he vends a dangerous and mislabled drug in its original package, he would ordinarily not be liable in tort if he was not negligent in so doing, but if he puts his name on as manufacturer, he would be liable though he knew nothing of the contents.

State Insurance Fund v. City Chemical Co. 290 N.Y. 64

To constitute an assault there must be (1) an intentional attempt to contact the body of the plaintiff; and *Cf. Meditz v. Liggett (167 Misc. 176, affd. 25 N.Y.S. Thus, pointing an unloaded firearm at another in a threatening manner constitutes an assault, where the party at whom it is pointed does not know that it is not loaded, or has no reason to believe that it is not loaded, and he is put in fear of bodily harm. 

People v.Tremaine 129 Misc. 650, 222 Ñ¸Y.S. 432 

The "battery" is the touching of the person or clothing of the plaintiff, or of some article held by him, as a result of an "assault." 

The tort must have been unwarranted but it need not have been committed in anger or with the thought of doing injury. 

McGovern v. Weis 265 A.D. 367, 370

Where a physician is confronted with an emergency which endangers the health of an infant patient or causes great pain, he must do that which occasion demands within the usual and customary practice of physicians in that locality. He need not wait to secure the consent of parents who may not be available. 

Sullivan v. Montgomery 155 Misc. 448, 279 N.Y.S. 575

The Effect of Death in Tort Suits 

The cause of action for injury to person or property is not lost either because of the death of the person liable for the injury or of the person in whose favor the cause of action existed. Under § 130 of the Decedent Estate Law an action lies where death results from injuries provided these five elements exist: (1) the action is brought by the administrator or executor of the deceased; (2) the decedent is survived by a spouse or next-of-kin; (3) death resulted from a wrongful act, neglect or default on the part of the defendant; (4) an action would exist in favor of the deceased had death not followed; (5) the action must be commenced within 2 years after the decedent's death.

Thus if the deceased had obtained a judgment which was paid or had released the tort-feasor, or had been guilty of contributory negligence barring his recovery, or the decedent during his lifetime had allowed the Statute of Limitations to expire before instituting suit. the representative cannot maintain the action. Furthermore, since the cause of action belongs to the representative, the infancy of the next of kin does not suspend the running of the twoyear period during such infancy. 

Fontheim v. Third Ave. Ry. Co. 257 A.D 147, affd. 281 N.Y. 392

Haas v. N.Y.P.G. Medical School 131 Misc. 395 Mossip v. F.H. Clement Co. 283 N.Y. 554 

Although the only existing next-of-kin and sole beneficiary may be the tort-feasor who caused the injuries resulting in death his action as administrator brought against another person who may also be liable, e.g., the owner of the car with whose permission it was driven by the next-of-kin, can be maintained. 

Rozewski v. Rozewski 181 Misc. 793 

Recovery under this section, be it noted, is for the benefit of a

spouse who had not abandoned the decedent or if the husband is the survivor, who had not neglected to support his wife and for the benefit of the next-of-kin. In the absence of a husband, wife or children damages are exclusively for the benefit of the father and mother of the deceased but in the event of abandonment of the deceased by either, the recovery shall be for the sole benefit of the other.

Decedent Estate Law § 130, 133 

In re Baker's Estate 252 A.D. 38; 297 N.Y.S. 353

The measure of the loss is determined solely from the standpoint of the survivor and is limited to the pecuniary loss. Accordingly a will executed by the deceased shortly before his death, which limited a bequest to the beneficiary of the death action, to one dollar is admissible to show the nature of the relationship between the beneficiary and the deceased and the expectancy of pecuniary advantages. 

Loetsch v. N.Y. City Omnibus Co. 291 N.Y. 308

Under § 120 of the Decedent Estate Law the executor or administrator has a cause of action for injuries and expenses sustained by the deceased in his lifetime. The recovery in this action is for the benefit of the estate and the damages are limited to the pain and suffering and pecuniary loss.*

Both of these actions when separately brought may be consolidated on motion of either party and on the trials any evidence of the deceased's admissions against interest would be admitted.** 

Kwiatkowski v. John Lowry, Inc. 276 N.Y. 126

Self-Defense 

One who finds himself in danger of being attacked is ordinarily obligated to retreat to a place of safety if that can reasonably be done. But if an attack is made upon a person or one in his company, he may resist with such force as is reasonable under the circumstances in order to repel the attack, and this even though he does not believe himself to be in peril. One attacked with a dangerous weapon, or under circumstances in which he was reasonable in believing that his life was in danger, may use a gun in defense. 

People v. Katz 263 N.Y. 883 

When a man is assailed in his home, or his home is invaded, he need not retreat even if he can avoid remaining in danger by retreating. He may stand his ground and he may protect his home by

Protection and Recapture of Property 

A person may use any amount of force necesary to protect his property from immediate injury, or to retain possession of his property about to be taken away without liability for assault and battery. The value of the property which X seeks to defend is of no importance whatever when seeking to determine the amount of force which X may use in the defense of that property. 

Where a person succeeds in taking the property of another, a later forceful recapture is not looked upon with favor by the law; it is taking the law into one's own hands. 

Bristor v. Burr 120 N.Y. 427 

False Imprisonment

There is a marked difference between an action for malicious prosecution and one for false imprisonment. The essential element of the former is the fact that a judicial proceeding has been commenced and prosecuted maliciously or without probable cause. The gist of the latter is an unlawful detention. The complaint must allege and show that the imprisonment was illegal or procured without a warrant, unless it was made pursuant to the statutory right of arrest without a warrant.

Accordingly, if A is arrested and detained by one not a peace of ficer without a warrant, when no crime has been committed by A, an action for false imprisonment lies, regardless of the innocence of the intention of the defendant.** 

McLoughlin v. N¸Y. Edison Co. 252 N.Y. 202 *This rule of self-defense is also applicable to criminal law.

The use of force upon the person of another is not unlawful in the following cases: (1) When committed to a reasonable degree by a person in arresting one who has committed a felony. (2) When committed in self-defense, as outlined above. (3) When committed by a parent, guardian or teacher in the exercise of lawful authority to restrain or correct a child, and the force used is reasonable. (4) When committed by a carrier in rightfully ejecting a person, provided the train is not in motion and the force is reasonable, **An officer may arrest without a warrant if the one arrested has attempted or committed a crime in his presence, or if the officer has reasonable ground to suspect that the person has committed a felony out of his presence. If the peace officer makes a mistake not unreasonably and gets the wrong party he is not liable in any way if a felony has actually been committed by someone. 

An arrest under these circumstances followed by a holding by the magistrate or an indictment by a Grand Jury is prima facie not unreasonable though there be a subsequent acquittal. A private person, however, is not authorized to arrest anyone unless that person has committed or attempted to commit a crime in his presence, or unless that person actually has committed a felony outside of his presence. Should he arrest the wrong person he is liable for the false imprisonment, without regard to the innocence of his intentions. Code of Criminal Procedure §§ 177, 179, 188; McLoughlin v. N. Y. Edison Co. 252 

N.Y. 202; Morgan v. N.Ÿ.C.R. Co. 256 A.D. 177, 9 N.Y.S. (2nd) 339

If the defendant directs an officer to take the plaintiff into custoday, he is liable for false imprisonment; but if he merely made his statement, leaving it to the officer to act or not as he thought proper, he is not liable.* 

Vernes v. Phillips 266 N.Y. 298 

Graves v. Rudman 235 A.D. 380, 257 N.Y.S. 212

It is not necessary to show that physical force was employed against the body of the plaintiff to restrain him in order to maintain an action for false imprisonment. It is enough that when force sufficient to dominate the situation was displayed, the plaintiff yielded submission.

Though an arrest is legal in its inception, the imprisonment becomes illegal ab initio if the defendant utilizes the period of detention for the illegal purpose of inflicting brutal treatment. 

Dumas v. Erie Ry. Co. 243 A.D. 792, 278 N.Y.S. 197

Detention of a person temporarily or partially deprived of reason by drunkenness where necessary to prevent him causing injury, does not constitute false imprisonment. 

Marks v. Brasser 244 A.D. 672, 280 N.Y.S. 435.

An action for false arrest will not lie if based upon an order of arrest issued out of the Supreme Court having jurisdiction, even though the order be erroneous and subsequently vacated. The showing of want of probable cause does not aid the plaintiff. In order to succeed in the action for false arrest, the plaintiff must show that the order of arrest was procured as the result of fraud, unfairness, malice or oppression. 

Skinner v. Asno Bussan Co. 130 Misc. 578, 224 N.Y.S. 643

Conversion Conversion has been defined as an unauthorized assumption and exercise of the right of ownership over goods, or personal chattels, ownership or immediate possession to which is in another, resulting in the alteration of their condition, or the exclusion of the owner's rights or the rights of the one entitled to possession. 

Melnick v. Kukla 228 A.D. 321, 239 N.Y.S. 16

In order to recover in conversion, a plaintiff must establish that he has title or the right to possession or some other property in the chattel. Wrongful intent is not a necessary element of conversion. 

The fact that the defendant was acting as an innocent agent of another is no defense at all. 

Spraights v. Hawley 39 N.Y. 441 

Suzuki v. Small 212 N.Y.S. 589, affd. 243 N.Y. 590 

Kaufman v. Simons Motor Sales Co. 261 N.Y. 146 

Riley v. Pierce Oil Corp. 245 N.Y. 152

The owner must make a demand if the defendant came into possession lawfully, and there must be a refusal before the plaintiff can maintain the action for conversion. The sole purpose of the demand is to turn an otherwise lawful possession into an unlawful one by non-compliance with it. The demand must include clear instructions as to manner of return and must be made under proper circumstances so as to make a return reasonably possible. Thus, under ordinary circumstances, a demand made several hundred miles away from the chattels involved, is not sufficient. 

Shea v. Chinn 223 A.D. 476, affd. 249 N.Y. 617

No demand is necessary before suing a thief in conversion. Where the property has passed into the hands of an innocent purchaser from the thief, a demand must be made before such purchaser who has not exercised an act of ownership and has acted in good faith, can be held liable as a wrongdoer for wrongful conversion. The in-

TORTS 

347 nocent purchaser may safely refuse to surrender until he has had a fair opportunity to clear up his doubts on the subject. 

Pease v. Smth 61 N.Y. 477; Gillett v. Robinson 57 N.Ÿ. 28

If the innocent purchaser learns that the articles he bought were stolen and also who the owner is, and despite this he continues to exercise dominion over the article, no demand need be made before commencing suit. 

Employers' Fire Ins. Co. v. Cotton 245 N.Y. 102

If an auctioneer sells stolen goods at an auction sale, he is liable in conversion to the true owners. His good faith is no excuse, nor that he sold the article in the course of business. The auctioneer must look to his principal for his indemnity. 

Levy v. Harp 134 Misc. 901, 209 N.Y.S. 720

In case of a deliberate conversion by a bailee or other person rightfully in possession from the owner, no demand is necessary as a condition precedent to the owner's right of action. 

Mullen v. Quinlan & Co. 195 N.Y. 109

If the articles converted were wearing apparel or household goods, the amount of recovery is not restricted to the price which could be realized by a sale in the market. The owner should be allowed to recover the value to him based on actual money loss, all the circumstances and conditions considered resulting from his being deprived of the property, not including, however, any sentimental value. 

Lake v. Dye 232 N.Y. 209

Although there may be a conversion, the plaintiff may, at his option, waive the tort and sue upon an implied promise to pay. 

Schuyler v. Smith 51 N.Y. 309, 314

If one wilfully and deliberately damages another's property, the jury can add punitive damages to the amount of the actual damages. He who causes the wilful damage cannot put up a defense that the plaintiff was guilty of contributory negligence. 

Magar v. Hammond 183 N.Y. 387 Blasting

If A, while blasting on his own land, throws some rocks on B's house, A is liable even though he was not negligent. There was an actual trespass on B's land and A is therefore liable, his care notwithstanding. But for damage resulting from concussions or vibrations of blasting, lawfully done without negligence, rather than by the contact, no recovery is allowed. If the vibrations amount to a nuisance there may be recovery for damages resulting from a nervous condition, alleged to have been caused by the blasting.

Dixon v. N. Y. Trap Rock Co. 293 N. Y. 509. Deceit*

There are four elements which must be present in order to establish a cause of action in deceit. *The reader is referred to the section on Rescission of Contracts, page 220.

(1) A material misrepresentation of something which appears to be a fact. A statement, "I think that the lot is worth $4,000," is not a misrepresentation of something that sounds like a fact even though it might have really been worth only $2,000. If one said, “I paid $4,000," whereas the amount paid was only $2,000, that would be a sufficient misrepresentation, for the statement sounded like a "fact"-the amount paid. 

Fairchild v. McMahon 139 N.Y. 290 

Clark v. Kirby 133 Misc. 229, affd. 256 N.Y. 600

Though the speaker merely voice an opinion of value, such expression will suffice to support an action based on a misrepresentation where there is such overmastering influence on one side, or such weakness on the other, that unfair advantage is rendered probable, and if the speaker, known to the plaintiff, had means of knowing the value which the plaintiff had not, and the false opinion was deliberately given so as to cause reliance thereon. Likewise, a declaration of present intention, false when made, to perform an act in the future, constitutes a false representation of an existing fact. 

Silence as to material fact is equivalent to a misrepresentation when in good faith one is bound to disclose the fact and the silence produces a false impression on the mind of the other party. 

Noved Realty Co. v. A & P Co. 250 A.D. 1, 293 N.Y.S. 336 (2) The speaker must intend to deceive by making the misrepresentation knowing it to be a falsehood. (3) And he must actually succeed in deceiving, so that tion.
