Libel and Slander

Written words, the effect of which is to invade privacy and bring undesired notoriety, are without remedy, unless they also appreciably affect reputation. It must also be shown that some third party heard or read the damaging words. A communication to a spouse is not a publication to a third person. The mere dictation of a letter by an employee of a corporation to the stenographer of the corporation has been held not to be a publication as the act of both was one joint act by the single corporate entity. The dictation of a letter by a private employer to his stenographer has been held to be a publication. The sending of a postcard through the mail is a publication as a matter of law. The absence of intent to defame anyone does not excuse the defendant.

The four elements of deceit also make up the elements of estoppel. 1

TORTS 

349 There is no presumption of fact or law that sealed matter addressed to one member of a family will be opened by another. In the absence of evidence that the sender knew of a custom or authority on the part of another not the plaintiff, to open the plaintiff's mail, there is no publication. 

Wells v. Belstrat 212 A.D. 366, 208 N.Y.S. 625 

Ostro v. Safir 165 Misc. 647, 1 N.Y.S. (2d) 377 

Kimmerle v. N.Y. Evening Journal 262 N.Y. 99 

Ostrowe v. Lee 256 N.Y. 36; Corrigan v. Bobbs-Merril Co. 228 N.Y. 58, 63 

Lawler v. Merritt 182 Misc. 648 

Weidman v. Ketcham 278 N.Y. 129

Any corporation, including a charitable or religious corporation not organized for profit and unincorporated associations, may sue or be sued for libel or slander the same as any individual. 

Kirkman v. Westchester Newspapers, Inc. 287 N.Y. 373 

N.Y. Society for the Supp. of Vice v. Macfadden Pub. 260 N.Y. 167

There is no cause of action for damages against one who publishes false and defamatory matter about the dead. It has even been held that there can be no recovery if the defendant falsely publishes that the deceased was a notorious criminal and that the plaintiffs were his wife and children. If the publication was maliciously libelous, it would be a basis for a criminal prosecution. 

Penal Law § 1340; Rose v. Daily Mirror 284 N. Y. 335 

In the following five instances it is not necessary to show any special damage regardless of whether the damaging words were oral or written. The existence of general damage is presumed. (1) If a woman is falsely called unchaste. (2) If one is falsely stated to be guilty of a crime, as "forger," "thief," "raper," "murderer," "pimp." 

Lander v. Wald 218 A.D. 514, affd. 245 N.Y. 590, Case 1

The Appellate Division in the Second Department has held that the word "crook" was slanderous per se. The First Department has held that it was not, if merely used as a general expression of opprobrium. When it is used to charge the plaintiff with unlawful conduct even the First Department holds it to be slander per se. 

The Court of Appeals has not passed on this point. 

Harris v. N. Y. W. & B. R Co. (1st Dept.) 244 A.D. 252 

Weiner v. Liviton (2nd Dept.) 230 A.D. 312, 244 N.Y.S. 176 (3) If one is called a name which is so derogatory that it would tend to hurt him in his office, profession, trade or business. Such would be calling a lawyer a "scheister," or a doctor a "quack," or a business man a "bankrupt," or publishing in the name of a wellknown author any literary work so badly done that those reading it would consider the author to be an ignoramus or bungler. 

Brown v. Tregoe 236 N.Y. 497 

Ben-Oliel v. Press Pub. Co. 251 N.Y. 250 (4) Falsely stating that a man has a disease which is loathsomeas leprosy and syphilis. 

Sleight v. Woods 145 Misc. 824 260 N.Y.S. 825 (5) In addition to these four, there is one case in which special damage need not be proved, provided the slanderous words were in writing. That case is when the plaintiff is held up to ridicule and

contempt. Setting in written form the statement that the plaintiff habitually fails to pay her hotel bills and has to be ejected for such non-payment, or that a married woman is the lady love of a man other than her husband is libelous per se. In a recent case the defendant newspaper placed, adjacent to an article on evolution, the photograph of the plaintiff and a young gorilla. Under the plaintiff's picture were placed the words "not fundamentally different from the gorilla in physique." The publication was held libelous per se. And it may be libel if the plaintiff has been written about as an object of pity, for though the article may create sympathy, it may tend to make the plaintiff be shunned or avoided. 

Sydney v. Macfadden Publications 242 N.Y. 208 

Wells v. Belstrat Hotel Corp. 212 A.D. 366, 208 N.Y.S. 625 

Zbyszko v. N. Y. American 228 A.D. 277, 239 N. Y. S. 411 

Katapodis v. Brooklyn Spectator Inc. 287 N. Y. 7

In cases of libel or slander per se, general damages are presumed. 

In all other cases special damages must be pleaded in order to state a cause of action. If the words, written or oral, appear harmless, the plaintiff can still show that there was a hidden meaning (innuendo) which others who heard or read the words could understand, and which caused the damage. The innuendo cannot be used to enlarge the natural meaning of a word. If the words are not susceptible of the meaning ascribed to them by the plaintiff, and do not sustain the innuendo, the case should not be sent to the jury. 

Werstein v. Postal Telegraph Cable Co. 131 Misc. 763 

Sydney v. Macfadden Publications, 242 N. Y. 208

If the words, as used in common usage, are susceptible of two meanings, it would be for the jury to say in which sense the words were used and understood. 

Rovira v. Bogetfi 240 N. Y. 314

Evidence of the repitition of a libel or a slander by the same party will not be considered competent for the sole purpose of enhancing damages. The plaintiff should bring a separate action on the new publication. However, if it be necessary to prove actual malice, e.g., to rebut a claim of privilege, any evidence which legitimately bears on the question of malice ought to be received, even though it might be the subject of another action. 

Taylor v. Friedman 214 Å. D. 198, 212 N.Y.S. 26

Defense in Libel and Slander Suits 

There are four defenses to a publication which is libelous per se, viz: (1) truth, (2) fair comment on official proceedings, (3) fair comment on matters of public interest, (4) privilege. (1) Truth.-Truth is a defense. But the fact that the defendant claims that he is simply repeating slanderous words which another had said, or that when he stated the slander he prefixed it by saying that he had heard so and so say it, does not excuse him. One cannot under such pretense escape the responsibility of having spread unfair and damaging news. A defendant may, however, in an action for libel or slander, prove mitigating circumstances, including the

TORTS 

351 sources of his information and the ground for his belief, notwithstanding that he has pleaded or attempted to prove a justification.* 

Civil Practice Act § 338 (2) Fair Comment on Official Proceedings. In the publication of a defamatory article in a newspaper publicly circulated there is but one publication, and that at the place where the newspaper is published. 

Fried v. Edmund Halstead Ltd. 203 A.D. 113, 196 N.Y.S. 285

A civil action is not maintainable against anyone who publishes a fair and true report of any judicial, legislative or of a public or official proceeding. The privilege does not include anything said or done at the proceeding which was not part thereof. That there was inaccuracy in the report does not destroy the protection if the report was substantially a fair account of what took place. 

Civil Practice Act § 337 

O'Connor v. Field 266 A.D. 121

By a "judicial" proceeding is meant a proceeding before any tribunal having attributes similar to those of a court. An appeal to the governor for a pardon or a hearing before the division of licenses are not judicial proceedings. A steamship company's letter to the Federal Radio Commission criticizing a radio operator's conduct in demanding a new contract just before sailing time was held privileged, since it is a charge made to a judicial body, the commission being authorized to subpoena witnesses and hear and determine charges. The publication of a slanderous talk by a convicted murderer immediately prior to his execution is not privileged. 

Sanford v. Bennett 24 N.Y. 20; Andrew v. Gardiner 224 NY. 440 

Alanga v. N.Y. & Cuba Mail Co. 155 Misc. 796, 279 N.Y.S. 319

Laganowicz v. Rome 240 A.D. 731, Case 4 

A law suit, at least from the time that a pleading is filed, is a judicial proceeding. So a newspaper report that the plaintiff was being sued on a swindle charge as set forth in the complaint as filed, is privileged. 

Campbell v. N. Y. Evening Post 245 N. Y. 320 (3) Comment on Matter of Public Interest.—A publication concerning a matter or person of public importance or interest, though false and slanderous, does not always give rise to a cause of action for damages. The publication is justified if it contains no imputations of corruption or dishonorable motive, except in so far as they are an inference which a fair-minded man might reasonably draw from the facts truly stated and represent the honest opinion of the *In an action for libel or slander the actual words used by the defendant must be pleaded and it must be alleged that they were written or spoken concerning the plaintiff. It is not sufficient to set forth the import, tenor and effect of the words alone. Durante v. Contanti 130 Misc. 632, 224 N.Y.S. 520. 

It is not necessary to state in the complaint any extrinsic fact for the purpose of showing the application to the plaintiff of the defamatory matter. It is when the allegation is put in issue that the plaintiff must prove the extrinsic facts showing the application of the defamatory matter to him. Rules of Civil 

Practice 896; Hernando Plantation Co. v. Slovak Press 223 A.D. 286, 228 

N.Y.S. 194.

writer. The defense of fair comment is available to every member of the community. 

Foley v. Press Pub. Co. 226 A.D. 535, 235 N.Y.S. 340

Books, prints, pictures, and statuary publicly exhibited, and the architecture of public buildings, ability of coaches, actors and exhibitors are all legitimate subjects of newspaper criticism, and such criticism fairly and honestly made is not legally a defamation. If it occasions damage, it is not compensable. No comment otherwise libelous is fair or just comment, if it be made through actual illwill or malice. By malice is meant personal spite or culpable negligence. 

Hoepner v. Dunkirk Printing Co. 254 N. Y. 95 (4) Privilege in Libel and Slander.—Privileges are of two kinds -absolute and qualified. Malice usually destroys the latter, not the former. A judge, sitting as a court, is absolutely privileged. He may say anything about anybody, whether relevant or not, and his motives are immaterial. This absolute privilege is not extended so as to protect a judge in his publication of a defamatory opinion to unofficial persons i.e., newspapers, law journals. Legislators are not liable because of slanderous statements uttered while acting at legislative sessions. 

Karelas v. Baldwin 237 A.D. 265, 261 N.Y.S. 518 

Murray v. Brancato 290 N. Y. 52

The privilege, as it applies to witnesses, parties or counsel in judicial proceedings, is absolutely privileged with respect to pertinent matters. It is only when the language used goes beyond the bounds of reason and is so clearly impertinent and needlessly defamatory as not to admit discussion that the privilege is lost. The determination of the question of privilege is a question of law. The receipt of a defamatory letter in evidence, definitely inadmissible because neither pertinent nor material, does not bar an action in libel. And this is so even if there was a failure to object to its admission. 

People ex rel Bensky v. Warden 258 N. Y. 55

Rusciano v. Miholyfi 165 Misc. 932, 1 N¸Y.S. (2d) 787 

A person has a qualified privilege in transmitting information of an alleged crime to the appropriate police officers. The privilege does not apply when the sender has no information or belief that the plaintiff has been guilty of any wrong. 

White v. Carroll 42 N.Y. 161 

Smith v. Lichterman 134 Misc. 150, 234 N.Y.S. 676 

Eisenberg v. Rosenberg 252 N. Y. 490 

Members of one family, employers asked for references concerning a former employee, and partners may, in good faith and with honest intentions and in order to protect one another's interest, say slanderous things about another to each other. A high school principal in communicating to the board of education the fact that rumors concerning a student were being circulated in school was held to have a qualified privilege, and in the absence of malice was held not liable for slander. Stockholders of a corporation may discuss the character of the directors, and their communications do not form the basis for an action in libel or slander, in the absence

TORTS 

353 of actual malice. Ordinarily a telegraph company in accepting, transmitting and delivering messages, is entitled to a qualified privilege. 

Forsythe v. Durham 270 N. Y. 141 

Ashcroft v. Hammond 197 N. Y. 488

Klein v. Western Union 257 A. D. 336 Partial Defenses 

Before the adoption of the Civil Practice Act, facts in mitigation of damages were required to be specially pleaded and proof in mitigation was not permitted where the defendant pleaded justification. 

A defendant is now permitted to prove facts in mitigation, even though he has attempted to justify, and even though the facts in mitigation might partially tend to establish justification. 

Partial defenses may be pleaded. Under § 339 of the Civil Practice 

Act, the defendant may prove at the trial facts not amounting to a total defense tending to mitigate or otherwise reduce plaintiff's damages if they are set forth in the answer. 

Goodrow v. Press Co. 233 A.D. 41, 251 N.Y.S. 364

A claim that the article published was based upon reports received from trustworthy sources and was published without malice, may be asserted as a partial defense in mitigation of damages. 

O'Conner v. Field 266 A. D. 121 *A tendency can be seen to relieve radio companies from full responsibility for statements made over its facilities. It is felt that if the management has used due care in the selection of sponsors and in inspection of the script, it should not be liable for their extemporaneous defamatory remarks. Josephson v. Knickerbocker Broadcasting Co. 179 Misc. 786.

General and Special Powers 

POWER is the right to create or make a charge on, or dispose of real property or personalty and is not limited in number as are trusts. Where a grantor, donor or testator confers upon someone, e.g., the life beneficiary, the absolute power to appoint an estate or fund by will to any person whatsoever, the donee has a general power. If the grantor restricts the appointment to a class or group, it is a special power. The general power is never coupled with a duty to make the appointment. The special power may be either discretionary or it may be coupled with a duty. In the case where the power is not discretionary, a court of equity will execute the power if the grantee failed to do so, just as it will not suffer a trust to fail for want of a trustee.

Real Property Law §§ 136, 157, 160 

Enforcement of the Power

A power must be in writing and may be created by deed or will. 

It may be implied from the language of another grant, as "A to B for life and whatever he does not dispose of, to C and his heirs." It is plain that B can dispose of the property, and so has a power. Any estate created by the execution of a power takes under the authority of and under the grantor of the power. 

In re Comey 173 Misc. 377, 17 N.Y.S. (2nd) 949

A gift to A, followed by a gift to B of such part as may remain at the death of A, can be enforced when the intention of the donor is clear and definite to limit the gift to A to a life estate with power to dispose of the principal during his lifetime, and give B such as is not disposed of in the lifetime of A. 

Callahan v. Volke 220 A. D. 379, 222 N.Y.S. 48

A power is deemed irrevocable unless the instrument creating it contains a reservation that it is irrevocable. If such a reservation is there, the grantor is deemed the absolute owner of the fee as regards purchasers from him and his creditors. 

Real Property Law §§ 144, 145, 148 

Where X's will gave his daughter power to appoint property to her lineal descendants, the daughter by her will cannot give the property to her husband. The exercise was declared void. 

In re Trowbridge's Estate 124 Misc. 317, 208 N.Y.S. 662

Where a power of sale of realty is vested in two or more, all must unite in its execution. If one donee dies, the power may be executed by the survivors.

Real Property Law § 166 

If R, the donee of a power to sell under a will, the power to be exercised at R's discretion, dies without having exercised the power and B is then appointed in R's place as administrator with the will 354

annexed, B cannot exercise the power of sale. If, however, the power were peremptory and imperative, involving no discretion, it would pass to the successor. 

Bettinger v. Montgomery 124 Misc. 906, 210 N.Y.S. 320

Where the donee of the power survives the donor, the right to exercise the power vests upon the latter's death and the right is not affected by the death of the donee before a primary life tenant. 

In re Carroll's Estate 153 Misc. 649, 247 A.D. 11

If B, an owner of a life estate or an estate for years, is given an absolute power of disposition not accompanied by a trust, the estate of B is changed into a fee absolute, in respect of the rights of creditors or bona fide purchasers, subject to any future estate limited on B's original estate in case the power of absolute disposition is not executed and the property is not sold for the satisfaction of debts. Therefore creditors of B may foreclose the exercise of this power for their benefit both during the lifetime of B or after his decease. B had an absolute fee as regards the creditors. 

In re Davies' Estate 242 N.Y. 196; Real Property Law § 149

If the beneficiary of a power may, under its terms, assign his interest, his creditors can compel its execution. The execution must be by an instrument in writing sufficient to pass the estate granted. 

Real Property Law § 162 

A power to appoint a fee includes the power to appoint a lesser estate. A general power to appoint in such sums as the donee desired was held sufficient to authorize an appointment in trust. 

Matter of Jackson 175 Misc. 882, 891 

Release of a Power

Any power, general or special, other than a power in trust which is imperative, is releasable by written instrument signed by the grantee. Consideration need not exist. The release may be with respect to all or part of the property subject to the power or it may reduce or limit the persons and objects in whose favor such power would otherwise be exerciseable. The instrument may by express provision, make imperative a power which was not imperative prior to the release.

The release must be delivered to any of the following: (a) a person specified for such purpose in the instrument creating the power; (b) a trustee of the property to which the power relates; (c) a person, other than the grantee, who might be adversely affected by an exercise of the power; (d) the county clerk of the county in which the grantee resides or has a place of business, or in which the instrument creating the power is filed. 

Real Property Law § 183 

Since a special power, if coupled with a trust and therefore involving a duty to act, may not be surrendered, if the grantee fails to appoint, the duty will be performed by the courts. 

Uses and Trusts

A trust will be created if an owner declares that he himself holds the party in trust for the person designated. In the absence of an in-

dication of a contrary design, a trust created by will has its inception on the day of the donor's death. 

In re Bird's Will 241 N. Y. 184

A contract to devise or establish a trust is void unless the contract or memorandum thereof is in writing and subscribed by the party to be charged therewith, or by his lawful authorized agent. The declaration need not be made to the beneficiary nor need the writing be given to him. His ignorance of the trust is immaterial. 

In re Brown's Will 252 N.Y. 366; Personal Property Law § 31 

In order to create an express trust, there must be: (1) a settlor, who may also be the trustee; (2) a trustee, who must not be the sole beneficiary; (3) a designated beneficiary; (4) a trust res sufficiently identified to enable title thereo to pass to the trustee: (5) actual delivery of a legal assignment of the property to the trustee, with the intention of passing title to him as trustee. An executory deed or conveyance in trust requires no consideration, yet, if made for a promised consideration which fails, the conveyance may be revoked. 

Hutchinson v. Ross 262 N. Y. 381, 397

Matter of Pantales 180 Misc. 423 

No act of the parties nor any court decree may terminate a valid trust before the expiration of the time designated by the testator nor may the remainder be accelerated. 

In re Hanna's Estate 155 Misc. 833, 280 N.Y.S. 662 

In re Leverick's Will 135 Misc. 774, affd. 224 A.D. 625

In cases where there is no trustee appointed, but the trust is otherwise valid, the vacancy will be filled by the court of equity, which will appoint a trustee or take the execution of the trust upon itself. This may not occur, however, where the requirements of the trust are such as to necessitate personal discretion of the trustee in the execution of the trust. In such case the trust will fail. 

Benedict v. Dunning 110 A.D. 303, 97 N.Y.S. 259 

Passive Trusts

Trusts in which the trustee is a mere depository of the legal estate, while possession and the beneficial use have been given to the cestui (dry or passive trusts), have been abolished, except where they arise by operation of law or statute. 

A person coming into possession and control of the property of another becomes a trustee thereof by implication of law. 

Little & Ives v. Acceptance Corp. 215 A.D. 427, 213 N.Y.S. 606

Passive trusts are considered legal estates. So where T is the sole trustee and beneficiary, the trust fades into the legal estate. And where a testator devised Blackacre in trust for his children, it was held that since there was no language to indicate the duration of the trust after the sale, the provision constituted a passive trust and the property passed to the children, the executors having merely a power of sale without title.

A mere trust as "X to the use of Y" gives Y everything. X has no duty to perform. He is merely a depository. Even if power to sell

42 had been given to X, Y would still have everything, except that Y's rights would be subject to be divested when X sold. 

Real Property Law §§ 92, 93 

Agent for Delivery It might be advisable at this point to discuss the legal position of the person who is given money by A to deliver to X-a situation which occurs frequently. It is apparent that the recipient may be intended by A to be his (A's) agent or to be a trustee for X. If the former, X will have no right of action to recover the moneys in the hands of the recipient; if the latter be A's intention, a cause of action for money had and received, will arise against the receiver and in favor of X. The right arises, not as a result of the receiver's promise to pay to X, but because of property rights acquired by X, to enforce an implied promise to pay over. X may sue in his own name.

If the recipient were a mere messenger to carry the property to X, no trust would be created and no cause for action in X would exist. 

Frequently money is given to a bank with instructions to pay to X. The bank is only an agent, and the agency is revocable at the will of the depositor. Of course, if an agreement existed that the bank was to pay to X, he would acquire an equitable interest permitting him to recover in an action for money had and received. 

The controlling factor is the intention of the owner plus an implied or expressed assumption of a trust duty, if a trust is intended. 

Sayer v. Wynkoop 248 N. Y. 54 

The Trustee

The ordinary business corporation cannot act as a trustee. Only corporations chartered as trust companies, and expressly authorized to act in such capacity, can serve as trustees. And in such cases, though some of the services required may invade the practice of law, if they are necessarily incident to the proper execution of the trust, they may be sanctioned. This, however, does not give a license to infringe upon the exclusive right of an individual to practice law. 

Rosenthal v. Lawyers County Tr. Co. 156 Misc. 910, 282 Ñ.Y.S. 868 

A person may create a trust for the benefit of another and make himself the trustee. The delivery of the trust instrument to another and notice to the beneficiary is not necessary. 

The trustee and beneficiary must be distinct personalities or otherwise there could be no trust, and the merger of interests in the same person would effect a legal state in him of the same duration as the beneficial interest designated. The legal and beneficial estate cannot exist and be maintained separately in the same person. 

Greene v. Greene 125 N.Y. 506

The settlor of a trust can grant the beneficiary unconditional power to change the trustee, and if the donee acts within the scope of the power conferred, he may make the change without cause. 

Guaranty Trust Co. v. Mackey 178 Misc. 862 

A trustee acting honestly with ordinary prudence is not liable for errors of judgment. Acting thus he is not liable for retaining in

a falling market, securities he was authorized by the testator to hold. 

The trustee must not, however, place himself in a position where his interest may be in conflict with his duty. Any such act is voidable at the instance of the person he represents, no matter how pure his intention. It may also result in surcharging him with a resulting loss. 

Matter of Ryan 291 N. Y. 376 

In re Clark's Will 257 N. Y. 132

Where a trustee mingles trust funds with his own funds and he spends part of the combined sum, it is presumed that he used his own money first. If the trustee speculates with, or spends the trust moneys unlawfully, the gain in the speculation or the articles purchased are held for the cestui. If the trustee has nothing to show for the money spent and he loses his own money as well, the following is the rule: If the amount left to the trustee was at any time less than the amount of the trust, the smallest sum so remaining is what the cestui has preference to over general creditors. If the trustee at no time had an amount less than what the trust amounted to, the cestui can follow the full amount. So if at any time the trustee had drawn out all the money, the cestui can get nothing as a preferred creditor, even if the trustee had put in a very large sum the next day. 

Scandinavian Imp. Co. v. Bachman 195 A.D. 297, 186 N.Y.S. 860

A withdrawal by a trustee of trust funds from the depositary and a redeposit in his personal account are not enough to charge the trustee with conversion nor the depositary with misfeasance. The funds remain a trust fund and the original depositary has the right to presume that the trustee will apply the funds to their proper place. It is only when the depositary has notice of a threatened misappropriation that it is chargeable with misfeasance. Adequate notice may come from circumstances which reasonably support the sole inference that a misappropriation is intended, as well as directly. 

Grace v. Corn Exchange Bank 287 N. Y. 94

A trustee cannot set off a claim against his beneficiary existing in the trustee's favor before his appointment. Under this rule security deposited under a lease to be returned at its termination, cannot be retained by the landlord because of the landlord's claim under an instrument foreign to the lease itself. 

People v. Klinger 164 Misc. 530, 300 N.Y.S. 408, 418

Trustees and executors are liable personally and not in their representative capacity for their torts. If the tort was committed by the trustee's own negligent act, he is not entitled to indemnity from the estate. Where the trustee was without personal fault, he is entitled to reimbursement from the estate. Thus, though the personal and fiduciary nature of a trust relationship prevents a trustee from delegating to another duties requiring the exercise of his own personal discretion, where the duties are of a purely ministerial nature, or of a type he could not reasonably be expected to perform per-

sonally, a trustee has the right to employ such asistants as may be necessary for the proper execution of the trust. As long as reasonable care has been exercised, in the choice and supervision of an agent selected for the performance of a properly delegable duty, the trustee is not liable for any loss occasioned by the negligence or dishonesty of the former. Thus a trustee is not liable for losses arising through the insolvency of an agent or attorney employed to collect debts, or of a banker with whom trust funds have been deposited, or through embezzlement of funds by a collection agent or clerk employed in carrying on the trust business. 

In re Lather's Will 137 Misc. 226, 243 N.Y.S. 366 

Kirchner v. Muller 280 N. Y. 23

As a general rule, where a trustee has made a contract upon a new and independent consideration and the liability created is not based upon any obligation of the creator of the trust, the third party may not look to the trust to satisfy the obligation. Although the contract was made for the benefit of the trust estate, the liability is a personal one. And the trustee does not avoid responsibility by adding his official character to his signature. The addition operates merely to identify the person. The trustee may absolve himself from personal liability by inserting in the instrument enough to show that the intent was that he be not held responsible. 

East River Savings Bank v. 245 Bway Corp. 284 N.Y. 470

As a general rule, a trustee who has not had possession of the assets of the estate and suffers the co-trustees to obtain them, and is not otherwise negligent in allowing the co-trustees to assume exclusive possession and management of the affairs, is not liable for waste or misappropriation. On the other hand, the acceptance of a trust duty imposes certain positive responsibilities. If the trustee surrenders the whole management to others and shows indifference or gross negligence in regard to the interests of the cestui que trust, he will be responsible. Where one trustee has permitted a co-trustee to manage the estate for fifteen years, acquiescing in all his acts, though not affirmatively, and making no effort to see that the provisions of the trust were properly carried out, this passive trustee was held liable for the misappropriation of the active trustee who had absconded and this despite the fact that the beneficiaries themselves had been lax in requiring proper accountings. 

Brown v. Phelan 223 A.D. 393, 228 N.Y.S. 466

Where one of several fiduciaries makes good a breach of trust for which all are jointly and severally liable, he is entitled to contribution from the others. This rule does not apply where the one seeking contribution committed the breach in bad faith or received a benefit from the breach or is a lawyer whose advice led to the breach of trust. 

Matter of Rosenfeld 180 Misc. 452

Legal proceedings against a third party for the protection of trust property must be brought by, or on behalf of, the trustee. The beneficiary or cestui que trust cannot proceed directly against the third

party, unless the trustee, after demand refuses to bring the action, in which case the cestui que trust may join the trustee and the third party as defendants.

Drucker v. Man. R. R. Co. 213 N. Y. 543 

Harvey v. McDownell 113 N. Y. 526

One who seeks to assert a lien upon a trust fund, or to set aside a deed of trust on the ground that it is fraudulent and void, can proceed against the trustee without joining the cestui que trust. 

The trustee represents the beneficiary and defends in his behalf. 

Jackson v. Talmadge 246 N. Y. 133

Distinction Between a Trust and a Debt 

In the case of a trust, the obligations of the trustee attach to definite property. In the case of a debt, the debtor is obligated to pay out of his general property. If the trust property is lost or destroyed without fault on the part of the trustee, the trustee is not liable. A debtor, however, remains liable for the debts no matter how blameless he was in the case of loss or destruction. 

Money deposited in a bank by a depositor creates a debt with the bank as debtor. This relationship is different in one respect from the ordinary case of debtor and creditor, because a formal demand for payment of a deposit is a condition precedent to the maintenance of any action by the depositor, unless the bank has disclaimed liability or for some other reason a demand would be futile. In the ordinary debtor and creditor relationship there is no need of any demand by the creditor as a condition to the maintenance of a suit for the recovery of the debt. 

Cottle v. Marine Bank 166 N. Y. 53

Whether a bank that collects money on commercial paper on behalf of the holder is a debtor or trustee, depends on this: If the arrangement or the course of dealing between the parties was such that the collecting bank was under a duty to preserve the proceeds intact and to keep them separate, it is a trust fund. If it was the custom of the bank to send money collected, immediately upon collection, to the client, the presumption is that a trust relationship was intended. If, however, the time for remittance was in the future and the bank in the meanwhile could rightfully mingle the proceeds with its own money, a debtor-creditor relationship is presumed. 

Natl. B. & D. Bank v. Hubbel, 117 N. Y. 384 

Baldwin's Bank v. Smith 215 N. Y. 76

Let us assume that the bank to whom the paper for collection was given sent that paper to another bank, which we shall call the subagent. Let us further suppose that the first bank had the right to use the proceeds collected until a like sum was to be transmitted to the client and the first bank. The sub-agent collects the money and, before it has turned the money over to the first bank, the first bank fails. Can the client claim the entire money in the hands of the subagent, or is he merely a general creditor of the first bank? The client can claim the money in full, as the relation of creditor and

361  debtor does not commence until the first bank obtains possession of the money. Until the money is so paid by the sub-agent, the proceeds are considered a trust fund. 

Importers & Traders' Natl. Bank v. Peters 123 N. Y. 272

A credit given by a bank for an item drawn on or payable at such bank shall be provisional, subject to revocation at or before the end of the day on which the item is deposited in the event the item is found not payable for any reason. Whenever a credit is given for an item deposited after banking hours, such right of revocation may be exercised during the following business day.

Negotiable Instruments Law § 350b 

Money received by a factor from the sale of his principal's goods constitutes trust money. 

Baker v. N. Y. Natl. Exchange Bank 100 N. Y. 31

If a bank has suspended, it ought not receive any payments upon business paper previously deposited with it for collection. Any proceeds received after the bank becomes insolvent, will be held in trust and may be recovered in full. 

Friede v. Natl. City Bank 222 A.D. 645, affå. 250 N.Y. 288

Where a party holding a certain fund for another is under an obligation to pay interest for the period the fund is so held, the relation between the holder of the fund and the beneficiary is presumed to be that of debtor and creditor. The payment of the interest negatives the contention that the fund is to be considered a trust fund. 

Euclid Holding Co. v. Kermarse 131 Misc. 466. 227 N.Y.S. 103 

Active Trusts

Active trusts of realty* are limited by statute to seven kinds in which the trustee has the legal title: (1) A trust to sell for the benefit of creditors. Note that is says "to sell" and not "to mortgage." A trust to mortgage would be a mere power and would give the trustee no title at all, as explained in the first part of this chapter. The direction to sell must be absolute and imperative. A discretionary right is not sufficient. 

Steinhardt v. Cunningham 130 N. Y. 292

Coupled with the right to sell, there must also be the right to receive and apply the rents until a sale is made. The life of the trust is ten years in the absence of any other provision. 

Real Property Law § 110 

(2) A trust to sell, mortgage or lease for a legatee's or annuitant's benefit, or to satisfy a charge on the realty. (3) A trust to apply or pay over the rent and profits to a person for life or for a term less than life. In this case the trustee may lease real property for five years or less without the approval of the Supreme Court, even though this term may extend beyond the du- *A trust of personalty may embrace any lawful purpose limited in the main by the rule of perpetuities and that of unlawful accumulations. Matter of Wilson 

182 Misc. 698

ration of the trust estate. In the latter event the lease is valid only for a period ending with the trust term. The lease properly made without court approval, may be modified by the trustee without court approval. When the authority to make the lease is dependent upon the approval of the court, then the authority to change its terms is dependent upon like approval. 

Raynolds v. Browning 217 N.Y.§. 15, affæ. 245 N. Y. 623 

City Bank Farmers' Trust Co. v. Smith 263 N¸Y. 292, 264 N.Y. 396 (4) A trust to accumulate the rents and profits for an infant. 

Real Property Law § 96 

To constitute an accumulation the funds must have the following elements: (a) There must be a prohibition or withholding of the present enjoyment or present expending of the rent, income or interest, and (b) This rent, income or interest so gathered must be added to the fund for the period of time mentioned Therefore, a testamentary trust to pay premiums on a life insurance policy taken out by the testator on the life of a son-in-law, payable to the son-in-law's 'wife as beneficiary, is not an accumulation, because there is no inhibition against the present enjoyment of the income. The upkeep of an insurance policy is a present enjoyment, and where a trustee is directed to expend income for the support of a beneficiary, a surplus for one year which may be all expended in addition to the whole annuity, in the succeeding year, would not be deemed an accumulation. 

In re Simpson's will 147 Misc. 817, 264 N.Y.S. 635

Where discretion is vested in a trustee to apply the income, the retention of a part is not a void accumulation. The unexpended balance always continues to be the property of the beneficiary and what is held at his death passes by will or intestacy. By statute, when a minor for whose benefit an accumulation of the income of personal property has been directed, is destitute, the Supreme Court, or where the accumulation is directed by a will, the Surrogate, may cause a sum to be taken from the accumulated money for his support or education. This section does not apply to a fund left by an insured for the benefit of a minor, pursuant to a contract with an insurance company. There was no trust relationship but only a contract obligation on the part of the insurance company to pay fixed amounts at certain times. It is essential that there be a trust. 

Personal Property Law § 17 

Matter of Nires 290 N. Y. 78

In re Littman's Estate 165 Misc. 285 1 An accumulation for the benefit of an individual ceases to be for his benefit when he becomes 21. It exists for the benefit of individuals while they are infants only and only for infants. If the accumulation is directed to continue for a longer period than the minority of the beneficiary, the accumulation is void only as to the time beyond the minority. 

Morris v. Morris 272 N. Y. 110

Where no valid direction for the accumulation is given, the surplus of rents and profits beyond the sum necessary for the education and support of the beneficiary is liable to the claims of his creditors. 

This applies to trusts of personal property and real property. 

Rowe v. Farmers L. & T. Co. 132 Misc. 651, 230 N.Y.S. 382

Where a will directed payment of income from a trust fund to support an infant or a married woman, the trustee must so apply the income notwithstanding the ability of the parent or husband to support the infant or wife respectively. 

In re Cohn's Estate 153 Misc. 757, 276 N.Y.S. 59

It is valid for the testator to provide that in case of the decease of the cestui during minority, accumulated income may go elsewhere. 

In re Levy's Will 238 A. D. 489, 264 N.Y.S. 795

When because of a valid limitation of an expectant estate, there is a suspension of the power of alienation or of ownership, during which rents and profits are undisposed of and no valid direction for the accumulation is given, these rents and profits belong to the persons presumptively entitled to the next eventual estate. The latter are entitled to anticipate the event which is to terminate the accumulation and to take at once the rents and profits undisposed of or unlawfully directed to be accumulated. A iife estate may be the "next eventual estate."

Real Property Law § 63; Matter of Saddington 260 A. D. 135 

By statute the following are permitted. (a) Income arising from personal property in trust created by an employer as part of stock bonus, pension, disability or death benefit plan, or profit sharing plan, for the exclusive benefit of some or all of the employees, to which contributions are made by the employer, employees or both, for the purpose of distributing to such employees the earnings and principal of the funds accumulated, may be permitted to accumulate until the fund shall be sufficient in the opinion of the employer, to accomplish the purposes of such plan. (b) If the instrument creating the accumulation of personal property directs the accumulation to commence from the date of the instrument, or from the death of the party executing the instrument, the accumulation is valid provided it is for the benefit of infants then in being, and to terminate before the majority of the infants. (c) If the accumulation is to commence after the execution of the instrument, or after the death of the creator, the accumulation in order to be valid, must commence within the time allowed for the suspension of alienation of personal property and during the minority of the beneficiary, and it must terminate before the majority. Any direction for an accumulation for a term longer than the minority of the beneficiary is void as respects the time beyond such minority.

(d) If the accumulation is for the benefit of a college or literary institution, or for the purpose of providing for the maintenance of teachers in grammar school, the income may be permitted to accumulate until it shall amount to a sum sufficient in the opinion of the New York State Regents, to carry its purpose into effect. (e) One-fourth of a trust fund of which the beneficiary is a religious, educational, charitable, or benevolent organization, may be permitted to accumulate. This fourth must not exceed $50,000 and the total sum accumulated must not be over $100,000. 

Personal Property Law § 16 

(5) A trust to reorganize property holdings under a guaranteed issue of participation mortgages when the reorganization is under the supervision of the superintendent of banking or of insurance; or (6) when the supervision is in the Federal Court under the Bankruptcy Act in such reorganizations. (7) A trust for general charitable purposes. Indefiniteness of purpose, if the purpose is clearly charitable, or indefiniteness of beneficiaries, is no objection to the validity of a charitable trust. The trust, however, must be entirely for a charitable purpose, which includes among other things, education and religion. The charitable trust is not subject to the rule against perpetuities. 

In re Cunningham 206 N. Y. 601 

St. Joseph's Hospital v. Bennett 281 N.Y. 115

The following have been held to be charitable gifts for a public use:

A trust for the promotion of research in agricultural chemistry; a trust providing for payments to persons who shall make greatest advancement in the discovery of a cure for cancer; a trust for the purpose of having masses said; a trust for the benefit of disabled ministers of a particular denomination; a legacy for the erection of a public monument. Since the spirit of the trust is charitable, the fact that a limited class will benefit will not defeat it. A bequest to be expended for the development of the Irish Republic, is not a charitable bequest. (In fact, it is void, as it tends to encourage a change in the fundamental law of a nation.) A trust to maintain a school for the Jones family is a private trust and not a general charitable one. 

In re Frasch's Estate 245 N. Y. 174 

In re Barnard's Estate 170 Misc. 875, 11 N.Y.S. (2nd) 115 

In re Perkins' Estate 245 N. Y. 469 

In re Beck's Estate 130 Misc. 765, 225 N.Y.S. 187 

In re Judd's Estate 242 A. D. 389, affd. 270 N.Y. 516

A trust to maintain a home for "refined, educated, Protestant women whose means were small and whose home was made unhappy by living with relatives who thought them in their way," was held to be a valid charitable bequest, although the testatrix provided that the preference was to be given to certain of her own relatives. 

In re MacDowell 217 N. Y. 460

7 If the trustee is allowed discretion as to the disposition of the property and he may apply it to purposes not charitable as well as charitable, the trust is not a charitable trust, even in part. 

If the trustees have several institutions from which to select and cannot agree upon the beneficiaries, the Attorney General is empowered to represent the beneficiaries in the enforcement of the trust. It is his duty to compel by judicial decree in the Supreme 

Court, the application of the fund to the public use contemplated by the testator.

Personal Property Law § 12 

In re Philipoteaux 138 Misc. 208, 245 N.Y.S. 303

If no trustee is named for the charitable trust, the Supreme Court becomes the trustee. 

In re Beekman's Estate 232 N. Y. 365

Gifts to foreign trustees will be upheld if valid in the places where the trust is to be administered. The New York courts will not administer such foreign charity, but will direct money devoted to it to be paid over to the proper parties, leaving it to the state where the charity is to be administered to provide for its administration. 

Real Property Law § 113 

In re Feehan's Estate 135 Misc. 903, 241 N.Y.S. 669

In re Donchian's Estate 120 Misc. 535, affd. 209 A. D. 806 

Lands may be conveyed in trust to (a) A college or unincorporated literary association to build an observatory, to found professorships, to maintain a cemetery, or for other purposes mentioned in its charter. (b) A municipal corporation for a public purpose. (c) School commissioners for the benefit of schools in their district. (d) For the perpetual care of cemetery lots. 

Real Property Law § 114 

Since the number and kind of trusts which can be treated are so limited, any "trust" which cannot take effect as such because it does not come under any of the seven headings above mentioned (pages 361-364) may be exercised as a power in trust. The legal title, not being in the trustee, descends to the heirs or devisees of the cestui, subject always to the exercise of the power by the trustee who has the power.

Real Property Law § 99 

Where land is conveyed to a trustee, and the instrument does not mention the fact that it is a trust, all bona fide purchasers for value are protected. What the trustee does with the money after receipt of it from the bona fide purchaser in no way affects the latter. But if the word "trustee" is in the instrument, it is equivalent to notice. 

Real Property Law § 104 Spendthrift Trusts 

The right of a beneficiary to enforce the performance of a trust to receive the income of personal property and to apply it to the use of any person, cannot be transferred. The right of a beneficiary of

an express trust to receive rents and profits of real property and to apply them to the use of any person, cannot be transferred. These restrictions do not apply to gifts of specific amounts payable out of both income and principal. The prohibition is limited to cases where the trust is to receive income and apply it to the use of any person. A discretionary right on the part of the trustee to invade principal does not remove the restrictions against alienability. 

Matter of Fowler 263 A.D. 255, affd. 288 N.Y. 697

Cy-Press Doctrine 

If the trustee cannot carry out the trust provisions, the court will administer the trust so as to effectually accomplish its purpose as nearly as possible. This is known as the cy pres doctrine. 

In re MacDowell 217 N. Y. 454

If the particular objects of a bequest to charity existed when the testator died, but they later ceased to function, the Supreme Court under the cy pres doctrine will carry out the trust. Thus a trust for the benefit of the Baptist Church of Lyons, N. Y., which ceased to function, was directed to be turned over to the Baptist Missionary Convention of New York, an organization having similar purposes. 

In a trust for maintenance of indigent females which directed the use of the homestead, where conditions had changed so that the homestead was not suitable, the court applied the cy pres doctrine and permitted the trustee to administer the trust by caring for indigent females in private or institutional homes.* 

In re Swan's Will 237 A. D. 454, affd. 263 N.Y. 638 

Graff v. Raymer 136 Misc. 297, 240 N.Y.S. 658 

In re Gary's Estate 248 A.D. 373, affd. 272 N.Y. 635

In a very recent case the trustees of a village were given property in trust with directions that the property be used as a hospital for the benefit of the people of the village, in memory of a named relative. The village accepted but later asked the court to permit the erection of a village administration building because the village had sufficient hospital facilities and not enough money to maintain another. Permission was granted on the ground that the main purpose of the creator of the trust was to make a gift to the village. 

Where, however, the will of a testator left a sum for the establishment and maintenance of a hospital and in addition thereto provided that if any bequest should prove to be inoperative it should be given to a designated person, the cy pres doctrine will not be applied if the amount is insufficient for the charitable purpose. The provision for an alternative recipient shows the intent of the testator not to have the doctrine applied. 

In re Neher's Will 279 Ñ. Y. 370; In re Fletcher 280 N. Y. 86.

The cy pres doctrine has been held to apply even where a trust in the technical sense is not created, as where there is a gift or bequest to a charitable corporation for a specific purpose. In this connection it should be noted that the corporate donee may not divert the funds from its original purpose unless the court applying the cy pres doctrine so commands, St. Joseph's Hospital v. Bennet 281 N. Y. 115.

The Rule Against Perpetuities Applied to Trusts 

Every future estate is void in its creation if it is impossible for a person in being to convey absolute ownership for more than any two lives in being at the creation of the estate. The suspension is not made valid even by agreement of all parties. Nor is it permitted to provide for a trust of realty for two lives in being and for the sale of realty and holding of the cash proceeds for further life. Where a trust term consists of the life of A, the life of B, with remainder to her issue, a further direction for the withholding of the payment of principal during the minority of the issue, creates no illegality. The vesting occurs at the death of B. It is only possession which is postponed. 

In re Froman's Estate 165 Misc. 400, 300 N.Y.S. 1088

A contingent remainder in fee may, however, be created on a prior remainder in fee if it takes effect in the event that the one to whom the first remainder is limited dies under 21. 

Real Property Law § 42 

It is settled law that where a secondary life estate is limited upon the life of the wife whom the primary life tenant might marry, it is void because such wife might be a person born after the estate begins and so not a person in being at that time. To render future estates valid, they must be so limited that in every possible contingency they will absolutely terminate within the prescribed period of two lives in being. 

Matter of Copp 176 Misc. 777

Only two trust forms are subject to the rule, to wit, to collect the income and pay it over, or to accumulate it. So whenever we have a suspension of the power of alienation (which means that there is no one capable of conveying the full fee), we must first determine whether these are involved.

A devise in trust to receive the income of realty for A for life, B for life, and C for life, is bad altogether, for there is a suspension of the power of alienation for more than two lives in being at the creation of the estate. And where a trust is voided, the remainder interests being contingent they cannot be accelerated. 

In re Trevor 239 N. Y. 6 

In re Wupperman 164 Misc. 900, 300 N.Y.S. 344

Although one of the three during whose life the trust is to exist survives the creator of the trust by only a few days, the trust would nevertheless be held bad. 

It is evident that a trust for a term of years would be bad, because any definite term, even for one year, might be longer than two lives. Thus a trust "for three years" was held bad. But should the trust provide for a termination at the end of a definite period "or at the end of two lives who were in being at the creation of the estate," it is valid. From this it has been held that a trust for a person until he attains a certain age is valid, for it is to last till he attains that age or sooner dies, and so is really for one life. Though

a trust "to collect rents during the joint lives of A, B and C" is bad, if in addition to this it said, "and the trustees may distribute the principal, when they desire it," it becomes valid, because of the alternative, for the trustees are persons in being who can at any time convey an absolute fee in possession. The direction to "pay the income to A for 5 years from my decease" is not valid and the death of A would terminate the trust. A bequest of a sum to be paid "when the cornerstone of the new hall is laid" (not for a charitable use) is void. The power of alienation might thus be suspended beyond the permitted period. A trust to continue until the subject matter could be sold for a stated sum is bad. It sets up a limitation which can create an unlawful suspension. 

In re Innerfield's Estate 153 Misc. 706, 276 N.Y.S. 63 

Matter of Hitchcock 222 N. Y. 57

In re Lynch's Will 102 Misc. 650, 169 N.Y.S. 321 

Petition of Bahrenberg 130 Misc. 196, affd. 244 N. Y. 561 

In re Fischer 181 Misc. 1044 

In re Kennedy's Estate 151 Misc. 193, 271 N.Y.S. 126

If there be any limitation on the power of the trustee to terminate the trust and there still remains a suspension of the power of alienation, then the rule against perpetuities is applicable. The following case will bring out the point. A testator directed that the residue of his estate be divided into three equal parts, one part to be held in trust for, and to pay the income to, his wife; one part for his son; and one for his daughter. On the death of his wife the fund held in trust for her was to be divided equally for the benefit of the children, and on the death of either, the principal was to be held in trust for the life of the survivor. Thus far, there is an invalid trust, as the trust is for three lives. The testator, however, provided that the trustees were permitted to convey the principal of the fund of any child to that child, if they considered the habits, capacity and ability of that child to warrant it. It was held that this latter clause did not validate the trust, because here existed a restriction of the trustee's right to alienate, for they might honestly find that the child was not fit to receive the fund before its natural termination. 

In re Perkins' Estate 245 N. Y. 478

The Court of Appeals opened the door to much litigation when it permitted a severance of a trust arrangement. By the terms of a will, the whole estate of the testator, amounting to a considerable sum, was given to a trustee in trust, to pay from the income $50 per month to one Mabel Crans, "so long as she may live." The balance of the income was to be paid to the testator's wife, and if the said wife was survived by a son, then the balance of the income to that son. "When the above payments ceased" by reason of the deaths of the beneficiaries, the trustee was to divide the estate and distribute it in certain definite ways. The dissenting opinion held the trust to be for three lives and violative of the statute. The majority said the care of the wife and son was the primary purpose of the trust and

made the phrase "when the above payments ceased,” read “as the, etc." The trifling provision for Mabel Grans was an incident and nothing more. Upon the death of the wife and son the trust would end and the division would be made. The trust was held to be for two lives, and the trust for Mabel Crans was severed from the main trust. The court said that it was clearly not the intention of the testator to require that the estate should be held in trust to protect a small payment of $600 per year. If such were the intention of the testator then the entire arrangement would be void. The court admittedly struggled hard to circumvent the rule and stretched a point to be practical and give effect to the intention of the testator. 

In re Gallien 247 N. Y. 195

In another case the testator created a trust of his residuary estate "to receive all rents and income and to pay out to my wife during her life, $7,500; to my brother for life, $1,250 yearly; to my nephew for life, $1,250 yearly; to my sister for life, $1,250 yearly." The court held this trust good, stating that there can be no question but that the testator intended to set up funds sufficient to provide the named sums for each beneficiary and that although under the said paragraph these funds were to remain in solido, there was positively no tenable objection to an interpretation which holds that the testator intended separate and severable trusts for the beneficiaries named. The influence of the decision in the Gallien case was apparent throughout the opinion of the court. 

In re Shapiro 124 Misc. 363, 208 N.Y.S. 35 

Matter of Saunders 176 Misc. 654, affd. 262 A. D. 578

Successive life estates must be limited to persons in being at the time of the creation thereof, but there cannot be more than two successive life estates: To A for life, remainder to B for life, remainder to C for life, remainder to D for life, remainder to E in fee, means that E gets the fee after B dies. Only the first two life estates are valid; those subsequent to the first two are void. This paragraph has no application to trusts, but only to the legal life estates. 

Real Property Law § 43; In re Soley's Estate 150 Misc. 839. 

A will provided that the three children of the testator were to Occupy certain property "for and during their respective lives or until they marry, and the property is to be distributed upon the expiration of all said life uses." The effect is that the three children are tenant in common. The devise lasts until two die or marry and will then be at an end and the third life estate will be void. 

Berdel v. Berdel 125 Misc. 496, affd. 215 A. D. 794

The Rule Against Perpetuities Applied to Powers 

The period during which the absolute right of alienation may be suspended by an instrument in which the power is created, is calculated from the time the power is created and not from the time it is to be executed. The doctrine of relation back is peculiar to the law of powers.

Real Property Law § 178

Thus an appointment by a donee acting under a will which made her children, who were not living at the date of the donor's death, the beneficiaries of the trust created by the donor, is void because it violates the rule against perpetuities. In one case a will set up a trust for the benefit of the testator's son for life, with power of appointment to the son by will. The son by will exercised the power by bequeathing this corpus in trust for division into as many shares as he had children surviving him, to pay each the income upon such divided shares, and upon their respective deaths to pay over such shares to his or her lawful issue. Thus, had children been born to the son (donee of the power), after his father's (donor) death, such after-born children would be entitled under the appointment to share. Since they were not in being at the time of the creation of the power, the trust for the children was held void. 

In re Baiter's Estate 152 Misc. 177, 273 N.Y.S. 962

A will bequeathed money in trust with a direction that the income was to be paid to A, and on his death the principal was to be divided among such members of the testator's family as A designated in his will. This, of course, was a power in A. A's will created a trust of this fund and the income was directed to be paid to X for life, then to Y for life, and on Y's death the principal was to be paid to Z. It is necessary to calculate from the time the power was created. 

Therefore, there was a suspension during the life of A, X and Y, and there being three lives, the suspension violated the rule against perpetuities. If X had predeceased A, one life would have been removed, and the trust would have been good. 

In re Dodge's Estate 129 Misc. 390, 222 N.Y.S. 247 99 1 "I authorize and empower and direct........the trustee of my estate to hereafter, and within three to five years, to sell and dispose of my real estate....... This was held a mandatory direction to sell and it was held not to be contra to the rule of perpetuities, despite the fact that a literal reading might justify a holding that the power of sale could not be exercised until three years had elapsed. The rule is that an executor or trustee being clothed with the power, and it being his imperative duty to sell the realty of the testator, the same will be deemed converted into personalty at once. The limit of time is inoperative. 

In re Smith's Estate 123 Misc. 69, 204 N.Y.S. 475

Similarly, where a general power of appointment or a power to revoke the trust has been reserved by the settlor, the period of suspension begins upon the expiration of the power, usually the death of the settlor, and not upon the creation of the trust. Remaindermen would have no vested interests until the power retained by the settlor is terminated, usually by death. 

City Bank Farmers' Trust Co. v. Cannon 291 N. Y. 125

Acceleration of Remainders 

The rule respecting remainders which are and are not capable of acceleration following the deletion of an invalid suspension is this.

Contingently vested and purely contingent remainders are treated alike. The inquiry is directed solely to the question of whether the testator desired that specified individuals should under every conceivable circumstance receive the remainder. Only if the question is decided in the affirmative will such remainder following an invalid trust provision be accelerated. In following case, therefore, there was no acceleration. A secondary trust created on a trust for one life was measured by two more lives, B and W, and was thus invalid. The remainder was directed to be paid to four named grandchildren "if they be then living" on the death of the survivor of B and W, but if they be not then living, it was to be paid to their issue per stirpes. By reason of the substitutional gift to the issue the remainders were contingently vested. Since their rights are subject to defeat if they should predecase B and W, the grandchildren are not entitled to have the principal accelerated. 

Matter of Oppenheim 175 Misc. 634 

Trusts of Personalty

The power of alienation of personalty cannot be suspended for more than two lives in being at the date of limitation or at the death of the testator if the limitation is set out in a will. 

A life or minority in being includes a child begotten before, though born after, the creation of the estate. In other respects all limitations of future estates in personalty are subject to the same rules as limitations upon realty. But the purposes for which trusts can be created are not limited in personalty matters as they are in realty.

Personal Property Law § 11 

So a trust in personalty to continue during the lifetime of T's daughter and during the minority of the youngest two of his grandchildren who should survive him suspends the ownership too long. 

The limitation is void. (A suspension of the power of alienation during a minority is equivalent to a possible suspension during a life.)

Suppose there is a trust of personalty for the lives of two sons and for the minority of the youngest grandchild, and at the end of the trust to be divided among X, Y and Z. The trust, of course, is void because of the perpetuity rule. But note that X, Y and Z's shares are not accelerated, because their legacies were not vested, but contingent, both as to time and person, and they were not separable from the rest of the invalid trust. It was one whole scheme and so if part is void, it must fall together. 

In re Douglass Estate 120 Misc. 193, 198 N.Y.S. 792 

In re Moore's Will 120 Misc. 825, 199 N.Y.S. 790

In charitable trusts of personalty the cy pres doctrine applies. 

Accumulations of income of personalty are allowed, just as in realty. 

Personal Property Law §§ 12, 13, 16 

In re Donchian's Estate 120 Misc. 535, affd. 209 A. D. 806

A creator of a trust of personalty who has not reserved the right

of revocation may revoke it in whole or in part, only upon the written consent of the persons beneficially interested in the trust. 

Thereupon the estate of the trustee ceases to the extent of the revocation. Any person who under the terms of the instrument has a right, whether present or future, whether vested or contingent, to income or principal of the trust fund, has a beneficial interest in the trust, and in determining what persons are entitled to such a beneficial interest the question to be decided is not who would be entitled to share in the estate if distribution were made at the time of the attempted revocation, but, rather, who may be entitled to share in the estate at the time of the distribution in accordance with the provisions of the indenture.* 

Schoelkopf v. Marine Trust Co. 267 N. Y. 358 Personal Property Law § 23 

In an action by a settlor to revoke the deed creating the trust, all the designated beneficiaries and the trustees are necessary parties. 

The exception to the rule which permits a trustee to represent the beneficiaries as sole party applies where a stranger to the transaction seeks to set aside the trust agreement under a right anterior to the making of the trust deed. 

McKnight v. Bank of New York 254 N. Y. 417

If the creator is the beneficiary of the trust and it is provided that after his death the corpus shall be distributed in the manner determined by the laws of New York, the creator by himself has the right to revoke, as there is no then existing person who has any interest in the trust fund outside of the creator of the trust. 

Stella v. N. Y. Trust Co. 224 A. D. 50, 229 N.Y.S. 166

A beneficiary of a trust cannot transfer his right to enforce the performance of the trust, to receive the income of personal property and to apply it to the use of any person. If the trust, however, was created by the party receiving the income, the income is assignable. 

Future income of a trust cannot be assigned. Therefore, any attempted transfer of future income by a beneficiary is not an assignment but is merely a direction for payment as sums accrue, and this direction is revocable as to payments not yet made to the transferee. 

In re Lynch's Estate 151 Misc. 549, 272 N.Y.S. 79 

In re Glover's Estate 246 A.D. 781, 284 N.Y.S. 487

Personal Property Law § 15; Schenck v. Barnes 156 N. Y. 316 

A transfer of personalty made in trust for the use of the transferor primarily, is void as against the present and subsequent creditors of such person.

Personal Property Law § 34 Liberty Storage Co. v. Van Wyck 256 A. D. 641, 11 N.Y.S. (2d) 92 

*The ultimate question is one of intention. Ordinarily a reservation to the heirs of the grantor is said to be the equivalent of a reversion to the grantor himself. Where the control of the principal by the settlor is the retention of the power of a testamentary disposition, it is an indication that a gift of the remainder was intended. This is merely a rule of thumb.

Savings Bank Trusts

A deposit by one person of his own money, in his own name as trustee for another standing alone, establishes not an irrevocable trust but only a tenative trust revocable at will, until the depositor dies or completes the gift in his lifetime by some unequivocal act or declaration, as delivery of the pass book or notice of such intent to the beneficiary. If the depositor dies before the beneficiary without revocation, or decisive act or declaration of disaffirmance, a rebuttable presumption arises that an absolute trust was created as to the balance on hand at the death of the depositor. It amounts to a judicial addition to the method permitted by statute for the transmission of property upon death. 

Matthews v. Bklyn. Savings Bank 208 N. Y. 508 

Matter of Totten 179 N. Y. 112, 125

The fund is subject to the claims of creditors of the depositor and they may assert their rights even after the death of the debtor. The court will not permit creditors to be defrauded by the creation of the savings bank trust. 

In re Weinberg's Estate 162 Misc. 867, 296 N.Y.S. 7 

Constructive Trusts

If A orally promises for a consideration to buy certain property in the name of the promisee or in the joint names of A and promisee, or he promises to hold the property in trust for the promisee, and he violates this oral promise, equity will not raise a constructive trust, because nothing has been done to induce equity to interfere.

There are, however, some exceptions to this rule. The court of equity will raise a constructive trust, regardless of the intention of the parties, where a confidential relation would be abused without the redress of a trust orally declared. The existence of the relation raises a presumption of constructive fraud. It is ordinarily applied to the relationship of guardian and ward; trustee and cestui que trust; attorney and client; physician and patient; or to other close relationships where it is affirmatively established that the parties are not dealing on an equal basis. The presumption does not arise from the mere relation of parent or child or of husband and wife. 

There must be proof of circumstances of inequality. Of course, since the relationship is so close, little affirmative proof is required in order to cast the burden upon one invoking an instrument executed under circumstances of equality and fairness. 

Where a son received realty from his mother under an oral promise to hold the property for her and her other children, a repudiation of that promise by the son gave rise to a constructive trust. 

Likewise a constructive trust of land arises where a confidential relationship would be abused by a repudiation by the person to whom the property was conveyed, without redress, of a trust orally declared. Thus if a husband paid for property, managed it, maintained it, paid for all upkeep and collected the rents, but took title

in his wife's name, a trust would be declared in the husband's favor if the wife even orally had at the time of the conveyance, promised to give him a deed upon demand or to dispose of the land in accordance with his wishes. 

Foreman v. Foreman 251 N. Y. 237 

Fraw Realty Co. v. Natanson 261 N. Y. 396 

Hifler v. Calmac Oil. Co.10 N.Y.S. (d) 531,540,affd.16 N.Y.S, (2d) 104 

Beatty v. Guggenheim Exploration Co. 225 N. Y. 380 

Resulting Trusts

The resulting trust arises by operation of law and is implied by equity from the acts of the parties according to their apparent intentions. It arises where a person makes or causes to be made a disposition of property under circumstances which raise an inference which is not rebuttable, that there is no intent that the one getting the property should have the beneficial interest therein and there is no disposition of that beneficial interest. 

In the ordinary case if land is conveyed to T and paid for by P, T takes full legal title. No trust results to P. But if P had creditors at that time, there arises a presumption of fraud and unless this presumption is rebutted, a trust results in favor of those persons who were creditors of P at the time of the transfer, up to the amount of their debt. A trust does not result in favor of those creditors who subsequently became creditors. Proof that one paying the consideration was at the time not insolvent but had, besides the consideration paid for the property granted, ample funds to pay his debts and that an inability to meet his obligations was not and could not be reasonably be supposed to have been in his mind, is sufficient to rebut this presumption. 

Preston v. Conroy 231 A. D. 442, 247 N.Y.S. 549

If P had no creditors, but the land was conveyed to T and paid for with P's money without P's knowledge or permission, a constructive trust would result in P's favor.

Real Property Law § 94

WILLS 

Who May Make a Will (1) A testator must be of the age of 18 years or more to validly bequeath personalty and 21 years or more to validly devise realty. (2) He must be sane enough to have the capacity to comprehend the nature of the transaction, to recall his property, to know of what it consisted, to understand his relation to those who are the objects of his bounty as affected by his will. 

His physical condition, hallucinations or religious beliefs are of no moment, unless of such a nature as to affect his sanity and therefore his knowledge of the condition of his property, his relationship to the object of his bounty, and the effects of his will. Delusion is insanity where one persistently believes facts which have no real existence except in the imagination, against all evidence and probability. But if there is some basis for the belief, though the conclusion be illogical or unreasonable, there is not insanity. 

In re Bossom's Will 195 A. D. 339, 186 N.Y.S. 782 

Lester v. Lester 178 A. D. 438, 165 N.Y.S. 592

Habitual and extreme intoxication does not of itself constitute an unsound mind or testamentary incapacity. There must be additional proof that at the time of the execution of the will the judgment of the testator was perverted or paralyzed because of intoxication.

The disposition which a man makes of his property by will is not invalidated because its provisions are unequal or unjust, or the result of passion, or other unjustifiable sentiment. Neither is the presumption in favor of a will overcome by showing that the testator was of advanced age or enfeebled in mind and body. 

In re Radley's Will 228 A. D. 119, 239 N.Y.S. 44

The Execution of The Will* 

There are four items to be remembered in determining whether the execution was proper or not. (1) be must be in 2) The will must be subscribed by the testator at the physical end, otherwise probate will be denied. The mark of the testator, his initials or fingerprints are sufficient if intended as a signature. Likewise the fact that a witness aided the testator to sign does not invalidate the will. A seal is not necessary. 

In re Caffrey's Will 174 A. D. 398, affd. 221 N. Y. 486 

In re Barger's Will 255 A. D. 674, affd. 256 N.Y. 585 *One who receives a will for safe-keeping is bound to return it to its maker upon demand and for probate after notice of death. N. Y. 249. 375

If after the signature there is more writing of a dispository nature the will is not signed at the end and is void in its entirety. But if the writing after the signature was not dispository, it does not void the will; the writing above the signature then constitutes the valid will. 

In re Ryan's Will 252 N. Y. 620

Where a will contained several bequests in this order, the signature, three names of people declared to be excutors, then the witnessed attestation clause, all done at one sitting and as part of one transaction, the will was held void. The appointment of executors is an important integral part of the testamentary disposition. 

Where a draftsman, after the testatrix had properly executed a will, wrote in the name of the decedent's son as executor after the signature, the added part was not admitted to probate, but the instrument actually subscribed by her, was her will.

Thus, the rule can be formulated that the addition of a clause at a time after proper execution and not as part of the execution, does not affect the will. The addition alone is disregarded. 

The will need not be written on separate and detached pages. 

One may paste pages on another sheet. And if on reading along, as one would from a pad, the signature is seen at the physical end, the signature is in the proper place.

Decedent Estate Law § 21 

In one case the will was written on a paper folded along the center making four pages. The pages were marked as follows: The outside page was marked "Page 1;" on turning over, back of page one was marked "Page 3" and what was the page opposite, was marked "Page 2." The signature was found on the page marked "Page 3."

The will was held invalid and void. Though this decision seems technical, the fact that pages one and two each ended a paragraph may have had some bearing on the decision. But a testamentary instrument written on a similar paper, where the writing began on the first folded sheet, 'was continued on the fourth, and from there on inside and signed at the end of that writing, was held signed at the end since there was no additional matter following the signature, the expressions were continuous and the language obviously written in that order. 

Matter of Andrews 162 N. Y. 1

(4) The testator must request the witnesses to sign, but there need be no direct testimony to that effect. A will may be admitted to probate even though the witnesses have no recollection that the testator requested them to sign. The appearance of the genuine signature at the proper place plus the attestation clause and an other-
