In re Katz's Will 277 N. Y. 470

These witnesses must sign and write their home address. If they do not write their addresses, they may be liable $50 each to an interested person who sues for it, but the will itself will not be affected.

Decedent Estate Law § 22 

The witnesses need not sign any attestation clause, but it is advisable that they do so. It makes out a prima facie case that the witnesses knew it was a will. The infancy of subscribing witnesses is insufficient by itself to invalidate the will.

In re Tannenbaum's Estate 154 Misc. 828, 278 N.Y.S. 253

The statute regulating the execution of a will must be strictly complied with even in the case of a holographic will.*

Where a testator refers to an actually existing state of things particularly itemizing his devises and bequests, his language refers to the date of the will and not of his death. Therefore such a devise will not carry after-acquired property.

Nuncupative and Holographic Wills 

The statute was amended effective May 6th, 1942, by which many radical changes were made in the law with respect to nuncupative and holographic wills. Under the present statute a nuncupative and holographic will may bequeath personal property and also devise real property if the will is made by the soldier or sailor in actual military or naval service or by a mariner while at sea. In the case of the nuncupative will, it must be made within the hearing of two persons and the execution and the tenor thereof must be proved by at least two witnesses. The holographic will, if entirely in the handwriting of the maker is valid even though the same be unattested. 

The disposition of property by a soldier or sailor either by a nuncupative or holographic will becomes invalid and unenforceable *But see next heading referring to holographic will of soldiers, sailors and mariners.

upon the expiration of one year following the discharge from military or naval service, provided he possesses testamentary capaciy at that time. The will continues to be valid and enforceable until the expiration of one year from the time he shall have regained testamentary capaciy if without it during that year. 

A soldier on leave from his military organization, or a mariner on shore, cannot èxecute an enforceable oral will. 

Decedent Estate Law § 16 Matter of McDonald 179 Misc. 285 The Probate* 

The purpose of a probate proceeding is to have a will declared a valid will. If the will has been proven to be genuine and its execution in accordance with the statute and the testator competent and not under restraint the will must be admitted to probate. 

Matter of Davis' Will 182 N. Y. 468; Surrogate's Court Act § 144 

The will, to be admitted to probate, must be proven by at least two subscribing witnesses, except those dead, absent from the state or incompetent. In the latter events, the will can still be admitted to probate on proof by others of the handwriting of the testator and of the witnesses and by any additional testimony which warrants the inference that statutory formalities were complied with. 

The will cannot be admitted to probate without proof of the handwriting of the requisite two subscribing witnesses.

Surrogate's Court Act §§ 141, 142 

In re Cann's Estate 136 Misc. 428, 240 N.Y.S. 840

It is no objection to the probate of a will that a testator has made a valid contract to dispose of his property in a different manner from that provided in his will, or that the will offered for probate revokes a will drawn in accordance with terms of that contract. 

Schley v. Donlan 131 Misc. 208, 225 N.Y.S. 453

Though a will has been lost or destroyed, it can be admitted to probate if there is evidence to justify a finding that the will was in existence after the testator's death, or that it was fraudulently destroyed before his death The provisions must be proven by at least two credible witnesses, or else by one such witness and a correct copy of the will, which latter would equal one witness. 

Surrogate's Court Act. § 143 

If a will, shown once to have existed and to have been in the testator's possession, cannot be found after his death, the legal presumption is that he destroyed it animo revocandi. Those seeking to establish the lost or destroyed will must assume the burden of proving that it was not destroyed animo revocandi. 

In re Staiger 243 N. Y. 468

Duplicate Wills 

When a testator executes a will in duplicate, one cannot be probated without producing the other or accounting for its non-pro- *The right to contest the validity of a will is confined to those persons who. would profit by its rejection.

379 duction, the theory being that a testator can destroy his will by destroying the one in his possession without repossessing the other from its custodian. Failure to produce one creates the presumption of destruction animo revocandi. 

In re Robinson's Will 257 A. D. 405

Abatement of Legacies 

When the assets of an estate are insufficient to pay all general legacies in full, in the absence of a contrary intent shown by the will, all legacies abate proportionately. There are three exceptions to this rule: (1) Where the legacy was for the maintenance and education of near relatives otherwise unprovided for; (2) a legacy to a widow in lieu of dower receives a preference on the ground that such a legatee takes as purchaser; (3) a legacy is preferred when it has been given for a valid consideration e.g., a contract exists between the legatee and the testator by the terms of which the legacy is to be preferred. Here also the legatee takes as a purchaser. 

In re Cameron's Estate 278 N. Y. 352

A general legacy or devise cannot generally be a charge on a specific legacy or devise, even in favor of a close relative, but a clear implication in the will of a different intent will control. 

Matter of Bauer 289 N.Y. 326 

Charge on Realty

A mortgage executed by the ancestor or testator of the receiver and other liens on the property thus received, are to be paid by the distributee or devisee out of his own property, unless there be an express direction in the will of the testator to the contrary.

Real Property Law § 250 General, Specific and Demonstrative Legacies* 

A general legacy is a gift of personalty not amounting to a bequest of a particular thing or of a particular fund not distinguished from all others of the same kind e.g. a bequest of the sum of $2,000. 

A specific legacy is a bequest of a certain thing, particularly described and distinguished from all others of the same kind belonging to the testator, usually at the time of the making of the will or in some cases at the date of his death e.g. a bequest of all proceeds of a bond and mortgage which is particularly described by the testator. The legacy is to be paid by the delivery only of the identical. thing specified and if it be disposed of or not in existence at the date of the testator's death the legatee does not get its equivalent out of the estate. 

In re Wheland's Estate 257 N.Y. 155

A demonstrative legacy is a bequest of a certain sum, stock or the like payable out of a particular fund or security e.g. bequest of $1,000 payable out of the proceeds of a specific bond and mort- An unincorporated association may not take a devise or bequest. In re 

Idem's Will 256 A. D. 124, affd. 280 N. Y. 756.

gage. If the fund pointed out for the payment of the legacies fails, resort may be had to the general assets of the estate. 

Crawford v. McCarthy 159 N. Y. 514

The courts are inclined to consider legacies as general rather than specific where the language used permits of such construction. 

In re Kilborn's Will 166 Misc. 627, 2 N.Y.S. (2d) 896

Interest On Legacies 

Whether the assets of the estate have been profitable or unproductive does not affect the rights of a legatee. He is like a creditor and may maintain an action at law. He is entitled to interest from the day he is entitled to bring such action, which by statute is at the end of seven months from the date of the letters testamentary. The same rule applies in the case of distributees of an intestate. 

Decedent Estate Law § 146 

Advancements

If A, standing in loco parentis* toward S, transfers property to S in aniticipation of the share of the donor's estate which the donee would receive if A died intestate, that transfer is an advancement. 

The amount of realty given to S is deducted from the realty left him, and the personalty from the personalty left. If there is not enough realty to deduct from, then the personalty must be used and vice versa. Note that the advances must have been made with a view to settlement. Giving money for a child's upkeep or education is not that. But money given for a business use now, instead of after death is money given with a view to a settlement. 

Decedent Estate Law §§ 85, 86 

If A disposes of his whole estate by will, the doctrine of advancements has no application, unless the will specifically refers to advancements and defines which previous gifts shall be so considered. 

Even if the will expressly states that the testator's property is to be distributed in accordance with the intestacy laws, the doctrine of advancements does not apply, for there is a will. The will cancels any effect that the advancements might have on the distribution. 

In re Bernhardi's Estate 151 Misc. 480, 273 N.Y.S. 250 Ademption

Ademption is the extinction or satisfaction of a specific legacy by some act of a testator or his committee if he has become insane after the making of the will. Ademption applies only to personalty and is equivalent to a revocation of a bequest in the will. 

Matter of Ireland 257 N.Y. 155

Payment by Beneficiary of Debt Owed to Testator 

Where a beneficiary of a trust created by will is indebted to the testator, the interest of the beneficiary is subject to a charge for the amount of the debt, unless the testator manifested a contrary *A person in loco parentis is one who means to put himself in the situation of the lawful parent. The relationship may be shown by acts and declarations of the decedent. The assumed office may exist between those not related.

WILLS intention. But if the trust is a spendthrift trust,* the inference is that the testator intended that the beneficiary should enjoy the whole interest given him under the trust. 

Matter of Chamberlain 289 N. Y. 456

Contract to Make or Alter Will 

If a testator is induced to make or not to change a will by an express or implied promise on the part of the legatee that he will apply the legacy to a stated lawful purpose, equity will compel the legatee to so apply the property obtained. Active co-operation or silent acquiescence has the same effect as an express promise. The promisor is held as a trustee ex maleficio.**

LaVin v. LaVin 179 Misc. 100 

Rules for Construction of a Will A will or part thereof may be construed in (1) A probate proceeding; (2) in an independent proceeding brought for the purpose of having the will construed, or (3) in an accounting proceeding. Questions of construction are to be determined by the Surrogate without a jury. 

In re Enright's' Will 138 Misc. 853, 247 N.Y.S. 514, 520

A petition for construction may be presented by a representative or executor, administrator with the will annexed, testamentary trustee or any person entitled to even contingently share in the estate in any manner except as a creditor. All the parties to a proceeding to construe a will are deemed parties to any appeal from the construction decree even though some do not appeal. The Appellate Court must render judgment on the rights of all. 

Surrogate's Court Act §§ 145, 314; 

In re Winburn 270 N.Y. 196 

In re Gardiner's Estate 154 Misc. 413, 278 N.Y.S. 52

The Court in construing a will should attempt to carry out the testator's intent as of the date of the execution of the will. Words used are to be given their ordinary meaning. Parol evidence cannot be admitted to contradict, enlarge or vary the words of the will nor to explain the intent of the testator except in three cases: (1)

Where there is a latent ambiguity arising dehors the will as to the person or subjects meant to be described e.g. two legatees of the same name, two chattels of similar description; (2) to rebut a resultant trust; (3) if giving the words their primary significance the will be rendered absurd. The Court may insert a word to complete the construction so as to carry out the obvious purpose of the testator. 

Dwight v. Fancher 245 N.Y. 71 

In re Burr's Estate 233 A.D. 290, affd. 258 N.Y. 592

The following are the leading canons of interpretation although *See ante p. 365 *See Seaver v. Ranson 224 N.Y. 233, in which the legatee was held liable to a third party beneficiary, on a similar promise made to the testatrix.

they give way to the intention of the testator as expressed in the will: (1) The law favors vesting all legacies. (2) The testator is presumed to have intended to dispose of all his property, and an interpretation which results in partial intestacy will not be favored. (3) Where the gift is only found in a direction to pay at a future time, time will be deemed to be of the essence of the gift; but if the amount of the gift is to be severed instanter from the general estate for the benefit of the legatee, and the interst thereon paid him until the period of distribution, a mere direction to pay at such a period will constitute a present gift. (4) Where a clause is capable of two interpretations, the one should be adopted which prefers persons of the testator's blood to strangers. (5) Where a testator has expressed two intentions, legally inconsistent, the court will give effect to that intention which the testator would have preferred if compelled to choose between the two. (6) When an estate is given in one part of a will, in clear and decisive terms, it is an established interpretive rule that the estate will not be taken away or cut down by raising a doubt as to the meaning or application in a subsequent clause, except by positive provision in words as clear and decisive as those giving the estate. (7) Where a sum in a legacy is repeated in a will, it is a rebuttable presumption that the latter sum is a substitution and is not to be taken cumulatively. But where the two bequests are in different instruments, as by will and codicil, the presumption is in favor of the legatee. 

In re Kelley's Estate 153 Misc. 445, 274 N.Y.S. 488 

In re Lindsay's Will 144 Misc. 89, 258 N.Y.S. 792 

In re McCready's Will 236 A.D. 390, affd. 263 N.Y. 602 

A gift of specific personal property speaks as of the date of the will. A residuary clause speaks as of the death of the testator. A devise also speaks as of the testator's death. All the estate of the testator which he then owns and could devise is included in the disposition. This rule differs from the common-law rule, which was that a devise passed title to real property owned at the time of the publication of the will. Under the common law, therefore, property acquired by the testator subsequent to the publication of the will was not carried along by the will. Under the statutory law, if a will shows an intention to dispose of all the testator's real estate, the will carries all after-acquired property. 

Decedent Estate Law § 14 

In re Frey's Will 154 Misc. 421, 277 N.Y.S. 269

In one case the testator devised "all my right, title and interest in parcels A, B, C and D to my sister Julia, and the rest, residue and remainder to Sarah." At the time of the execution of the will the testator had a one-half interest in those four parcels and he owned a fifth parcel "E." Subsequent to the execution of the will the tes-

WILLS tator sold parcel "E" and obtained the full interest in parcels "A. 

B, C and D." It was held that Julia was entitled to all and Sarah to nothing. If the testator had stated that he devised "all my right, title and interest which I now possess, etc." Julia would have been limited to the interest of the testator at the time of the execution of the will.

U. S. Security Trust Co. v. Petrillo 129 Misc. 15, 220 N.Y.S. 635 

When a will speaks of the death of a devisee or legatee without issue, it means such death occurring during the life of the testator. 

So that where there is a devise to one person in fee, and in case of his death to another, the contingency referred to is the death of the first named devisee during the lifetime of the testator, and if such devisee survives the testator, he takes an absolute fee; the words of contingency do not create a remainder over to take effect upon death, at any time, of the first taker. 

In re Martin's Will 225 A.D. 502, 233 N.Y.S. 602

A child en ventre sa mere, which is subsequently born alive and capable of living, is considered a child living from the date of conception (which date is presumed to be 280 days before actual birth, unless conception is shown to have occurred later or earlier) in order to take a beneficial interest in a bequest or devise, where the description is "child living." 

Farmer's L. & Tr. Co. v. Pierson 130 Misc. 110, 222 N.Y.S. 532 

In re Well's Will 129 Misc. 447, 221 N.Y.S. 714

When an estate in fee simple is granted, a condition that the grantee shall not alienate the land or be limited in his right to do so, is void. Therefore, a condition that a grantee in a fee simple shall alienate it only to those having the testator's family name, is void, for the reason that a fee-simple estate and such a restraint upon its alienation cannot in their nature coexist. A codicil which provided that the said property "should be kept in possession, and that neither Joseph J. Steffan nor Anthony J. Steffan, the grantees, can force a sale of said property at this time or at any other time in the future unless satisfactory to both Joseph J. Steffan and Anthony 

J. Steffan," was declared void. 

Steffan v. Steffan 135 Misc. 568

If a will devises property to the wife of the testator, to be her absolute property, provided that on death or remarriage whatever property is undisposed of should go to A, B, and C, etc., the wife has no power to dispose of the property by will. The wife may use the property liberally for her own use, comfort, benefit and support, but such user has to be in good faith. 

Vincent v. Putnam 248 N.Y. 76

A gift of the income arising from personal property not providing for the disposition of the principal, is equivalent to a general gift of the property itself, unless the income is given for a specified time. Therefore the gift of income for the duration of the beneficiary's life does not carry with it a gift of the principal, though no disposition of the latter is made. 

In re Frayer's Estate 155 Misc. 811, affd. 246 A.D. 703

Where general legacies are given, followed by a gift of the residue of the realty and personalty, the general legacies will not be charged upon the lands included in the residuary devise. The primary rule is that where the personal estate is sufficient to pay legacies, they abate proportionally and no recourse may be had to the realty to make up the deficiency unless the will shows an intention to charge the realty. A decedent's realty is, however, the primary source of payment of incumbrances thereon in the absence of clear testamentary intent to the contrary. 

In re Parker's Estate 151 Misc. 394, 273 N.Y.S. 86 

McGoldick v. Bodkin 140 A.D. 196, 125 N.Y.S. 101 

In re Burrow's Estate 167 Misc. 1, 3 N.Y.S. (2d) 350

In the absence of clear direction to the contrary, debts and funeral expenses are paid out of the residuary estate. 

Matter of Hund 266 A.D. 379

Meaning of Terms 

A bequest to "my children me surviving" includes only such children as are alive at the death of the testator. Without an expression in the will tending to contradict, the use of the word "child" denotes legitimate, immediate offspring, and grandchildren or living dependents or pre-deceased child of the testator, are not included in the legacy. The word "issue" includes legitimate descendants generally of every generation, unless the testator has shown other intent. Therefore an adopted child is not ordinarily an "issue." The distribution would be per capita, but the gift will be distributed per stripes whenever there is slight evidence that the author so desires. The term "heirs," "heirs-at-law," "next-of-kin" and "distributees" and terms of like import all mean distributees under the Intestacy Laws.* The term "descendant" means only the issue of a deceased person and does not describe the child of a parent who is still living. 

Matter of Underhill 176 Misc. 737

Matter of Burke 178 Misc. 684 

Matter of Plaster 179 Misc. 80, affd. 266 A.D. 926

Decedent Estate Law § 47c 

Trowbridge v. Trowbridge 182 Misc. 191

In the Harris' Will 138 Misc. 287; In re Sander's Estate 148 Misc. 776. 

It has been held that the terms "nephews" and "nieces" in their primary and ordinary sense do not include grandnephews and grandnieces, or more remote descendants, unless there is something in the will to show that the words were used in a broader sense. "Cousins" has been interpreted to mean first cousins. 

In re Salyer's Estate 142 Misc. 300, 255 N.Y.S. 81

A gift to a "wife" of a beneficiary is a gift to one who occupies that relation at the time of making the will, if the beneficiary is then married. 

Matter of Friend 283 N.Y. 200 *The meaning of such terms is controlled by their meaning as of the date of the death of the testator. A deed of trust inter vivos not being ambulatory in character, speaks as of the day of its execution and delivery. Trowbridge v. 

First Stamford Bank 182 Misc. 180, affd. 268 A.D. 768

WILLS 

385 A gift to a class has been defined as the gift of a sum to a body of persons uncertain in number at the time of the gift, to be ascertained at a future time, and who are all to take in equal or in some other definite proportions, the share of each being dependent for its amount upon the ultimate number of persons. The distribution is made among the persons who comprise the class at the date of distribution. If there is a bequest to certain persons nominatum or so described as to be fixed at the time of the gift, so that there can be no fluctuation, then if one of them dies in the lifetime of the testator his share lapses. 

Matter of Koch 282 N. Y. 462

A will directed payment "to my nieces and nephews Edna, Rose, Nettie, William and Floyd" after the death of A, who was given a life interest. Edna died before A. Was the estate of Edna entitled to the share of Edna or were the other four surviving A entitled? 

Since the beneficiaries were named, the individuals were meant. It was not a gift to a class. Since payment was postponed only to let in an intermediate estate-A's life estate-Edna's estate vested upon the death of the testator. A legacy is contingent when the legacy does not vest immediately, but when the enjoyment of it depends upon some particular event, e.g., the arrival of the legatee at a certain age. 

In re Rochester Trust Co. 129 Misc. 318, 222 N.Y.S. 256 "Divide and Pay Over" Rule

Where there are no words of present gift and the gift is to be found only in a direction to divide and pay over at a future time, so that it must necessarily remain dependent upon a future event whether a gift is to exist at all, the vesting is suspended. It will not run counter to the intent of the testator. There is, however, this point to be noted. If the postponement of the payment is for the purpose of letting in an intermediate estate, the right to the remainder vests immediately upon the death of the testator, and the legatees are determined as of that date, since futurity is not annexed to the substance of the gift. Only enjoyment and possession were intended to be postponed. 

Matter of Crane 164 N.Y. 71

Since it is the policy of the law to favor vesting, the “divide and pay over" rule will yield to a slight indication of a contrary intent. 

In re Levy's Will 171 Misc. 431, 12 N.Y.S. (2nd) 799

Special Circumstances Affecting Rights Under a Will 

(1) Children Born or Adopted. If a testator has or adopts a child after the execution of his will and this will made no mention of any future children, such children unprovided for by any settlement made by the testator are entitled to the same rights in the estate of the testator that they would have had if no will had been made. The child so born or adopted cannot contest the probate on this ground but recovers his portion from the devisees and legatees in proportion to and out of the parts devised and bequeathed

to them by the will.* The statute does not provide that the afterborn child must survive the testator in order to share, consequently a predeceased child born after the execution of the will does share. 

In re Horst 264 N.Y. 236; Decedent Estate Laws § 26

Matter of Bostwick 178 Misc. 695 

It is not required that the mention of after-born children be specific or that such thought of the future be expressly stated. Any testamentary mention that may reasonably be interpreted as indicative of a concurrent contemplation of the possibility of future parenthood bars children thereafter born from any right under the statute. An after-born child is mentioned in a way sufficient to satisfy the statute if the testator has made some reference to a class in terms broad.enough to include such child, e.g., "any issue surviving me.' 19 In re Land's Estate 160 Misc. 780, 290 N.Y.S. 637 

Matter of Kelly 182 Misc. 481 (2) Marriage of a Testator.—If a testator marries after making a will and the spouse survives the testator the will is deemed revoked as to the survivor unless provision shall have been made for the survivor by a written ante-nuptial agreement; and the survivor is entitled to the same portion of the estate as she would have had if no will had been made. The other legatees pay the spouse from their share in proportion.

Decedent Estate Law § 35 

(3) The Witness as a Legatee.—Where a devisee or legatee was a witness to the will, without whose testimony there could be no probate, he loses his legacy unless he would have inherited had the testator died intestate. In the latter event he takes the legacy or the intestate share, whichever is the smaller. And even though a surrogate may, where only one witness is available, probate the instrument on the testimony of one subscribing witness, no subscribing witness can take under the will unless there are two other subscribing witnesses who are not beneficiaries thereunder. Thus an absent witness may not take under the will when he left the jurisdiction in order to avoid giving testimony and make the probate possible, unless there were two others, not beneficiaries.

Decedent Estate Law § 27; Surrogate's Court Act § 142 

Matter of Hohn 180 Misc. 384

It is to be noted that those entitled to share because they were married or born to the testator after the making of the will, or a subscribing necessary witness who gets a share, can get that share by an action against the other beneficiaries. They cannot contest the probate of the will because of that fact. 

Decedent Estate Law § 28 

(4) Renunciation of the Legacy.—If a legatee renounces his legacy, it falls into the residuary estate. The legacy does not pass as intestate property.

In re Southmayd's Estate 124 Misc. 647, affd. 216 A¸D. 746 *The burden of establishing the right of inheritance is upon the person asserting it.

WILLS 

387 A legatee or distributee who murdered the decedent loses his legacy or claim because the law will not permit a criminal to create a legal or equitable interest for himself. 

Riggs v. Palmer 115 N. Y. 506 

In re Spark's Estate 172 Misc. 642, 15 N.Y.S. (2d) 926 (5) Executor as Distributor.-Where the residue is given to an executor to be distributed among persons, including himself, in such amount as he deems right, he must either waive the right to take thereunder or refuse to act as executor. 

In re Lawler's Will 215 A.D. 506, 213 N.Y.S. 723、

Survivorship Among Beneficiaries 

Where title to property or its devolution depends upon the priority of death, and there is no evidence that the persons died otherwise than simultaneously, the property of each is disposed of as if he had survived, with these exceptions: (1) If those who thus died were joint tenants or tenants by the entirety, the property so held is distributed one-half as if one had survived and one-half as if the other had survived, and if there were more than two and all so died, then distribution is made in the proportion that each bears to the whole number. (2) If a testamentary disposition depends upon the time of death, beneficiaries designated to take alternatively by reason of survivorship, if there is no evidence that they died otherwise than simultaneously the property is divided and distributed in equal proportions among those who would have taken the whole property if the beneficiary through whom they take, had survived. (3) If an insured and the beneficiary in a policy of life or accident insurance had so died, the proceeds are to be distrbuted as if the insured had survived the beneficiary. (4) In cases of wills, trusts inter vivos, deeds or contracts of insurance wherein other provisions are made, those other provisions control.

Decedent Estate Law § 89 Lapsed Legacies 

The general rule is that a legacy to a person who predeceases the testator, lapses. There are two exceptions to this rule: (1) If the deceased legatee is (a) a descendant, or (b) a brother or sister, mentioned by name and not as a member of a class (as "to my brother John," and not as "to all my brothers") and this devisee or legatee left a descendant, the devise or legacy, if the testator has not otherwise provided, vests in this descendant, as if this deceased devisee or legatee had left no will. This applies even if this deceased devise or legatee had left a will. The descendant of this deceased devisee or legatee may be an adopted child. 

Decedent Estate Law § 29; In re Walter's Estate 270 N.Y. 201

Matter of McKeon 182 Misc. 906 

Suppose the testator left "my land to be divided among my brothers, share and share alike." If one of the brothers had predeceased

the testator leaving a child, this child would not take, as in such a case only those surviving in the class take.* 

Matter of Agrella 175 Misc. 456

In a devise to X absolutely, and in case of his death to Y, Y can take only if X predeceases the testator. 

In re Fort's Estate 126 Misc. 28, 211 N.Y.S. 772 (2) Even though the predeceased legatee or devisee is a stranger, it will not lapse where it was given in discharge of a legal or moral obligation and not as a mere bounty. Such legacy is also entitled to priority over general legacies which are mere bounties, the legatee being a purchaser and not a mere volunteer. 

In re Shardlow's Estate 173 Misc. 795, 18 N.Y.S. (2d) 662

Clause Prohibiting a Contest 

Although generally a declaration in a will that a named legatee forfeits his legacy if he contests the will is respected, this condition has not been enforced against infants. And a condition attached to a bequest that if other persons should present claims against the estate the legacy would be invalid, is void, since the legatee is placed at the mercy of the others over whom he has no control. 

In re Kempf's Estate 252 A.D. 28, 33, affd. 287 N.Y. 613 

Clause Restricting the Legatee

A testator ordinarily may annex a condition which is to be met before the legatee may receive his legacy. If the condition is contrary to public policy it will be disregared. A condition calculated to induce a beneficiary to marry, even to marry in a manner desired by the testator is not against public policy. A condition calculated to induce a beneficiary to live in celibacy or adultery is against public policy. A condition annexed to a bequest designed to prevent a marriage with a particular person, or to limit the marriage to one of a particular faith, is valid. A condition, however, which required an adult legatee to obtain the consent of his brother or sister to his marriage and in the event no such consent was obtained, the brother and sister would take his share, was held invalid, as an unreasonable restraint, the tendency of which might be to induce the legatee to live in celibacy or adultery. Each case is to be decided on its own facts. 

In re Liberman 279 N.Y. 458 

The Codicil

A codicil has been defined as an addition to a will or an explanation or alteration of the former disposition of the testator and is to be taken as part of the will, all making but one testament. But the revocation of a codicil does not operate as a revocation of the antecedent will. 

Brown v. Clark 77 N.Y. 369, 375; Matter of Hill 176 Misc. 774. *Since a testator is deemed to draw his will against the background of the laws of his domicile, if the will is there drawn the laws of that place will control in deciding whether a legacy lapses because a legatee predeceased the testator. 

Matter of Duke 181 Misc. 529.

WILLS The codicil to be probated must have been executed with all the formality required by the statute for the execution of wills and when so executed operates as a repudiation of the will. The date of the execution of the codicil would then be the date of execution of the will. 

In re Greenberg's Estate 261 N.Y. 474 

Gifts to Charity

If a deceased leaves a spouse, child, descendant or parent surviving, he cannot, if any one of these objects, leave more than one-half of his estate for any charitable, benevolent, literary, scientific, or religious purpose. The bequest or devise exceeding the one-half is distributed to legatees and what then remains will go to the residuary legatee. The validity of a devise or bequest for more than such one-half may be contested only by a surviving spouse, descendant or parent.*

Decedent Estate Law § 17 

Matter of Morris 175 Misc. 773, affd. 287 N.Y. 624

To ascertain whether a testator has given more than one-half of his estate, the whole estate is treated as converted into money at his death, the debts but not the administration expenses deducted, and if the money value of the portion given is not more than one-half, then the statute has not been violated. No interest is figured for a beneficiary, because of a postponement in payment. Yet where the bequest reads "One-half of my estate is hereby bequeathed to (naming the charity)," one-half of any increase between the date of death and the date of distribution belongs to the legatee. There cannot be a violation of the staute as the will expressly limits the legatee to one-half of the estate. 

In re Opdyke's Will 255 N.Y. 255; Decedent Estate Law § 17 

In re Lord's Estate 155 Misc. 628, 279 N.Y.S. 613

A gift in a will "to distribute where my executor shall consider it will be most effective in the advancement of Christ's Kingdom on Earth” was held to be a valid bequest, and not void for indefiniteness and uncertainty of purpose. The court held that the express purpose of the clause was to promote the cause of the Christian religion in a most general sense and was therefore for charitable, religious uses. 

In re Durbrow 245 N. Y. 469

A gift to a charitable organization, although in outright terms, is nevertheless a gift in trust for the general purpose of the institution, if it is reasonably certain that the testator intended a bequest for purposes of charity. A gift in trust will be implied. In such case the cy pres doctrine will be applied when necessary. 

In re Walter's Estate 150 Misc. 512, 269 N.Y.S. 402, 405 

Prudential Ins. Co. v. N. Y. Guild 252 A.D. 493, 299 N.Y.S. 917 *Since "descendant" means issue of a deceased, grandchildren of a testator cannot object to the gifts if their parent who is a child of the testator, is alive at the time of the testator's death. Matter of Plaster 179 Misc. 80, affd. 266 

N. Y. 439.

Mutual Wills 

Parties may agree not to revoke a will or to execute mutual and reciprocal wills. Where one of the parties in violation of the agreement, makes a later will making other disposition of his property, the later will and not the first joint will should be admitted to probate as the mutual will is not the last will of the decedent. The agreement is enforceable in equity even as against the legatees of the probated will. The contract will be enforced though oral if there has been a change of position of the parties otherwise than through marriage, since every agreement made in consideration of marriage, except mutual promises to marry, must be in writing and subscribed by the party to be charged or his lawful agent. 

In re Higgin's Will 264 N.Y. 226 

In re Goldberg's Estate 275 N.Y. 186

If one party dies before either will has been revoked, the wills become fixed obligations. Equity will enforce them if the survivor attempts to impair his will by subsequent testamentary provisions. 

The courts tend to respect contracts made by a testator during his lifetime, even though the effect be to distribute the property of a testator after his death. 

Conditional Will

Suppose A leaving the country on business, executes a will "to be effective if I should die before I return home." He gets back safely, but he fails to destroy the will. That will cannot be probated, as it expressly states that it is a conditional will. If, however, T had not written the condition into the will but intended to change it later and did not, it cannot be refused probate on the ground that it is a conditional will. 

In re Poonarman's Will 234 N.Y. 329

In re Webb's Estate 122 Misc. 129, affd. 208 A.D. 793 

Incorporation by Reference 

66 A testator may not import into his will an unattested memorandum of his mere desire and expectations, or his unexecuted plans. 

In one case the will bequeathed capital stock mentioned in a certain agreement subject to all the terms and provisions of the said agreement." It was held that the agreement mentioned was not incorporated in the will by reference and that it should not be included in the probate. The will itself, if properly executed, may be probated. 

In re Martindale's Will 69 Misc. 622, 127 N.Y.S. 887

Where the will incorporates by reference another accomplished fact, it is not necessary to incorporate in the will the details of the thing referred to. Thus in one case the testator conferred a power on his daughter to dispose of his estate and then added a provision in substance, that in case of her death before him and her consequent inability to execute the power, the legatees under her will should be deemed, none the less, to be the legatees under his own. 

The daughter died before her father. It was held that her will

391 might be referred to for the purpose of determining the legatees entitled to take under his and the extent of their respective shares. 

In re Pifford 111 N. Y. 410

A bequest to a trust company in trust for the testator's daughter under the terms of a previous and existing trust agreement, "made part of this will as if fully set forth herein," was held not invalid for failure to restate the purpose of the trust referred to. So a bequest to a son by cancelling whatever indebtedness appears upon the other's books, is a valid gift, though to understand the extent of the legacy one must go beyond the will itself. 

In re Rausch's Will 258 N. Y. 327 

A gift or devise of realty or personalty may be incorporated by reference in a validly executed will, regardless of the above discussion, provided all of the following elements are present. (1) The gift or devise must be for general charitable purposes. (2) The resolution, declaration or deed of trust referred to in the will must be identified as existing prior to the execution of such will and made to a corporation authorized by law to accept such devise or gift. (3) A copy of the resolution, declaration or deed of trust, certified by the secretary or assistant secretary or cashier or assistant cashier of the corporation, under the corporate seal, shall have been filed in the office of the Secretary of State of New York and in the office in which real property conveyances are to be recorded in the county where the corporation has its principal place of business. 

Personal Property Law § 12; Real Property Law § 113 

Revocation

A will may be revoked in one of three ways. The first is by another will in writing, which must be executed in accordance with regular statutory requirements. This second will in so far as it is inconsistent with the first will, revokes the first. So if the first will left a house to T's son, and a later executed writing left it to his daughter, the latter would get the house. The latter writing may be in the form of interlineations, provided it was executed as any will would have to be. Note that part of the will may thus be revoked. 

The second method is by some other writing declaring such revocation. In such case there is a revocation even though the second writing was not inconsistent with the first or omitted to mention certain dispositions. The second writing must be executed with all statutory formalities. By this method part of a will may be revoked. 

The third method is by burning, cancelling, obliterating, tearing or destroying a will with intent to revoke the whole will. It has been held that words of revocation written by the testator upon the margin, were not an effective revocation. Where the words are written across the will, the will is revoked. A line drawn through the signature of the testator or of the signatures of the witnesses, with evidence of intent to revoke, was held a good revocation. 

Matter of Semler 176 Misc. 687

A testator may also tell another to burn, cancel, obliterate, tear or destroy his will for him, but this order and destruction must be proved by at least two other witnesses. 

Decedent Estate Law § 34 

If a testator tears up or destroys a part of a will, intending to cancel that part alone, the will is not affected in any way. If the original language can be ascertained by competent evidence, the original will may be admitted to probate in the form and condition in which it was when originally executed. So it is clear that by tearing, etc., you cannot revoke a part of a will, if what the part contained can be ascertained. If what has been destroyed cannot be ascertained, that part of the will which remains can be probated as the testator's last will, unless it can be seen that the missing parts would affect or alter the remaining parts.* 

In re Fox's Estate 118 Misc. 352, 193 N.Y.S. 232

In re Bescher's Estate 132 Misc. 625, 229 N.Y.S. 821 

If T executes a will, and later a second, the destruction, cancellation or revocation of the second will does not revive the first unless (1) by the terms of the revocation he revives the first or (2) T duly republished the first will. In the first case, a writing executed with the same formalities as are required for the execution of a will must exist. A revocation because of an intent to make changes or because of a mistaken belief that the will was inoperative with the idea of making necessary changes is an effective revocation, and though death occur before the changes are made, intestacy results. The doctrine of dependent relative revocation is not now recognized in this state.

Decedent Estate Law § 41 

In re O'Donavan's Will 168 Misc. 362 

In re Steckney's Will 161 N. Y. 42 

Matter of McCaffrey 174 Misc. 162

So it follows that if a testator revokes a codicil by which a $1,000 bequest had been taken from A, it does not put the $1,000 back into the will. The codicil in its effect revokes a $1,000 part of the will. There is an intestacy as to that $1,000, unless there is the proper republication. 

In re Cable's Will 123 Misc. 894, affd. 242 N. Y. 510

The law presumes that a will proved to have had existence and not found after the death of the testator was destroyed animo revocandi. Mistakes

These are two kinds-those that go to the essence, and those that do not.

Suppose T writes a will and is about to sign. Unobserved, his aunt changes it for another in which the only change is that she gets $100 more. The will is void, as it is not T's will. The mistake *There is conflict of authority as to whether there is a presumption that alterations were made either prior or substquent to the execution of a will, or whether there is any presumption. Matter of Thomson 181 Misc. 385.

WILLS goes to the essence. The point is brought out even more strongly in a case where a husband and wife drew identical wills, making each other beneficiaries. By mistake he signed hers and she his. Both wills were void. No testimony is admissible to correct the situation. 

They did not sign their wills. 

Nelson v. McDonald 61 Hun. 406, 16 N.Y.S. 273

Suppose the will is written by T and through absent-mindedness he puts in a $10,000 legacy for S instead of the $1,000, and he signs. 

The will stands as signed and executed. The mistake cannot be rectified. But if T's lawyer had written the will for him and T did not read the will before he signed, the court on probate would allow evidence to show the mistake and would throw out the mistaken part, as not being T's wish, for T was not in a position to be held accountable for the error. If the will had been read to T, and he signed, it would be the same as if T had written the will and signed it.

The court, if it put out the erroneous bequest, would not put in the correct one, because after the bequest is denied there is a blank, and the court, though it will correct an evident error so as to make sense, will not, however, add anything for the testator and thus actually write a part of the will for him. 

Where the testator at the time was very ill or illiterate, there is no presumption that he knew what he was doing. The character of the will and the contents must be proven. The court cannot assume that the will was read to the testator.

Parol evidence may be admitted to explain a will where a latent ambiguity exists arising outside the instrument. It can never supply, contradict, enlarge or vary the written words. Where ordinary English words are used by the testator, parol evidence is inadmissible to show that the testator attached a peculiar meaning to them. It cannot be shown that the testator habitually, or at the execution of the will, used the plain English words in some peculiar manner. 

In re Quackenbush's Will 127 Misc. 731, 217 N.Y.S. 493

A will left $50 to the "Erieville Church." There was no church in Erieville by that specific name, but there was a church there, a Methodist church. The bequest was paid to the trustees of that institution. 

In re Card's Estate 145 Misc. 686, 260 N.Y.S. 764

The surrounding facts and circumstances can be used to show what T's attitude was toward his beneficiaries and the disposition of his property. But this extraneous evidence cannot supply, contradict or vary the written words. 

Fraud and Undue Influence 

Not every fraud or use of influence invalidates a will. The giving of advice and use of argument and persuasion do not constitute ground for voiding a will even though the will is made in conformity with the advice given. To avoid a will the influence exerted must be so potent at the time the will was made as to overcome the

power of the testator at the time to act freely and upon his own volition. If the testator because of a falsehood told by a neighbor about Y, leaves nothing to the latter, the will would be probated as written even though it could be shown that in the absence of the falsehood a $1,000 bequest would have been left. X would be limited to his action against the falsifier. A will would exist. The fraud to vitiate the will must go to the very essence. 

Smith v. Keller 205 N. Y. 39

A case where undue influence seems clear is where the one who was made the sole beneficiary became acquainted with the testator two weeks before the testator's death, superintended the execution, selected the witnesses and the draftsmen. Proof that the instrument designates as the principal beneficiary the attorney who drew the will and superintended its execution together with the fact that the decedent was old, mentally weak and had previously expressed a contrary testamentary intention, presented a prima facie case of undue influence.

In re Alfaya's Will 122 Misc. 771, affd. 213 A.D. 877 

In re Zimmerman's Estate 254 A.D. 630, affd. 279 N. Y. 659

The burden of proof is upon the contestant upon an issue of undue influence. 

In re Kindberg's Will 207 N. Y. 220, 228

If a proponent be content to remain passive and refrain from explaining a legitimate inference flowing from his adversary's evidence his case must necessarily go against him; he cannot be al lowed to ignore evidence advanced by one whose affirmative duty it is to bear the burden and produce the proof. 

In re Schellinger's Will 258 N.Y. 186

Rights of Surviving Spouse of a Testator 

If a testator dies and leaves either a will or a codicil executed after August 31, 1930, the surviving spouse may, if he or she so desires, renounce both will and codicil and take his or her share as intestacy, subject to the limitations outlined below. The right of election exists as to realty and personalty of the testator domiciled in this state at the time of his death. If not so domiciled, it exists only as to realty located in the state. 

Matter of McGlone 284 N. Y. 527 (1) The spouse cannot get more than one-half of the estate after deductions are made for debts, taxes, surviving spouse's exemption, funeral and administration expenses. By "estate" is meant all property of every nature, wheresoever situated. (2) Where the aggregate amount for the benefit of the surviving spouse, including the principal of a trust, is less than the intestate share, the surviving spouse can elect to take the difference between such aggregate amount and the share as in intestacy, the rest of the will remaining unaffected. In every estate the surviving spouse has the right to withdraw $2,500 if the intestate share is at least that amount. This sum is inclusive of any legacy or devise. If a trust fund is created for his or her benefit for life, the $2,500 sum or any part

WILLS 

395 thereof is payable from the principal of the trust fund. For example, suppose the intestate share is $5,000. The will gives the spouse a legacy of $100 and the income from a $4,800 trust fund. The spouse gets the $100 legacy, plus $100 which is the difference between the aggregate amount and the intestate share, and an additional $2,300 out of the trust fund of $4,800. 

Decedent Estate Law § 18; Matter of Goldsmith 177 Misc. 298 

It should be noted that the above provisions regarding trusts, with income payable for life to the surviving spouse, apply to legal life estates or to annuities. In computing the value of the provisions under the will, the capital value of the fund producing the income is the value of the life estate. 

In re Byrne's Will 260 N. Y. 405

The right of election does not exist 1. If a decree of divorce recognized as valid in New York has been obtained. 

2. If the surviving spouse has been an unsuccessful defendant in a separation action brought by the deceased. 

3. If the surviving spouse obtained a divorce from the deceased in another state, even though the decree is not recognized as valid in New York. 

4. If the surviving husband has failed to support the deceased wife. 

5. If the survivor had abandoned the deceased.

Where the spouses had separated voluntarily, the right to election is not lost. The burden is upon him who opposes the right to elect. 

Matter of Maiden 284 N. Y. 429 

In re Lorch's Will 254 A.D. 680, affd. 279 N.Y. 574

It is therefore the rule that even an adulterous spouse or one who has been guilty of cruel and inhuman treatment or whose conduct makes it unsafe and improper to cohabit with him is entitled to a right of election if he continues to live in the matrimonial domicile. 

Matter of Green 155 Misc. 641, 645, affd. 246 A.D. 583

The election may be made by the general guardian of an infant when permitted by the Surrogate having jurisdiction, or on behalf of an incompetent when permitted by the Supreme Court. But the infant must be alive when the notice of election is served and filed. 

An election made under this section is in lieu of any dower in lands acquired by the husband prior to September 1, 1930. The notice of election must be served upon the representatives of the decedent's estate personally or in such manner as the surrogate may direct and by filing a copy with proof of service in the surrogate's court. This service and filing may occur at any time within 6 months after letters have been issued unless the time is extended by the surrogate, and during the lifetime of the surviving spouse. The surrogate may relieve the defaulting spouse for good cause shown, by extending the time for one or more fixed periods extending beyond the six months' period, provided no decree settling the ac-

count of the fiduciary has been made, and twelve months have not elapsed since the issuance of the letters. Where it was proven that the petitioner was not aware of her right to elect and thought that the lawyer for the estate was under a duty to advise her of her rights, a reasonable cause for being relieved of her default was shown. If the surviving spouse is an infant or incompetent, the surrogate may permit an election up to a time not later than the entry of the decree on the first judicial account of a permanent representative made more than seven months after the issuance of letters.* 

In re Coffin's Estate 152 Misc. 619, 273 N.Y.S. 974 

In re Altman's Estate 160 Misc. 812, 290 N.Y.S. 803 

In re Schmidt's Estate 168 Misc. 534, 6 N.Y.S. (2d) 213

Though the will makes no provision for the surviving spouse, it remains valid and otherwise unobjectionable except in so far as the terms of the will are defeated by the exercise of the right of election. 

In re Mihlman's Will 140 Misc. 565, 251 N.Y.S. 146

A spouse during the lifetime of the other may waive the right to elect and to take against a particular will by an instrument subscribed and duly acknowledged. A waiver to take against any will of the other must be evidenced by an agreement based on consideration moving to the one who surrendered the potential right. 

Decedent Estate Law § 18, sub. 9 

Intestacy Laws Affecting Estates of Decedents 

If a person dies intestate, his property is distributed in accordance with a schedule entirely different from the above. The rules make uniform the devolution of both realty and personalty. 

The real property and surplus of personal property not devised, after payment of debts, shall be distributed as follows: (1) One-third share of the personalty and realty belongs to the surviving spouse if any children or grandchildren survive, and the residue in equal portions to the children and such persons per stirpes as legally represent the predeceased children of the intestate. (2) If a spouse and parents (but no descendants) survive, the former takes $5,000 and half the remainder and the parents divide the balance between them. If only one parent survives, that parent takes the balance. If the deceased in such case was illegitimate, the mother receives the share of both parents. (3) If there be no spouse or descendant surviving, the parents of the deceased take all in equal amounts. (4) If there be a spouse surviving and no descendant, parent, brother, sister, nephew or niece, the spouse takes all. (5) If there be a brother, sister, nephew or niece surviving, the spouse receives $10,000 and half the residue and the balance descends to the brothers and sisters and their representatives per stirpes. The $10,000 are taken from the personalty before resorting to the realty. *The notice of election may be written by the spouse or by a duly authorized agent or attorney in fact. Matter of Zalewski 292 Ñ. Y. 332.

WILLS 

397 2 (6) If descendants survive and there is no surviving spouse, the children and such as legally represent them, take all, per stirpes.* (7) If there be no surviving spouse, no children, no representative of a child, and no parent, the whole is distributed to the next of kin, in equal degree to the deceased. Brothers and sisters and children of any deceased brother or sister take equally per stirpes. 

Relatives of half blood and their representatives take equally with those of the whole blood; posthumous children take equally with those born in the lifetime of the deceased and who survive him. 

Decedent Estate Law § 83 

In re Karp's Estate 163 Misc. 855, 298 N.Y.S. 903

Beyond brothers and sisters and their descendants, only persons within the nearest degree of relationship to the decedent are entitled to inherit intestate real or personal property. In other words, where there is a group of first cousins, as the nearest relatives, they alone are entitled to inherit. In such case if there are children or grandchildren of deceased first cousins, they are not entitled to inherit. The same rule applies to the ascertainment of the class of next of kin or heirs where there are second cousins or third cousins or more distant classes of relatives. When persons of the nearest degree establish their standing, those more remote are excluded. 

In re Wendel's Will 143 Misc. 480, 257 N.Y.S. 87

No distributive share is allowed a spouse whose marriage with the deceased has been dissolved under a decree which is valid in this state. If the decree is not valid here, the spouse is not entitled to a share if he or she were the plaintiff in that action. Nor is a distributive share allowed to a husband who had neglected or failed to provide for his wife or had abandoned her, or to a wife who had abandoned her husband. The fact that a separation decree has been obtained against the surviving spouse does not prevent him from sharing unless there was a failure to provide for the deceased.* 

A parent who had failed to provide for or who has abandoned a child, during the latter's infancy, may not take in the estate of the child, unless the parental relationship and duties were resumed and continued until the death of the child. 

In re Sidman's Estate 153 Misc. 735, 276 N.Y.S. 56

Decedent Estate Law § 87 Matter of Bennett 178 Misc. 442 

A child though legitimate, of a mother who was illegitimate, cannot inherit from a collateral relation. Nor can an illegitimate child share in the estate of a deceased brother of the mother. 

Matter of Simpson 175 Misc. 718, 723, affd. 262 A.D. 1001

A man can deliberately strip himself of all inheritable property and leave nothing to his wife by a valid transfer during his life. A *A spouse finally sentenced to life imprisonment, even in the absence of a remarriage by the innocent spouse, does not continue to be a spouse and may not claim a right as distributee under a will of the innocent spouse. In re 

Lindewall 287 N.Y. 347 **Contrast this with the case of a right to elect against a will. In such case a separation decree destroys the right of the unsuccessful defendant.

spouse of one who leaves a will has an interest in the estate of the decedent. Property which is not part of the estate at death does not come within the protection of the statute. The creation of a trust with one's assets reserving the enjoyment of the income during life and the right to revoke the trust at will and keeping the trustee subject to the settlor's control, is an illusory trust. The owner has not actually stripped himself of his property and the surviving spouse's right of election would be recognized. Likewise the opening of an account in a savings bank in trust for a designated person permits of the inference that the depositor intended to create a trust, but intended to reserve power to deal with it as he chose. The transfer is illusory The same rule was not applied to life insurance policies, where the testator had reserved the right during his lifetime to change the beneficiaries. It is also settled that a transfer will be set aside where it is made by a decedent in contemplation of marriage or in contemplation of a reconciliation with his spouse and with intent to strip himself of his inheritable property in fraud of the rights of the spouse and where he has falsely represented that he has sufficient property in which she will be entitled to share on his decease. 

Mitchell v. Mitchell 290 N.Y. 779 

Newman v. Dore 275 N.Y. 371; Krause v. Krause 285 N.Y. 27

It has been held, however, that the claim of beneficiaries under a Totten trust* created by an intestate prevails over the right of election of a surviving spouse, since the right of election given by the Decedent Estate Law exists only where a will has been left. Section 239 (3) of the Banking Law expressly provides that when a deposit is made in a savings bank in form to be paid to the depositor or another or to the survivor, the deposit and any additions thereto become the property of the persons named as joint tenants and may be paid to either during the lifetime of both or to the survivor after the death of one. In the absence of fraud or undue influence, a deposit in this form becomes conclusive evidence of the intention of both depositors to vest title to the deposit in the survivor. The intent of the intestate is immaterial and the right of election of a surviving spouse cannot be exercised because that right depends upon the existence of a will. 

Matter of Colaci 288 N.Y. 158 

Inda v. Inda 288 N.Y. 315

Where the person entitled to a legacy or distributive share is unknown, the decree must direct the executor, administrator, guardian or trustee to pay the amount to the state comptroller, to be held for the person who may later appear to be entitled to it.
